News.title: Stop calling 999 to dob in your neighbours for having a barbecue, fire service begs after being swamped with calls
News.content:
FIRE services have begged Brits not to dob in their neighbours for having a barbecue after they were swamped with calls.

Millions of people across England and Wales received an emergency alert on their phones at around 7pm on Friday evening warning them of the risk of wildfires.



The government issued the alert warning people “not to light anything that could spark a fire, including barbecues, campfires, and fireworks” with the country in the middle of another heatwave.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the request “came directly from Fire and Rescue Services”.



He urged Brits to take the alert “seriously” and “follow the guidance in place” as the UK contends with a series of devastating wildfires.

But the blaring alert sent panic across the nation, as fire services urged people not to call 999 to report their neighbours.



Surrey Fire and Rescue Service posted to X that they had received a “high volume of calls” urging people to call only if there “is an emergency or fire producing significant smoke”.

“We understand residents may be concerned, but we are unable to respond to reports of neighbours having BBQs, bonfires or campfires in their gardens unless there is an emergency,” they said.



“We support the Government’s message on this and would strongly advise against having bonfires, fireworks, campfires or disposable BBQs during this period.

“Fires can spread quickly and become difficult to control, putting your home and neighbouring properties at risk.”

Meanwhile, Gloucestershire Fire and Rescue said they were also experiencing “exceptionally high call volumes”.

They added that they understood the public’s “vigilance” but said to only call 999 if there is a “genuine emergency or immediate risk to life, property or the environment”.

The message was also echoed by South Wales Fire and Rescue Service who urged the public to only call for ” a new emergency”.



It comes after nineteen homes were destroyed after a wildfire grew out of control in Stourbridge, West Midlands, on Thursday.

The blaze left “extensive damage” and resulted in dozens of people needing to be treated by paramedics and evacuated from their homes.

Other locations in the UK have also been affected by wildfires in recent days.

There were multiple reported across the Midlands yesterday, including also in Stoke-on-Trent, Birmingham, Warwickshire and Worcestershire – as well as others in Norfolk and Wales.

Chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) Phil Garrigan told BBC Breakfast that fire services have been called to 43 new wildfires in the last 24 hours with 11 major incidents declared in the last two days.



He added that nine firefighters have been taken to hospital in the last 48 hours for smoke inhalation after “taking courageous actions”.

The surge in fires came as the UK officially broke its 2026 record for the hottest day on Thursday, with the mercury hitting 38.5C in Kew Gardens, London.

Louise Haigh, the First Secretary of State, said the UK’s Emergency Alert system “reflects the seriousness with which the government is acting to safeguard people and property”.

“During this period of extreme heat, we are asking people to take simple steps to limit the risk of further fires,” she continued.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The government will continue to provide every assistance to communities being impacted by these fires, including the deployment of 100 additional military personnel in major incident areas.”



But the deafening siren sparked a furious backlash with some questioning whether the ear-splitting warning was necessary.

News.title: Glam fitness influencer, 28, among seven killed in horror head on smash in high speed police chase
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FATAL CHASE Glam fitness influencer, 28, among seven killed in horror head on smash in high speed police chase

AN INFLUENCER has been killed alongside six other people in a head-on crash while fleeing police.

Alana Alves da Silva, 28, was allegedly hauling 137kg of cannabis when the Fiat Cronos she was travelling in smashed into an oncoming car.



Better known online as Vampira 085, the content creator was pronounced dead at the scene in Minas Gerais State, Brazil.

The incident unfolded on the BR-251 highway on Saturday last week.



Police had attempted to stop the vehicle near the town of Salinas but the driver allegedly ignored their order and sped away.

A high-speed pursuit then continued for six miles before the Fiat swerved into oncoming traffic while overtaking on a bend and then crashed into a Chevrolet Astra.



Alana was one of four people in the Fiat. Two young men who were also travelling with her died in hospital.

A woman, 20, survived but remains in a critical condition with severe head injuries and multiple fractures.

All four men travelling in the Chevrolet, aged between 46 and 79, were killed in the disaster.

Police identified the suspected driver of the Fiat as Pedro Yan Linhares Gutierrez, 24.



Officers said he did not have a driving licence, was wearing an electronic tag and was already facing drug trafficking charges.

In the aftermath, the highway was completely shut off.

Alana had built a large online fanbase – boasting over 59,000 followers on Instagram and TikTok – by sharing daily workout tips and healthy living content and comedy skits.



She also ran her own online fitness fashion shop from her home in the city of Fortaleza.

The investigation into the fatal crash remains ongoing.

News.title: Our chocolate-box village was made famous by Downton Abbey – now plans for 200 new homes could destroy our countryside
News.content:
FEELING DOWN Our chocolate-box village was made famous by Downton Abbey – now plans for 200 new homes could destroy our countryside

LOCALS are outraged that their scenic village, once the backdrop to a beloved British TV series, could be swamped with 200 newbuilds.

The quaint community of Bampton, Oxfordshire, was once the location for the fictional Yorkshire village in Downton Abbey.



ITV began filming on the cobbled streets of the picturesque village in 2010, with Bampton becoming a global tourist attraction almost overnight.

Several scenes in the series, including the Old Rectory and parish church, were filmed in the village – with the iconic Highclere Castle located just 40 miles away.



Residents now fear plans for 200 new homes could risk overdeveloping the site, with several complaints lodged with the West Oxfordshire District Council.

Dr William Outhwaite wrote: “Bampton has already been massively damaged by excessive and insensitive building programmes which have overloaded its medical, educational and other infrastructure.





“This proposal would add the loss of agricultural land and of a still attractive site on the edge of the village.”

Hourigan Planning submitted a blueprint for 190 homes, 40 per cent of which they claim would be affordable housing.

But many locals fear the added strain on resources and existing infrastructure could cause flooding, as seen back in 2007.

One said: “We moved here 28 years ago because we wanted to live in a village – it’s a shame how places like Bampton become overdeveloped with no real infrastructure to cope with such influx of houses.



”Very sad that countryside is being lost at such a colossal rate affecting wildlife and country life.”

Another asked: “Do we really need more homes?

“My water pressure is already poor and no need to mention doctors appointments.”

Locals have previously spoken out about the perils of living in a tourist hotspot – despite the handsome cash flow – with many objecting to the “brash American accents” on their doorsteps.



Bus loads of American fans, intrigued by the historical drama’s depiction of early 20th-century Britain, come armed with cameras and selfie sticks to Bampton.

“My friend overheard a tour guide say that Bampton was nothing before Downton Abbey,” said village local Fabrizio Manerba, 62.

”Let me tell you – Bampton was a beautiful, expensive place to live long beforehand.”

Just last year, the village was named as one of the most beautiful chocolate box villages in England, according to Independent Cottages.

Qualifying factors include the number of historic buildings, the oldest recorded existence of the village and whether it’s classed as an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.



Fabrizio, who lives in the main square, complains that the tourists often stand in his driveway and “just go everywhere”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Around 10 buses a day were seen during the town’s peak popularity, according to locals, with visitors lingering and posing for photographs.

A spokesperson for Hourigan Planning said: “The scheme would comprise a mix of both open market homes and affordable homes, and includes significant areas of accessible open space.”

News.title: Brutal storm strikes Brit holiday hotspot as torrential rain & hailstones wreak havoc with flood alert triggered
News.content:
A BRUTAL storm has struck the Costa del Sol with torrential rain and hailstones sparking a flood alert in the Brit holiday hotspot.

Urgent weather warnings have been issued across Spain‘s southern coast as thunderstorms wreak havoc during the peak summer getaway season.



Shocked holidaymakers arriving at Malaga Airport in the early hours of this morning were met with biblical rain and powerful gusts of wind.

Jaw-dropping footage showed scores of panicked Brit tourists waiting out the dramatic downpour.



Hailstones were also seen striking the airport tarmac while lightning bolts were filmed tearing through the night sky.

The heavy deluge battered the Costa del Sol and Malaga City – with tourists currently flocking to the region for summer trips.

The harsh weather – which could trigger flash flooding – is expected to continue throughout this weekend.

Large swathes of the Andalusia region are expected to see drastic changes in weather with storms, flooding, and large hailstones, local authorities say.



Spanish weather agency Aemet has predicted a so-called Dana system to sweep through the region.

It is essentially a cold drop isolated depression – meaning huge amounts of rain can fall in just hours.

Up to 20mm of rain could fall in just one hour, according to Aemet.



The yellow warnings for thunderstorms will be in place from 2pm to 10pm today.

On Friday, Almería, Granada and Jaén issued storm warnings.

But the region will see stark contrasts between showers and sun as record-breaking levels of heat also continue to persist.



Amber alerts for the heatwave remained in place in Córdoba and Jaén, where temperatures could reach 40C.

Cádiz, Granada, Huelva and Seville are also set to remain on yellow alert.

Over the weekend, showers and thunderstorms are expected to batter the Costa del Sol as well as the Balearic Islands of Ibiza, Mallorca and Menorca.

Hailstones are expected to develop during the weather phenomenon.

From Monday onwards, the risk of widespread storms is set to decrease.



Over the weekend, today is estimated to be the most challenging day of the shocking turn of weather.

The heaviest showers will hit the north of Catalonia and Aragón, according to local media.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Throughout the day, rain is expected to hit many eastern regions, including Valencia, Murcia and eastern Andalusia.

News.title: Infamous ‘killer nanny’ Louise Woodward pictured for first time in years as she shops in UK town after TV show announced
News.content:
FLASH BACK Infamous ‘killer nanny’ Louise Woodward pictured for first time in years as she shops in UK town after TV show announced

INFAMOUS nanny, Louise Woodward, who was accused of murdering an eight-month-old baby, has been pictured for the first time in years as she shops in a UK town.

Woodward’s gripping trial for the murder of baby Matthew Eappen in Massachusettts sent shockwaves around the globe in 1997.



The former au pair, from Elton, Cheshire, was convicted of involuntary manslaughter after the eight-month-old died under her care.

The then 18-year-old had initially been found guilty of second-degree murder, accused of shaking Matthew to death just ten weeks after flying to the US.



But her conviction was soon reduced to involuntary manslaughter and, after spending 289 days in jail, she returned to the UK.

Woodward, now 48, was pictured on August 1 for the first time in years, where she was seen shopping in Shropshire, 29 years after the horror unfolded.



The story of Woodward’s life and trial is now set to enter the limelight once again after HBO announced a major new drama.

A five-part limited series, The Trial Of Louise Woodward, will re-tell the shocking story which became a media sensation.



Directed by Welsh producer, Matthew Barry, the show will feature The White Lotus star and two-time Emmy nominee, Meghann Fahy.

Woodward’s story began when she swapped Cheshire for Boston in 1996, flying 3,100 miles to work as an au pair after finishing her A-Levels.

She was hired Sunil and Deborah Eappen, both 30-year-old doctors, to take care of their young son Matthew, that November.

But the following February, Woodward called an ambulance after the eight-month old suddenly stopped breathing.

He was raced to Boston Children’s Hospital and put on a life support machine – but six days later, he tragically died of a brain haemorrhage.



Woodward was arrested on February 5, and experts said Matthew’s injuries were classic symptoms of Shaken Baby Syndrome – a forceful action that causes serious brain damage or death.

In a polarising trial that split opinion across the Atlantic, both sides of the aisle hammered home their arguments.

Woodward maintained her innocence throughout with her defence arguing that Matthew’s horror injuries were sustained at an earlier date.



But the prosecution alleged she killed the baby in a “frustrated, unhappy and relentless rage” – a claim the au pair’s lawyers strongly rejected.

Woodward was also criticised for for appearing “cold” and “remorseless”.

While under cross-examination, Woodward clarified that she had “popped” and not “dropped” the baby – as police officers had previously claimed.

Later, she explained that to “pop” was an English term meaning to “lay” or to “place” but had admitted to playing “a little roughly” with the child days before his death.

In October 1977, Woodward wept in the docks as she was found guilty of a lesser second-degree murder charge and was later sentenced to life in prison.



Outside the court, the teen’s mother said: “They’ve made a horrendous mistake and they need to put it right.”

Just days after her conviction, it emerged that the jury was split before they were convinced in favour of finding the teen guilty.

According to one jury member, none of them “thought she tried to murder” Matthew.

The defence launched an appeal and within 10 days of being sentenced to life in prison, Woodward was released.

Judge Hiller Zobel overturned the jury’s verdict and ruled that she was guilty of involuntary manslaughter.



He sentenced her to 278 days in jail at MCI-Framingham, a maximum security-unit – the amount of time she had already spent behind bars.

The following day, the prosecution vowed to “pull out every stop” to get Woodward back in jail and her lawyers promised “total vindication”.

By June 1998, Judge Zobel’s verdict had been overturned after it was claimed he “abused his statutory discretion” and the decision moved to the Supreme Court.

By four votes to three, his verdict of involuntary manslaughter and the reduced sentence was upheld, which finally allowed Woodward to return home to the UK as a free woman.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Woodward later went on to graduate with a law degree and tied the knot with her husband, Anthony Elkes, in 2013.



Louise and Anthony also have a daughter together, who would now be over 12-years-old.

News.title: Hailed a hero refugee ‘suitcase killer’ felt untouchable – cops are convinced he killed Brit but mystery motive remains
News.content:
ONCE hailed as a fresh-faced teen with a brutally compelling story to tell, Afghan refugee Sharif Ahmadzai is now being branded a monster.

A decade after first arriving in Greece, the 26-year-old is now locked up in an Athens jail cell accused of killing Brit Elisabeth Ross before disposing of her body in a suitcase and looting her bank account.



Ahmadzai became one of the posterboys of child refugee missions in Europe when he fled the murderous Taliban regime at just 16 years old.

Once settled in Greece, he would go on to be accepted by the country as a proud national boxing champion before falling in love with an American woman and becoming a father.



But this adoration is feared to have made him feel untouchable, a well-placed insider with first-hand knowledge of the shocking murder case told The Sun.

They revealed: “Our view is that he internalised his heroic status as a child refugee, with all the praise he received from international organisations, and then as a champion boxer.



“Both made him feel he could do and get away with anything.”

Ten years ago, international volunteers assisting the thousands of refugees landing on the shores of Lesvos in dinghies were immediately drawn to a young Ahmadzai.

He was drawn to them too as in record time the young Afghan had reportedly learned English.

This newfound skill saw him help interpret for aid workers stationed in Moria, the island’s notoriously overcrowded migrant camp.



Field workers with the International Red Cross also quickly took a shine to the boy.

They heard his miraculous story of survival as he made the journey on foot to Europe after seeing his father, brother, mother and sister die at the hands of the blood-thirsty Taliban.



In 2016, an animated video released by the organisation devoted nearly ten minutes to telling his remarkable story.

There was nothing, it seemed, the teen could do wrong.

But today he sits in a prison awaiting trial for murder.

The American grandmother who Ahmadzai calls “mom” after he was adopted by her and her relief worker husband in Lesvos reacted to the news saying: “When I heard it, I couldn’t imagine it to be true.”



“Not in a million years.”

Veterans in the solidarity movement expressed similar disbelief this week.

One volunteer said: “At our core we were a small group and Sharif was extra special because he had been a refugee himself.

“It all seemed so natural when he met Alaina [Hall], fell in love with her, married her and decided to stay on in Greece.



“None of us can get our heads around the fact that he is now detained in Korydallos [prison] and is the prime suspect in such a horrific case.”

By the time Ahmadzai crossed paths with the Elisabeth, he had converted to Christianity and had a child with wife Alaina.

His social media was littered with images from his boxing days including snaps of championship belts and pictures of his sculpted physique.

Alongside his partner, Ahmadzai would also start up a Christian-backed NGO called Love Every Nation.



This was where Elisabeth, the Scottish aid worker killed in Athens, and her alleged murderer Ahmadzai would become friends.

The NGO would regularly meet up in Elisabeth’s flat – a first floor apartment in a nondescript 1970’s building.

It was here that the 38-year-old, described as “an angel, full of kindness” by friends, is believed to have been killed on the night of July 15.

With no signs of injury to her body, forensic scientists concluded she had likely been asphyxiated.

They are still awaiting analysis of her blood and vital organs as advanced decomposition had made an on-site post-mortem almost impossible to conduct.



“The toxicological tests will reveal the exact cause of death,” George Kalliakmanis, honorary president of the union of police officers told the Sun.

“But police are 100 per cent sure it was murder. The big question, of course, is why?”

What was sure to George and investigators was that Ahmadzai was a “cunning” man.



Brought in for questioning on July 30 – twelve days after Elisabeth’s body was found by a homeless man inside the suitcase – Ahmadzai had reportedly appeared “calculating and evasive”.

The suspect allegedly admitted to moving the Brit’s body using a trolley-art, according to Kalliakmanis.

But the Afghan continues to deny murder insisting he had found Elisabeth slumped on the bathroom floor when he entered her flat.

“Panic-stricken”, Ahmadzai had decided to move her elsewhere for a still unknown reason.

On the third day of interrogation, he confessed to withdrawing more than 10,000 euros from ATMs using the victim’s credit cards.



He also admitted to sending misleading text messages from her mobile phones to family and friends.

“From the get-go he rejected the accusation of murder,” added Kalliakmanis.

“And to this day he has never been forthcoming about how he got the card codes that enabled him to withdraw the money.



“It became clear to my colleagues that they were dealing with a cunning individual.”

Police would go on to charge Ahmadzai with intentional homicide after “significant” testimony from his wife Alaina.

A cop for more than 30 years, Kalliakmanis said: “She came in, she expressed her fears, she was very helpful.

“She is revolted by what he has done.”

Dozens of tributes have been laid at the site where Elisabeth’s body was found last month – just several kilometres away from the Afghan’s home in Kypseli.



Among them are flowers and handwritten cards with one reading: “Elizabeth Jane Ross forever in our memories.”

A friend in the volunteer community even claimed: “Alaina may well have placed one of them there.

Her thoughts are with her, not Sharif. She feels distraught.”

In her own testimony to police, leaked to the local media, the 26-year-old American had spoken of her husband’s “stubbornness”.

She said: “Even if you put all the evidence, all the hard facts, right in front of him, he never admits anything.”



Holed up in Korydallos, home to some of Greece’s most hardened criminals, Ahmadzai is not thought to have received any visit requests.

At summer’s peak, he has been left with his own thoughts in a cell shared with eight other men.

But he has wasted no time hiring a “boutique” Athens-based law firm whose clients “range from large companies to private companies and individuals”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Representing the Afghan in court last week, Christos Erdas invoked his client’s right to remain silent saying the presumption of innocence in the case of the Afghan had been violated by continuous leaks.

As such, he said, Ahmedzai would not be speaking until the results of toxicological and vital organ tests were returned.

News.title: Powerful earthquake hits Spain as cars crushed under rocks & giant crack slices through road with emergency declared
News.content:
A POWERFUL 5-magnitude earthquake has struck Spain as authorities declare an emergency after buildings collapsed and rocks crushed cars.

Panic spread across the southern city of Granada after the tremor hit around 1am local time.



Footage circulating on social media shows people fleeing their homes and tourists running out of hotels in the middle of the night.

Andalusian ‌emergency services have rescued a ‌number of people from damaged buildings.



Homes and cars have been heavily damaged – and an entire road has been split in half by a crack caused by the powerful jolt.

Antonio Sanz Cabello, vice-president of the Andalusian government, said that authorities had declared an emergency.



“If you are in Granada, you have felt the earthquake, you are okay, and your home shows no damage, stay calm and avoid entering and exiting buildings unnecessarily,” he wrote on X.

“On the street, stay away from facades, cornices, balconies, walls, and other elements that could fall.”



Regional authorities reported that emergency services received around 200 calls, but no casualties have been reported so far.

Callers reported falling objects, shaking furniture and rattling doors and windows.

The earthquake caused structural damage across the area, with residents reporting cracks in structures, collapses – including entire walls – and damage to several buildings.



In nearby Armilla and other parts of the region, pieces of facades and roof tiles came crashing down on the streets under.

Firefighters and police have been working to seal off affected spots after carrying out inspections through the night.

The epicentre was located near the town of Alendin, a few miles from Granada, with a depth of 1.2 miles.



A smaller 2.6 tremor followed a few minutes later near the village of Gojar.

Destructive earthquakes are rare in Spain, where the risk is classified as medium.

The neighbouring regions of Andalusia and Murcia, stretching along the Betic Cordillera through Granada, Málaga, Almería, and Murcia, are the most active.

The earthquake in Granada comes just two weeks after a 4.1 quake hit the town of Librilla in the Murcia region.

News.title: Granada earthquake - live: Tourists flee and homes wrecked as tremor hits Spain
News.content:
Residents fled their homes and tourists ran from hotels in panic in the city of Granada, Spain, after the powerful 5-magnitude earthquake struck

A powerful 5-magnitude earthquake has hit part of Spain popular with tourists, leaving a trail of destruction with panicking tourists running from their hotels.

The southern city of Granada, known for its stunning Alhambra Palace, was rocked by the tremor at around 1am local time. Homes and cars have been heavily damaged.

Antonio Sanz Cabello, vice-president of the Andalusian government, said in a post on X that authorities had declared an emergency.

"If you're in Granada, you've felt the earthquake, you're okay, and your home shows no damage, stay calm and avoid entering and exiting buildings unnecessarily," he said. "On the street, stay away from facades, cornices, balconies, walls, and other elements that could fall."

Today's earthquake follows another tremor in Granada in July which measured 3.7 on the Richter scale.

News.title: Indonesia earthquake - live: At least 38 dead as huge 7.7 quake rocks tourist spot
News.content:
The 7.7-magnitude quake has struck not far from the coast of Flores Island with buildings in multiple towns destroyed

A massive earthquake has struck in a popular tourist spot in Indonesia with at least 38 dead and rescuers desperately searching for survivors in the rubble.

The 7.7-magnitude tremor struck off the country's Flores Island, to the east of Bali and a tourist destination known for its stunning scenery, shortly before 5am local time (11pm UK time) on Saturday at a depth of 10 kilometres, the United States Geological Survey (USGS) said.

Rescue official Fathur Rahman told AFP the people confirmed dead so far are from four different towns on the island. "Our focus will be on locating the victims who are buried under the rubble" said Fathur, adding that the rescue effort had been complicated by landslides cutting off roads.

Following the quake, the country's Weather, Climate, and Earthquake Information office (BMKG) issued an early tsunami warning which has now been lifted.

The first, massive, tremor was followed by at least two other powerful quakes at 5.9 and 5.6 magnitude respectively.

News.title: Heathrow flooding - live: Airport in urgent 'do not drive' warning to passengers
News.content:
There is a massive disruption at Heathrow Airport

Flooding at Heathrow Airport is preventing access by road to Terminals 2 and 3 with passengers urged to use rail and underground services instead

Heathrow flooding - live: Airport in urgent 'do not drive' warning to passengers

Heathrow Airport has issued an urgent "do not drive" warning after major flooding left access to two terminals restricted.

Water in the airport's central terminal area is barring drivers from reaching or leaving Terminals 2 and 3 by road.

People headed to Heathrow are now being strongly urged to use rail and underground services instead.

Those who must travel by car are urged to use Park and Ride, head to Terminals 4 or 5 and take free rail services from there, or change at local rail stations.

"Our teams are working to resolve the situation as quickly as possible, we apologise for any disruption caused," airport officials said.

Flights from Terminals 2 and 3 go to major global destinations across Europe, North America, Asia, and the Middle East such as Chicago, Tokyo or Mumbai.

News.title: Jason Arday told friend 'he couldn't go on' before his death after Cambridge plagiarism scandal
News.content:
Jason Arday told friend 'he couldn't go on' before his death after Cambridge plagiarism scandal

The Metropolitan Police said the 41-year-old former Cambridge University professor's death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.

View 2 Images Jason Arday has been found dead at home (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

Former University of Cambridge professor Jason Arday said he "couldn’t go on" hours before he died, a friend of his has said.

‌



Mr Arday, who resigned after a plagiarism row, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to Daley Thompson Way, in Battersea, just after 3pm on Friday to reports that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property.

‌



The Metropolitan Police said his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.

‌



University of Cambridge professor, and director of the Autism Research Centre, Sir Simon Baron-Cohen has now told the BBC he spoke to Mr Arday.

Sir Simon told Radio 4’s Today programme: "He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he couldn't go on."

"He used those words in voice notes," he added. Sir Simon said: "At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.

‌



"He was a vulnerable child, a vulnerable teenager, and a vulnerable adult, so he needed and deserved safeguarding and support and reasonable adjustment every step of the way."

View 2 Images Jason Arday was 'subjected to relentless scrutiny' the BBC has been told (Image: University of Cambridge Faculty SWNS)

Youngest Black Cambridge professor's extraordinary rise after autism diagnosis aged 3 READ MORE :

Sir Simon said Mr Arday was a "kind and gentle" man who had been and used as a "lightning rod" to examine diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.

‌



Mr Arday, a professor of sociology of education who became Cambridge's youngest black professor in 2023, quit following a series of reports alleging he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research. An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Mr Arday of wrongdoing.

Sir Simon said he had grown concerned about the mental health of Mr Arday, a "vulnerable autistic man" that he could see was struggling.

He said: "We need to let the investigations proceed, we need to understand how this tragedy has happened, but there has to be accountability at lots of levels."

News.title: Met Office issues grim drought warning as rain forecast to break heatwave grip on UK
News.content:
Met Office issues grim drought warning as rain forecast to break heatwave grip on UK

Following the driest July on record for England and Wales in nearly two centuries, the Environment Agency declared official drought conditions across more than half of the country

View 4 Images More than two-thirds of England is now in drought (Image: Getty Images)

A Met Office weather expert has warned that not even an Autumn deluge could guarantee a reversal of the drought conditions impacting most of Britain.

‌



The government has warned that conditions could last until October after officials declared 71.3 per cent of England is now in drought, after the nation recorded its driest six months since 1976. Last week, the East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and Sussex moved into drought status, joining half of England and the whole of Wales.

‌



Rainfall totals for July ranged from 26 per cent of the expected average for North West England to as little as 1 per cent in the South East. Parts of Hampshire, the Isle of Wight and West Sussex have not had a single drop for 59 days. Over the next two days, there could be relief for many, with rain expected for the first time in weeks.

‌



Will Lang, the organisation’s chief meteorologist says although rain is on its way, there remains a question mark over how much would fall. Asked whether the Met Office expected rainfall, Mr Lang said: “Having seen virtually no rainfall in southern parts of the UK, we will see some rainfall.

View 4 Images Some areas have not seen a drop of rain for almost 60 days (Image: Getty Images)

Four teens arrested on suspicion of arson after massive wildfire spread across Porth READ MORE :

"How much is the question. The answer is probably not too much compared with our forecast. It’s looking like the overall amount of rain will still be below normal for the time of year.”

‌



He continued: “Looking forward into the autumn, though, that’s when we’d normally see a change of conditions. We do see wetter and windier conditions and we will see more rainfall. Again, ‘how much?’ is the question – and whether that’s enough to alleviate things like the current drought problems, we don’t know yet.”

Mr Lang spoke to the Press Association following a visit to the Met Office in Exeter, Devon, by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who met apprentices and staff at the centre.

Brits were left shocked last night after millions across England and Wales were sent a blaring Government emergency alert tonight with a stark warning against 'any activity that could start a fire'

‌



View 4 Images A Government emergency alert arrived on Friday night (Image: Jeff Moore)

On Friday, Mr Burnham was at the scene of a wildfire in Stourbridge in the West Midlands where 54 people have been treated by paramedics, including 19 who were admitted to hospital.

This morning, the Prince of Wales thanked the emergency services battling wildfires across the country in a personal statement, saying: “Our thoughts are with everyone affected, particularly those who have lost their homes, and with those working tirelessly to protect communities, homes and the countryside.”

‌



The Prime Minister told broadcasters: “We might be in for a wet autumn and winter straight after this, because of El Nino and some of the issues there, which was reported to Cobra.

“So, after fire could come floods. We have to face up to the changing climate. I think we need a different debate about that.

“There’s no point denying where we are – we need to face up to it, we need more clean energy, we need to see that transition accelerate. Those are all of the issues that, you know, are right now in discussion.”

‌



View 4 Images PM Andy Burnham made a visit to Stourbridge on Friday before the alert was issued (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

El Nino is declared when sea temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise 0.5C above the long-term average.

The Met Office’s Professor Adam Scaife previously said that this year’s El Nino will likely cause “a temporary spike in global annual temperature with the residual heat potentially making next year the hottest in the global series from 1850”.

‌



Chris Hinchliff, the Labour MP for North East Hertfordshire, last week wrote to Mr Burnham urging him to take “urgent action” to prepare for the hotter weather.

“Climate breakdown is the greatest threat to our way of life since the Second World War,” he wrote in his letter.

“If we do not prepare in the short window available to us, the looming El Nino will compound these challenges and inflict devastating consequences on our already struggling country.”

‌



Mr Hinchliff called for a national “nature restoration workforce” to plant trees and restore wetland to bolster water storage, a review of how resilient national infrastructure is in the face of heat, and an acceleration of “food security planning, including measures to support domestic food production, particularly at a local, community scale”.

Asked what sort of effects El Nino might have on the country’s weather, Mr Lang replied: “El Nino can start to have an effect on the UK winter.

“So, one of the things it can do is give a little bit of a boost to rainfall in the latter part of the autumn and as we head into early winter.

Article continues below

“We’re not sure that that will happen at this stage, but it’s something that can happen in El Nino conditions. So, that’s one thing we’re looking out for in our forecasts and our models. Beyond that, it’s really too early to tell.”

News.title: Doctor issues collagen 'evidence' skin warning as millions take supplement
News.content:
Doctor issues collagen 'evidence' skin warning as millions take supplement

Skin expert says collagen isn't a 'miracle cure' and reveals what actually helps protect your skin

View 3 Images Collagen is an important structural protein in the skin (Image: Getty)

A health expert has issued a warning to anyone taking collagen. It comes as the supplement has become one of the UK's biggest beauty and wellness trends - and consumers are increasingly putting their money where their interest lies.

‌



According to YouGov research, 10% of UK adults (roughly 5.3 million people) have used collagen since January 2025, rising to 15% of women, making it the most popular of the emerging wellness supplements measured. But while collagen powders, drinks and gummies often promise firmer skin and fewer wrinkles, new research suggests consumers may want to think twice before spending money on them.

‌



A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 randomised controlled trials involving 1,474 people found that collagen supplementation appeared to improve skin hydration, elasticity and wrinkles when all studies were considered. However, the researchers found no significant benefits in higher-quality studies or in studies without pharmaceutical industry funding, concluding that there is currently insufficient clinical evidence to support the use of collagen supplements to prevent or treat skin ageing.

‌



Dr Conal Perrett, consultant dermatologist at The Devonshire Clinic, says consumers should therefore be wary of taking marketing claims at face value. He said: "Collagen is an important structural protein in the skin, but that doesn't automatically mean that consuming collagen will make your skin younger."

He warned: "The evidence around oral collagen is interesting, but it remains mixed and the quality of the studies varies." The dermatologist says, unlike the impression often given by beauty marketing, collagen consumed in a drink or powder isn't simply transported directly to the skin.

View 3 Images "Your body doesn't simply take the collagen from a supplement and deliver it directly to your skin"

‌



The digestive system breaks down collagen into amino acids and smaller peptides that the body can then use. "Your body doesn't simply take the collagen from a supplement and deliver it directly to your skin," explains Dr Perrett.

"Some research suggests certain collagen peptides may have biological effects. But this shouldn't be interpreted as proof that every collagen product will reduce wrinkles or improve skin firmness."

Dr Perrett says consumers shouldn't overlook the basics of nutrition when considering skin health. Vitamin C is essential for normal collagen production, while protein provides the amino acids the body needs to make proteins. Foods including peppers, citrus fruits, berries, broccoli, eggs, fish, dairy, beans, and lentils can all be part of a diet that supports healthy skin.

‌



Dr Perrett said: "Before spending money on an expensive beauty supplement, I'd focus on the fundamentals: a varied diet, adequate protein, plenty of fruit and vegetables and good sun protection. These are far more important foundations for skin health than relying on a single supplement."

View 3 Images Dr Perrett says consumers shouldn't overlook the basics of nutrition when considering skin health

What are five ways to support your skin's natural collagen?

According to Dr Conal Perrett, supporting healthy collagen starts with the basics:

‌



1. Eat a varied diet

Include a variety of colourful fruit and vegetables alongside a good source of protein at your meals. "Don't look for one miracle food for your skin. A varied diet containing plenty of fruit and vegetables, alongside adequate protein, gives your body the nutrients it needs to maintain healthy skin," Dr Perrett said.

2. Prioritise vitamin C

Add vitamin C-rich foods such as peppers, citrus fruits, berries, broccoli and tomatoes to your diet regularly. "Vitamin C is essential for collagen production, so it's an important nutrient when it comes to skin health. Fortunately, it's easy to get through food."

3. Don't overlook protein

Include protein-rich foods such as eggs, fish, meat, dairy, beans and lentils throughout the day. "Collagen is a protein, so it's important not to overlook your overall protein intake while focusing on collagen supplements. Your body needs amino acids to produce its own proteins."

‌



4. Don't rely on supplements alone

Think of supplements as an optional addition, not a replacement for good nutrition and skincare. Dr Perrett added: "A collagen supplement isn't a shortcut to younger-looking skin. The evidence is still mixed, so I'd prioritise a balanced diet and healthy lifestyle before spending money on an expensive supplement."

5. Protect your skin from UV

Use broad-spectrum sunscreen daily and take practical steps to reduce prolonged UV exposure, particularly on the face, neck and hands. "When it comes to collagen, we shouldn't just think about making more, we should also think about protecting what we already have. UV exposure is a major contributor to premature skin ageing."

Article continues below

Dr Perrett's 'miracle cure' warning:

The dermatologist says that while collagen isn't necessarily a scam, but it isn't a 'miracle cure' either. With collagen use continuing to grow despite seven in 10 adults saying most wellness supplements are overhyped, Dr Perrett's advice is to approach the trend with realistic expectations.

“If someone enjoys taking a collagen supplement and understands that the evidence is still developing, there may be a place for it within their routine. But I wouldn't want people to feel that they need to spend significant amounts of money on collagen to have healthy skin,” Dr Perrett added.

“The biggest mistake is to confuse a popular wellness trend with an established medical treatment. Collagen is an important protein in our skin, but that doesn't automatically mean that consuming collagen will reverse skin ageing.”

News.title: Teenage boy, 17, 'murdered' after reports of 'possible burglary' as police issue plea
News.content:
Teenage boy, 17, 'murdered' after reports of 'possible burglary' as police issue plea

A man was arrested at the scene in Linslade, near Leighton Buzzard, and is now in custody on suspicion of murder

View Image Bedfordshire Police are at the scene in Linslade (Image: PA)

A 17-year-old boy has died and a murder investigation is underway after police were called to a "possible break-in" in Bedfordshire.

Police rushed to what they called "initial reports of suspicious activity" in Soulbury Road, Linslade, near Leighton Buzzard.

They found the boy unresponsive and, despite desperate attempts to save him, he was pronounced dead shortly afterwards. Bedfordshire Police said there was no evidence the victim had been involved in a burglary and that his next of kin had been informed.

A man was arrested at the scene and is currently in custody on suspicion of murder. Three other men were also arrested in connection with the incident late on Thursday which is being investigated by the Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire Major Crime Unit.

Detective Inspector Caeva Taylor said: "This is an incredibly tragic incident in which a 17-year-old boy has lost his life and our thoughts are with his loved ones at this unimaginably difficult time.

"We currently have one person in custody on suspicion of murder, and three other men are also assisting us with our enquiries.

"Our team is working hard to establish what has led to the boy’s death and we understand the concern this will cause in the community.

"The initial 999 call to police was to report a possible break-in in progress, however our enquiries so far have found no evidence whatsoever that the victim was carrying out, or attempting to carry out, a burglary.

Article continues below

"We have been carrying out a number of enquiries including reviewing CCTV and speaking to people in the area, and we’re urging the public to help us by letting us know any information they may have. In particular we’re urging anyone with any doorbell or CCTV footage to get in touch immediately."

News.title: All we know on Brit girl, 12, missing on family holiday in Japan
News.content:
All we know on Brit girl, 12, missing on family holiday in Japan

Schoolgirl Carmelita Lakdesha Paul, 12, went missing on family holiday in Japan, sparking a huge search operation as her with the country swept by a wave of severe rainstorms

View 3 Images Carmelita Lakdesha Paul travelled to Japan with her parents and older brother on July 21 (Image: ANNnewsCH)

Fears are growing for a 12-year-old British girl who vanished on family holiday to Japan.

‌



A desperate search is under way for Carmelita Lakdesha Paul, who disappeared while on a sightseeing trip after her parents woke up to discover she was no longer at their accommodation. They raised the alarm at the Tokyo apartment where they were staying on August 12 after finding her gone.

‌



Carmelita's phone and passport behind were left behind in the room with her parents having no way of getting in touch with her. She is believed to have been carrying only a few thousand yen, worth around £65. She is described as being five feet three inches and a medium build with curly black hair.

‌



Here is all we know about her disappearance, as her frantic parents and older brother wait for answers.

Spotted on CCTV

View 3 Images She was last seen in Kamata, near to the family's hotel (Image: The Asahi Shimbun via Getty Images)

Footage analysed by investigators shows the schoolgirl dressed in a blue sleeveless top, black and white skirt, black pumps and carrying a pink handbag.

‌



She was captured on shop CCTV walking in the Nichome section of Kamata, close to where the family were staying, later that morning.

Police said she then boarded a train at Kamata station and travelled 20 minutes south to Yokohama Station. No-one has been able to trace her movements since.

Last conversation with parents

The youngster was reported missing to police at 9.30am on August 13, when her parents woke to find her gone.

‌



Carmelita's father says he had spoken to her before she went to bed the night before.

He told police said there was nothing at all suspicious about her behaviour. It is unclear what time she left their apartment.

Severe rainstorm concern

View 3 Images Severe floods have killed eight people so far (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Japan has been swept by a wave of severe rainstorms in the past few days, heightening family's fears over the need for proper shelter. The girl has little money - not enough for an extended hotel or hostel stay.

At least eight people have died after "unprecedented" rainfall caused flooding with nearly 7,000 people left stranded at Tokyo's Narita airport and evacuation orders were issued for more than 400,000 people.

Japan's Meteorological Agency has issued the highest level-5 warning for heavy rain and landslides.

Article continues below

What the authorities say

Police are now urging anyone with information that could help find the schoolgirl to contact Tokyo Metropolitan Police's Kamata Station.

Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office spokesman said: "We are supporting the family of a British child who has been reported missing in Japan and are in contact with the local authorities."

News.title: Tributes paid to Jason Arday after ex-Cambridge professor found dead
News.content:
Tributes have been paid to Jason Arday, the former Cambridge professor, after he was found dead at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.

In a statement issued by his publisher Simon & Schuster UK, Arday's family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They said a "campaign of misinformation" had been too much for him.

Arday, 41, resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.

The University of Cambridge vice-chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice led the tributes, saying the faculty was "desperately saddened" to learn of his death.

"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" to hear about the death and she urged people to "remember there are real people with loved ones involved".

Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan is among those who have said Arday was subjected to unrelenting media scrutiny.

He said Arday had faced "an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse", adding that he was a victim of "a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced".

"His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake up call for all of us," he posted on X.

Jo Grady, General secretary of the University and College Union said the "level of harassment he suffered and the racism he was subjected to has been sickening" and "must be investigated".

Lord Paul Boateng, who became the UK's first black cabinet minister in 2002 when he was appointed Chief Secretary to the Treasury under Tony Blair, told BBC Newsnight he was " horrified, shocked and deeply saddened".

"Racism in academia is a fact of life and needs to be addressed," he added in a written statement.

In a statement on Saturday, National Education Union (NEU) general secretary Daniel Kebede said Arday had been subjected to "a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism".

"The effect has been chilling. It tells black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target," he said.

Director of the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge, Prof Simon Baron-Cohen told the Today programme Arday had been "bombarded by every media outlet to paint him as a fraud".

"He was an incredibly, kind and gentle and caring man," he said.

He spoke to Arday the morning of his death, and said the academic had felt unable to leave the house.

"He has experienced what he described as a campaign against him, for the last three years," he previously told BBC News.

"What he was saying to me was 'they've destroyed my life' - it's not clear who they were but I think he was referring to the media."

"The personal attacks on him have been so immense.

"This isn't to point fingers, and its not a single media outlet, but in the last few weeks since he resigned, I must have received a hundred new requests - to comment on his life."

News.title: Temporary ban on disposable BBQs as military deployed to help battle wildfires
News.content:
As part of the military deployment, Gurkha logistics teams equipped with water tankers and military engineers are now assisting fire services in South Wales.

Andy Burnham has promised more military personnel will be deployed elsewhere if needed.

Crews in England and Wales tackled multiple blazes on Friday and an emergency alert was sent to millions of phones.

A total of 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), which matches last year's record.

As well as devastating blazes in the West Midlands which saw dozens of homes destroyed, fire crews have been in action across the two countries.

In Wales, a major incident was declared near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, after dozens of homes were evacuated and roads closed.

In Hampshire, firefighters have spent a sixth day tackling a wildfire in the New Forest, which broke out on Sunday.

Sixteen emergencies were tackled by Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service on Thursday afternoon, including a fire at Mousehold Heath in the city.

On Friday evening, an emergency alert was sent to mobile phones warning of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" across England and Wales.

The message asked residents, landowners and visitors to not undertake any activity that could cause a fire "including disposable barbecues, firepits, garden incinerators of fireworks".

It was the most extensive use of the system to date, according to the government.

News.title: Heathrow Airport pipe leak causes flood disruption
News.content:
Heathrow Airport has warned access to Terminals 2 and 3 is restricted because of flooding caused by a leak in a pipe within the grounds of the airport.

Water in the central terminal area means anyone trying to travel to or from either of these terminals cannot travel by road. Instead passengers are being advised to travel by rail and Tube and to avoid using cars.

An airport spokesperson said: "Our teams are working to resolve the situation as quickly as possible, we apologise for any disruption caused," adding: "The leak has been isolated and repairs are on-going."

The disruption comes during the school holidays, one of the busiest periods for the airport.

Heathrow said 19 July was its busiest day of the year so far as many schools broke up for summer, with 267,000 passengers passing through.

The airport was recently affected by disruption to railway services, after a water leak prompted the closure of a tunnel.

News.title: Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?
News.content:
But now, even this is being squeezed too. Recent rules say women have to ask men to take their products to market, and only men can sit at their stalls to show their wares at trade fairs. The Taliban gives various reasons for this, including claiming that women aren't wearing proper hijab or head covering.

"The world has to talk to the Taliban in a different way because it's just not working," says Najia. "The lives of Afghan women have to change because we're losing hope."

Five years after this ultra-conservative Islamist movement took charge, women are banned from much of the public sphere and girls are prohibited from going to school over the age of 12. Many inside and outside Afghanistan are asking the same pressing question: what's the best way to engage the Taliban to try to achieve meaningful change?

The issue is deeply divisive. There are fissures between many groups, with a huge array of conflicting issues at stake. These include women's rights, unpredictable Taliban edicts, international sanctions and aid cuts during a spiralling humanitarian crisis. The international response is split between Western countries often focused on human rights and others more interested in investment opportunities. And the West itself is divided on the best response.

Many now accept that whatever they're doing, it's not working.

News.title: Europe's scorched landscapes seen from space after summer heatwaves
News.content:
The impact of this summer's extreme temperatures on western Europe can now be seen from space after successive heatwaves since May.

Satellite images examined by BBC Verify show shrunken glaciers, scorched areas left by wildfires, green fields turned arid and lower river levels.

And some landmarks have been affected, too. The Palace of Versailles, south of the French capital Paris, appears as an island of trees surrounded by brown fields in these images.

News.title: Many Canadians are boycotting the US - here's where they're travelling instead
News.content:
Prior to US President Donald Trump's re-election, Kent Truscott and his family, from London, Ontario, had taken multiple trips south of the border, including to California and most recently New York in 2023.

But since late 2024, "my family and I have completely decided to boycott the United States", he told BBC.

That meant cancelling a trip last spring to Texas to watch the SpaceX Starship launch with his brother. The two had planned to fly down from Toronto, rent a car and stay a week to watch the launch, likely spending "thousands of dollars".

Truscott and his wife decided to spend that money in Canada instead â the Atlantic provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, to be exact.

Their decision is a response to US tariffs and the president's comments about annexing their country. More than a year after Trump's return to the White House, many Canadians like Truscott are still holding firm on their boycott on travel to the US.

News.title: When my dog died, my grief was overwhelming and complicated
News.content:
Gemma Champ, a writer from north London, rescued her cat Frankie as a kitten 17 years ago, when she lived in Abu Dhabi. Frankie died at home in January, and at first she felt "ridiculous for making such a fuss".

"I sent out a WhatsApp to all who'd known and loved him - and it turned out everyone had amazing memories of him. He wasn't just a cat. One friend said it was like 'a legendary beast from the great plains has left us.'

"We can see from social media that there's a whole community of people out there who have gone through the same experience and the same pain, so you don't feel like you're just being a drama queen - I think that's definitely how it would have been seen years ago."

After Greg James' dog died, the presenter said he wouldn't be on his show the next day. But getting employers to agree to this isn't always easy.

In 2019, Emma McNulty's 14-year-old terrier Millie died suddenly. Feeling sick with grief, McNulty, from Glasgow, said she was too upset to go into work. Unable to find someone to cover her shift, she said her part-time job in a sandwich shop was terminated. She then launched an online petition asking for employers to recognise pet bereavement.

No country mandates that employers offer paid time off after the death of a pet. Kara Stott, head of in-house legal and general counsel at law firm Peninsula, said more UK employers were starting to show flexibility with workers whose pets had died, even if a change to the law does not appear imminent.

But introducing formal pet bereavement policies has its challenges, Stott tells the BBC.

"Points to consider include how do you define a pet - does the policy just cover cats and dogs or would hamsters, rabbits, goldfish, horses, snakes, or other animals be included?"

Gemma, who is freelance, took a few days off work after Frankie's death, with the support of her "incredibly kind" client. "I doubt I could have done that if I'd been employed," she says, "and I think I'd have been weeping in the toilets at the office."

The reaction from friends and family to Frankie's passing confirmed that her sense of grief was real, she says, and she appreciated that people took it seriously.

"I do think, or hope, that people are learning not to dismiss this very profound and long-lasting relationship so easily."

News.title: I wish I had been a more rebellious teenager, says Bella Ramsey
News.content:
Bella Ramsey spent many teenage years working with adults so never really went through the moody, rebellious phase often associated with being a teenager.

The British actor, who debuted in Game of Thrones aged 11 and uses they/them pronouns, says they had consciously decided not to behave like a stereotypical teenager after hearing criticisms from adults.

"I was like, I'm not going to be that."

So when Sunny Dancer, a film about a summer camp for young people affected by cancer, gave Ramsey seven weeks to experience teenage freedom, it was an opportunity to dive straight in.

"I got to be a teenager aged 21, which was brilliant," Ramsey tells BBC News. "It was really nice - and liberating."

Looking back, Ramsey says the experience made them wonder whether they had missed out by being quite so sensible the first time around.

"I kind of wish that I had made the most of being a teenager and getting away with things and being a bit rebellious."

In Sunny Dancer, Ramsey plays Ivy, a young female cancer survivor in remission who reluctantly heads to a "chemo camp" where she finds an unexpected group of friends and has a summer that changes her.

News.title: Fires prompt national alert as 19 homes destroyed
News.content:
Fires across England and Wales have prompted a national government alert warning people not to light anything that could spark a wildfire.

The warning on Friday evening came as it was revealed 19 homes were destroyed and a further 18 damaged in a huge fire in Stourbridge, West Midlands, that spread rapidly through grass and woodland on Thursday before damaging homes.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told members of the public to take the warning "seriously", adding it was triggered at the request of firefighters.

West Midlands Fire Service chief fire officer Simon Tuhill said the Stourbridge blaze was one of the most significant incidents the service had ever dealt with.

It was one of several fires being dealt with across England and Wales on Friday.

In Wales, a major incident was declared near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, after dozens of homes were evacuated and roads closed

Overnight in to Saturday, four 14-year-olds from Porth, South Wales, have all been arrested on suspicion of arson and have since been bailed under investigation

In Hampshire, firefighters spent a sixth day tackling a wildfire in the New Forest, Hampshire, which broke out on Sunday.

Sixteen emergencies were tackled by Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service on Thursday afternoon, including a fire at Mousehold Heath, off Gurney Road in the city.

Elsewhere in the West Midlands fires caused extensive damage in Warstock and Kings Norton, Birmingham on Thursday. A 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of arson with intent to endanger life .

In Stoke-on-Trent on Thursday four homes in Sandyford were destroyed, with other properties damaged. Two people were arrested on suspicion of arson. Six firefighters were taken to hospital due to smoke inhalation and heat exhaustion.

In Willenhall, West Midlands, at least three homes and several gardens were destroyed in fires on Stonehouse Avenue and Harry Perks Street.

Investigators said they were working with other emergency services to establish how the Stourbridge fire started, with police saying they were keeping an open mind.

Some of the worst-affected areas have been cordoned off and many residents who were evacuated, including the Bishop of Dudley, the Right Reverend Martin Gorick, have not been able to return home.

News.title: Weekend to bring significant drop in temperatures as heatwave ends
News.content:
Temperatures are set to tumble this weekend as the fifth heatwave to scorch the UK this year comes to an end.

After Thursday marked the hottest day of 2026 so far, conditions will be noticeably cooler on Saturday and Sunday.

Temperatures will fall by 10-15 degrees Celsius by the end of the weekend, bringing them much closer to the seasonal average.

The change in weather pattern that is bringing this cooler air will also result in an increased chance of rain, including in areas currently in drought.

News.title: New Forest fire fully contained, fire service says
News.content:
A wildfire that broke out in the New Forest on Sunday is now "fully surrounded", says the fire service.

The blaze began when a van caught fire on the A31 last Sunday, with 23 drivers having to abandon their vehicles as the fire took hold.

The A31 will remain closed until at least Thursday 20 August, says National Highways.

In an update on Saturday, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said: "Overnight, firefighters continued working incredibly hard at the scene, and the fire is now fully surrounded. We will still be on scene for a number of days as we damp down and extinguish hotspots."

The fire service revealed on Friday evening that the blaze has affected an area of approximately 1.6 sq km (0.6 sq miles) and 169 fire appliances have attended from 93 fire stations.

In the update on Friday, assistant chief fire officer for HIWFRS Rob Cole said: "I'm pleased to say we are getting on top of this. However there are many days of work ahead of us to ensure that this fire doesn't spread when the wind blows or when other hotspots start to occur."

On Friday evening the UK's mobile phone alert system was used to warn people not to light anything which could spark a wildfire, including barbecues and garden incinerators.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told members of the public to take the warning "seriously" and said it was triggered at the request of firefighters.

News.title: Six people arrested after man abducted in Edinburgh
News.content:
Six people have been arrested in East Lothian after a man was abducted in Edinburgh.

Police Scotland said it received a report that a man had been abducted in the Canonmills area of the capital at about 22:30 on Thursday.

A 22-year-old man was later traced in Longniddry on Friday and taken to hospital as a precaution.

Five men - aged 21, 21, 22, 23 and 45 - and a 40-year-old woman have been arrested and police say inquiries are ongoing.

A section of the A198, which runs through the village of Longniddry, has been shut by police and a diversion is in place.

Officers believe this was a targeted incident and there is no risk to the wider public.

Det Insp Robbie Wallace said: "We understand an incident of this nature will be concerning but please be assured our inquiries are ongoing.

"Police will remain in the Longniddry area while this investigation continues and anyone with any concerns, or information, can approach these officers."

One report on social media said armed officers had been seen removing someone from a car.

Lothian Buses posted that some services were unable to serve the village and its routes had been diverted due to the road closure.

Longniddry is a coastal village about 15 miles (24km) from Canonmills.

News.title: Derailed Essex train leads to travel chaos
News.content:
Martin Frobisher, of Network Rail, said the summer's hot weather had "presented exceptional challenges to the railway".

In an interview with the BBC Transport Correspondent Katy Austin, Frobisher also confirmed speed restrictions were not in place in either Wickford or Lewes.

On the possible impact of the hot weather, he said "yes, that's one of the things that we're looking at.

"We've got our investigations underway. We've got technical engineers on site, our best experts who are on site with the Rail Accident Investigation Branch.

"They're looking very thoroughly at what's happened. And based on that, we will act on what we learn."

However, he added it was "too early to speculate on the full findings".

The investigation would specifically assess "whether or not this was weather-related", said Mark Francois, the Conservative MP for Rayleigh and Wickford.

The Department for Transport stressed Britain's railways were "among the safest in the world" as it reacted to the incident.

It said derailments were "incredibly rare" events.

An East of England Ambulance Service spokesperson said: "Our crews assessed 62 patients who were on board the train.

"Following assessment, all patients were discharged at the scene.

"We also assisted with the evacuation of a second train that was unable to continue its journey due to the derailment.

"There were no casualties among those on board."

A spokesperson for BTP also confirmed there were no reported injuries.

Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below.

News.title: Bride dazzles in thrifty wedding with £2 charity shop dress
News.content:
A couple tied the knot in a thrifty-themed wedding with the bride dazzling in a Â£2 charity shop wedding dress.

Gina and Jacob Dodds, from Hoole in Chester, said "I do" in a ceremony held at the city's Storyhouse arts and cultural centre on Wednesday.

Both Gina's dress and engagement ring were bought from the Hope House Children's Hospice outlet while guests were also invited to wear outfits sourced from charity shops - raising money for a range of good causes.

"If we were going to have a wedding then we wanted it to be about more than just us - we wanted it to be about helping other people," she said.

News.title: Baby puffins make uninhabited island their new home
News.content:
Footage of a puffling - a baby puffin - bred on the Copeland Islands off the County Down coast has been captured for the first time.

The seabirds, synonymous with Rathlin Island off County Antrim, are not indigenous to the uninhabited Lighthouse Island, so no population existed there until an introduction scheme was launched around 2013.

There are now around 30 breeding pairs of puffins, which is being seen as a real success story.

They arrive to the island each April, and this year - in fact, just last month - trail cameras near their burrows in the ground filmed a young puffling out of its burrow, and an adult puffin bringing fish back to feed its young.

Attempts to attract puffins to Lighthouse Island included setting up fake "decoy" puffins, and a solar powered speaker system broadcasting its call.

News.title: Two dead after light aircraft crash
News.content:
Two people have died following a light aircraft crash in north Wales.

The aircraft was found in a remote location close to Trawsfynydd, Gwynedd, with the two people on board pronounced dead at the scene, North Wales Police said.

The force received reports shortly after 12:00 BST that a light aircraft travelling from an airfield in England had not arrived at Caernarfon Airport as scheduled.

Multi-agency air and ground searches were carried out until the aircraft was found.

A team of investigators have since been deployed by the Air Accidents Investigations Branch (AAIB).

A quick-thinking air traffic controller averted a potential disaster on Friday after noticing two American Airlines jets were mistakenly flying the same flight number.

Audio of the incident shortly after midnight Friday shows how the Phoenix controller found a solution to ensure the planes that were both called American 2482 maintained proper separation as one plane arrived from Chicago shortly after the other had taken off.

“I’ve been working air traffic for 25 years. I’ve never seen two aircraft pretty much merge with the same call sign. That’s pretty incredible,” the controller said after the departing plane had safely cleared the area.

If both pilots thought the controller was telling them to fly at the same altitude as they headed toward each other, they might have collided.

Therefore, it was crucial that the two pilots knew which plane he was directing.

The audio posted by ATC.com shows how the controller quickly started referring to “American 2482 on the arrival” and “American 2482 on the departure” to keep the two planes straight.

The controller kept the arriving plane safely above the departing plane even as their flight paths converged and made sure that the pilots of both airlines saw each other when they were still miles apart. He also directed the departing plane not to climb too high, so a gap would remain between the planes.

“It could have been disastrous, but I’m glad it worked out,” the controller said afterwards.

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal ‘lead race’ to sign £50m target, Tottenham reach Gakpo agreement, Fernandez latest
News.content:
Arsenal could turn their attention to Brighton’s £51m-rated midfielder Jack Hinshelwood as they continue talks with Bayer Leverkusen over signing England international Jarell Quansah. The Premier League champions have been keen to sign a defender following the injury to William Saliba and the 23-year-old Quansah, formerly of Liverpool, would be able to cover both centre-back and right back positions.

Meanwhile, Barcelona are set to make a third bid of around £60m for Rodri, but are still set to fall £10m short of Manchester City’s valuation of the Ballon d’Or winner. The deal could yet influence the speed of any move for Enzo Fernandez, with his former Chelsea manager Enzo Maresca pushing for the midfielder's signature. Chelsea’s deadline of 5pm on Friday passed without City submitting their £120m bid, and the club expect Fernandez to now stay for the upcoming season.

Tottenham have agreed personal terms with Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo, according to reports in the Netherlands, while Spurs are also close to signing Manchester City winger Savinho and have joined Manchester United and Arsenal in expressing interest in Galatasaray forward Victor Osimhen. Arsenal’s Gabriel Martinelli has rejected the chance to join the Turkish club as part of a deal.

In other news, Tottenham captain Cristian Romero has completed his transfer to Atletico Madrid, while Paris Saint-Germain have confirmed the signing of Ferran Torres, the scorer of the winning goal in the World Cup final, from Barcelona. Crystal Palace have completed the signing of right-sided player Anan Khalaili on a five-year contract.

Former University of Cambridge professor Jason Arday has been found dead at a property in London, police have said.

The former professor, who resigned following a plagiarism row, was found dead at a property in Battersea on Friday afternoon.

The family of the former University of Cambridge professor said they are “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”, adding “the campaign of misinformation was too much” for him.

Prof Arday told a friend he felt he “couldn’t go on” in a voice note sent hours before he died, it emerged on Saturday.

open image in gallery ( St Mary's University Twickenham )

University of Cambridge professor and director of the Autism Research Centre, Sir Simon Baron-Cohen, told the BBC he spoke to Prof Arday on Friday morning.

Sir Simon told Radio 4’s Today programme: “He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he couldn’t go on.”

“He used those words in voice notes,” he added.

Sir Simon said Prof Arday was a “kind and gentle” man who had been “bombarded by every media outlet” and used as a “lightning rod” to examine diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.

“At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.

“He was a vulnerable child, a vulnerable teenager, and a vulnerable adult, so he needed and deserved safeguarding and support and reasonable adjustment every step of the way,” he added.

In a statement issued by Prof Arday’s publisher Simon & Schuster UK, Prof Arday’s family said: “Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for the more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him.

“The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.

open image in gallery Jason Arday carries the Olympic Torch in 2012 ( PA Wire )

“We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son.

A spokesman for the Metropolitan Police said officers were alerted on the death by the London Ambulance Service at 3.12pm on Friday.

A force spokesman said: “Sadly, a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers.

“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s Central South Command Unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner.”

A London Ambulance Service spokesperson said: “We were called at 3.06pm on Friday 14 August to reports of an incident on Daley Thompson Way, SW8.

“We sent a number of resources to the scene, including an ambulance crew, an advanced paramedic in a fast response car and members of our Hazardous Area Response Team.

“Sadly, a person was pronounced dead at the scene.”

Prof Arday, a professor of sociology of education who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, quit following a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research.

Further questions were asked in the press about the truth of other claims he made, including saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5 million for charity.

open image in gallery ( Supplied )

An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Prof Arday of wrongdoing.

Durham and Glasgow universities are investigating the circumstances around Prof Arday’s appointment to academic posts there .

Prof Arday said in his open resignation letter that the “only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away”.

He said: “This decision should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge.

“Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me.

“It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.”

University of Cambridge Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said she was “desperately saddened” by the death Prof Arday, adding: “Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”

Mr Arday’s death has prompted an outpouring of anger.

Labour MP for Liverpool Riverside Kim Johnson, said “serious questions need to be answered” over the “relentless media attacks Jason faced”, as she sent her condolences to his family.

News.title: Toddler who was taught by parents how to call 999 saves mum after she collapses
News.content:
A three-year-old, who was taught by his parents to call 999, rang emergency services after he saw his mother collapse.

James dialled 999 after his mother, Georgia, suffered a sudden drop in blood pressure caused by postural hypotension and severe dehydration, as she was putting her five-month-old down for a nap.

The call was answered by South Yorkshire Police Handler Jen, who asked James if he could “tickle mummy to wake her up”. Georgia later regained consciousness whilst James was still on the call.

Appearing on BBC Breakfast, Georgia explained that she and her husband had taught James what to do in an emergency following a visit to the National Emergency Services Museum in Sheffield.

"It was a fantastic opportunity to teach James who to call, what to do if there was ever an emergency and he needed something, especially when I'm on my own with him at home when I was pregnant.”
