Sports.title: Europe’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsed
Sports.content:
Europe’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped.

In a letter to the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, the influential European Football Clubs (EFC) group warned that its cooperation with future tournaments would hinge on Infantino backing down. It said the threat would hold unless a joint venture between EFC and Fifa – a framework for which has already been agreed – is completed before television rights can be sold for the 2028 Women’s Club World Cup.

The letter, dated 31 July and signed by the EFC chief executive, Charlie Marshall, said Infantino’s actions could constitute a “substantial breach” of the bodies’ existing memorandum of understanding (MoU) and suggested this could be grounds for its termination. It floated the idea that EFC and its clubs may push back against the international match calendar and its player release rules, which are crucial to ensuring national team tournaments can function. Infantino shelved the privately backed Football Forward Enterprise (FFE) in the early hours of 1 August after widespread condemnation.

Fundamental to EFC’s complaints was the impression FFE would bring all broadcasting, commercial and sponsorship rights under its own umbrella. The letter asked Fifa to confirm this and said it would take decisive action if these elements were not included in the long-proposed joint venture, whose creation is enshrined in the MoU and intended to involve managing the commercial side of global club competitions. It witheringly wrote that the tie-in had, “unlike the FFE proposal, made no meaningful progress over the past year”. EFC already has a similar joint venture with Uefa, named UC3, which was launched in 2025.

A potentially incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”

In theory the threat still holds although Fifa, in a response to EFC’s letter since Infantino climbed down, is understood to have promised a swift meeting to keep the joint venture on track. EFC’s position followed concerns raised by a vast number of clubs around Europe, who were angered by the lack of consultation around the design of FFE. One major European club expressed concerns in its own letter saying it would support EFC in any “firmer collective action” if necessary and called for “more rigorous and transparent governance processes”.

Any European withdrawal from Club World Cups would in practice mean those tournaments could not run. EFC and Fifa operated last year’s Club World Cup, the first to take place with 32 teams, using a short-term prototype for any future joint venture. No hosts have yet been announced for the new-look Women’s Club World Cup or the next edition of the men’s tournament in 2029.

View image in fullscreen Chelsea won the Club World Cup in July 2025 by beating Paris Saint-Germain in the final. Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty Images

EFC’s letter also raised the continuing delay, first reported in February, in distributing £185m of solidarity money to clubs that did not participate in the Club World Cup. Transparency over the event’s financial performance was also requested.

“We ask that you urgently share the final surplus revenue generated by the 2025 Fifa WC, together with a full profit and loss statement, so that all revenues, expenses and costs can be properly assessed in line with our partnership in this competition,” it said. “The absence of information on this matter, as with the lack of a solution on CWC solidarity for over a year, is also of serious concern and disappointment to EFC and our member clubs.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is understood there is increasing optimism that this issue is on the verge of resolution, although a notional average £50,000 windfall for every global top-flight club, if the pot was divided equally, pales in comparison with the £84m reward long since banked by last year’s winners, Chelsea.

Referring to clubs releasing players for international duty, EFC continued: “Our memorandum of understanding, set to expire on 30 December 2030, includes EFC’s and its member clubs’ acceptance of the international match calendar and the release rules. Both are directly relevant for Fifa’s non-European member associations and to any value FFE may have.” It said Fifa’s apparent commercial vision for FFE constituted a “serious breach of trust” and warned the MoU could be jeopardised.

The letter demonstrates the extraordinary level of leverage EFC, which is chaired by the Paris Saint-Germain president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, can claim over Fifa and its increasing influence on football’s future. The organisation, set up in 2008 as a lobby group for clubs around the continent, now has well over 800 members although only a minority hold full voting rights. Some stakeholders elsewhere in football’s ecosystem have expressed fears about the level of power it has assumed. A separate representative body, the Union of European Clubs, was created in 2023 to represent smaller sides but is not recognised by Uefa.

One potential consequence of EFC’s discussions with Fifa could, in the medium term, be its expansion into a group representing clubs around the world. More immediately, last month’s letter demanded that Fifa deliver on a previous promise to fully integrate Al-Khelaifi into the Fifa council, which is purportedly its main decision-making body.

Sports.title: London City Lionesses’ Mapi León: ‘It is a club created for women. It is beautiful and exciting’
Sports.content:
‘No, I can’t, I’m sorry, it’s a secret!” Mapi León roars with laughter, in response to being asked what persuaded her to join London City Lionesses. Does this bode badly for our interview? Fear not, the Spain centre-back is in as banterous and jovial a mood as you could imagine any new signing to be, as she embarks on her first major interview since signing for the Women’s Super League club.

Across the course of our conversation, in bright sunshine outside a quiet hotel near Maidstone, it is evident that the 31-year-old could scarcely be happier about her decision to swap Barcelona for south-east England. She is sorely missing her cat, Bagheera (“Here, you ask for so many things for pets, you can’t [really] fly with them, it’s so many documents, so many things”) but, that aside, she is buoyant, relaxed and clearly embracing English life. She says she likes the “little bread” in the morning, and we eventually establish she is referring to crumpets, and reveals: “I like the beans in the morning. It’s really interesting. My Spanish teammates like Alexia [Putellas] and Jana [Fernández] are like: ‘What are you doing eating beans in the morning? You need to train.’ I go: ‘No, it’s fine I like it.’”

However, English breakfasts were surely not what attracted her to Kent to play for London City Lionesses so, returning to that first question, she explains thoughtfully: “My body was craving something different. I spent many years in a comfortable position, because playing at Barça has been absolutely wonderful and very nice; it is a style of game that suits me a lot and coming to England, the football is very different from the Spanish one, at first glance. So, I think [the reason was] being able to challenge myself and see if I am capable. I am going to make an effort to adapt to this league and also to show myself that I’m able to compete in another style of play that is not the one that makes me stand out the most.”

An undisputed club legend at Barcelona, León certainly stood out in Spain as the best ball-playing centre-back of her generation, and won seven league titles, seven Copa de la Reina’s and – most impressively – four Champions League titles, during a nine-year period of relentless dominance with Barcelona, whom she joined from Atlético Madrid in 2017.

Allow Instagram content? This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue

This summer she was one of four members of the Spain starting XI that beat England 4-0 in June in Mallorca to leave Barcelona, together with Arsenal’s new signing Ona Batlle, OL Lyonnes’ new winger Salma Paralluelo and, most notably, her London City Lionesses teammate Alexia Putellas. Together, León and Putellas drew raised eyebrows across the women’s game by swapping the reigning European champions for a lesser-known team that finished sixth in the WSL last term, but they have been joined by a series of other world-renowned names including the former England goalkeeper Mary Earps and the France winger Kadidiatou Diani.

The club’s new signings meet the vision of their ambitious owner, the American businesswoman Michele Kang, of whom León says: “The impression I get is of an empowered woman, with a winning mindset, driven by a desire to see things improve and a drive to win. And that is a competitive and winning mentality. And if in the end, I want to be part of it because it is a club created for women and that is not common, I think it is beautiful and exciting.

“Everything counts when you make this kind of a decision, and of course, [Kang] was an important part because seeing another woman doing so much to help women’s sports, and women’s football grow, I think it’s impossible not to value that. I think it’s something very powerful.”

View image in fullscreen Mapi León hugs the Champions League trophy after Barcelona’s victory over Wolfsburg in 2023, the second of four WCL titles the defender had won with the club. Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images

The club’s signings of Putellas and León were announced five days apart in July, which prompts the question: did they discuss their decision with one another and was it a case of “If you go, I’ll go too”?

“No, not really, no. I think we take the issue of personal matters very seriously,” León says. “It’s a very different challenge. You come from a league where you win every year. Where you have achieved great things internationally and you come to a club that finished mid-table with some different challenges. And I think it is a very personal decision for each individual to make, choosing what is best for you personally.

“[You ask yourself] what do you really need right now? What is your body telling you? What do you think is best for you to keep improving, to keep pushing yourself, and to maintain that ambition? And I think each person needs different things. So, there wasn’t much communication between us. And that the decision wasn’t planned.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The more she reflects on her move, the tactical differences between Liga F and the WSL become clear as a key factor, as the Zaragoza-born defender continues: “The English league can give me a lot. You can learn a lot. The transitions, the style of play, playing with more space. The pressing is different too because I’m used to teams often sitting back in a mid-to-low block, whereas here, it’s probably more of a high press. I’d like to bring a bit of calm to the game.

“I don’t know if that really fits with English football, but no, of course, I don’t want to change the system, but simply the timings as a centre-back. I am a centre-back so I see everything. And I like to control a little bit of the timings so maybe we can try to have a little bit more of the ball. Or there are many spaces, so we can go. So I like to have a bit of control.

View image in fullscreen Mapi León is one of several big summer signings made by London City Lionesses was attracted by the competitive nature of the WSL. Photograph: Sally Rawlins/London City Lionesses

“The league is so competitive, the commitment the league is making, the clubs, I mean, I think everything makes it very attractive to come because I have been following the English league over these years and it feels like it can’t let you relax even for a second, not in any match, not during the match. Not a single second can relax you, because the English league is much more competitive.”

Her new side open the season at home to Manchester United on 4 September. Until then, she is embracing a comparatively quiet life and enjoying not being recognised in public, adding: “It’s so different [here]. It’s not a bad thing but, I can just walk to buy food, and no one recognises me! And sometimes it’s nice, because in Barcelona we are not ‘famous’ but people know us. It’s one of the many amazing things. But also sometimes you miss this freedom. Like, just go and shop.”

How long that newfound anonymity will continue is hard to tell, as it will surely not take long for León to become one of the most recognisable faces in the WSL if she can bring her form for Spain and Barcelona straight to London City Lionesses. For now, she can enjoy her beans and her crumpets in peace.

Sports.title: Farewell Cristian Romero, you actually always were ‘that type of player’ | Max Rushden
Sports.content:
“He’s not that kind of player” is perhaps the greatest of the co-commentators’ meaningless banalities. Used shortly after a “nice guy” has scythed someone in half about a day after the ball has gone, it is by definition nonsense because if you have scythed someone in half about a day after the ball has gone, then you are indeed that kind of player.

But I don’t recall ever hearing anyone saying “the thing is Clive/Brian, he is that kind of player”. I haven’t analysed every foul in Premier League history to tell if you those kinds of challenges are carried out by players all of us would consider to be “that kind of player” as opposed to the opposite – but the list of players with the most red cards suggests a pattern – Richard Dunne, Duncan Ferguson, Patrick Vieira with eight reds, Lee Cattermole and Roy Keane on seven, Vinnie Jones, Joey Barton and Alan Smith (obviously not that one) among those on six.

This article is about Cristian Romero – who I would have in tier A of “that kind of player” if I had any idea how to do one of those Instagram reels where you rank things (posh hotels you can’t afford, non weight-bearing exercises for middle-aged people, biscuits of the 80s etc). There is not a debate about the category in which he belongs.

A player with a permanent look of mild confusion about the situation he finds himself in – am I really playing for Spurs? Consistently inconsistent. And always just a moment away from just giving the whole game a Falling-Down-full-Michael-Douglas-ing.

Six red cards in his Spurs career. It feels like so many more. The one that sticks in my mind is in the Champions League last-16 exit to Milan in 2023. Hopefully you don’t remember the game, it was awful. 1-0 going into the second leg, it’s goalless in the 77th minute at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Spurs aren’t doing much. Romero’s already on a booking for lunging into Rafael Leão. And then for no apparent reason he flies into Théo Hernandez on the touchline.

It’s peak Romero. That sense that he was just a bit annoyed he wasn’t playing for someone better and so he needed a release. And in this case Hernandez was that release.

His four Premier League red cards feature all your favourites. Two yellows against Manchester City featuring a wild late tackle on Erling Haaland deep in the City half – really letting him know he was there.

There are a couple of straight red get-the-ball-really-get-the-man challenges that he probably would have got away with in 1986. One against Chelsea when Spurs were top of the league and 1-0 up early in the Ange Postecoglou tenure earned a “oh nooooo Romero, you … you … you …” from Gary Neville. The other on Casemiro last season came shortly after he criticised the club on social media prompting calls for Thomas Frank to strip him of the captaincy. It was his second red of the season after getting two yellows for dissent and kicking Ibrahima Konaté on the floor against Liverpool last December. “What’s he doing?” Neville again.

View image in fullscreen Cristian Romero is sent off at Old Trafford last season with his international defensive teammate Lisandro Martínez celebrating in the background for good measure. Photograph: James Gill/Danehouse/Getty Images

It’s often said the great defenders don’t go to ground – but it feels like that is exactly where Romero spent his entire Spurs career.

And yet. And yet – he spent most of the Europa League final win against Manchester United on the floor – hurling himself at shots, and United players, in a man-of-the-match performance. People rightly remember the Micky van de Ven goalline clearance, but Romero was unbeatable in that game. He can’t not be good. Gasperini, Scaloni, Conte, Postecoglou, Frank, Simeone all like him. He has played in two World Cup Finals (if you accept any Argentinians actually played in the last one).

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

All fans like a player who flies into challenges – we like to think we’re subtle, but we evolved from primates – one of your own putting in a reducer, an oof into the turf perhaps it takes us back somewhere deep into our past. And he scored vital goals too.

Atlético Madrid feels so perfect. The people I talk to who watch Spanish football (ie Sid Lowe once he’s actually replied to a WhatsApp) tell me Atléti aren’t the Atleti we want them to be anymore. It’s not all Godín Giménez and Juanfran. Perhaps Simeone is taking them back there. But we should all be thankful that he has arrived in his spiritual home.

As soon as the Atleti rumours began it felt perfect – it is rare for a player to feel like they fit at a club before they’ve even worn the colours. But in the same way James Maddison always looked like he should be in a Spurs shirt, perhaps Romero never did, even when he was wearing it – even when he was playing brilliantly in a gritty backs-to-the-wall job in a Europa League final. Is that really emblematic of what a Spurs centre-back should be? At their best Spurs centre-backs are Gary Mabbutt or Ledley King, Jan Vertonghen or Toby Alderweireld – solid, reliable, measured. At their worst – well there have been lots of them, but not many as rash as Romero.

It is perhaps a fault of mine, or a fault of how we watch and consume football, that I’ve already made my mind up. Watching Romero I was either annoyed by something he’d done, or annoyed that I was going to be annoyed about something he was going to do later. This permanent pre-annoyance rendered an objective judgment impossible.

So when people talk about his leadership and especially his ability on the ball, I was never totally convinced. But good luck Cristian, I get the feeling it will be much less stressful watching you play for a team I am less invested in. He might leave Spurs a club legend, it’s hard to say for sure; but if he does, he leaves as an incredibly infuriating one.

Sports.title: La Liga 2026-27 preview: Madrid look to Mourinho in bid to dethrone Barcelona
Sports.content:
A lot has changed since José Mourinho was last appointed Real Madrid manager, but a lot has also not changed. Before his first game in charge in 2010, Spain had just become world champions, their extra-time winner in the final scored by a Barcelona player after their opponents, who had been reduced to 10 men, had tried to kick them off the park. Like then, Mourinho’s task is to take down a Barcelona team that have won two La Liga titles in succession. And like then, he has a host of world-class talent at his disposal.

Florentino Pérez is also still around – and he is largely the reason why Mourinho is back. After the chief executive, José Ángel Sánchez, was said to have led the charge to appoint Xabi Alonso last summer, the 79-year-old club president has made the decision his own this time. He promised Mourinho, who won La Liga with 100 points in his first spell, would return if he was re-elected in snap elections in June and the announcement came, in true Pérez style, on the opening day of the World Cup.

Jorge Valdano, the former Madrid player and manager who worked upstairs during Mourinho’s first tenure, was of the opinion that a lot has indeed changed since then. “Almost 15 years have passed: football is no longer the same, society is not the same, Florentino is no longer the same, and Mourinho certainly won’t be either,” he told A Bola.

View image in fullscreen It was champagne all round at Real Madrid at Christmas of 2012. But by the end of that season, José Mourinho had left, after having public rows with both Iker Casillas (left) and Sergio Ramos (second left). Photograph: Ángel Martínez/Real Madrid/Getty Images

But Mourinho was the outstanding law-and-order candidate. Even after Alonso’s sacking last January, Madrid’s season continued its descent into chaos under Álvaro Arbeloa. In May, Federico Valverde was taken to hospital for stitches after a bust-up with his teammate Aurélien Tchouaméni. A few days later, Madrid conceded the league title in the clásico and would finish the campaign trophyless. By then an online petition calling for Kylian Mbappé to leave had reached 30 million signatures. Speculation about the future of Vinícius Júnior, who had 12 months left on his contract, would not go away.

Not everything has gone right since – a £129m bid for Julián Álvarez was turned down by Atlético Madrid, while Barcelona look more likely to sign Rodri from Manchester City – but Madrid’s preparations for the new campaign have exuded an air of calm. Mourinho began work a month before his contract started and has not had an official unveiling in front of the media. “It’s not about working at Real Madrid, it is working for Real Madrid,” he said sternly in a short in-house interview at the start of pre-season. The soundbites are limited to his new Netflix documentary. There has been no globetrotting summer tour either; just a series of low-key friendlies across Europe.

Perhaps most importantly, after all that Arsenal talk, Vinícius has signed a new six-year deal. “Vinícius has become one of the most important players in one of the most successful periods in our history,” the club said. Mourinho will have to find a system that gets the best out of him, Mbappé and Jude Bellingham, not to mention a new galáctico, the £115m winger Yan Diomandé, who was playing across town for Leganés B in Spain’s fifth tier only last year.

View image in fullscreen Yan Diomandé caught the eye at the World Cup, and has now become the most expensive player in Real Madrid’s history. Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty Images

Diomandé made his Leganés first-team debut at the Bernabéu in March 2025. “Who makes their debut at 18 against Real Madrid? It was a dream. And then it was a nightmare,” Diomandé wrote in the Players’ Tribune this summer, while he was shining for Côte d’Ivoire at the World Cup, in a raw and emotional article dedicated to his sister Roxane, who died aged 15 after her drink was spiked at a party, just weeks after her brother’s La Liga debut.

Supporting Diomandé and Vinícius down the left wing will be Marc Cucurella who, along with Bernardo Silva, Ibrahima Konaté, Denzel Dumfries and the 6ft 4in striker Carlos Espí, are all signings that should adapt easily to Mourinho’s coaching. But of all the star quality on the pitch, it is the Portuguese coach who will attract the most attention.

By landing the Real Madrid job again, Mourinho has staged a comeback few expected after his later struggles in the Premier League and a tour of Europe that delivered mixed results. His orchestrating of Benfica’s remarkable Champions League escape against Madrid last season, with the goalkeeper Anatoliy Trubin’s late goal, thrust him back into the spotlight. But his disappointing comments after Vinícius accused Benfica’s Gianluca Prestianni of racist abuse – Prestianni was ultimately banned by Uefa for “homophobic conduct” – were criticised by Kick It Out as “a form of gaslighting”. “Mourinho is Mourinho,” said Arbeloa.

View image in fullscreen It looked unlikely at points last season and even this summer, but Vinícius Junior has signed a new long-term contract at Real Madrid. Photograph: Bernadett Szabó/Reuters

After returning for pre-season, Vinícius said: “It has gone very well, getting to know the new coach … Mourinho wants me to be as I have always been: happy, cheerful and playing my football.” There has been no suggestion of any lingering bad blood.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is not only Mourinho who is returning to La Liga after a lengthy absence. Racing Santander are back for the first time since 2012 and have welcomed back one of their own in Sergio Canales, now 35, who left aged 19 to join Mourinho’s Real Madrid in that summer of 2010. “I’m still struggling to believe this is real,” the midfielder said last month. Deportivo and Málaga also return to La Liga for the first time since 2018 having both dropped to the third tier in that time. Depor’s marquee signing has been a 37-year-old Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang.

Diego Simeone, beginning his 15th full season in charge of Atlético, reunites with Mourinho in the dugout for the Madrid derby. Atlético have started life after Antoine Griezmann with investment in their squad that has included signing Lee Kang-in from Paris Saint-Germain and giving him Griezmann’s No 7 shirt. Manuel Pellegrini, Mourinho’s predecessor in his first spell at the Bernabéu, remains in charge of Real Betis while Villarreal, the other of Spain’s five clubs in the Champions League this season, have appointed Iñigo Pérez after his feats at Rayo Vallecano.

View image in fullscreen Diego Simeone took Atlético Madrid to the Champions League semi-finals, but his team finished third in La Liga, 22 points off the champions, Barcelona. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Pellegrino Matarazzo, the American in charge of Real Sociedad, will be looking to build on the club’s Copa del Rey triumph in April. The other hotseat in the Basque Country, at Athletic Club, is occupied by a German for the first time since Jupp Heynckes in 2003. “Athletic is the only club where a handshake is more important than a signature,” Heynckes told the new man, Edin Terzic, before he took the job.

It is Barcelona, though, who remain favourites for the title. Like Griezmann, Robert Lewandowski has departed for Major League Soccer in the US, and there is still a gap up front while Atlético stand firm on Álvarez. Anthony Gordon has replaced Marcus Rashford to fight for a place with the injury-prone Raphinha on the left wing, but, with respect to Karim Adeyemi, there is no real competition on the other flank. Lamine Yamal did not take the World Cup by storm as many expected but he has returned from America as a world champion and, let’s remember, a 19-year-old. He will probably be the ringleader once more if Hansi Flick is to match Pep Guardiola’s achievement of three successive league titles. The first clásico is at the Camp Nou at the end of October.

View image in fullscreen Barcelona have won the last two La Liga titles, sealing last season’s against Real Madrid, who they finished eight points clear of at the top of the table. Photograph: Joan Monfort/AP

Unlike Europe’s other major leagues, La Liga is staggering the start of its new season. Owing to their players’ involvement in the later stages of the extended World Cup, none of Madrid, Barcelona and Atlético are in action on the opening weekend. The league’s president, Javier Tebas, is one of Gianni Infantino’s loudest critics and said on Sunday that the Fifa president’s projects are “destroying” the national leagues. All this means José Bordalás’s Getafe, soon embarking on a European campaign, will raise the curtain at Quique Sánchez Flores’s Alavés on Saturday evening – what more could you ask for?

Sports.title: Liverpool owner FSG seals £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff Bezos
Sports.content:
Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, has confirmed it has agreed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin. The deal is understood to be worth £1.65bn, valuing Liverpool at £5.5bn, and will see Bhatia become the club’s new vice-chair on an expanded board.

Bhatia, the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, initiated and led talks with FSG on behalf of the 1892 Holdings consortium, a reference to Liverpool’s founding year. The former co-owner of Queens Park Rangers has received financial backing from the Mittal Family Trust, the K5 Sports fund, of which Bezos is the lead investor, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Eduardo Saverin.

Elaine Saverin, wife of Eduardo, and Bryan Baum, co-founder and managing partner of K5 Global, will also join the Liverpool board. Bezos is considered a passive investor and will not have a seat on the board.

Despite the involvement of Bezos, the third richest man in the world with $272bn (£201bn), Eduardo Saverin, worth an estimated $33bn and the Mittal family, worth around $17bn, FSG will remain in operational control of Liverpool as well as majority owners. 1892 Holdings’ investment remains subject to regulatory approval, which could take up to 90 days, and will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. There is also no change to the leadership or day-to-day running of Liverpool.

FSG insist the deal is not part of an exit strategy from a club they acquired in 2010 for £300m after the near-ruinous ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett. The transaction does not compel FSG to sell more of the club to 1892 at a future date, or include obligations for 1892 to increase their stake, but it does give Bhatia’s consortium options to purchase more of Liverpool should the majority owners eventually decide to sell.

It is the makeup of Bhatia’s consortium, rather than any financial need, that FSG claim attracted them to the British-Indian businessman’s proposal. The FSG leadership team of principal owner John W Henry, chair Tom Werner and president Mike Gordon have spent almost a year getting to know Bhatia and believe the deal will create further opportunities for Liverpool in global business, technology and investment, including in the important markets of India and Asia.

View image in fullscreen The sale will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Gordon, who has resumed a more hands-on role at Liverpool following the departure of Michael Edwards as chief executive of football at FSG, said: “Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club’s long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world.

“As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special. Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together.”

With Premier League and Uefa financial regulations linking a club’s spending to turnover, the new investment will not have an immediate benefit for head coach Andoni Iraola and his Liverpool team. However, the commercial opportunities presented by the involvement of Bezos, Bhatia and Saverin will enable the Anfield club to grow their annual revenue significantly. Liverpool’s annual revenue increased to a record £703m in the year ending May 2025.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Speaking on behalf of 1892 Holdings, Bhatia said: “We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield.

“To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club’s continued success for years to come.”

Bhatia was involved in QPR for almost 19 years and took on numerous roles, from chair of the club to chair of the club’s community trust, until transferring his shareholding in July. He is likely to have a more visible presence at Anfield than fellow members of his consortium or FSG.

Sports.title: Raúl Jiménez’s injury-time penalty salvages point for Wolves against Blackburn
Sports.content:
Raúl Jiménez marked his return to Wolves with the stoppage-time equaliser that saved them from an embarrassing start to their return to the Championship. The Mexico striker, who scored against England during the World Cup, came off the bench to convert a penalty given for handball by Ryan Alebiosu that would have had VAR questioning whether the defender was in the area when Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross struck his arm.

One minor consolation from Wolves’ relegation is that the video assistant referee is no longer their problem. Jiménez, who had bought scarves for all supporters in the South Bank in gratitude for their welcome home, tucked away his first goal in this second spell for the club he graced during their recent heyday before leaving for Fulham.

“He’s an important striker,” César Peixoto, Wolves’ new head coach said. “He lives for scoring and making goals. Raúl is a key player for us. He helped the team inside and outside the pitch but we have to go slowly with him because he is 35 years old and comes back from the World Cup. We want him to stay good and scoring for us is good for him and for the team.”

Goals from Sean McLoughlin and Andri Gudjohnsen allowed Blackburn to provide Wolves with a reality check after Marshall Munetsi had scored early. Confidence is a fragile commodity and, after their decision to replace Rob Edwards with a manager with no experience of English football, the Wolves board know that their supporters’ patience is thin. Leading Gil Vicente to sixth place in the Portuguese first division does not make Peixoto a guaranteed winner.

Conceding the equaliser, through Jiménez’s first goal for Wolves in 1,311 days, denied unfancied Blackburn a deserved victory after Wolves lost their shape. Tony Mowbray, their head coach, felt the penalty decision was harsh. “I’ve just been shown an angle by my analyst where he [Alebiosu] is outside the box; another angle I’m told shows he’s just inside the box. I just felt like more and more decisions were starting to sway their way,” the former West Brom manager said. “It’s harsh to take because I don’t think they deserved that second goal.”

Molineux was awash with fading golden sunlight and rising optimism at kick-off. A summer that started with such a surprising managerial departure was promising to end with renewed faith in the team’s direction of travel, until Peixoto’s admired high press came unstuck as his team started to “play with their hearts more than their heads”.

View image in fullscreen Marshall Munetsi (right) celebrates scoring Woves’ first goal with Fer López. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

The Blackburn defence had split generously to allow Munetsi a clean run through on to Fer López’s sumptuous pass. The left-footed finish from the Zimbabwean, himself coming back to Molineux after a loan at Paris FC, strengthened the feelgood factor.

Peixoto’s tactics do currently lead to gaps on transition. Blackburn, who have not done so much in the transfer market to suggest they should aim higher than last season’s 20th place, got behind Wolves on several occasions. It was no great surprise when, from Ryoya Morishita’s superb right-wing cross, McLoughlin headed beyond Dan Bentley to equalise.

Some of Wolves’ best business this summer has been bringing players back to Molineux. While Jiménez started the night on the bench, after a late start to pre-season following his impressive World Cup for Mexico, López was the classiest player on view. Back from a loan at Celta Vigo, he has been invited to make the No 10 position his own, and the Spaniard nearly regained Wolves the lead only to curl his shot wide.

View image in fullscreen Blackburn’s Andri Gudjohnsen gives his side a 2-1 lead early in the second half. Photograph: Simon Davies/ProSports/Shutterstock

Blackburn continued to benefit from Wolves’ soft centre however. Oladapo Afolayan’s shot needed tipping over by Bentley before the right winger again got space down Wolves’ left – where David Møller Wolfe, in for the injured Hugo Bueno, showed he is still not match fit after his World Cup endeavours with Norway – to cross for Gudjohnsen to turn in Rovers’ second goal. “The team lost some organisation and played with their heart rather than their head and brains,” Peixoto said. “It’s a lesson for us in the future, we need to stay with mental stability for the 90 minutes.”

By the hour mark, the South Bank were swirling their Jiménez scarves above their heads and chanting “Si Señor” in honour of the veteran striker who was such an esteemed figure at Molineux for five of the club’s best years in modern times. Before his horrific head injury, he was the pivotal attacking player as Nuno Espírito Santo’s team reached the later stages of the FA Cup and Europa League. The scene was set for the Mexican. Could he deliver? Si, señor.

Sports.title: ‘Not going to be an issue’: Mikel Arteta relaxed about Arsenal contract situation
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has said he is relaxed about his Arsenal contract expiring at the end of the new season and believes his side will need to be better than last year to defend their title successfully.

The Premier League champions will face Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City in the Community Shield in Cardiff on Sunday and are heavy favourites to win back-to-back league titles for the first time since the 1930s. The departure of Pep Guardiola from their traditional rivals City means Arteta is now the Premier League’s longest-serving manager, with the Spaniard having joined in December 2019.

He signed a three-year contract extension in September 2024 after Arsenal finished as runners-up to City and had been expected to agree a new deal over the summer that would make him one of the highest-paid managers in the world. Arteta acknowledged on Friday that his priorities have been elsewhere this summer as he attempts to strengthen his squad before the new season but reassured supporters that he is fully committed to the club.

“They don’t have to worry about any of that, because I want to be here. I am extremely happy. I feel very grateful to work with the people that I work with and when we have the possibility, we will resolve that. And that’s it,” he said.

Asked if he expects talks over a new contract to continue after the transfer window, Arteta added: “There is always another priority, I think. And that’s the way we have been treating it, I think because everybody feels comfortable that the time on the contract is not going to be an issue. I think because my will, certainly, is to be here and I am very happy here. My feeling from the club is the same one. That is why everyone is doing things in a really organic way.”

Arsenal have opened negotiations with Bayer Leverkusen over a move for Jarell Quansah as they seek cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber, while they are still in the market for another attacker if they can offload Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus. After missing out on Vinícius Júnior when the Brazil forward opted to sign a new deal with Real Madrid, Arteta defended Arsenal’s strategy this summer and is hoping that they can still add to their squad.

“I am really happy with the squad, the players that I have and I am really happy with the ambition of the club. There is zero question about that. We have shown that in the manner we have tried to act,” he said.

“But I think we need to do it our own way. We have super strengths and we have other areas we need to be very conscious [of] because we don’t have the elements or the structure that other clubs have. We need to do it our way. We are always on it that way and we will do what we believe is the right thing to do. To have the best possibility to compete in every competition that’s for sure.”

Arteta added: “We’re going to prepare to elevate our level, expecting that the rest will do the same. That’s traditionally what happened in the league in the last few years, and that’s the way we have planned the season, and the way we want to evolve the team.”

Sports.title: Crystal Palace complete £21m signing of full back Anan Khalaili, while Southampton reject Benfica's opening bid for Harwood-Bellis: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period as clubs look to make big signings ahead of the new season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

Benfica offer for Harwood-Bellis rejected

Southampton have rejected a £17.5million offer from Benfica for defender Taylor Harwood-Bellis.

The Portuguese side, coached by Marco Silva, turned to the 24-year-old after initial interest in Chelsea's Tosin Adarabioyo who wants to stay at Stamford Bridge.

Benfica are considering an improved offer with Harwood-Bellis interested in the move.

Benfica are considering an improved offer for Saints' Harwood-Bellis after having their initial bid of £17.5million rejected, while the 24-year-old is interested in the move

Eagles sign £21m right back Khalaili

Crystal Palace have completed the £21million signing of Union Saint-Gilloise full-back Anan Khalaili.

Khalaili's move to Inter Milan fell through earlier this summer over a health issue, but he passed his medical with Palace last weekend.

The 21-year-old is being brought in to provide competition for Daniel Munoz at right wing-back.

However, there is no guarantee that the £20m-rated Colombian will stay beyond this summer amid interest from the likes of Tottenham and Everton. He has two years left on his deal.

Khalaili, who has won 16 caps for Israel, said: 'I'm happy to be here, I'm excited, and I can't wait to start.

'I’ve followed the Premier League. It's a new challenge for me, and I've followed Crystal Palace for a long time. I'm happy to be here.'

Khalaili's move to Inter Milan fell through earlier this summer over a health issue, but he passed his medical with Palace last weekend

The deal is worth £2.9m guaranteed, plus add-ons and a 10 per cent sell-on clause.

'I’m really happy to have this experience. I got a chance to play in the Champions League, Serie A and Ligue 1.

'I've learned a lot and I’m really happy to put this experience on the pitch in the Premier League. The Premier League is the dream of all footballers. Now, I have a chance to play in the Premier League, so I am excited to play.'
