World.title: International Youth Day 2026 Unites Young African Leaders Around Common Aspirations
World.content:
Cllr. Charlyne M. Brumskine, Judge of the ECOWAS Court served as a special guest.

On August 12, 2026, over 100 young political and civic leaders from across Africa gathered for a two-hour hybrid celebration of International Youth Day under the theme, “Different Contexts, Common Aspirations.”

Hosted by Naymote Partners for Democratic Development and the Young Political Leadership School Africa (YPLS Africa), in collaboration with the African Democratic Alliance for Freedom and Progress (ADAFP), the event was broadcast live from the Democracy Innovation Hub in Monrovia, Liberia. More than 100 participants joined online, while 12 attended in person.

Opening the program, Eddie D. Jarwolo, Executive Director of Naymote and Secretary-General of ADAFP, emphasized the importance of creating opportunities for young Africans to connect, exchange experiences, and actively shape the continent’s future.

Hon. Nobuntu Hlazo-Webster, Deputy President of Build One South Africa and Member of the South African Parliament, offered practical insights on youth representation and leadership in democratic institutions. She challenged participants to recognize their power and responsibility:

“Nobody is coming to save you but you. You have so much power and resources at your disposal. I encourage you to leverage that power to change our continent.”

Alphia Faith Kemokai, Manager of YPLS Africa and Global Democracy Fellow, shared lessons from her work with emerging political and civic leaders across the continent, while YPLS Africa alumna Kadiatu Koroma spoke on “Values That Count Across Different Contexts: Leading Toward Our Common Aspirations.”

Special Guest Cllr. Charlyne M. Brumskine, Judge of the ECOWAS Court of Justice and former vice-presidential candidate of Liberia, encouraged participants to translate their aspirations into purposeful leadership, integrity, civic responsibility, and practical action. She declared:

“To every young person who boards a boat, gets on an airplane to another country, or crosses boundaries, there is a verdict on my leadership and on your leadership. Your charge is to make staying in Africa an act of opportunity, not an act of sacrifice.”

Moderated by Cameroonian media practitioner and YPLS Africa alumna Njix Sharon Nabeseh, the discussion examined the diverse political, social, and economic realities confronting young Africans. Participants identified the aspirations that unite them with dignity, opportunity, inclusion, economic security, accountable leadership, and meaningful participation in shaping their countries and continent.

The event also strengthened engagement with the emerging Continental Young Forum of Political Parties, a platform created to unit young members of political parties across Africa, an initiative of ADAFP and YPLS Africa that connects young political leaders across national, institutional, and partisan boundaries.

Through interactive discussions, participants exchanged experiences, raised questions, and explored opportunities for cross-border learning, networking, and collaboration.

The celebration reaffirmed a clear message: Africa’s young people may live in different contexts, but they share common aspirations and a collective responsibility to shape the continent’s future.

Different Contexts. Common Aspirations. One Generation. One Africa.

World.title: Liberia: Prophet Key Walks Free, Says Prison Experience Rehabilitated Him After Six-Month Contempt Sentence
World.content:
MONROVIA — Justin Oldpa Yeazehn, popularly known as “Prophet Key,” has regained his freedom after spending six months at the Monrovia Central Prison following a contempt conviction by the Supreme Court of Liberia.

By Webster Clayeh

Upon his release, Prophet Key said his time behind bars had changed him, describing the experience as a period of rehabilitation and personal transformation.

He also indicated that he had been relocated following his release, suggesting that his return to society would be accompanied by a deliberate effort to distance himself from some of the circumstances and conduct that preceded his imprisonment.

His release brings to an end one of the most closely followed contempt cases involving a Liberian social media personality in recent years. The case attracted widespread public attention after the Supreme Court took action against Yeazehn over statements made against Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay, members of the judiciary and the Chief Justice’s mother.

The Supreme Court sentenced Yeazehn on February 13, 2026, after he appeared before the Full Bench and admitted wrongdoing while appealing to the justices for mercy.

The Court found his conduct contemptuous and damaging to the dignity and authority of the judiciary. Its official record says the proceedings arose from a podcast in which Yeazehn accused the Chief Justice and Associate Justices of corruption and directed derogatory and vulgar remarks at the judiciary.

The sentence was not limited to imprisonment. The Court also ordered Prophet Key to publish an apology in three local newspapers for five consecutive days and to execute a bond committing himself to refrain from the kind of insulting and inflammatory language that had brought him before the Court.

Reports on the judgment said the apology was directed to the Chief Justice, Associate Justices, judges, magistrates and the judiciary generally, as well as Liberian women whom he had previously insulted.

In the months that followed, the controversial social media personality appeared to move from confrontation to contrition. A handwritten apology dated July 28 surfaced publicly in early August, in which he expressed regret for accusing members of the judiciary of corruption without proof. He also apologized to Liberian women for his offensive remarks and pledged not to repeat such conduct.

That apology became an important part of the public narrative surrounding his anticipated release. While supporters focused on the expiration of the six-month custodial sentence, questions emerged over whether every requirement attached to the Supreme Court’s judgment had been satisfied and whether the prison authorities had received the necessary legal authorization to release him.

Although August 13 had widely been identified as the date on which Prophet Key would complete his six-month sentence, he did not walk out of the Monrovia Central Prison that day.

The delay was linked to the fact that his imprisonment originated directly from an order of the Supreme Court. Current reports indicate that the prison authorities were awaiting a formal release order from the Court before they could discharge him. In other words, the expiration of the custodial period did not, by itself, result in an immediate physical release because the institution holding him required the appropriate judicial authorization.

That distinction became the center of public debate on August 13, with supporters gathering around the prison expecting his release while the necessary documentation had apparently not yet reached the correctional authorities. Reports later indicated that the Supreme Court issued the release order on August 14, clearing the way for his departure from custody.

World.title: Liberia: President Boakai Signs Port Decentralization Bill in Middle of Biggest Drug Crisis
World.content:
A year ago, the Liberian president said breaking up Liberia’s ports would risk the country’s maritime security. This week, with a mystery vessel case still unresolved and a cocaine scandal reaching his own drug chief, he signed the bill anyway — and left the question of who’s watching the new ports unanswered.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – President Joseph Boakai has signed into law the legislation dismantling the National Port Authority’s decades-long monopoly, ending centralized control of Liberia’s ports and handing operational power to autonomous boards in Monrovia, Buchanan, Greenville and Harper under a newly created Independent Seaport and Inland Ports Regulatory Authority.

What is not yet clear is whether the final law includes the safeguards needed to keep four newly independent ports from becoming easier targets for drug traffickers than the single, centralized system it replaces.

The President had twice vetoed earlier versions of this legislation, citing legal conflicts, overlapping regulatory mandates, and risks to Liberia’s international maritime security obligations; the Senate responded by revising and repassing the bill, and the president has now signed the revised version. The timing is difficult to overstate: the signing comes as Liberia remains consumed by its largest drug scandal in years, one that has already produced a record $317 million cocaine seizure, criminal charges against an LDEA officer and a Paynesville bar owner, the recusal of the LDEA’s own acting chief over an unresolved vehicle allegation, and months of unanswered questions about a mystery vessel, the IB Atlantic IV, that first exposed how little visibility Liberia’s port and maritime system has over what moves through it.

A Reversal, Not Just a Signature

Somewhere in the Executive Mansion this week, a pen crossed a line the president himself drew twice before. That is what makes this signing newsworthy — not simply that a major piece of legislation became law, but that the man signing it is the same man who, on two separate occasions, told the Legislature in writing that it was not ready to pass. Boakai’s earlier vetoes of the port decentralization and autonomy bills were not procedural throat-clearing. He cited legal conflicts between the new port boards and existing regulatory bodies, overlapping mandates that risked institutional confusion, fragmentation of executive oversight, and — most pointedly, given everything that has happened since — risks to Liberia’s international maritime security obligations. Those were not small concerns when he raised them, and nothing about the summer that followed made them smaller. What changed, in the end, was not the risk. It was the political weather around it — enough pressure to pass some version of port reform that it eventually outweighed the president’s own stated reservations, at least enough to move his hand to the page.

An Eighteen-Month Runway

Two details emerged after the signing that reshape, without resolving, the questions surrounding it. The Minister of State, Samuel A. Stevequoah, confirmed to FrontPageAfrica that President Boakai signed the bill on the advice of the Minister of Justice — a detail that matters given the Justice Ministry’s own past warnings about the legislation’s legal conflicts, and one that suggests the administration’s internal legal objections were addressed, or at least set aside, before the president put pen to paper.

FrontPageAfrica has also confirmed that the legislation carries an 18-month transitional clause, meaning the new decentralized port structure will not actually take effect until 2028. That transition period cuts two ways, and which way it ultimately cuts is now the real story. Read generously, an 18-month runway is exactly the kind of window FrontPageAfrica previously argued was missing from the original, undelayed version of the bill — time to build a unified maritime security and counternarcotics framework before four independent ports go live, rather than discovering the gaps after the fact. Read skeptically, an 18-month delay is also a convenient way to defuse the immediate political pressure of signing security-sensitive legislation in the middle of a cocaine scandal, without requiring the administration to specify, today, what it plans to do with the time. Nothing announced alongside the signing indicates which of those two readings is closer to the truth. The next 18 months, not this week’s signature, will settle it.

What the Law Actually Does

The legislation ends the National Port Authority’s roughly 70-year monopoly over Liberia’s seaports, replacing centralized control with autonomous, county-based port boards responsible for the Freeport of Monrovia and the ports of Buchanan, Greenville and Harper. Overseeing the new structure is an Independent Seaport and Inland Ports Regulatory Authority, intended to regulate the newly decentralized system rather than run it directly. Supporters have framed the change as a long-overdue correction to decades of Monrovia-centered control that left Liberia’s secondary ports starved of investment and local say over infrastructure sitting in their own backyards — a legitimate grievance this newspaper has acknowledged even while warning against the timing of this fix.

The Missing Safety Net

Here is the question nobody in Monrovia seems eager to answer out loud, and it happens to be the one that matters most given the year Liberia has just had: does the final version of this law include anything resembling a unified maritime security and counter-narcotics framework spanning all four newly independent ports, or does security oversight now sit as fragmented as everything else the bill decentralizes? Neither the legislative history nor the president’s own remarks upon signing, as reported so far, make that clear one way or the other. A port system split four ways multiplies the number of doors traffickers can walk through, and multiplies the number of agencies each with a plausible-sounding answer for why detecting the next shipment wasn’t quite their job — precisely the dynamic this newspaper warned about when it urged caution on this bill last month, before the president had signed it and before the IB Atlantic IV had become a household name in Liberia’s drug scandal.

The mystery vessel case is not incidental background here; it is the clearest evidence available that Liberia’s current, centralized port and maritime security apparatus already struggles to answer basic questions about what is moving through its own waters. A ship sat off Liberia’s coast for the better part of a week before anyone acted, tied by a rejected letter to a now-dismissed RIA official, eventually chased by AFL boats that turned out to be too small to catch it once it ran for open water. If a single, centralized system produced that outcome, the burden was always on this bill’s supporters to explain, convincingly and in public, why four separate, newly formed authorities would do better rather than worse. Nobody has offered that explanation yet, at least not one this newspaper has been able to find.

Signed Amid the Worst Possible Timing

Whatever the merits of port decentralization as policy, the timing of this signature could hardly have landed at a more uncomfortable moment. Liberia is currently working through the fallout of a record $317 million cocaine seizure in Duazon, on top of a $19.2 million bust at Roberts International Airport in June. LDEA officer Moses Jallah and Paynesville bar owner George Harris are facing prosecution. The LDEA’s own Officer-in-Charge, Fitzgerald Biago, has recused himself from the investigation amid allegations he accepted vehicles from a bar owner tied to the case, with President Boakai personally giving the Minister of Justice 48 hours to report on the matter. Senator Amara Konneh has taken to calling the whole affair “Cocainegate.” Signing a bill that fragments port oversight into four pieces, in the middle of a scandal that has repeatedly exposed how poorly Liberia’s existing, unified institutions have policed themselves, is the kind of decision that will be read by critics as tone-deaf regardless of the bill’s underlying merits — and the administration has offered little public messaging so far to counter that reading.

What Critics Warned

Opposition to the bill was neither quiet nor limited to the presidency. Representative Musa Hassan Bility condemned the Legislature’s handling of the reform, calling the Port Autonomy Law “improper” and “dangerous.” The head of the Liberia Revenue Authority separately urged Boakai to reject the bill again, warning of revenue risks and unresolved legal conflicts between the new port authorities and existing agencies. Those warnings were about institutional and fiscal risk more than security specifically, but they reinforce the same underlying picture: a piece of legislation that even before its security implications are considered, drew sustained warnings from officials inside the government about how much this reform could go wrong in the execution.

The Question Nobody’s Answered

None of this means port decentralization was the wrong idea in principle, and FrontPageAfrica has said as much before. Buchanan, Greenville and Harper have real grievances about decades of Monrovia-centered control, and those grievances deserve a serious legislative answer eventually. But “eventually” and “in the middle of the country’s worst drug scandal in years, with the underlying security gaps still unaddressed” are not the same moment, and the president’s own vetoes once made exactly that argument. What Liberians deserve now, at minimum, is a clear public accounting from the administration of what changed between the version Boakai rejected and the version he signed — specifically, what safeguards, if any, will exist by 2028 to keep four independent ports from being four times as vulnerable as the single system that just spent a summer failing to catch a ship sitting in plain view off its own coast. The 18-month transition period is, in effect, the administration’s own self-imposed deadline for answering that question. Until it does, the safest assumption is the least reassuring one: that the law changed, and the vulnerability it was meant to address is being left for 2028 to sort out.

World.title: How a Liberia “Cartel” Took a 71-Year-old Canadian $100k
World.content:
A Canadian retiree’s search for African gold turned into a months-long con involving fake shipping companies, a phony “minister,” strongbox theater, and a scheme so elaborate he compares it to “an academy award performance.”

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – Gerry Pettle wants one thing understood before anything else: he isn’t writing to embarrass himself.



“I am writing you on the advice of two friends of your country,” the 71-year-old Canadian says in a note to FrontPageAfrica explaining why he’s going public, “and not necessarily in agreement to make this complaint a public humiliation of myself.” He calls himself “a Canadian, born young fellow at the age of 71” — a wry touch from a man who, by his own account, was taken for more than $100,000 USD by a network of scammers in Liberia over the course of several months this year.

It started, as these things often do, with a friend of a friend.



A Favor from Sam



Pettle knew a man named Sam Berkel, who in turn knew a man named Paul — a Liberian expatriate originally from Toronto. Paul, Sam said, had a way to get gold out of Liberia. Pettle now calls it what it was: “a scheme.” At the time, he had no reason to doubt it.



Paul asked Pettle and Sam for $20,000 to secure a shipment of gold he’d bring back to Toronto himself. The two split the cost and wired the money in installments — a few thousand dollars a day, spread out to avoid suspicion. The gold never arrived. Paul never flew back. When Pettle finally reached him, the excuses began: a delay, then another delay, then the claim that Paul himself had been robbed — the gold and the money “switched” out from under him by unnamed thieves.



It should have ended there. It didn’t.



The Dubai Pitch



A week later, Paul had a new plan: he’d have a kilo of gold worked into jewelry and meet Pettle in Dubai, where Pettle could collect it, pay off the man Paul supposedly owed, and recoup his original $20,000 plus a profit. The cost of entry this time was smaller — $3,500 for airfare and jewelry-making — but the outcome was the same. The money vanished. So, for a while, did Paul.



When Paul resurfaced, he offered something even more improbable: a stranger claiming to have millions in marked American cash that needed “washing” for a fee. Pettle refused outright. “Paul, F off,” he recalls telling him. “You’re mental.”



Two days later, Paul was back on the phone with yet another connection — a man with a diplomatic passport, capable of moving gold across borders without permits. Paul said he didn’t trust the man directly but knew someone who did: a fixer who went by “Boylan,” whose real name, Pettle later learned, was Jensen Gonkarnue.



Boylan, Peter, and the Compound



Jensen — “Boylan” — called Pettle personally, addressing him warmly as “Doc.” He vouched for a Liberian gold trader named Peter John, describing a house near the residence of Liberia’s president as proof of legitimacy. On a call, Peter told Pettle he had hundreds of kilos of gold sourced from local miners and sent a photograph appearing to show roughly a thousand kilos stacked on a floor. All Pettle had to do, Peter said, was cover the shipping tax.



It was the first of many taxes.



Pettle sent $12,500 by USDT for the initial tax. Then came a $14,500 charge for air freight and insurance to a company calling itself Noble Shipping — complete with an invoice and a bank routing number, giving Pettle, for the first time, something resembling a paper trail. He and a new partner, Robert, paid it. The package, he was told, was on its way.



It was around this time a second trader, a man named Ben, contacted Pettle claiming to have five kilos of his own gold and to have heard of Pettle’s reputation through a woman named Bernice. A pattern was forming — taxes, shipping fees, insurance, one new stranger after another — but Pettle, already deep in, kept going.

Flying to Liberia



By the time Pettle boarded a flight to Liberia in June, he had lost thousands and gained nothing but promises. He was met at the airport by Boylan, carrying a single assayed kilo of gold as “collateral” against the money already spent.



The next day brought a scene Pettle still describes in almost cinematic terms: a drive down a rough, barely marked road to a barbed-wire compound, a honked horn, a gate that opened and closed behind the car, a second gate, and finally a run-down exterior giving way to a surprisingly polished interior — televisions, desks, a busy office floor.



There, in the office of a man identified only as “Mr. Hill,” security guards produced strongboxes belonging to Peter and Ben. Each man opened his own box with his own key, revealing, Pettle says, ten kilos in one and thirty in the other. Then two more men — introduced as Moses and Patrick — arrived unannounced with five kilos of their own.



Pettle agreed to take five kilos total, combined from all three sources, with Peter — who held a diplomatic passport — set to fly back to Canada with him and the gold. The running total by then was roughly $68,000.



Then came the final charges: $6,000 to expedite an “expired” export license, and additional tax for the extra kilos, bringing the total to nearly $29,000 more. Robert wired it. Everyone, Pettle recalls, seemed satisfied when the meeting ended.



The Passport Standoff



Afterward, Peter asked for the one kilo Pettle was still holding as collateral. Pettle refused — it was the only tangible thing he had for his money. He offered a trade instead: the gold for Peter’s passport, so that if he’d been cheated, he’d at least have a photograph to bring to authorities. Peter refused and left angrily.



Days later, a man named Elijah Teahjay — who Pettle says “looked the most legitimate” of everyone he’d met — invited him to a second compound, even more polished than the first, complete with flags and a formal reception area. There, armed guards wheeled in a case holding what Pettle estimates was 300 kilos of gold and told him to take his pick. The new deal: $24,000 up front, $110,000 per kilo on delivery in Canada, payable within 72 hours. The gold, Elijah assured him, would simply be handed to him after customs. “We do it all the time,” he said.



The Man in the Yellow Shirt



The unraveling began with a knock at Pettle’s hotel room door. A representative from Noble Shipping arrived unannounced with an official-looking export license and a new tax bill — $21,000, then, minutes later, a second bill for $27,500. When Pettle tried to photograph the documents, the man blocked his camera, insisting they weren’t his to keep, even though he’d paid for them.



Suspicious, Pettle called Elijah and sent him a photo of the receipt, threatening to involve police if it wasn’t legitimate. Within minutes, a large man in a yellow shirt appeared at the hotel, identifying himself as “Todd” — Liberia’s minister of minerals, he claimed, though he carried no badge, only a worn business card.



What followed, Pettle says, played out “like the end of a lousy movie”: Todd confronted the Noble Shipping representative in front of him, questioned him about the missing export license, and asked Pettle to get into a car. Pettle refused to get in fully, kept one foot on the pavement, and agreed only to meet again the next morning. Within minutes of that encounter ending, his phone lit up with calls from what felt like a dozen different people connected to the scheme, all anxious to know why he’d mentioned police.



Getting Out



By his final night in Liberia, Pettle believed he might be in real danger. As far as the network knew, he’d genuinely gone to authorities. A woman named Grace — another gold contact who’d surfaced days earlier — offered to come collect him from the hotel. He nearly accepted, then reconsidered: if Grace was part of the same web, leaving with her might not be safe either. Instead, a hotel worker moved him quietly to a different room for the night. He slept, and the next morning, he left the country.



An Unlikely Postscript



Pettle did file a report with local police — six officers, he says, took his statement and had him sign it. What strikes him most, looking back, is what they never asked for: the names of the men involved, which he had; the passport used, which he had; or a single phone number from the dozens who called him during the ordeal.



“This is the beginning of a dormant complaint,” Pettle writes. But his closing line is the one that lingers: despite everything, he says his real ambition is still “to come back and bring investment to your beautiful country” — if Liberia will have him.

World.title: After 35 Years, Liberia Reopens Embassy in India
World.content:
NEW DELHI, India — Liberia has officially reopened its Embassy in New Delhi after more than 35 years without a resident diplomatic mission in India, marking a major step in efforts to strengthen bilateral relations between the two countries.

Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti is in New Delhi to formally inaugurate the Embassy on behalf of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and the Government and people of Liberia.

The Liberian Embassy in India was closed more than three decades ago amid geopolitical and other challenges facing the country. Successive administrations subsequently sought to restore a permanent diplomatic presence in India, recognizing the country’s growing importance as a partner in Asia.

The reopening culminates years of efforts spanning several administrations. The Government said President Boakai’s administration has built on earlier initiatives to complete the process and restore Liberia’s resident diplomatic presence in New Delhi.

Speaking ahead of the inauguration, Minister Nyanti described the reopening as both a diplomatic milestone and an opportunity to deliver practical benefits to Liberians.

“After more than three decades, Liberia once again has a permanent diplomatic home in India,” Nyanti said. “This is a major milestone for our country and a testament to President Boakai’s commitment to strengthening Liberia’s global partnerships and ensuring that our diplomacy delivers tangible results for our people.”

She also acknowledged the efforts of successive administrations that worked toward reestablishing the mission.

The reopening is particularly significant given the growing number of Liberian students pursuing education and professional training in India, as well as Liberians traveling there for medical treatment.

The resident Embassy is expected to strengthen consular services and provide more direct assistance to Liberian citizens while creating opportunities for scholarships, education, healthcare and professional capacity building.

Beyond consular services, the Embassy is expected to serve as Liberia’s principal diplomatic and economic platform in India, with a focus on attracting investment, promoting trade and private-sector partnerships, and expanding cooperation in agriculture, technology, infrastructure and healthcare.

The mission will also support Liberia’s broader economic diplomacy and national development priorities by helping mobilize technical assistance and development partnerships.

India remains an important development and economic partner for Liberia, with bilateral cooperation spanning education, health, agriculture, technology, infrastructure, capacity building, trade and private-sector development.

The Government of Liberia expressed appreciation to India for its cooperation and support in facilitating the reopening of the Embassy and said the development marks a new chapter in Liberia–India relations.

World.title: Liberia: Gongloe Demands Independent Probe Into Cocaine Crisis
World.content:
Monrovia — As Liberia grapples with the fallout from its largest-ever cocaine seizures, renowned Liberian lawyer and politician Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe has issued one of his strongest warnings yet, describing the country’s escalating narcotics problem as a national security emergency and cautioning that Liberia must not follow the path of Haiti, where criminal networks have severely weakened state authority.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

In a lengthy commentary, Gongloe called on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to establish an independent Commission of Inquiry to investigate the cocaine seizures, trace the money behind the alleged trafficking network and determine whether individuals within Liberia’s security and political establishment helped facilitate the operation.

“Liberia must not become Haiti,” Gongloe declared, warning that the country could face a gradual erosion of state authority if corruption, organized crime and compromised security institutions are not confronted decisively.

Gongloe, a former standard-bearer of the Liberian People’s Party who contested the 2023 presidential election, said the scale of the cocaine seizures demonstrates that Liberia is confronting more than a conventional law-enforcement problem.

According to authorities, approximately 237.6 kilograms of cocaine, valued at more than US$19 million, were seized at Roberts International Airport in June. The country was subsequently rocked by the discovery of approximately 3,971 kilograms — nearly four metric tons — of cocaine, estimated to be worth about US$317 million, in the Duazon area.

Gongloe said the volume and value of the drugs point to an organized and well-financed international criminal enterprise.

“This is not the work of a few young people selling drugs on a street corner,” he said. “The sheer volume and value point to an organized and well-financed international criminal enterprise.”

He said investigators must determine who imported the drugs, who received and transported them, who provided protection, and whether anyone within the Liberian state facilitated the operation.

‘Follow the Money’

Central to Gongloe’s proposed response is a comprehensive financial investigation.

“The central principle must be simple: follow the money,” he said.

He argued that the investigation should extend beyond the cocaine itself to financial transactions, unexplained wealth, properties, businesses, bank accounts, communications, airport records, immigration records, shipping records and political relationships.

“Cocaine is the commodity. Money is the motive. Corruption is often the bridge between criminal money and legitimate institutions,” Gongloe said.

He stressed that allegations against individuals must not be treated as established facts and that anyone accused of wrongdoing must be afforded due process and presumed innocent until proven guilty.

But he said due process cannot become an excuse for government inaction.

“The rule of law does not mean that government should remain silent when credible allegations of criminal conduct reach into the highest levels of government,” he said. “The rule of law requires a fearless, impartial and professional investigation.”

Calls for Independent Commission

Gongloe acknowledged actions already taken by the Boakai administration, including reported suspensions, dismissals, arrests, charges and detentions involving individuals connected to the investigation.

He praised the administration for taking steps in the direction of accountability but said the measures remain insufficient given the magnitude of the crisis.

“Mr. President, this is not enough,” Gongloe said.

He urged President Boakai to establish a commission composed of experts in criminal investigation, narcotics trafficking, financial intelligence, forensic accounting, money laundering, organized crime, constitutional and criminal law, cybersecurity, border security and asset tracing.

The commission, he said, should have the authority to obtain documents and testimony, trace financial transactions and examine relevant communications and movements.

Its findings, he added, should be made public, subject only to legitimate national-security restrictions.

Warning About State Capture

Gongloe said Liberia should study Haiti’s experience as a warning of what could happen when criminal organizations become stronger than state institutions.

He argued that institutional collapse does not happen overnight, but through a gradual process in which corruption becomes normalized, criminal networks purchase protection, security institutions become compromised, and young people are recruited into criminal enterprises.

“A country does not wake up one morning and discover that gangs control its streets,” he said. “Institutional deterioration occurs gradually.”

He warned that Liberia must confront the warning signs before organized crime becomes entrenched.

“That is the road Liberia must refuse to travel,” he said.

Beyond Cocaine

Gongloe linked the cocaine crisis to what he described as deeper problems of governance, corruption, weak institutions, impunity and unexplained wealth.

He raised questions about several other national controversies, including the multimillion-dollar project in Foya, Lofa County, and allegations surrounding illegal mining activities along the Liberia-Guinea border.

Gongloe was careful to distinguish questions from accusations, emphasizing that he was not alleging that the Foya project was financed with drug money.

Instead, he argued that the government should provide complete transparency about the project’s financing, procurement and authorization.

“If the money is legitimate, transparency should establish that fact,” he said. “If the procurement was lawful, the records should establish it.”

He similarly called for investigations into allegations of illegal mining along the Makona River, saying illicit mineral extraction could become a corruption, revenue, border-security and national-security problem.

A Message to Boakai

Gongloe also invoked President Boakai’s 2023 campaign-era remark that he could “dance with the devil” if doing so would help him win the presidency.

He said he was not suggesting that Boakai had any agreement with drug traffickers or that the president’s statement was connected to the cocaine crisis. Instead, Gongloe used the remark as a broader warning about political compromises.

“Every compromise with corruption has a price. Every accommodation with criminality has a price,” he said.

He described the “devil” metaphorically as corruption, greed, impunity, political patronage and abuse of public office.

“The real devil in Liberia is not a supernatural being,” Gongloe said. “The real devil is corruption. The real devil is greed. The real devil is impunity.”

Youth at Risk

Gongloe said Liberia’s young population is particularly vulnerable to recruitment by international narcotics networks because of unemployment, poverty and limited economic opportunities.

He warned that drug traffickers have the financial resources to offer young people opportunities that legitimate employment cannot match.

“What happens when a young Liberian begins to believe that a drug dealer has more opportunities than a university graduate?” he asked.

He said Liberia’s response must therefore go beyond arrests and prosecutions to include education, employment, public health, youth development, criminal justice and border security.

“Arrests alone will not solve it,” he said. “We must destroy the economic ecosystem that makes narcotics profitable.”

‘No One Should Be Above the Law’

Gongloe urged the government to investigate anyone connected to the drug-trafficking network regardless of political affiliation, social status or proximity to power.

“If the evidence leads to a poor man, investigate him. If it leads to a police officer, investigate him. If it leads to a businessman, investigate him. If it leads to a minister, investigate him,” he said.

“If it leads to someone close to the President, investigate him.”

He emphasized that the objective should not be to target individuals but to establish the truth and protect the Republic.

“No one should be above the law,” he said. “Not because we want to destroy people, but because we want to save Liberia.”

‘The System Must Be Examined’

Gongloe said the eventual destruction of the seized cocaine should not mark the end of the investigation.

“The cocaine may be destroyed. The suspects may eventually be convicted or acquitted. But the system that allowed such an enormous criminal enterprise to operate in Liberia must be examined,” he said.

He called on the government to identify the facilitators, protectors and beneficiaries of the alleged trafficking network and ensure that prosecutions follow where evidence warrants.

He also urged Liberians to resist turning the crisis into another partisan political dispute.

“Do not ask first whether the matter involves the Unity Party, the CDC or the LPP,” he said. “Ask whether Liberia is safe.”

Gongloe said the crisis represents a test for the presidency, security institutions, courts, Legislature and political parties — but ultimately, a test for the Liberian nation.

“We survived civil war. We survived Ebola. We survived political instability. We must not now lose Liberia to organized crime,” he said.

His central demand to President Boakai was repeated throughout the commentary: establish an independent inquiry, follow the money, follow the evidence, and ensure that justice reaches everyone implicated.

“Liberia deserves the truth,” Gongloe said.

“The cocaine may be seized. The cocaine may be destroyed. But the lesson must not be destroyed with it.”

He concluded with a stark warning: “If we do not control the criminals, the criminals may eventually control us. If we do not defeat corruption, corruption may eventually defeat the Republic.”

“Liberia must answer those questions, and Liberia must answer them now.”

World.title: UN does not have electoral observation mandate – Mutali
World.content:
The United Nations (UN) in Zambia has clarified that it has no electoral observation mandate in the country and has therefore not deployed any election observers for the 13 August 2026 polls.

Reacting to claims on social media suggesting that the UN had congratulated a presidential candidate following the elections held in Zambia yesterday, UN Resident Coordinator, Beatrice Mutali, explained that the UN does not observe national electoral processes unless mandated by the General Assembly or the Security Council.

“While the UN supports Member States in strengthening democratic institutions and encourages compliance with international obligations and commitments, it does not pronounce itself on the validity of an electoral process or the legitimacy of electoral outcomes,” Ms Mutali said in a press statement issued in Lusaka today.

The UN has since strongly condemned the inappropriate and unlawful use of UN emblems and urged the public and media institutions to verify information through official UN communication channels and to refrain from sharing unverified content.

She explained that unverified content may contribute to misinformation and disinformation.

“The UN also stresses the importance of dialogue to defuse tensions and calls on political leaders to adhere to the political parties’ peace pledge and their supporters to reject any form of violence while awaiting the announcement of results.

World.title: ECZ announces first batch of results
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has announced the first consolidated presidential results from four constituencies out of the 226 constituencies in the country.

The four constituencies are Dongwe in Mufumbwe district in North-western Province, Feira in Luangwa district in Lusaka Province, Kundabwika in Kaputa district of Northern Province and Chisamba constituency in Central Province.

ECZ Chairperson, Mwangala Zaloumis, announced that the incumbent President, Hakainde Hichilema of the United Party for National Development (UPND) has garnered 22,476 votes from the four constituencies while Brian Mundubile of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) got 14,388 voted.

Mrs Zaloumis said Kelvin Bwalya of Zambia Must Prosper (ZMP) got 91 votes ahead of Socialist Party leader, Fred Mmembe with 83, while Harry Kalaba of the Citizens First has 59 votes and Movement for Economic Emancipation (MEE) president, Given Chansa got 58 votes.

Others are Brian Mushimba for the Organised People’s Party (OPP) who got 40 votes, Richard Silumbe of the Leadership Movement with 27 votes, while an Independent presidential candidate Given Katuta has 21 votes and Ackim Njobvu of the Democratic Union got 15 votes.

The rest are Howard Kunda of the Zambia Wake Up Party (ZAWAP) who got 14 while Richwell Siamunene of New Focus Party got 11 and Daniel Pule of the Christian Democratic Party has 5 votes from the four constituencies.

In Kundabwika constituency, President Hichilema got 4,160 votes while Mr Mundubile scored 3,180 and in Feira, the former received 4,900 votes and the latter got 7,885 votes.

In Dongwe constituency, Mr Hichilema got 6,848 votes while Mr Mundubile scored 143 votes and in Chisamba constituency, President Hichilema polled 6,568 and the NRPUP president got 3,180 votes.

Meanwhile, ECZ Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) Brown Kasaro, announced that the Commission will this morning issue a notice indicating when the next announcement will be done.

World.title: Mundubile confirms Army interrogation as questions emerge over Friday night incident
World.content:
Mundubile confirms Army interrogation as questions emerge over Friday night incident

NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile has confirmed that he was interrogated by officers from the Zambia Army, as conflicting accounts continue to emerge about events surrounding his Lusaka residence and the whereabouts of some people reportedly with him at the time.

The development followed several claims circulated on social media on Friday suggesting that Mundubile had been arrested, shot or detained at Ibex Hill Police Station. Some reports went further and falsely claimed that he had died.

The Zambia Police Service denied that Mundubile had been arrested or was being held in police custody. Police spokesperson Godfrey Chilabi described the reports as false and misleading and urged members of the public not to circulate unverified information during the sensitive election period.

However, Mundubile later confirmed that he had been questioned by Zambia Army officers rather than the police.

“Just to confirm that I am being interrogated by officers from the Zambia Army over the two videos I released earlier today. I appeal for calm from all our supporters as we allow the due process to proceed,” Mundubile said in a message reported by News Diggers.

Mundubile subsequently appeared on Emmanuel Mwamba’s online platform, where he made further allegations about what happened at his residence. He claimed soldiers had entered and searched the property and alleged that former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya had been “shot at twice.”

There has, however, been no independent confirmation that Kafwaya was struck by gunfire or injured. Some social media accounts have presented the allegation as confirmation that he was shot, something Lusaka Times has not established.

Questions have also been raised about Patrick Mwansa, husband of former Chawama Member of Parliament Tasila Lungu, who was reportedly among people associated with Mundubile during the incident. Opposition-aligned accounts have described Mwansa and several others as unaccounted for, but Lusaka Times has not independently established that he was arrested, injured or remains missing.

Other people mentioned in circulating accounts include lawyer and presidential spokesperson George Chisanga, Mundubile’s driver, a Mr Banda and members of his security detail. Their circumstances immediately following the reported incident have similarly not been independently established.

The incident has also generated commentary comparing Mundubile’s current circumstances with the treatment President Hakainde Hichilema and his family experienced while he was in opposition.

One commentary circulating under the title The Tribulations of BM8 and His Family argues that the distress allegedly being experienced by Mundubile’s family recalls the experiences of Hichilema’s family during his encounters with security forces under the administration of late President Edgar Lungu.

The commentary argues that families of political leaders should not become casualties of political confrontation and calls for solidarity with spouses and children who may find themselves affected by events arising from political disputes.

It also recalls previous periods of political tension involving former presidents Kenneth Kaunda and Frederick Chiluba, arguing that successive administrations should learn from the country’s history rather than repeat conduct they condemned while in opposition.

These are the views and comparisons advanced by the author of the commentary and should not be interpreted as independently established facts about Friday’s events.

We as Lusaka Times have seen no independently verified evidence establishing that President Hichilema personally ordered the reported operation at Mundubile’s residence. Claims attributing responsibility directly to the President therefore remain allegations unless supported by evidence or confirmed by the relevant authorities.

Similarly, Mundubile’s allegations concerning the conduct of military personnel have not been independently verified in their entirety. What has been confirmed through Mundubile’s own statement is that Zambia Army officers interrogated him. This is separate from the Zambia Police statement, which specifically denied that he had been arrested and detained in police custody.

The circumstances surrounding the Army’s involvement therefore remain unclear, including the legal basis of the interrogation, whether anyone else was taken away, whether firearms were discharged and the circumstances under which the reported operation occurred.

The Zambia Police Service has meanwhile warned that anyone deliberately creating or circulating false information intended to mislead the public may face legal action.

With vote counting and verification continuing following Thursday’s general election, authoritative clarification from the relevant security authorities could help establish precisely what happened, the condition and whereabouts of those reportedly involved, and separate verified events from the numerous conflicting claims circulating online.

World.title: Mundubile names Northern Province official in ballot claim
World.content:
National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity presidential candidate Brian Mundubile has named a senior Northern Province official in connection with what he alleges was the unlawful movement of ballot boxes during the presidential count, as he pressed his claim to have won Thursday’s election.

Addressing the nation, Mundubile said his party’s parallel voter tabulation indicated he had won at presidential, parliamentary and local government level, and accused unnamed officials of orchestrating delays designed to manipulate the outcome.

“According to the results received and compiled through our parallel voter tabulation, PVT, based on information transmitted to us from polling stations and totalling centres across the country, our tabulation indicates that we have won this election,” he said.

Mundubile said well-known senior government officials in Northern Province were involved in the illegal movement of ballot boxes, and directed a specific warning at one official by name.

“I would like to issue a timely warning to my dear sister, Deputy PS Undi in Kasama, who has been mentioned in this particular case. So my dear sister Undi, stop what you are doing. Let the will of the Zambian people prevail,” he said.

The reference appeared to be to Beauty Undi-Phiri, Northern Province’s acting permanent secretary, who separately confirmed this week that Government had set a target date to reopen Chikokola Bridge in Kasama District. Undi-Phiri had not publicly responded to Mundubile’s allegation at the time of publication.

Mundubile’s claim comes against a wider backdrop of reported incidents around the count. He said members of the military had taken control of certain totalling centres in Mufulira, where Gen 20 forms, the official results declaration documents completed at constituency level, were allegedly being removed.

“These reports must be addressed immediately,” he said.

He also raised concern over reported incidents involving ballot boxes in Chawama, Matero and Mandevu constituencies, saying any allegation of boxes being unlawfully removed, stolen, interfered with or transported outside established procedures should be investigated immediately and transparently.

“Those responsible, if these allegations are established, must be held accountable under the law,” he said.

In North-Western Province, Mundubile said returning and presiding officers had been instructed to stop issuing results and Gen 20 forms, a claim that, if confirmed, would represent a further disruption to the constitutionally mandated counting process.

He called on the Electoral Commission of Zambia to preserve every ballot box, Gen 20 form and other electoral record, maintain the chain of custody, and allow accredited party agents and observers to carry out their lawful duties.

“No ballot box should be diverted from a legally prescribed chain of custody,” he said.

Mundubile framed the continued delay in announcing results as cause for concern rather than a routine part of the counting process.

“We therefore view the continued delay in the transparent announcement and verification of presidential results with grave concern. The pattern of reports reaching us raises legitimate fears that this delay could create an opportunity for interference with or manipulation of the results,” he said.

He demanded the immediate publication of results in accordance with the law and called for all stakeholders to be given access to relevant electoral records so the outcome could be independently verified.

Despite the pointed allegations, Mundubile appealed to his party’s agents, supporters and the wider public to remain peaceful and to operate within the law, saying protection of the vote should not extend to violence or confrontation with security personnel.

President Hakainde Hichilema, for his part, said his camp continued to receive encouraging results as the count proceeded, and made no direct reference to Mundubile’s allegations.

“We continue to receive encouraging results and reports of peace, unity and solidarity across our country as the votes come in. There is much in this moment to be grateful for,” Hichilema said, urging Zambians to await the official outcome rather than celebrate early.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia has not issued a public response to the specific allegation concerning Northern Province officials. ECZ chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis has repeatedly stressed that only the Commission holds legal authority to announce and declare results, warning that premature declarations by candidates constitute an offence under Section 89(1) of the Electoral Process Act.

The allegation against a named provincial official adds a new dimension to a count already marked by a brief nationwide suspension of results announcements, reports of violence at several tallying centres, and competing claims of victory from the two leading candidates. Zambians continue to await ECZ’s official declaration, with the commission’s own roadmap pointing toward an announcement by Monday.

World.title: Hichilema takes commanding early lead as parliamentary battle produces major upsets
World.content:
Hichilema takes commanding early lead as parliamentary battle produces major upsets

President Hakainde Hichilema has opened a commanding lead in the first presidential results reflected on the Electoral Commission of Zambia results platform, taking 69.9 percent of the valid votes counted from the first five of the country’s 226 constituencies, while opposition leader Brian Mundubile trails with 29.7 percent.

The ECZ dashboard shows Hichilema with 37,060 votes against Mundubile’s 15,748, from 53,017 valid votes counted. Socialist Party candidate Fred M’membe follows with 71 votes, while Harry Kalaba and Kelvin Fube Bwalya have 56 and 52 votes respectively.

But the presidential numbers remain extremely early. Only five constituencies, representing about two percent of the country’s 226 constituencies, are reflected in the count. The dashboard itself warns that early declarations tend to cluster geographically and may therefore not provide a representative picture of the national vote. Its presidential projection only becomes available after 20 percent of constituencies have declared.

Away from the presidential tally, however, a much broader political picture is beginning to emerge from parliamentary results coming out of constituency tallying centres. Some of those declarations are still making their way through the ECZ verification process before appearing on the national dashboard, but they already point to a fiercely contested National Assembly race, with NRPUP making gains in several constituencies while UPND, Independents and other opposition parties pick up seats elsewhere.

In Kabwe Central, former Kabwe Mayor Patrick Chishala has secured his return to elected office, this time as Member of Parliament, after defeating incumbent UPND MP Chrizoster Halwindi Phiri. Results from the constituency put Chishala on 15,600 votes against Phiri’s 8,099, handing NRPUP one of its notable parliamentary gains outside the Copperbelt.

The Copperbelt is producing some of the opposition’s strongest results. Former Nkana MP Alexander Chiteme has reclaimed Nkana Constituency, defeating UPND candidate Francis Mukuka and booking his return to Parliament. Wusakile has gone to Pavyuma Kalobo, while Frank Ng’ambi has taken Chifubu, adding two more seats to the changing parliamentary landscape in the province.

The shift extends beyond Kitwe. Tilus Sichinga has taken Kabushi, while Michelle Phiri Kazala has emerged victorious in Chingola Central. Rosemary Chipoya has secured Nchanga, with Boris Chansa taking Chingola West. Taken together, the results show the Copperbelt becoming one of the major parliamentary battlegrounds of the election.

Muchinga Province is also sending new and returning faces to Parliament. Francis Kapyanga has secured Mpika North, while Kanungwe Chota Kanyanyamina has taken Lwitikila Constituency. In Nakonde, Lukas Simumba has prevailed in Mwenzo Constituency. The developing results have also brought defeat for incumbent Kanchibiya MP Sunday Chanda, although the complete result identifying his successor still requires confirmation.

In Malambo West, Patrick Mwale has emerged victorious on the NRPUP ticket, adding another constituency to the party’s growing parliamentary tally. The result is among those emerging from constituency-level counting while the national ECZ platform continues catching up with declarations being made around the country.

Lusaka Province is producing a more mixed picture. Danny Yenga has taken Kabwata Constituency, while former Cabinet minister Jean Kapata has secured Mandevu, marking her return to Parliament. Former Lusaka Mayor Chilando Chitangala is also among the candidates emerging from the parliamentary contests as constituency results continue to arrive.

The gains by NRPUP and other opposition candidates do not amount to a one-way parliamentary contest. UPND is collecting seats of its own across the country. Ross Kasikili has secured the newly created Roma Constituency, while Emmanuel Kasambo, popularly known as Lamba Bull, has taken Mpongwe West. In Chilanga South, UPND candidate Ngenda Situmbeko has also secured the parliamentary seat.

Southern Province continues to provide victories for the ruling party. UPND candidate Vincent Lilanda has won the Mazabuka parliamentary seat with 20,420 votes. The party also entered polling day with a number of parliamentary seats already secured after its candidates went through unopposed, including Trevor Mwiinde Sialunga in Choma South, Edgar Siakachoma in Kalomo South, Vumango Musumali in Zambezi West, Clement Andeleki in Kazungula North, Siakole Nchimunya in Sinazongwe and Jack Mwiimbu in Monze East.

There are surprises beyond the two largest political formations. Former minister Dr Chishimba Kambwili has captured Roan Constituency on the Citizens First ticket, putting the veteran politician back on course for Parliament. Independent candidate Iris Kaingu Kamwi has taken Mwandi, while Jeffrey Mulebwa has secured Kafulafuta. In Chongwe East, Independent Anita Kamanga has defeated former Health Minister Sylvia Masebo, adding another high-profile upset to the parliamentary contest.

Another result requiring careful distinction is Ndola Central, where Emmanuel Mulenga has emerged victorious on the Resolute Party ticket after defeating UPND’s Frank Tayali. Mulenga should therefore not be included among NRPUP’s parliamentary victories when calculating the opposition party’s seat tally.

The stream of constituency declarations also explains the apparent contradiction between what is happening around the country and what is visible on the ECZ dashboard. At the point captured by the latest dashboard, the National Assembly section showed only one constituency seat incorporated into the central system, even as winners were already being announced from numerous constituency tallying centres.

That gap does not necessarily mean the constituency results are missing. Election documents move through verification before they are incorporated into the national results management system, creating a period in which a candidate may already have prevailed at constituency level while the ECZ dashboard continues showing the seat as pending.

The distinction is particularly important at this early stage. Parliamentary elections are determined constituency by constituency, meaning a succession of local declarations can quickly provide a picture of how the National Assembly is taking shape. The presidential election, on the other hand, requires the national accumulation of votes from all constituencies before the true balance of the race becomes clear.

For Hichilema, the opening presidential figures are nevertheless emphatic. His 37,060 votes give him more than twice Mundubile’s 15,748 in the five constituencies currently reflected on the dashboard. But with 221 constituencies still outstanding in that snapshot, the overwhelming majority of the presidential vote remains outside the published national tally.

The parliamentary contest is already offering a different story. NRPUP has broken through in a number of constituencies, particularly on the Copperbelt, while UPND continues to secure seats of its own. Independents are also making their presence felt, and smaller opposition parties have begun putting MPs into the next National Assembly.

Zambia is therefore watching two election contests developing at different speeds. The first official presidential figures have given Hichilema a commanding 69.9 percent lead, but the parliamentary declarations are producing a far more fragmented map, with seats changing hands and several established political figures either returning to Parliament or being defeated.

With most presidential constituency results still to be incorporated into the national count and parliamentary declarations continuing across the country, neither picture is complete. What is already clear is that the race for State House and the battle for control of the National Assembly are not necessarily following the same political pattern.

Attention now turns to the next official ECZ update, expected at about 09:00 hours today, when more verified constituency results are expected to be added to the national tally. That update should provide a clearer indication of whether Hichilema’s commanding 69.9 percent opening lead is holding as results arrive from a wider geographical spread of the country, or whether the gap between him and Mundubile begins to narrow.

It should also bring the official dashboard closer to the picture already emerging from constituency tallying centres, where parliamentary winners have been declared faster than they are appearing on the central results platform.

For now, Hichilema leads the presidential race by a wide margin in the results officially reflected so far, while the parliamentary contest is producing a much more fragmented political map. The 09:00 hours ECZ update could give the first substantially broader indication of where Zambia’s 2026 election is heading.

World.title: Nine Arrested in Matero Over Polling Agent Murder
World.content:
THE Zambia Police Service has confirmed multiple arrests following isolated incidents during and after the August 13 General Elections.

In Matero, Lusaka Province, nine suspects have been arrested in connection with the alleged murder of 57-year-old polling agent LOVEMORE CHISHIMA.

Mr. CHISHIMA was allegedly assaulted at Kasamba Polling Station and later died.

According to a statement issued by Inspector General of Police GRAPHEL MUSAMBA, the suspects are in police custody as investigations continue.

In a separate incident, police arrested six men allegedly found in possession of offensive weapons, 22 rounds of ammunition and a Toyota Land Cruiser.

Police say they are seeking SEAN TEMBO to assist with investigations.

Meanwhile, in Kalomo, Southern Province, one suspect was arrested following an incident in which four people were assaulted, with one victim sustaining a gunshot wound.

Police recovered a firearm and ammunition.

In Kasama, Northern Province, police are also investigating an attack on the residence of Acting Permanent Secretary BEAUTY UNDI-PHIRI, allegedly carried out by armed supporters of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity.

One suspect has since been apprehended.

Mr. MUSAMBA says although the overall conduct of the elections was peaceful, police are taking the reported incidents seriously.

He has warned against incitement, unlawful activities and the spread of false information, while urging citizens to remain calm and allow the Electoral Commission of Zambia to professionally manage and announce the election results.

World.title: ECZ lifts suspension, sets 22:00 for first results after security review
World.content:
ECZ lifts suspension, sets 22:00 for first results after security review

The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has lifted, with immediate effect, its suspension of the counting and announcement of results in the 2026 general election, and says the first set of results will be announced at 22:00 tonight.

ECZ Chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis told a press briefing on Friday that a review of the security situation, carried out in consultation with law enforcement agencies, found that the threat to the electoral process had been contained and that measures were now in place to allow counting to resume.

The Commission had earlier suspended counting and the announcement of results nationwide after reports of violence directed at polling staff and, in some instances, the theft of marked ballot papers from ballot boxes. That suspension was to be reviewed within 24 hours depending on the security situation.

“Following a review of the security situation and consultations with the relevant law enforcement agencies, I am pleased to inform you and to inform the nation that the security threat to the electoral process has been contained,” Zaloumis said.

She said polling had been successfully conducted at all polling stations across the country, with the last station closing in the early hours of Friday at 02:00.

“We therefore wish to advise all stakeholders that the suspension of the counting and announcement of results has been lifted, with immediate effect,” she said.

Zaloumis appealed to political parties, candidates, their supporters and members of the public to remain peaceful and allow polling staff to work without interference, intimidation or violence. She said the safety of polling staff, the security of electoral materials and the integrity of the process remained paramount, and that law enforcement agencies would continue providing security as counting and the announcement of results proceed.

She reminded the nation that official results are only those announced by the ECZ in accordance with prescribed procedures, and warned candidates against self-declaration.

“It is an offence under Section 89(1) of the Electoral Process Amendment Act No. 32 of 2021 for any person without lawful authority to announce and declare the results of an election,” she said, urging all presidential and other candidates to desist from declaring themselves winners and to allow the Commission to complete its constitutional duty of counting, verifying and announcing results.

Zaloumis thanked Zambians for their patience and cooperation, acknowledged the work of law enforcement in maintaining order, and commended ECZ staff for their commitment to duty. She said the Commission would continue to update the nation as the process progresses, and that stakeholders were invited to join at 22:00 as the first results begin to stream in.

The suspension, and now its lifting, come after opposition leader Brian Mundubile declared himself the winner of the presidential election on Friday, citing his alliance’s parallel vote tabulation, a claim that remains a Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance position rather than an official result. President Hakainde Hichilema had called on Zambians to remain calm as the count continued.

World.title: HICHILEMA SAYS EARLY ELECTION RESULTS ENCOURAGING
World.content:
PRESIDENT HAKAINDE HICHILEMA says he has continued to receive encouraging results following yesterday’s voting.

President HICHILEMA says he has also received reports of peace, unity and solidarity across the country as the counting process continues.

In a statement posted on his Facebook page, President HICHILEMA has urged Zambians to remain peaceful, patient and patriotic while awaiting the official results from the Electoral Commission of Zambia — ECZ.

Meanwhile, UPND National Management Committee representative MULAMBO HAIMBE says early indications from tallying centres are encouraging for President HICHILEMA.

Mr. HAIMBE says reported trends point to a strong performance for the incumbent, with high voter turnout recorded in Southern, Western and North-Western Provinces.

He says the picture in Central Province is favourable, while the party is also seeing gains in Northern Province.

However, Mr. HAIMBE has stressed that the information being shared represents early indications and not official election results.

He says only the ECZ has the constitutional authority to declare the winner of the presidential election.

Mr. HAIMBE has further cautioned political parties and members of the public against circulating unverified claims of victory, saying the ECZ should be allowed to complete the process of collation, verification and announcement of results.

The UPND has since called on citizens to exercise patience and restraint and respect the conclusion of the democratic process.
