IKEA lands on Falabella’s website

The launch is set for the last days of August 2026. It starts with a slice of the catalogue — storage, decoration, dining, bedroom, desks and living-room pieces.

This matters more than it sounds. Chile is only the third country where IKEA has let an outside marketplace sell its products.

The other two are Indonesia, through Shopee, and China, through Tmall and JD.com. Chile is the first outside Asia.

There is a clear split of jobs here. Falabella.com is the storefront where you browse and pay. IKEA looks after the stock, the delivery and the after-sales help.

This is not the same as the IKEA stores

Falabella already knows IKEA well. Back in 2018 it signed a franchise deal to build and run physical IKEA stores in Chile, Peru and Colombia.

The first store opened in Santiago in 2022, with Lima and Bogotá following. Under that deal, Falabella owns and operates the shops.

The new website tie-up is a different animal. Here IKEA is the seller and Falabella.com is simply the channel. Think of it as IKEA renting a huge, ready-made shopfront online.

A new man in the chair

The online move comes as Falabella changes hands at the top. Fernando de Peña became chairman of the board in March 2026.

He is not a newcomer. De Peña spent about 35 years at Mallplaza, Falabella’s shopping-centre arm, and built it into one of the region’s largest mall operators.

He replaced Enrique Ostalé and won backing from the founding families who control the group. In plain terms, the owners picked a steady, in-house hand rather than an outsider.

Back in profit after a rough patch

The timing is not an accident. In 2023 Falabella carried heavy debt and lost its investment-grade credit rating, which spooked lenders.

Since then it has sold assets, cut debt and steadied the ship. The second quarter of 2026 showed the recovery in the figures.

Adjusted profit rose about 14% to CLP 223.6 billion (~US$245 million). Revenue grew almost 7% to CLP 2.87 trillion (~US$3.14 billion).

The group’s bank did much of the heavy lifting. Its credit cards and loans grew fast, and that fed straight through to the bottom line.

Why you should care

If you live in Latin America, this is about choice and prices. More sellers on one trusted website usually means easier comparison and better deals for you.

If you invest in the region, the signal is bigger. A brand as careful as IKEA rarely lends its name to a partner it does not trust — and it just picked Falabella over the whole Western hemisphere.

It also shows where retail is heading here. The winners are building online marketplaces, banks and physical stores into one system, and Falabella is betting it can run all three.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I buy IKEA on Falabella.com right now? Yes, in Chile. IKEA products go live on Falabella.com in the last days of August 2026, starting with storage, decoration, dining, bedroom and living-room items rather than the full catalogue. Is this the same as the IKEA stores in Chile? No. Falabella runs physical IKEA stores under a separate 2018 franchise deal. On Falabella.com, IKEA itself is the seller and handles the stock, shipping and customer service, while Falabella provides the website. Who is Fernando de Peña? He is Falabella’s new chairman of the board, in the role since March 18, 2026. He previously ran the group’s mall business, Mallplaza, for about 35 years and replaced Enrique Ostalé. Is Falabella financially healthy again? It has recovered strongly from its 2023 debt troubles. Adjusted second-quarter 2026 profit rose about 14% to CLP 223.6 billion (~US$245 million), helped mainly by fast growth at its bank.

Sources: Diario Financiero (DF.cl); La Tercera; Emol; Forbes Chile; CNN Chile; IKEA Global newsroom; FashionNetwork. Currency converted at CLP 914 per US$1.

World.title: Codelco Overhauls Its Leadership With Five New Vice Presidents and Four Division Chiefs
World.content:
Chile · Mining

Key Facts What happened: On August 14, 2026, Codelco reshuffled its top ranks, naming five vice presidents and new managers at four mining divisions.

On August 14, 2026, Codelco reshuffled its top ranks, naming five vice presidents and new managers at four mining divisions. New CEO: Jorge Gómez, former head of the Collahuasi mine, took over on July 13, 2026, replacing Rubén Alvarado.

Jorge Gómez, former head of the Collahuasi mine, took over on July 13, 2026, replacing Rubén Alvarado. New chairman: Bernardo Fontaine, appointed by President José Antonio Kast in May 2026.

Bernardo Fontaine, appointed by President José Antonio Kast in May 2026. Divisions affected: El Teniente, Chuquicamata, Ventanas and Ministro Hales.

El Teniente, Chuquicamata, Ventanas and Ministro Hales. Backdrop: A production-reporting scandal and a deadly 2025 accident at El Teniente.

A production-reporting scandal and a deadly 2025 accident at El Teniente. 2025 output: About 1.332 million tonnes of copper; the old 1.7-million-tonne goal has been dropped.

About 1.332 million tonnes of copper; the old 1.7-million-tonne goal has been dropped. Lithium: Codelco’s venture with SQM controls Salar de Atacama lithium production until 2060.

The world’s largest copper miner is betting new faces can fix old problems — a fatal accident, a bookkeeping scandal, and ore that keeps getting poorer.

Chile’s state copper company just rebuilt its command team from the top down. On August 14, 2026, Codelco named five new vice presidents and replaced the general managers at four of its mining divisions.

Codelco, the world’s largest copper miner, has rebuilt its leadership team. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Who is moving where

New CEO Jorge Gómez has split the mines into two operating blocks. Lindor Quiroga Bugueño takes charge of the northern operations.

Those cover Chuquicamata, Radomiro Tomic, Ministro Hales and Gabriela Mistral. Francisco Carvajal Palacios — the former head of iron miner CMP — leads the center-south block.

That group holds El Teniente, Andina, El Salvador and Ventanas. So two people now oversee almost every mine Codelco runs.

Three more vice presidents round out the team. Mario Quiñones will run mining resources, development and innovation.

Leonardo Biaggini takes strategy and management control. Pablo Villarino, a lawyer, handles corporate affairs and sustainability.

Several of them come from Collahuasi, the private mine Gómez used to lead. He is clearly bringing trusted people with him.

Four divisions, new bosses

The divisions got fresh leadership too. Julio Díaz moves in to run El Teniente, the flagship mine.

Ricardo Weishaupt takes over Chuquicamata from August 15. Claudio Flores steps in at Ventanas, and Thomas Gleisner Rivas at Ministro Hales — both for now on an interim basis.

Most of the other appointments start on September 1. It is one of the deepest reshuffles Codelco has done in years.

Why the shake-up, and why now

Codelco has had a rough year — and a rough decade. Gómez only took the top job on July 13, 2026.

He replaced Rubén Alvarado, who resigned after an audit found the company had overstated its 2025 copper output. The gap was about 27,000 tonnes.

That may sound small. But for a company built on trust with the Chilean state, a reporting error like that is a serious blow.

The board changed too. In May 2026, President José Antonio Kast named economist Bernardo Fontaine as chairman.

He replaced Máximo Pacheco, the chairman under the previous government. So the new team reflects a change of government, not just a change of managers.

Gómez has said little that is flashy. He describes the goal as reinforcing a team of excellence with deep industry experience.

The plainer translation is steady hands and fewer surprises — and a hard focus on getting the numbers right.

The El Teniente shadow

Safety is the quiet theme behind all of this. On July 31, 2025, a violent rock burst tore through El Teniente.

Six workers died. The mine — Codelco’s biggest — lost roughly 48,000 tonnes of copper that year.

Codelco now expects little real growth there for several years. Putting a trusted manager in that seat is not a small decision.

Copper is getting harder to dig

There is a slower problem underneath the headlines. Chile’s copper is getting harder and costlier to pull out of the ground.

Ore grades — the amount of metal in each tonne of rock — keep falling. So miners must move more rock to get the same copper.

Codelco produced about 1.332 million tonnes of copper in 2025. It has quietly dropped its old dream of 1.7 million tonnes, calling that target out of reach.

The lithium bet

Copper is not the only bet on the table. In late 2025, Codelco and private miner SQM sealed a lithium partnership in the Salar de Atacama.

The venture will control lithium in that salt flat — the world’s richest — until 2060. It hands the state a bigger share of a metal used in electric-car batteries.

Gómez now has to make both plans work at once. That means fixing the copper business while standing up a whole new lithium one.

Why this matters if you live in or invest in Latin America

Codelco alone hands billions of dollars a year to Chile’s treasury. That money funds schools, roads and pensions across the country.

When its output slips, the whole nation feels the pinch. And because Chile supplies so much of the world’s copper, its troubles ripple into the price of everything from home wiring to electric cars.

A steadier Codelco is good news well beyond Santiago. This shake-up is the clearest sign yet that its new leaders know the stakes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Codelco’s new CEO? Jorge Gómez, who ran the Collahuasi mine for more than a decade. He became Codelco’s chief executive on July 13, 2026, replacing Rubén Alvarado. How many executives changed in the shake-up? Codelco named five new vice presidents and new general managers at four divisions — El Teniente, Chuquicamata, Ventanas and Ministro Hales. Most changes take effect on September 1, 2026. Why is Codelco restructuring now? The company is recovering from a production-reporting scandal, a deadly 2025 accident at El Teniente, and years of falling ore grades. A new CEO and a new chairman are trying to steady the business. What happened at the El Teniente mine? On July 31, 2025, a rock burst killed six workers at El Teniente, Codelco’s largest mine. It cost about 48,000 tonnes of copper output and stalled growth there for years.

Sources: Codelco; Diario Financiero; La Tercera; Reuters via Mining.com; Bloomberg.

World.title: Havanna Sales Drop 9.7% as Argentina’s Alfajor Icon Falls Into the Red
World.content:
Argentina · Business

Key Facts Net result: Havanna swung to a loss of ARS 747 million (~US$502,000) in the second quarter of 2026, from an ARS 1,044 million profit a year earlier.

Havanna swung to a loss of ARS 747 million (~US$502,000) in the second quarter of 2026, from an ARS 1,044 million profit a year earlier. Revenue: ARS 32,288 million (~US$21.7 million) in the quarter, down 9.7% in real terms.

ARS 32,288 million (~US$21.7 million) in the quarter, down 9.7% in real terms. Core products: Alfajores, cookies and Havannets sold ARS 21,673 million (~US$14.6 million), with volume down 3.1%.

Alfajores, cookies and Havannets sold ARS 21,673 million (~US$14.6 million), with volume down 3.1%. Half-year: Revenue of ARS 87,198 million (~US$58.6 million) and a still-positive net profit of ARS 7,841 million (~US$5.3 million).

Revenue of ARS 87,198 million (~US$58.6 million) and a still-positive net profit of ARS 7,841 million (~US$5.3 million). Stores: About 250 in Argentina and roughly 230 abroad, with Brazil the biggest foreign market at 191 shops.

About 250 in Argentina and roughly 230 abroad, with Brazil the biggest foreign market at 191 shops. Ownership: Controlled by the Argentine investment fund Inverlat since 2016; about 7% trades on BYMA under the ticker HAVA.

Controlled by the Argentine investment fund Inverlat since 2016; about 7% trades on BYMA under the ticker HAVA. Why: A weak Argentine consumer, plus a decision to hold back price rises to protect sales.

An alfajor is one of the cheapest joys in Argentina. When even that gets cut from the shopping list, it tells you how tight household budgets have really become.

Argentina’s most famous alfajor maker just had a sour quarter. Havanna slipped into the red between April and June 2026. Sales fell almost 10% from a year earlier, and the company swung from profit to a net loss of ARS 747 million (~US$502,000).

Havanna’s alfajor sales fell as Argentine shoppers tightened their budgets. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The brand comes from Mar del Plata. It is known for dulce de leche sandwich cookies and its café counters across the country.

What the numbers show

Revenue reached ARS 32,288 million (~US$21.7 million) in the second quarter. That is down 9.7% from a year earlier.

The figure is measured in constant June 2026 pesos. That strips out inflation, so the drop is a real fall in sales — not just a currency effect.

The core business felt it most. Sales of alfajores, cookies and Havannets came to ARS 21,673 million (~US$14.6 million), with volume down 3.1%.

Margins thinned as costs climbed. The operating result dropped 55.5% to ARS 1,553 million (~US$1 million).

Then inflation did the rest. A financial loss of ARS 2,113 million (~US$1.4 million) came mostly from the erosion of cash holdings. That pushed the bottom line into a loss.

Why sales fell

The simple answer is that Argentines are spending less. A treat like an alfajor is easy to skip when money is tight.

Havanna also made a deliberate choice. It held back on raising shelf prices, hoping to keep customers buying.

The company said it chose not to pass the full weight of inflation on to shoppers. That protected sales volumes a little — but it squeezed what Havanna earned on each sale.

The half-year is still positive

Zoom out, and the picture looks less grim. Over the first six months of 2026, Havanna still turned a profit.

Half-year revenue was ARS 87,198 million (~US$58.6 million), down a milder 3.4%. Net profit came in at ARS 7,841 million (~US$5.3 million).

That profit is 15.8% lower than a year before. So the second quarter was the weak stretch, while a stronger start to the year kept the six-month result in the black.

Who owns Havanna, and the stock angle

Havanna was founded in Mar del Plata in 1948. Today it runs about 250 stores across Argentina and roughly 230 more abroad.

Brazil is its biggest foreign market, with 191 shops. Smaller networks operate in Peru, Paraguay, Chile, Spain and Bolivia.

The brand has been controlled by the local investment fund Inverlat since 2016. About 7% of the company trades publicly on BYMA — Argentina’s stock exchange — under the ticker HAVA.

Why this matters to you

Havanna is more than a sweet shop. It works as a thermometer for the Argentine consumer.

When people cut back on a beloved, affordable treat, household budgets are truly stretched. If you live in the region or invest here, that signal is worth watching.

It also hints at how the government’s tough anti-inflation drive is landing on everyday spending. Falling sales at a brand this loved suggest the squeeze is real — and still biting.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Havanna lose in the second quarter of 2026? Havanna reported a net loss of ARS 747 million (about US$502,000) for the second quarter of 2026. That reversed a profit of ARS 1,044 million from the same quarter a year earlier. Why did Havanna’s sales fall? Argentine shoppers cut back on treats as budgets tightened. Havanna also held back price increases to keep customers, which protected volumes but squeezed its margins. Is Havanna still profitable in 2026? Yes, over the first half of the year. Havanna earned a net profit of ARS 7,841 million (about US$5.3 million) in the six months to June, down 15.8% from a year earlier. Who owns Havanna? The brand has been controlled by the Argentine investment fund Inverlat since 2016. About 7% of the shares trade publicly on the BYMA exchange under the ticker HAVA. How many stores does Havanna have? Havanna runs about 250 stores in Argentina. It has roughly 230 more abroad, with Brazil its largest foreign market at 191 shops.

Sources: Ámbito Financiero; El Destape; Minuto Uno; iProfesional; La Nación; Bloomberg Línea; and Havanna Holding S.A. filings to BYMA.

World.title: Argentina’s YPF Luz and Genneia Hit Pause on Their New York IPOs
World.content:
Argentina · Markets

Key Facts Both delayed: Power generators YPF Luz and Genneia have postponed their planned New York (NYSE) share sales.

Power generators YPF Luz and Genneia have postponed their planned New York (NYSE) share sales. Why: Their banks advised waiting for a better market window, likely September or October 2026.

Their banks advised waiting for a better market window, likely September or October 2026. Genneia: Argentina’s largest wind and solar producer, planning to list as “GENN” and sought to raise about US$100 million.

Argentina’s largest wind and solar producer, planning to list as “GENN” and sought to raise about US$100 million. YPF Luz: Majority owned by state oil firm YPF (75.01%), planning to list as “YLUZ”; the seller was a minority stake split between US-based GE Vernova and China’s Silk Road Fund.

Majority owned by state oil firm YPF (75.01%), planning to list as “YLUZ”; the seller was a minority stake split between US-based GE Vernova and China’s Silk Road Fund. The trigger: Argentina’s Merval stock index sold off in early August and country risk climbed to about 480 basis points.

Argentina’s Merval stock index sold off in early August and country risk climbed to about 480 basis points. The stakes: These would have been among Argentina’s first US equity listings since 2019.

A door that looked wide open in July suddenly feels stuck. The delay is a quiet test of how much fresh money Wall Street will really send to Argentina.

Two Argentine power companies were ready to ring the bell in New York. Now they are waiting. YPF Luz and Genneia both filed paperwork in July to sell shares on the New York Stock Exchange, and both have now put those plans on hold.

YPF Luz and Genneia have delayed their planned New York listings. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The reason is timing, not cold feet. Their advisers told them to wait for calmer markets — most likely September or October.

What just happened

Genneia moved first, filing for what would have been a rare US listing. It planned to trade under the ticker “GENN” and aimed to raise roughly US$100 million.

YPF Luz followed on July 13, filing to list as “YLUZ.” It planned a dual listing — shares in New York and in Buenos Aires at the same time.

Then the mood changed. Argentina’s main stock index, the Merval, slid in early August. It gave back the 3-million-point level it had just reached.

At the same time, country risk — a gauge of how nervous investors are about lending to Argentina — rose about 10%. It reached roughly 480 basis points, its highest since June.

That is exactly the kind of backdrop that scares off buyers of new shares. So both companies chose to wait rather than sell into a falling market.

The company operates through the Upstream, Midstream and Downstream, LNG and Integrated Gas, and New Energies segments. It is involved in the exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbon fields and production of…

Who owns these companies

YPF Luz is the power arm of YPF, Argentina’s state-controlled oil giant. YPF owns 75.01% and will stay firmly in charge after any sale.

The shares on offer belonged to the minority owner, BNR Power Investments, which holds 24.99%. That stake is split between GE Vernova of the United States and China’s Silk Road Fund.

Genneia is controlled by Fintech Energy, the investment vehicle of Argentine-born financier David Martínez. The company has drawn outside backers over the years as it built out clean-energy projects.

What the two firms do

YPF Luz runs 17 power plants with about 3,764 megawatts of capacity. That is roughly 8% of Argentina’s entire grid.

Most of that power is thermal — plants that burn gas to make electricity. The rest comes from wind and solar farms spread across several provinces.

Its business is steadier than it sounds. It sells power under long dollar contracts to names like Toyota, Ford and Femsa. Revenue reached US$640.8 million in 2025.

Genneia is the country’s biggest wind and solar generator. It runs close to 2 gigawatts of capacity, mostly from wind farms in Patagonia and solar plants in the northwest.

It, too, earns almost entirely in dollars — about 98% of sales. That brought in roughly US$361 million last year, with net income near US$95 million.

Why they blinked

Both companies were riding a wave. Under President Javier Milei, Argentine firms have raised billions on international markets as investors warmed to his cuts and reforms.

In the first half of 2026 alone, Argentine companies sold about US$9.6 billion in bonds abroad. More than half of that came from the energy sector.

Selling stock is harder than selling bonds. A share sale needs buyers who believe the price will rise, and that belief fades fast when the local market wobbles.

The early-August selloff had homegrown causes. Investors grew wary ahead of a congressional fight over central-bank reform and a key fiscal bill, and over reports of political pressure on monetary policy.

Why this matters to you

If you live in Latin America or invest here, this is a live signal about confidence. Argentina’s recovery leans on a steady flow of foreign dollars, and stock sales are part of that pipeline.

A short delay is normal and not a crisis. But if the window stays shut, it hints that global money is less sure about Milei’s Argentina than the headline numbers suggest — and that caution tends to ripple across the region.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did YPF Luz and Genneia postpone their New York IPOs? Their advisers recommended waiting for better market conditions. Argentina’s Merval index sold off in early August 2026 and country risk rose to about 480 basis points, a poor backdrop for selling new shares. Bankers pointed to a possible window in September or October. Who owns YPF Luz and Genneia? YPF Luz is 75.01% owned by YPF, Argentina’s state-controlled oil company. The minority 24.99% stake, held by BNR Power Investments, is split between GE Vernova of the US and China’s Silk Road Fund. Genneia is controlled by Fintech Energy, the vehicle of financier David Martínez. What do the two companies do? YPF Luz operates 17 power plants totaling about 3,764 megawatts, mostly gas-fired thermal generation, and supplies roughly 8% of Argentina’s grid. Genneia is the country’s largest wind and solar generator, running close to 2 gigawatts of mostly renewable capacity. How much were they trying to raise, and when? Genneia sought to raise around US$100 million and would have traded as “GENN,” while YPF Luz planned to list as “YLUZ” without naming a size. Both filed in July 2026 and now aim for a possible relaunch in September or October.

Sources: La Política Online; Bloomberg; MercoPress; Buenos Aires Times; Renaissance Capital; company filings.

World.title: Terpel’s First-Half 2026 Sales Reach US$6.4 Billion as Profit Jumps 25%
World.content:
Colombia · Business

Key Facts Revenue: COP 19.94 trillion (~US$6.38 billion) in the first half of 2026, up 5.9% year on year.

COP 19.94 trillion (~US$6.38 billion) in the first half of 2026, up 5.9% year on year. Net profit: COP 409.25 billion (~US$131 million), up 25.4% from a year earlier.

COP 409.25 billion (~US$131 million), up 25.4% from a year earlier. Operating profit: COP 794.52 billion (~US$254 million), up 25.7%.

COP 794.52 billion (~US$254 million), up 25.7%. Gross profit: COP 2.01 trillion (~US$643 million).

COP 2.01 trillion (~US$643 million). Market share: 42.6% of fuel dispatched to Colombian service stations — four in every ten gallons.

42.6% of fuel dispatched to Colombian service stations — four in every ten gallons. Dividends paid: COP 300.58 billion (~US$96 million).

COP 300.58 billion (~US$96 million). Owner: Chile’s Empresas Copec, part of the Angelini group.

A slow-growth top line hides a fast-growth bottom line — and a quiet read on whether Colombians are still driving, flying and spending.

Colombia’s biggest fuel seller just closed a strong six months. Organización Terpel booked sales of COP 19.94 trillion (~US$6.38 billion) in the first half of 2026. That is up 5.9% from a year earlier. Profit rose far faster.

Terpel supplies more than four in ten gallons sold at Colombia’s service stations. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The numbers behind the headline

Net profit reached COP 409.25 billion (~US$131 million). That is 25.4% more than the same period last year.

Operating profit climbed 25.7% to COP 794.52 billion (~US$254 million). Gross profit came in at COP 2.01 trillion (~US$643 million).

So sales grew slowly, yet earnings grew quickly. Terpel sold a little more fuel and kept a firmer grip on its costs.

The company also rewarded its owners. It paid out COP 300.58 billion (~US$96 million) in dividends over the half.

What drove the results

Fuel and lubricant volumes rose about 2%. Aviation fuel — the jet fuel Terpel pumps at airports — grew 1.3%.

Convenience stores were the bright spot. Sales there jumped 6% in pesos, helped by store brands like Altoque and Va&ven.

Natural gas for vehicles also beat plan in Colombia. Volumes hit 104% of budget, margins improved, and running costs fell.

One line went the other way. Industrial sales dropped sharply, mostly because Terpel is dropping lower-value clients in Ecuador.

Colombia’s fuel king

Terpel rules its home market. It supplied 42.6% of all fuel dispatched to service stations in the first half.

That is four out of every ten gallons. Picture that ratio the next time you fill up in Bogotá.

Its nearest rival, Primax, held 21.4%. Chevron, Biomax and Petromil trailed well behind.

The top five distributors together moved 85.7% of the market. Terpel has widened its lead for years, from roughly 36% in 2010.

A retreat from Ecuador

The big strategic move of 2026 is a pullback. Terpel is selling its network of about 110 stations in Ecuador.

Primax is the buyer. Terpel is leaving that market after two decades to focus on its stronger lines of business.

The parent company has not changed. Terpel remains controlled by Empresas Copec, the fuel arm of Chile’s Angelini group.

Copec has owned Terpel since 2010. It still runs the business today, and there is no public sign of a sale to any new owner.

Why this matters to you

Here is why to care if you live in or invest across Latin America. Terpel is a rare regional consumer champion that touches daily life.

If you drive, fly, or grab a coffee at a highway stop in Colombia, Panama or Peru, you probably use it. Its results are also a simple gauge of the wider economy.

Strong fuel and store sales suggest people are still on the move and still spending. And as a company listed on Colombia’s stock exchange, Terpel sits in many regional funds.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Terpel earn in the first half of 2026? Terpel reported net profit of COP 409.25 billion (~US$131 million), up 25.4% from a year earlier. Sales reached COP 19.94 trillion (~US$6.38 billion). What is Terpel’s share of Colombia’s fuel market? Terpel supplied 42.6% of the fuel dispatched to Colombian service stations in the first half of 2026. That is about four out of every ten gallons, far ahead of second-place Primax at 21.4%. Who owns Terpel? Terpel is controlled by Empresas Copec, the fuel company of Chile’s Angelini group. Copec has owned Terpel since 2010, and there is no public record of a sale to a new owner. Why is Terpel leaving Ecuador? Terpel is selling its roughly 110 service stations in Ecuador to Primax after two decades in that market. The company wants to focus its money and attention on stronger lines of business.

Sources: Organización Terpel first-half 2026 results, via La República and Valora Analítik; market-share data from Surtidores LATAM (SICOM); Ecuador exit reporting from La Tercera, El Universo and Diario Financiero.

World.title: Karol G and Miguel Bosé Headline a Bogotá Solidarity Concert for Quake Victims

— Where Vive Claro Distrito Cultural, the city’s largest venue, in the Salitre district beside Parque Simón Bolívar.

— How to get in It is donation-based: give from COP 100,000 (about US$32) through Ticketmaster.co, and your donation is your entry.

— Who Karol G, Miguel Bosé, Sebastián Yatra and Silvestre Dangond lead a bill of more than 20 artists.

It is a donation-for-entry night, not a normal ticket sale — and if you cannot make it to Bogotá. Karol G’s set will stream so you can still chip in.

A star-studded solidarity concert is coming to Bogotá on Sunday, 23 August 2026. And it is built around one simple idea: turn a big night of music into rebuilt homes.

Karol G and Miguel Bosé lead the bill for “Voces por la Vida,” a benefit for the families hit hardest by Colombia’s August earthquake.

If you live in or near the capital, here is exactly how to be part of it.

What the Bogotá solidarity concert is

The show is called “Voces por la Vida,” and it is a one-night fundraiser rather than a regular gig. Colombia’s music industry.

Artists, promoters, producers and crews — agreed to donate their work so that every peso raised can go to relief. For an expat or newcomer, that framing matters.

You are not just buying a ticket; you are making a donation that happens to come with a seat. So think of the price less as an entry fee and more as a contribution with a great soundtrack attached.

When and where it happens

Mark Sunday, 23 August 2026 on your calendar. The concert takes place at Vive Claro Distrito Cultural, currently the largest venue in the country.

Vive Claro sits in the Salitre area of western Bogotá, right beside Parque Simón Bolívar. Roughly between Calle 53 and Calle 26 near Carrera 60.

It is a part of town locals already associate with big open-air events. So the surroundings are familiar even if the venue itself is new.

Who is performing

The headliners are a genuine who’s-who of Colombian and Latin music: Karol G, Miguel Bosé, Sebastián Yatra and Silvestre Dangond. That alone would fill a stadium on any normal weekend.

The supporting bill runs deep, too. Reporting lists more than 20 acts in total, among them Grupo Niche.

Andrés Cepeda, ChocQuibTown, Pedro Capó, Manuel Medrano, Draco Rosa, Eladio Carrión and Beéle. In short, it spans reggaeton, salsa, pop, vallenato and ballads, so almost every taste is covered.

How to get in and what it costs

Here is the practical part. Entry is donation-based, and the minimum contribution is COP 100,000.

Or roughly US$32 at mid-August 2026 exchange rates of about 3,145 pesos to the dollar. You make that donation through Ticketmaster.

co, and the donation itself serves as your admission. Because organizers have not published a full tier list of higher-priced zones.

Treat COP 100,000 as the floor and expect the option to give more if you wish.

Can’t make it? How to watch

If you are outside Bogotá, travelling, or simply cannot attend in person, you are not shut out. Karol G’s participation is confirmed to include a livestream, so you can follow at least part of the night from home.

A full broadcast and streaming schedule had not been published as of mid-August. So keep an eye on the artists’ official channels closer to the date.

Even from a laptop abroad, you can still donate through the same platform and count yourself in.

Where your money actually goes

This is the reassuring bit. Organizers say 100% of the proceeds will go to Presentes Corporación, the same foundation channeling other quake-relief efforts in Colombia.

The stated goal is concrete: rebuild in the hardest-hit areas and help families who lost their homes. A committee is meant to oversee how the funds are spent.

So the aim is reconstruction on the ground rather than a vague general pot.

The earthquake behind the show

The concert is a response to the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia on Monday. 10 August 2026, with its epicentre in Chocó near San José del Palmar.

The damage spread across Chocó, Valle del Cauca and the coffee-growing departments of Risaralda, Caldas and Quindío. By mid-August the death toll had climbed past 280, and thousands more were left without safe housing.

Which is why the rebuilding focus is so pointed.

How this differs from the other benefit shows

It is easy to mix these up, because Colombia’s artists launched several benefits at once. This Bogotá concert is a separate, third event.

It is not the Medellín show “Colombia, Medellín te quiere,” held on Saturday, 15 August at Centro de Eventos La Macarena. Nor the Miami telethon “Unidos por los nuestros” on Sunday, 16 August with Marc Anthony.

Those have already passed; the Bogotá night is the one still ahead of you.

Getting to Vive Claro

Because Vive Claro sits beside Parque Simón Bolívar, it is well served by the city’s main west-side corridors. If you are coming by TransMilenio.

Aim for stations along the Calle 26 or Avenida NQS lines and plan for a short walk into the Salitre complex. Big nights here draw big crowds, so give yourself extra time.

Ride-hailing and taxis are widely used in Bogotá, but expect heavy traffic and surge pricing around the venue. Especially as tens of thousands arrive for a single show.

Practical tips for the night

Bogotá sits at about 2,600 metres, so evenings turn cold quickly. Bring a warm layer and a light rain jacket, even if the afternoon feels mild, because open-air venues offer little shelter.

Carry a charged phone for your digital entry, keep your donation confirmation handy. And set a meeting point with friends in case signal drops in the crowd.

A little planning turns a good cause into a genuinely enjoyable evening.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the solidarity concert?

It is on Sunday, 23 August 2026 at Vive Claro Distrito Cultural in the Salitre area of western Bogotá. Beside Parque Simón Bolívar.

How much does it cost and how do I get in?

Entry is donation-based, starting at COP 100,000 (about US$32). You donate through Ticketmaster.

Can I watch if I’m not in Bogotá?

Yes. Karol G’s set is confirmed to include a livestream.

Where does the money go?

Organizers say 100% of proceeds go to Presentes Corporación to rebuild homes and help families in the areas worst hit by the 10 August 2026 earthquake.

Sources: El Tiempo; Publimetro Colombia; El Sol de México (OEM); U.S. Embassy Colombia; NPR; Wikipedia.

World.title: Coco 2 Confirmed for November 2029 With a First-Look Reveal
World.content:
Latin America · Culture

Key Facts — Release window Pixar confirmed Coco 2 is heading to theaters in November 2029; no exact calendar day has been set yet.

— Where it was announced the reveal came at the Disney Entertainment Showcase during D23 Expo 2026 in Anaheim on Friday, 14 August 2026.

— First look concept art shows a now-teenage Miguel with his dog Dante, plus an emotional reunion with Grandma Coco in the Land of the Dead.

— Cast and crew Benjamin Bratt returns to voice Ernesto de la Cruz; Lee Unkrich directs, Adrian Molina co-directs, and Mark Nielsen produces.

— Dia de Muertos the holiday at the heart of the story falls on 1-2 November each year; in 2026 that is Sunday 1 and Monday 2 November.

For anyone raising a family in Mexico or building a life across Latin America. The Land of the Dead is heading back to the big screen. Here is what Pixar actually confirmed, and how to enjoy the tradition while you wait.

Illustrative photo: a monumental Dia de Muertos ofrenda, the tradition at the heart of Coco, which returns with Coco 2 in November 2029. (Photo: Mario Yair TS, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)
