World.title: Croatian MP Josip Dabro Pushes Harsh Measures Against Illegal Migrants
World.content:
August the 14th, 2026 – Croatian MP Josip Dabro has pushed harsh measures against illegal migrants, stating that “you can’t talk with evil, you need to shoot at evil”.

Index reports that the former DP minister and MP Josip Dabro reacted clearly and sharply to the case of a Pakistani man who imprisoned and raped a Nepalese citizen in a house near Zagreb, stating that Croatia must act significantly more harshly toward illegal migrants who commit criminal offences.

“there’s no talking with evil, you have to shoot at evil”

In a statement titled “The principle of state prevention toward illegal migrants: There is no talking with evil, you have to shoot at evil!”, he called for stricter border protection, including the use of force, and the possibility of temporarily suspending the right to seek asylum.

Dabro referred to the case of Mohamad Sh., whom he claims has been moving for years throughout Croatia and other European countries, repeatedly committing extremely serious crimes, and after police and court proceedings again seeks asylum in order to avoid deportation. He believes this case demonstrates the powerlessness of European states in dealing with people who abuse the asylum system. “What we are witnessing in this case is a public demonstration of the powerlessness and paralysis of state orders, and at the same time an invitation to everyone in the world to come and calmly, with impunity, fulfil their most perverse urges and desires,” Dabro said.

sharp criticism of lax approach by other countries

Dabro claims that the way European countries handle such cases sends the wrong message to potential perpetrators.

“Come, do whatever you want, no one can do anything to you, and on top of that you will have free accommodation, food, pocket money for condoms, possibly knives or even firearms,” he wrote, describing the message which, in his opinion, the existing system sends.

He also criticised political debates about human rights, the European legal order and the possible deployment of the army on the borders. As a positive example he highlighted the policy of US President Donald Trump, whom he claims shows how a responsible state should behave. Dabro also linked the case to earlier attacks on police officers, beatings, murders and mass brawls in Zagreb and other European cities. He claims that because of this “increasingly serious insecurity is becoming a legal European acquis”.

he advocates the use of force at the border

Dabro then set out a series of measures he considers necessary. He stated that “there is no mercy or concessions toward evil” and that nothing that is illegal must subsequently become legal. The security of the population, he believes, must primarily be defended at the state borders.

“The security of one’s own people is primarily defended at the borders, by all means and by shooting if and when necessary,” Dabro wrote. He also claims that international norms must not limit the state if it assesses that national security is threatened. In his view, in the event of a conflict between international rules and national security, such norms should be suspended. “No international norm can legally suspend the sovereign and exclusive right of the state to protect its national security by all available means,” he stated.

suspending the right to asylum

Dabro believes the state must act immediately and without, as he puts it, “false legal labyrinths”, and publicly promote such a policy in order to deter people who intend to cross the border illegally and commit criminal offences. He also called on those who oppose this approach to personally take care of illegal migrants.

“All those who have a moral objection to such state policies, instead of rhetorical one-upmanship – take in the illegal migrants, take them home, feed and care for them, share your security, prosperity and home with them, stop sharing other people’s,” he wrote. As examples of the messages the state should, in his opinion, send, he cited a case in which security forces would kill an illegal migrant during a violent attempt to cross the border, the expulsion of a perpetrator of sexual violence after a police intervention, and the temporary suspension of the right of illegal migrants to submit asylum applications.

Dabro believes such messages can have a stronger deterrent effect than increasing the number of security force members at the border, but only if the state shows it is prepared to implement them. “Whoever plans to enter Croatia illegally and cause disorder in the country must know that persecution or death awaits him, not protection and super-rights,” he said. “Let us be a nation, not a humanitarian refuge for the world’s evil,” Dabro concluded.

World.title: Anton Aleksejev: Putin does not know the people he lives among
World.content:
By allowing Yabloko to participate in the State Duma elections and failing to anticipate its rise in popularity, Vladimir Putin's administration has confirmed that it does not understand the people it governs, writes Anton Aleksejev.

A legend says that when Yuri Andropov came to power in 1982 after Leonid Brezhnev's death, he told a Politburo meeting: "We do not know the people among whom we live."

More than forty years later, Vladimir Putin — also with a KGB background — has clearly ended up in the same situation. He prefers to believe that people who oppose the war are marginal in number and that the overwhelming majority is actually pleased about it.

In early August, Putin quoted volunteers he had previously met. They asked the president: "When the 'special military operation'"— the official term for the war in Russia — "eventually ends, what will we do then?" Putin did not say what he answered. He likely does not know himself.

Life goes on, however, and since — unlike in Ukraine — martial law has not been declared in Russia, State Duma elections will be held on September 20. "Elections" is a conditional term, because in such cases the Kremlin has long been simply appointing the next composition of parliament.

On July 30, the Central Election Commission registered 11 parties to participate. All share unconditional loyalty to the Kremlin, but as usual only four or five will actually enter parliament. United Russia will get the majority. The Communists, Liberal Democrats, A Just Russia, and the supposedly liberal New People will divide the remaining seats the Kremlin leaves for them.

Among those who have never had access to parliamentary mandates is Yabloko, founded in 1993 and considered democratic and liberal.

"'Elections' is a conditional term, because in such cases the Kremlin has long been simply appointing the next composition of parliament."

They last entered the Duma almost 20 years ago. Since then, their chances have steadily declined — partly because the party refused cooperation with potential allies (including the then‑alive Alexei Navalny), and partly because the Kremlin decided once and for all that the Duma podium would not be given to "odd characters." Even so, Yabloko was regarded as an "old party," one Putin treated with a certain respect, and they never skipped an election.

As befits a marginal party, Yabloko entered the elections with a slogan marginal in today's Russia: "For peace and freedom!"

Sergei Kiriyenko, the first deputy head of the presidential administration responsible for elections, reasoned that Yabloko would again get its two to three percent, fail to enter parliament, and prove to all anti‑war citizens that they are vanishingly few.

But within a week of registration, support for the party rose from three percent to seven — with a month and a half still to go. The outsider and marginal force was becoming a poorly controllable threat right before the presidential administration's eyes.

Of course, according to Stalin's principle — "it doesn't matter how people vote, but how the votes are counted" — no level of public support would have changed anything. No one intended to let Yabloko into the Duma.

Still, the mere fact that during the fifth year of the war, the slogan "For peace and freedom!" would appear on television and in newspapers for six weeks could have unpredictable consequences.

Yabloko did not speak about who Crimea belongs to, did not oppose holding elections in occupied Ukrainian territories, and so on. Two words were enough to signal clearly: if you want the war to end as soon as possible, here are people who share your view. And voting would show how many of you there are.

The FSB's 2nd Service — responsible for protecting constitutional order — understood the problem first. Action had to be swift and decisive. On August 7, it filed a lawsuit with the Supreme Court to remove Yabloko from the elections.

As usual, the FSB chose a suitable executor. Official parties — Communists, Liberal Democrats — rushed to accuse Yabloko of extremism and near‑treason, but none dared go to court demanding a ban.

The role fit perfectly for State Duma deputy Alexei Zhuravlyov of the Rodina party. The party itself is not represented in the Duma, but Zhuravlyov was allowed in during the previous elections, presumably in hopes he might be useful.

So far, his usefulness has consisted mainly of appearances on propaganda TV shows, where he has called for killing at least two million Ukrainians and claimed that Europe has special zoophile zoos where perverts can pay to have sex with animals, even turtles.

"As befits a marginal party, Yabloko entered the elections with a slogan marginal in today's Russia: "For peace and freedom!""

Zhuravlyov did not disappoint his superiors. In his lawsuit, he accused Yabloko of extremism, foreign funding, and even copyright infringement. One Yabloko poster depicted a nuclear explosion as a symbol of war. Zhuravlyov claimed the photo showed the 1945 Hiroshima bombing and that the rights belonged to the U.S. Army.

Even the judge was surprised and asked whether Zhuravlyov could prove his claims. He was unfazed: the photo could not exist without the bombing, and since the bomb belonged to the United States, the image of its explosion must also be U.S. property.

By that logic, anyone wishing to use a photo of a nuclear explosion in the future must build a nuclear bomb, detonate it themselves, and photograph the blast — otherwise they risk being crushed by the Russian legal system.

Despite the absurdity, on August 10 the Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the elections — the first time in Russian history that a party was banned just ten days after being allowed to run.

As the murdered Boris Nemtsov said, in the absence of fair elections and fair polling, the only way to understand a political force's popularity in Russia is through the authorities' reaction.

Everything happened exactly in line with Andropov's words. By allowing Yabloko to run and failing to foresee its rise, the presidential administration confirmed it does not know the people it lives among. The FSB, by removing Yabloko with Zhuravlyov and the Supreme Court, clarified: we do not know them and do not want to know them.

Meanwhile, such unwillingness to know the governed is characteristic of many governments. Volodymyr Zelenskyy likely did not expect that his July decision to dismiss former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov would bring thousands of young people into the streets in protest.

Last Monday, several hundred young Yabloko supporters gathered outside the Supreme Court in Moscow. For a city of millions, that is not many, but in a country where all unsanctioned street gatherings are effectively banned, it is a significant number.

The motivation of young Russians who do not want to go to war and fear mobilization coincides strikingly with the motivation of at least two million Ukrainians trying to avoid mobilization.

And if Yabloko's slogan "For peace!" is interpreted as a call to freeze fighting along the front line immediately and begin negotiations, then nearly 60 percent of Ukrainians today share that view.

How many Russians share it, we will not know — but judging by the authorities' reaction, enough to cast doubt on the continuation of the war. And as Vladimir Putin said: "When the war ends, what will we do then?"

World.title: Mounting public interest seeing teachers brush up on drone knowledge
World.content:
Over the next five months, 20 science and mathematics teachers will visit various companies to gain practical insights and work together to create teaching materials for the future.

The "Lae end" ("Charge Yourself") education program is aimed at middle school physics and mathematics teachers, helping them bring more practical examples and real-life connections into the teaching of science and mathematics. This year, 72 teachers applied to the program, of whom 20 were selected. Participants include both new and more experienced teachers who began the program at Metrosert's drone and defense technology testing laboratory.

"We have a whole range of laboratories here for testing subsystems. What is important about all of these laboratories is that the tests can be replicated," said Rainer Kivimäe, head of Metrosert's drone unit.

Interest in drones and artificial intelligence is also growing in schools, meaning teachers increasingly need to be able to explain these topics to students.

"Starting this academic year, as far as I know, some schools will begin talking more about drones. An educational program is also being developed in Tallinn where young people will be able to play drone soccer themselves. So young people's interest in the field is gradually beginning to grow and teachers naturally need to be knowledgeable enough to discuss it in the first place," said "Lae end" program manager Valentina Moskaljova.

For teachers, this means getting up to speed on subjects they have not encountered before.

"I knew as much about drones as I'd read in the news, basically, and as much as has recently been said about introducing a drone curriculum in schools," said Getriin Kokk, a mathematics teacher at Lodijärve School.

The program will also produce teaching materials for students in grades seven through nine.

"Young people need to understand which formulas they can use in both mathematics and physics. Right now, we're giving teachers the opportunity to work together in groups to create materials specifically designed to support that learning," Moskaljova said.

World.title: Gallery: Ukrainian children's fairytale art from Kharkiv reaches Estonia
World.content:
More than a dozen works by young artists in Kharkiv are now on display in Pärnu, blending forgotten legends and untold tales with new mythologies in large, colorful scenes.

"Lost Fairy Tales" opened at the Pärnu Museum of New Art (MONA) this week, showcasing 14 monumental original works created by about 40 children and teens ages 5–17.

Kharkiv's Aza Nizi Maza art studio continues to operate from a World War II-era bomb shelter, where kids still meet, learn and create amid ongoing drone, missile and guided-bomb strikes on the city.

The exhibition grew from the idea of a "missing museum" — a world made up of forgotten legends, untold stories and new mythologies inspired by the Baroque collections of European museums.

The young artists first drew elements found in ancient frescoes, botanical atlases, medieval maps and manuscripts before developing characters and building narratives around them.

Details like rosehips, seashells, bones, bats, lions and musical instruments meet characters ranging from beggars, saints and witches to princesses, children and those who have seen it all.

The scale of the works, which measure 2.5 x 1.5 meters, allows viewers to step into these visual worlds and become part of the unfolding narratives.

Curated by Mykola Kolomiiets and Iryna Hrytska, "Lost Fairy Tales" will remain on view in Pärnu through October 4.

World.title: Reform Party wants former EKRE MP as next Riigikogu Defense Committee chair
World.content:
The coalition Reform Party has proposed a former Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) MP as next chair of the Riigikogu's National Defense Committee, Postimees reported .

The move if successful may help the now-minority Reform-Eesti 200 coalition get votes passed at the Riigikogu.

The MP, Leo Kunnas, now sits as an independent, and Reform's secretary general, Kristo Enn Vaga, told Postimees his name had been discussed favorably.

However, Vaga said, Kunnas has not formally been agreed on within the party as candidate for the next Riigikogu Defense Committee chair to replace Kalev Stoicescu, who stepped down this week.

"He has served as deputy chair, has said he will not run for anything else, and his work there would be guided not by political interests but by national defense interests," Vaga said, noting it is not yet known whether Kunnas would agree to run for the post.

Kristo Enn Vaga. Source: Arp Müller/ERR

That a former EKRE member has been floated for the role by Reform – the parties were very much at loggerheads when EKRE was in office 2019–2021 – is likely the result of the Reform-Eesti 200 coalition now being a minority government; courting Kunnas could mean he will vote with the government on the state budget come autumn, and on other key matters.

Additionally, the current composition of the Defense Committee is such that electing a coalition MP to the post could prove complicated, while as noted Kunnas has served as deputy chair in any case. He is also a retired military officer.

The vote on the new Defense Committee chair is to take place on September 14, after parliament has reconvened from its summer break.

Kalev Stoicescu announced Sunday evening he was quitting Eesti 200, and he is stepping down as Defense Committee chief as well.

His departure and that of Meelis Kiili from the Reform Party a day later left the coalition with 50 seats at the 101-seat Riigikogu; Kiili himself told Postimees that Kunnas would make a good candidate for the Defense Committee job.

Other important votes coming up include the presidential election ballots on September 2 and 3; there are 20 independent MPs at the Riigikogu now, making them a significant demographic within parliament – 68 or more votes are required to elect a head of state.

World.title: Drone surveillance system starts work on Narva River
World.content:
A new drone surveillance system has been launched on the Narva River. Initially, border guards will be able to monitor aircraft movements along about a third of the river border, with the entire border river to be covered next year.

The first five radar masts were erected along the Narva River in the spring. They have now been equipped with surveillance equipment and for the first time border guards can monitor drone movements at and near the border. Even Russian reconnaissance aircraft flying along the border show up on the radar.

"These systems are now operational. We can see drones — not just small, civilian drones. In principle, if a military drone appears near our border, it will also show up on the radar screen. This is a significant step forward," Interior Minister Igor Taro said.

Just a few years ago, border guards said they could see about 70 percent of what was happening on the Narva River. By next year, the remaining blind spots are expected to disappear.

"We have state-of-the-art radar systems that, in addition to conventional monitoring of the airspace, can now also track different types of drone traffic. Better eyes and better systems give us a clearer picture to respond to," said Veiko Kommusaar, deputy director general of the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA).

While border guards can currently only monitor drone movements, the next step will be to counter drones both along the eastern border and inland.

"We are currently in the final stages of procuring an experimental site. Once the procurement is complete, an experimental site will be built where various counter-drone solutions will also be tested. If these solutions prove successful, they can then be deployed elsewhere across Estonia where they could be useful," Taro said.

Estonian border guards currently have drone surveillance coverage from Narva to Narva-Jõesuu. Construction of radars that will cover the Narva River as far as Lake Peipus is still underway and they are expected to become operational next year.

World.title: Demand for specialists remains high as Estonia's unemployment falls slightly
World.content:
The unemployment rate fell slightly in the second quarter, but the overall employment situation did not improve significantly. Employers say the greatest challenge is hiring specialists, for whom competition is fierce.

According to Statistics Estonia, Estonia's unemployment rate was 6.6 percent in the second quarter, slightly lower than a year earlier. The employment rate, at 68.6 percent, was also slightly below last year's level.

SEB economic analyst Mihkel Nestor said the figures are to be expected given the economy's gradual growth.

"Our economic growth is also relatively slow, which means there is no record-fast demand for new workers. I'm afraid unemployment will remain at around 6 percent for quite some time," Nestor said.

Southern Estonia and Harju County were the only regions where employment increased. Paulig is moving an entire production unit from Sweden to Saue, creating nearly 100 new jobs. Plant manager Margo Kuslap said there is no shortage of applicants.

"Our experience in Saue so far shows that people are willing to commute to work in Saue if the workplace is accessible, stable and offers opportunities for development," Kuslap said.

Kuslap added that hiring specialists is more difficult.

"There are roles that require specific expertise and those people are a little harder to find because many companies are competing for the same specialists," Kuslap said.

Martti Kork, CEO of Võru-based wood processing company Barrus, which was recently named Factory of the Year, said low investment has left the sector in a difficult position and forced his company to lay off employees this year as well. According to Kork, most local wood processing companies are in the same situation.

"The unfortunate thing is that all these companies are in rural areas, so jobs in rural areas are taking the hit," Kork said.

Barrus has created new opportunities in the region by shifting some work to computer-based roles. Kork said data specialists are now easier to recruit than machine operators.

"Our most recent recruitment process for a senior data architect position brought in 80 résumés here in Võru, which is quite surprising," Kork said.

The unemployment rate among 15- to 24-year-olds in Estonia was 22.4 percent in the second quarter. That is relatively high, although significantly lower than last year. Nestor sees this as a sign of society's growing prosperity.

"Families today can afford for young people's childhoods to last a little longer," Nestor said.

World.title: EDF in so-called gap year but active-duty personnel training still not underway
World.content:
The Estonian Defense Forces accepted several times fewer conscripts this year to allow active-duty personnel to focus on further training and professional development. However, such activities have yet to begin.

2026 is a so-called gap year for the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF). While around 4,000 conscripts were previously taken into service each year, in 2026 that number is just 1,200, with many of them being young people who intend to pursue a career with the Defense Forces.

The aim is to give active-duty personnel an opportunity to undergo more extensive further training and professional development.

However, according to the Defense Forces, the intensive period of further training is only now getting underway, as all conscripts who began their service last year have now been transferred to the reserve.

"In terms of the training courses being redesigned, changes to the soldiers' basic training course have now been prepared, as have instructors who will introduce the updated course curriculum and training methods in units. To this end, instructors' training levels have been standardized and the way further training will be conducted has been established," the Defense Forces told ERR.

Broadly speaking, the EDF is focusing its training on three areas: improving soldiers' basic skills, counter-drone training and firearms training.

Basic skills refers to helping each soldier, figuratively speaking, stay alive longer — in other words, protecting personnel, weapons and equipment from detection and the effects of enemy weapons. Both drone and firearms training involve the latest expertise, which is constantly evolving in light of developments in the war in Ukraine.

Although the number of conscripts is more than three times lower than usual, the reduction has not been evenly distributed. Some units simply require the same number of conscripts to operate, meaning this year is much the same as any other for them.

With the Defense Forces hoping to take in 4,100 conscripts next year, more than in previous years, how does it plan to find enough people?

Each year, the Defense Resources Agency (KRA) assesses the health of nearly 10,000 young people between the ages of 18 and 27. To meet the target of 4,100 conscripts in 2027, the agency is focusing intensively on those who have not yet entered service.

"It is not yet known how many of the young people who did not enter conscript service this year will receive a deferment. We will only be able to assess that once school admissions have concluded and we know how many young people will continue their studies and apply for deferment. Those who do not begin their studies and have no other grounds for postponing conscript service will be assigned to service in 2027," KRA Marketing and Communications Director Daisi Želizko-Kask said.

The agency currently believes that calling up around 4,000 conscripts a year will remain realistic until 2040, when the effects of the earlier low birth rate among boys will begin to have a significant impact.

However, according to KRA, the gap year has not affected the number of active-duty personnel.

World.title: Estonia's traffic deaths up compared to the same period last year
World.content:
Although the total number of serious traffic accidents and injuries declined in the first seven months of this year, 30 people have lost their lives on Estonia's roads and streets, four more than during the same period last year.

Estonia's road safety picture has been mixed this year. According to preliminary police data, 55 fewer people have been injured in traffic accidents than last year, while the number of fatalities has moved in the opposite direction, with four more deaths than last year, Transport Administration traffic expert Villu Vane said.

Compared with the Nordic countries and other European countries, Estonia's rate of road deaths per million inhabitants remains too high. According to a 2024 Europe-wide study, most European countries, including Norway, Denmark and Germany, had fewer traffic fatalities per million inhabitants than Estonia. With 50 deaths per million inhabitants, Estonia was also well above the European average of 44. Estonia's improvement in road safety over a 10-year period was also modest, at just 12 percent.

Vane said the root causes of the high number of fatalities lie in road users' habits and attitudes.

"This probably reflects our behavior in traffic, which isn't always what it should be and perhaps also reflects our attitudes toward things like obeying speed limits. It illustrates how we behave on the road," Vane said.

According to Vane, the situation has improved compared with 10 or 20 years ago. Seat belt use, for example, has become the norm, but there has been no comparable progress when it comes to speeding.

"If we look back, it took a little while for people to get used to wearing seat belts, but we've accepted it now. The overall picture is relatively good, with 99 percent of drivers and passengers in the front seats wearing seat belts, or 98 percent in some years. Unfortunately, when we look at fatal accidents, every year several people die in crashes because they weren't wearing a seat belt," Vane said.

When it comes to speeding, Vane said there has been improvement over the longer term, but Estonia has made little progress in recent years.

"One year we take half a step forward and the next year we take a step back," he said, describing the situation on Estonia's roads.

Vane said it is still too early to say what effect recent legislative changes — which introduced warning signs ahead of mobile speed cameras and lowered the speeding threshold at which fines are issued — have had on road safety.

"First of all, it's still relatively early to say because the signs were only recently installed ahead of mobile cameras — signs have been in place for fixed cameras for a long time. I think the impact so far has been relatively negligible. But there's always the question of whether the sign really needs to be there," Vane said.

Vane cited the legacy of the past as one reason for poor behavior on the roads. Asked what shapes the attitudes of young people who have grown up in Estonia since the country regained independence, Vane pointed to the influence of role models and their surroundings.

"It's probably the traffic environment and what they see, as well as how people behave at home. There are quite a lot of factors at play here," he said.

Elderly the most at-risk group in traffic

Looking at the profile of those killed, Vane highlighted two main risk groups. "Quite often, the road user is elderly, while young men also continue to account for a high proportion of fatalities," Vane said.

Asked who the typical person responsible for a traffic accident is, Vane said he could not give a clear answer. "We haven't specifically profiled them and it varies widely," he added.

According to 2024 European Union statistics, the most vulnerable age groups are people ages 25 to 49 and those over 65, each accounting for 31 percent. Men predominate both among those responsible for traffic accidents and among victims. The difference between the number of male and female victims is smallest among pedestrians.

Although Tallinn's traffic strategy calls for reducing road deaths to zero, there have already been several traffic fatalities in the city this year. What is Tallinn doing wrong?

Vane said the city may not necessarily be doing anything wrong as such, but the traffic environment has not been made safe everywhere and there are still places where improvements could be made.

"In cities in particular, speeds could be reduced in areas where pedestrians are present. Unfortunately, there are also fatal accidents where it's difficult to do much to prevent them. One possible example — we don't know for sure yet — is the most recent fatality in Tallinn where a person was struck by a car while directing traffic. There is a possibility that the driver suffered a medical emergency at the wheel," Vane said.

"Accidents that occur while vehicles are reversing are also relatively difficult to prevent, although there are measures that can be taken in certain cases. When it comes to freight transport, traffic arrangements can be designed so that vehicles only have to reverse short distances and pedestrians don't inadvertently enter those areas," Vane said.

People who shouldn't be driving

Speaking about medical conditions and medical certificates, Vane pointed to gaps in the system and its oversight.

"A person's health changes over time. People can develop illnesses while their medical certificate is still valid, but as I understand it, if someone develops a condition that means they are no longer allowed to drive, their medical certificate is not currently revoked automatically. That means someone can become ill and be told they must not drive, but still get behind the wheel. That's clearly dangerous," Vane said.

Doctors' decisions are also influenced by the social realities of rural areas and the availability of public transportation.

"Whether a doctor renews a medical certificate also depends on where the person lives and how accessible basic services are — whether they can take a bus to the store and back in a reasonable amount of time or whether there is no bus service at all. In that case, how are they supposed to get to a store 10 kilometers or even farther away? Unfortunately, a rural doctor may sometimes turn a blind eye and issue the certificate so the person can at least manage their day-to-day life somehow," Vane said.

Solutions: Enforcement and safer living environment

Vane said reducing traffic fatalities and improving road safety culture requires more than isolated technological solutions, with consistent work needed in three main areas.

"We need to continue doing what we've been doing. That means making the traffic environment safer as much as possible, particularly for pedestrians, and we probably also need to continue with prevention campaigns to some extent. Their impact may not be very large, but over time they do have an effect and probably influence certain groups in society. Police enforcement is, of course, another essential element. If there is no enforcement, things aren't going to improve. If drivers sense that there are certain violations the police don't respond to or don't have the resources to respond to, some drivers will start taking advantage of that," Vane said.

Vane also noted that under the implementation plan for Estonia's national road safety program, one important measure is lowering speed limits in built-up areas, which directly improves pedestrians' chances of surviving a collision.

Vane said traffic conditions in municipalities are largely determined by political decisions made by local authorities, although the state can still set the overall direction.

"The state can do that through the road safety program's implementation plan, which includes lowering speed limits in built-up areas as one of its measures. The question is always whether it will actually be implemented — that's often a political decision that leads to endless wrangling, but the state has set out the direction and the idea," Vane said.

World.title: Iraq Ministry of Oil inks deal with Japan’s JGC to resume FCC project
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Friday, August 14, 2026, an agreement with Japan’s JGC Corporation to officially resume construction and operational work on the massive Fluid Catalytic Cracking (FCC) complex at the South Refineries Company (SRC) in Basra.

The deal follows negotiations led by a ministerial committee under directives from Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair Al-Abadi, chaired by Ministry Advisor Hamid Younis alongside SRC Director General Hussam Hussein Wali. Under the finalized agreement, JGC remobilized its technical personnel to the Basra site starting August 10 to prepare processing units for full design-capacity operations, advancing Iraq’s target of refined petroleum self-sufficiency.

Key Operational Deliverables & Production Capacity

High-Octane Gasoline: Adding 5 million liters per day to domestic fuel supplies.

Gas Oil (Diesel): Producing approximately 7 million liters per day.

Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG): Delivering 400 metric tons per day for commercial and domestic consumption.

Project Milestone: Mobilization of JGC engineering teams began on August 10, 2026, to finalize site preparations and run commissioning sequences.

Strategic Objective: Eliminating fuel import expenditures and converting heavy refining residues into high-value white petroleum products.

The FCC complex at the Shuaiba refinery in Basra is among Iraq’s most critical downstream modernization projects, designed to upgrade heavy vacuum gas oil into premium fuels.

By adding 12 million combined liters of daily gasoline and diesel alongside substantial LPG yields, the facility will significantly curtail state spending on imported refined fuels and support domestic market stability.

World.title: Iraq customs revenues hit 2.5 trillion IQD in Seven Months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s General Customs Authority collected 2.5 trillion Iraqi Dinars (approximately $1.9 billion) in revenues during the first seven months of 2026, matching total receipts recorded for the entirety of 2025, Director-General Thamer Qasim Al-Taie announced on Saturday, August 15, 2026.

Speaking to state-run Al Iraqiya News, Al-Taie stated that July alone generated 560 billion IQD, representing a 150% year-on-year surge compared to July 2025. With revenue collection accelerating across all federal border crossings, full-year receipts are projected to surpass 3.5 trillion IQD ($2.67 billion)—the highest annual total in modern Iraqi state history.

Key Revenue Indicators & Technical Upgrades

Seven-Month Total:2.5 trillion IQD (~$1.9B) collected through July 2026, equaling full-year 2025 custom receipts.

July Revenue Surge: Recorded 560 billion IQD, a 150% increase compared to July 2025.

Annual Projection: Forecasted to exceed 3.5 trillion IQD (~$2.67B) by year-end 2026, setting a national historical record.

Automation & Anti-Corruption: Revenue jumps were driven by the nationwide rollout of SCADA systems, automated customs processing, and integrated digital networks connecting border crossings with government agencies, drastically curbing tariff evasion and illicit clearances.

The sharp rise in customs collections reflects Baghdad’s wider push to modernize border controls, plug financial leakages, and reduce structural dependence on crude oil sales amid regional market volatility.

By implementing mandatory automated documentation and digital data-sharing across federal transit checkpoints, the Customs Authority has systematically reduced tariff evasion, accelerated cargo clearances, and fortified federal non-oil revenue streams.

World.title: Popular Lebanese restaurant Al Beiruti to open in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Al Beiruti, a popular Lebanese restaurant, is set to build its first Iraqi branch in Iraq Mall in Baghdad, adding another significant regional dining name to the capital’s growing restaurant scene.

The Baghdad inauguration will be the next chapter of Al Beiruti’s regional development, after previous launches in Jordan and Qatar, as well as its established presence in the UAE.

The restaurant announced that its Iraq Mall restaurant is about to open, with a local franchise arrangement handling the expansion.

Al Beiruti has become a renowned location for Lebanese food in the Middle East, providing both classic dishes and a more modern restaurant experience.

The menu includes Lebanese favorites, including manakish, fattoush, hummus, baba ghanouj, and grilled halloumi, as well as shawarma, wraps, and mixed grills. Larger meals include steak, chicken escalope, and grilled salmon.

Al Beiruti joins a growing number of international and regional food and beverage companies in Baghdad, as new malls and commercial expansions change the city’s retail and entertainment markets.

Iraq Mall has emerged as a focal point of that expansion, drawing new restaurants, boutiques, and entertainment ideas as consumer spending and private-sector investment continue to rise in the capital.

World.title: Baghdad and Erbil agree on unified digital customs system across Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Baghdad and Erbil have agreed to fully adopt the digital ASYCUDA customs system across border crossings, with non-oil border earnings shared equally by the federal and Kurdistan regional governments.

The deal is a significant step toward standardizing customs processes across Iraq and addressing long-standing disagreements over border revenues and claimed import quantities.

ASYCUDA, designed by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), digitizes customs declarations, payments, and clearing processes, allowing authorities to better monitor products entering the nation and the income they earn.

Linking customs operations to Iraq’s banking and electronic payment systems may help limit the potential for underreporting, revenue leakage, and corruption at border crossings.

The deal comes as Iraq’s Finance Ministry and Central Bank work to digitize customs, payments, and government financial data in collaboration with UNCTAD.

A combined computerized customs system for Baghdad and Erbil might give more accurate revenue data while resolving one of the two governments’ ongoing financial issues.

The change is also significant for Iraq’s overall economy.

More open and uniform customs processes might facilitate cross-border commerce, boost governmental revenues, and enhance the business climate as Iraq pursues more foreign investment and closer integration with international markets.

World.title: Iraq’s Chief Justice Faiq Zidan meets Syrian President Al-Sharaa in Damascus
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zidan met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus on Thursday, marking another high-level Iraqi outreach to a neighboring Arab state as Baghdad seeks to bolster regional relations under rising security problems.

Al-Sharaa welcomed Zidan and an Iraqi delegation to the People’s Palace, which also included Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Justice Minister Mazhar al-Wais.

According to the Syrian president, the talks focused on extending judicial and legal cooperation between Iraq and Syria, as well as resolving mutual concerns.

The visit also resulted in more practical conversations among the two nations’ judicial officials. Iraqi and Syrian authorities agreed to set up joint judicial committees to continue working on cases involving Syrian prisoners and other cross-border legal issues.

Zidan’s visit is crucial as he is one of the most prominent persons in Iraq’s state institutions, and it coincides with Baghdad’s increased diplomatic, security, and judicial interaction with its neighbors.

The Damascus meetings come after a separate Iraqi security group visited Riyadh, where senior military official Abdul Amir al-Shammari met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman.

Zidan had also just visited Ankara as part of a larger Iraqi effort to build ties with Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Turkey.

That approach has become more urgent in light of the regional escalation involving Iran-backed Iraqi forces.

In late July, the United States and Saudi Arabia conducted synchronized attacks against locations used by Iran-aligned organizations in Iraq, after Riyadh accused militias operating from Iraqi territory of firing drones against Saudi energy infrastructure.

The incident put Baghdad under strong pressure to prevent armed organizations from exploiting Iraqi territory to launch assaults on neighboring nations and also highlighted the potential that militia activity may harm Iraq’s improved ties with Arab governments.

Against this setting, Zidan’s encounter with Al-Sharaa is significant beyond regular court cooperation.

Iraq and Syria share a long border and confront shared concerns such as terrorism, organized crime, prisoners, and cross-border security. Baghdad also has a strategic interest in preserving stable ties with Damascus, as Iraq strives to boost regional connections and prevent unrest from spilling over its borders.

Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s administration sees recent diplomatic efforts as part of a larger effort to strengthen Iraq’s ties with its neighbors while keeping the nation out of the developing conflict between Iran and its regional adversaries.

Baghdad has increasingly emphasized that choices on security, armament, and relations with neighboring governments must be made by Iraqi official authorities rather than armed groupings.

The travels to Damascus and Riyadh therefore convey an essential message: although Iran-aligned militias have exacerbated tensions between Iraq and certain of its neighbors, Iraqi official institutions are working directly with those nations to restore cooperation and avoid further escalation.

Strengthening judicial, diplomatic, and security ties with Syria, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey might serve as an essential regional buffer for Iraq as it seeks to safeguard its sovereignty, control armed groups, and avoid being drawn further into the region’s crises.

World.title: Iraq’s Al-Shammari visits Riyadh to meet Saudi Defense Minister
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — A top Iraqi security team has traveled to Riyadh for meetings with Saudi Arabia’s leadership, as Baghdad and the Kingdom work to improve security and military cooperation after weeks of heightened tensions in Iraq involving Iran-backed militias.

First Lieutenant General Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman on Thursday to discuss military cooperation, regional developments, and increased coordination between the two nations.

According to reports from the visit, the conversations included cross-border drone concerns, air defense, and intelligence collaboration.

The conference is especially significant in light of the combined US-Saudi attacks on Iran-linked militia locations in Iraq on July 29.

Washington and Riyadh said the operation targeted Iran-backed terrorists’ weapons and logistical facilities in response to a series of drone assaults on Saudi oil installations that they said originated in Iraqi territory.

The strikes drastically escalated tensions between Baghdad and Riyadh, highlighting the Iraqi government’s problems in preventing armed groups from exploiting its territory to target neighboring nations.

Thursday’s visit indicates that both parties are now attempting to move beyond that conflict via direct military and intelligence collaboration.

Prince Khalid underlined Saudi Arabia’s commitment to Iraq’s security, stability, and economic growth, identifying it as an essential neighbor with whom the Kingdom has strong political and social relations.

The meetings in Riyadh follow Saudi intelligence head Khalid bin Ali al-Humaidan’s visit to Baghdad last week, during which he met with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and reiterated an offer for the Iraqi leader to visit Saudi Arabia.

Baghdad’s security cooperation with Riyadh has grown more vital as the government seeks to prevent Iran-backed militias from drawing Iraq into a larger regional conflict.

Al-Zaidi has frequently said that Iraqi soil should not be used to attack other nations and has stepped up efforts for weaponry to be put solely under state control.

The most recent Iraqi trip to Riyadh symbolizes more than just normal defense diplomacy. It is part of a joint effort by Baghdad and Saudi Arabia to restore security trust after the July escalation and prevent militia activities from dragging the two neighboring nations into conflict.

World.title: Rare blind fish found in underground river in Iraq’s Anbar desert
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security and environmental teams have discovered a fascinating underground water system deep under the dry Anbar desert, where rare eyeless fish thrive in total darkness.

The location is in the Al-Khasfa region near Haditha, and crews traveled through a remote desert cave and sinkhole system to access running groundwater hundreds of meters under the surface.

The expedition’s footage shows little, pale fish moving in the subterranean water in the lack of sunshine.

The fish have evolved to live in darkness by losing their eyes and pigmentation, giving them a characteristic white-to-pink look.

The crew traveled more than 500 meters into the cave system despite challenging terrain and low oxygen levels.

The difference between above- and underground has piqued interest: underneath what seems to be an isolated and very arid stretch of western Iraqi desert, there is flowing freshwater and a specialized ecology.

Initial investigations have also suggested a link between the subterranean water system and the Euphrates basin, with the watercourse possibly running for a long distance under the desert.

However, environmental experts have highlighted that the blind fish themselves are not a novel finding.

Qais Najeh, the chairman of the Anbar Environment Directorate, stated that experts first confirmed the occurrence of eyeless fish in Al-Khasfa in 2010.

Similar fish have also been discovered in subterranean water near the Sheik Hadid mausoleum in Haditha district.

According to experts, the fish may grow to be roughly 49 millimeters long and survive in rather steady groundwater temperatures ranging from 20 to 22 degrees Celsius.

Their lack of vision and pigmentation are adaptations to generations of living in perpetually dark subterranean habitats.

The recent mission is nonetheless noteworthy because it has refocused attention on one of Iraq’s least-known natural ecosystems, perhaps allowing scientists to better research the subterranean water network, its geology, and the creatures that rely on it.

The fish’s severely limited environment renders it vulnerable.

Changes in groundwater levels, pollution, or human intervention might endanger a population that has acclimated to highly particular subsurface circumstances.

The Al-Khasfa location offers a unique dimension to Anbar, a region best known for its wide western desert and the Euphrates.

Hidden under that terrain lies an environment few Iraqis have ever seen: flowing subterranean water that feeds fish who have evolved to survive their entire lives without sunshine.

World.title: Israel reopens once-closed West Bank settlement
World.content:
GANIM – Israel officially reopened the West Bank settlement of Ganim on Thursday, more than 20 years after it withdrew from the community, in a move emblematic of the current government’s policy of rapid settlement expansion.

The smell of freshly-poured asphalt hung in the air above Ganim’s new and only street, where future residents and their families — who had come to help with the move — smiled at the sight of their pre-fabricated homes.

“A month ago there was nothing here. A rocky mountain, barely any trees, barely any shade. We’re arriving now,” new resident Reut Baran, 35, told AFP in front of her new home.

In a nearby truck, dozens of brand new air conditioning units still in their boxes were waiting to be installed.

Matan Berkovitch, a 25-year-old who moved into the new settlement with his wife and child, said he was satisfied with the government’s policy towards settlements as he looked around a brand new home just connected to the electric grid.

“I’m happy to be part of a time like this where there are ministers in the government who support and guide us in the right direction and know how to get things done properly,” he said.

Berkovitch’s mother Carmit, who came from Jerusalem to move him in, said another one of her sons would soon study at the religious school in the settlement, and expressed pride at their active part in the settler movement.

“Here, this is the Land of Israel. Here, we are staying forever,” Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said at the ceremony, after arriving by helicopter.

Ganim is one of four Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank that Israel evacuated under former prime minister Ariel Sharon’s disengagement plan in 2005.

The move came partly because of their isolated location in the north of the territory among many Palestinian cities and villages.

Under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, settlement construction and expansion have soared, including with the official re-establishment of three of the four evacuated communities — Ganim, Sa-Nur and Homesh.

In Ganim, about two dozen pre-fabricated homes have already been installed, while steamrollers and other construction machinery busily created new space for future houses on the hillside on Thursday.

About a hundred people from Israel and other West Bank settlements attended the ceremony, including Katz and Yossi Dagan, head of the Israeli authority in charge of settlements in the northern West Bank.

“The era of evacuation is over — from here, we only build,” Dagan said.

In the valley below, Palestinians who spoke to AFP feared Ganim’s construction would make their lives harder, or even mean eventual displacement.

On both sides of the road leading to the settlement from Israel, the army has demolished stores in recent days and blocked several dirt roads to Palestinian communities with piles of rubble.

Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the territory, which are illegal under international law, among some three million Palestinians.

Violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers has increased dramatically since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas from the Gaza Strip.

World.title: 100GW of nuclear power by 2047, 5 reactors this decade: Inside PM Modi's energy self-reliance plan
World.content:
Target of 100 GW of nuclear energy by 2047, 5 new nuclear reactors to be operational within 6-7 years: PM Modi

India enters second stage of three-stage nuclear programme

Why PFBR matters for India's nuclear expansion

Nuclear power seen as key to meeting rising electricity demand

India targets 500 GW renewable energy by 2030

SHANTI Act seeks to reshape India's nuclear power framework

Indiaâs nuclear capacity to expand from 8.78 GW

Five reactors to be operationalised this decade

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Nuclear power and India's 2070 net-zero target

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday announced an expansion of India's ambitious nuclear power programme, setting a target of 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047.PM Modi said five new nuclear reactors would be operationalised during this decade as the country seeks greater energy security and self-reliance.Addressing the nation from the ramparts of the Red Fort on the 80th Independence Day, PM Modi said India had taken an important step towards self-reliance in nuclear energy with the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu attaining first criticality in April this year.PM Modi said nuclear power would be an important component of India's energy security as demand for electricity rises with the expansion of technologies such as semiconductors, artificial intelligence and data centres. He also referred to the government's nuclear policy reforms and the SHANTI Act, enacted in December 2025, as part of efforts to expand the sector.âThe new world cannot run without energy. Whether they are (semiconductor) chips, AI or data centres, the country needs lots of electricity â¦ Thatâs why we have already taken strong steps to ensure energy security,â he added.PM Modi said India had set the goal of reaching 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047, with five new reactors expected to become operational in the current decade.The PFBR at Kalpakkam marks India's entry into the second stage of its three-stage nuclear power programme, originally conceived by Homi J Bhabha.The 500 MWe reactor, developed and built indigenously at the Kalpakkam Nuclear Complex, attained first criticality on April 6, 2026. It is being built by Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited, or BHAVINI, under the Department of Atomic Energy, with technology developed by the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research.The first stage of India's nuclear programme relies on Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors, or PHWRs, which use natural uranium as fuel and produce plutonium as a byproduct.The second stage uses this plutonium in fast breeder reactors. The PFBR uses uranium-plutonium mixed oxide, or MOX, fuel and is designed to produce more fissile material than it consumes.The third stage of the programme is aimed at using India's large thorium reserves to produce uranium-233 for nuclear power generation.The PFBR is therefore intended to serve as a bridge between India's existing uranium-based nuclear programme and its longer-term thorium-based energy strategy.The PFBR is a 500 MWe sodium-cooled fast breeder reactor designed to use plutonium-based fuel while breeding additional fissile material.A blanket of uranium-238 around the reactor core can be converted into plutonium-239 through the action of fast neutrons. This allows the reactor to generate electricity while producing additional fuel.The reactor's technology is particularly relevant to India's nuclear strategy because the country has relatively limited uranium resources but substantial thorium reserves.The Department of Atomic Energy has said the PFBR will eventually help lay the foundation for the third stage of India's nuclear programme, in which thorium would be used to produce uranium-233.PM Modi had earlier described the PFBR milestone as a major development in India's civil nuclear programme.âToday, India takes a defining step in its civil nuclear journey, advancing the second stage of its nuclear programme.âPM Modi had also said, âThis advanced reactor, capable of producing more fuel than it consumes, reflects the depth of our scientific capability and the strength of our engineering enterprise. It is a decisive step towards harnessing our vast thorium reserves in the third stage of the programme.âIn his Independence Day address, PM Modi linked India's nuclear expansion with the country's rapidly increasing demand for electricity.He pointed to the growing power requirements of semiconductor manufacturing, artificial intelligence and data centres, saying energy security would become increasingly important as India expands its technology and manufacturing sectors.âIt is difficult to build a new world. That is why, whether it is a chip, AI, or data centre, we need electricity in large quantity. The new era demands energy.âPM Modi said India had taken steps to strengthen energy security by expanding both nuclear and renewable energy capacity.He said nuclear energy was vital for ensuring a stable supply of electricity while the country simultaneously expands solar, wind and other renewable sources.Alongside the nuclear expansion, PM Modi highlighted the growth of India's renewable energy capacity.He said India's solar energy capacity had risen from 2 GW in 2014 to 160 GW, while the country had set a target of 500 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030.PM Modi also referred to the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, saying around 50 lakh households had been covered under the rooftop solar programme.Thousands of consumers, he said, were also earning through electricity generated from rooftop solar systems.Beneficiaries under the scheme can receive a subsidy of up to Rs 80,000 per household for installing rooftop solar systems.PM Modi also said India's railway electrification had expanded sharply, helping reduce diesel consumption and imports.He said India had also started work on a hydrogen train as part of its broader clean-energy transition.PM Modi also referred to the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India, or SHANTI Act, enacted in December 2025.The legislation is intended to modernise India's nuclear legal framework and facilitate greater participation in the nuclear sector under regulatory oversight.The law forms part of the government's broader effort to expand nuclear power capacity and bring new investment and technology into the sector.The Union Budget 2025-26 had also announced a Nuclear Energy Mission with an allocation of Rs 20,000 crore for the design, development and deployment of Small Modular Reactors.The government has set a target of having at least five indigenously designed small modular reactors operational by 2033.India's installed nuclear power capacity currently stands at around 8.78 GW, according to government data.Nuclear power accounted for about 3.1% of India's electricity generation in 2024-25, when nuclear plants generated 56,681 million units of electricity.The government has projected that India's nuclear capacity could reach around 22.38 GW by 2031-32 through the development of indigenous 700 MW reactors and larger reactors being developed through international cooperation.The 100 GW target by 2047 would therefore require a substantial expansion in both the number and scale of nuclear power projects over the next two decades.PM Modi said India would operationalise five nuclear reactors during the current decade as part of its push towards greater nuclear capacity.The expansion is expected to involve multiple reactor technologies, including India's indigenous PHWR designs and advanced reactor technologies.The government is also developing small modular reactor designs, including the 200 MWe Bharat Small Modular Reactor and the 55 MWe SMR-55, as well as other advanced reactor concepts.The expansion is aimed at increasing the contribution of nuclear energy to India's electricity mix while maintaining the country's broader clean-energy and net-zero commitments.The expansion of nuclear power is also linked to India's commitment to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2070.Unlike solar and wind power, nuclear reactors can provide continuous electricity and are not dependent on weather conditions. This makes nuclear generation a potential source of firm, low-carbon electricity alongside renewable energy.The government has therefore positioned nuclear power as part of a wider energy mix that includes solar, wind, hydrogen and other clean-energy sources.PM Modi's announcement of the 100 GW target marks a substantial increase in India's long-term nuclear ambitions and places nuclear power at the centre of the country's energy security strategy as it works towards the Viksit Bharat 2047 goal.

World.title: 'Public services neglected': CJP's new campaign to check facilities at public hospitals
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on Saturday announced its plans to launch a statewide campaign to assess the condition of public hospitals in Maharashtra. The organisation's founder, Abhijeet Dipke, alleged that patients are forced to endure long delays and poor facilities in government-run healthcare institutions.

The announcement came as the party expanded its broader push to scrutinise public welfare infrastructure after launching its âSchool Thik Karoâ campaign, which seeks to audit basic amenities in government schools across Maharashtra and eventually nationwide.

Addressing reporters during a visit to his native village in Hingoli district, Dipke said the CJP would now focus on healthcare facilities in public hospitals.

âWe are going to raise health-related issues. When we visit public hospitals, we see people sleeping on the floor. People have to wait for surgeries. For a CT scan, the wait extends to one week,â he alleged.

Dipke said the proposed campaign would examine the condition of government hospitals and document deficiencies in infrastructure and access to treatment. He further argued that essential public services have been neglected.





The hospital initiative follows the launch of the CJPâs âSchool Thik Karoâ campaign, under which party workers are collecting data on basic facilities in government schools, including drinking water, toilets, benches, windows and overall infrastructure. Dipke has repeatedly argued that the government must improve public institutions that serve ordinary citizens, particularly students and patients.

He said the party believes that public well-being facilities, including schools and hospitals, require greater accountability and better utilisation of government funds.

During the school campaign launch, Dipke had questioned why basic amenities remained unavailable in many government schools despite decades of public spending, and accused successive governments of neglecting state-run institutions. He has also alleged that poor infrastructure in public facilities disproportionately affects children and low-income families.

The CJP convenor said the hospital campaign would similarly highlight issues faced by patients who depend on government healthcare, including overcrowding, delays in surgeries and diagnostic tests, and inadequate infrastructure.

The party has said it intends to use findings from both campaigns to press governments for improvements in public education and healthcare infrastructure across Maharashtra.

World.title: ‘Ireland’s Independence Day?’ Congress mocks PM Modi over Tricolour pocket square
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The

on Saturday took a swipe at Prime Minister Narendra Modi over the tricolour pocket square he wore during his Independence Day address from the Red Fort.

Congress leader Pawan Khera shared a picture of Modi's outfit on X and sarcastically questioned the design of the pocket square, suggesting that it resembled the Irish tricolour.

In his post, Khera wrote, "

Lagta hai sahib ne Urdu mein Tiranga pehna hai. Ya phir Bharat India ki jagah Ireland ka Independence Day mana rahay hain

. (Looks like the sahib is wearing the Tricolour in Urdu. Or perhaps, instead of India, he is celebrating Ireland's Independence Day)."

The remark came as India marked its 80th Independence Day, with this year's celebrations being held under the theme 'Yuva Shakti for Viksit Bharat@2047'.

Modi delivered his 13th consecutive Independence Day address from the Red Fort, continuing a tradition that began with his first such speech in 2014.

For the occasion, the Prime Minister wore a red safa featuring yellow and white Bandhani patterns, along with a white kurta and pyjama. He completed the outfit with a brown Nehru jacket and a tricolour pocket square.

World.title: BJP says Sonia objected to full Vande Mataram; Congress says she was seeking chair for Kharge
World.content:
Sonia Gandhiâs Vande Mataram row: BJP alleges âhatredâ, Congress calls claim false

Congress rejects BJP's allegation

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

BJP escalates attack

NEW DELHI: A political row erupted on Saturday over the rendition of the full version of Vande Mataram at the Congress's Independence Day event, with the BJP accusing grand old party's former chief Sonia Gandhi of objecting to the national song and the opposition party rejecting the allegation.The BJP shared video footage from the Congress's event at Indira Bhawan and alleged that Sonia questioned party workers while Vande Mataram was being played. Congress, however, said there was no attempt to stop the full rendition and that Sonia was merely asking for a chair for party president Mallikarjun Kharge, who had been standing for some time.BJP spokesperson Gopal Krishna Agarwal, sharing the footage on X, accused the Congress of showing disrespect towards the national song. "The scene that has come to light today on Independence Day is utterly shameful."He said, "Sonia Gandhi's objection during the rendition of India's national song, 'Vande Mataram', and her questioning of Congress workers as to why it was being played exposes the Congress party's mindset."Agarwal said Vande Mataram represented more than a patriotic song, calling it a symbol of India's freedom struggle and national consciousness."Is this the same Congress that lays claim to the legacy of the nation's freedom struggle?" he asked.He also alleged that the Congress's alleged approach towards the national song reflected the party's "Emergency mindset"."The people of the country have rejected this mindset and will continue to reject it," he said.The Congress dismissed the BJP's claim and maintained that the full version of Vande Mataram was sung at its Independence Day programme.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh cited the party's historical association with the song and referred to a 1937 meeting of the Congress Working Committee in Calcutta, attended by several prominent leaders of the freedom movement."On October 28, 1937, in Calcutta, a meeting of the Congress Working Committee was held in the presence of Mahatma Gandhi, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, Jawaharlal Nehru, Govind Ballabh Pant and C Rajagopalachari, and on the advice of Gurudev Rabindranath Tagore, they decided that the initial stanzas of Vande Mataram would be sung at the Congress sessions," Ramesh said.Ramesh said Tagore had advised Nehru and Bose that the opening portions of the song should be used at Congress gatherings."Tagore gave the advice to Nehru and Bose that the first few paragraphs of Vande Mataram should be used, he said."We have been singing those lines in every session since them, our Seva Dal sings it, our workers sing it, there is no controversy over that," Ramesh said."He stressed that the complete version was sung at Saturday's event and said the issue had already been debated extensively in Parliament."This was discussed in Parliament for 16 hours. We put forward our views. I narrated the whole history around it which the prime minister and the home minister did not know. I informed MPs of the context in which the Vande Mataram decision was taken," Ramesh said."But today, at Indira Bhawan, the full version was sung, there is no question of a controversy over it," he added.Asked specifically about the BJP's allegation that Sonia had tried to stop the full rendition, Ramesh offered a different explanation for what was seen in the video."As the Congress president was standing for a long time, Soniaji was asking for a chair for him," he said.BJP spokesperson R P Singh also targeted Sonia over the controversy, questioning her alleged opposition to the national song."Why does Antonio Maino Ji hate Vande Mataram so much? When Vande Mataram was being sung, Antonio Maino Ji reportedly became so angry that she allegedly got agitated and asked her party workers to stop it. Why such hatred for Vande Mataram?"The row over Vande Mataram comes shortly after Parliament passed legislation dealing with disrespect towards the national song. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, was passed by the Lok Sabha through a voice vote on July 30, a day after the Rajya Sabha cleared it.The legislation grants Vande Mataram a status on par with the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana.

World.title: Arunachal Pradesh flash floods: Four killed, five Army personnel missing after landslide
World.content:
Five Army personnel missing after flash flood

NEW DELHI: Five Army personnel went missing after a heavy rain-triggered flash flood washed away two shelters in Arunachal Pradesh's Dibang Valley district, while a major landslide at a road construction site in Upper Subansiri district claimed four lives, officials told news agency PTI on Saturday.Both incidents took place on Friday evening, according to the state emergency operations centre.In Upper Subansiri district, a major landslide struck the Keojaring-Byaching road construction site, burying several people under debris. Four people, Tadu Baki, Taji Rai, Markosh Basumatari and Babul Ali, were reported dead.The body of Babul Ali has been recovered, the district disaster management officer of Upper Subansiri said.Personnel from Nacho Police Station have been deployed for search and recovery operations. Fire and Emergency Services teams are being mobilised from Daporijo, while a State Disaster Response Force team will join the operation.In Dibang Valley district, a flash flood triggered by heavy rainfall swept away two shelters at the 5th Grenadier's Pasu Pani Army camp on Friday evening.Seven Army personnel were swept away in the flash flood, officials said.Two were rescued, while five remain missing.The missing personnel have been identified as Havaldar Upendar and Army personnel Kundan, Vinod, Aditya and Samunda.Two search and rescue teams from the 5th Grenadier have been deployed to locate the missing personnel.Teams from the 58th Battalion of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), 62 RCC of the General Reserve Engineer Force, Arunachal Pradesh Police and local volunteers have also been rushed to the area.An SDRF team from Pasighat is proceeding to Anini to assist in the search and rescue operation.

World.title: 'Warmest congratulations': World leaders wish India 80th Independence Day, hail growing ties
World.content:
NEW DELHI: From Washington and Jerusalem to Singapore and Kathmandu, leaders and institutions across the world extended greetings to India on Saturday as the country marked its 80th Independence Day, highlighting the strength of bilateral ties and the breadth of cooperation with New Delhi.

Israel

Israelâs president Isaac Herzog congratulated President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the people of India.

âOn behalf of the State of Israel, I warmly congratulate President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and the wonderful people of India on your 80th Independence Day! May we continue to strengthen the beautiful friendship between Israel and India,â Herzog wrote on X. He also posted his wishes in Hindi.

The message came after Modi and his Israeli counterpart Benjamin Netanyahu reviewed progress in the India-Israel Special Strategic Partnership and discussed the situation in West Asia during a recent phone call.

United States

US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the India-US relationship continues to grow and is âstronger than everâ.

âOn behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm congratulations to the people of India on their Independence Day.





Thanks to the personal relationship between President Trump and Prime Minister Modi, the U.S.-India relationship continues to grow and is stronger than ever,â Rubio said.

He highlighted cooperation in defence, energy security, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, space cooperation and commerce.

âFrom defence and energy security to critical minerals, artificial intelligence, space cooperation, and commerce, our collaboration is making both of our nations, and the broader Indian Ocean region, safer, stronger, and more prosperous,â Rubio said.

He added: âThe United States looks forward to the future our two countries will build together.â

Singapore

Singapore president Tharman Shanmugaratnam congratulated India on the âjoyous occasionâ and underscored the countriesâ Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.

âOn behalf of the people of Singapore, I extend my warmest congratulations to Your Excellency and the people of India on the joyous occasion of India's 80th Independence Day,â Tharman wrote in a letter addressed to President Murmu.

He also pointed to close people-to-people ties and expanding cooperation in skills development, digitalisation, sustainability and advanced manufacturing.

Nepal

Nepal prime minister Balendra âBalenâ Shah extended greetings and best wishes to PM Modi, the Government of India and the people of India.

âOn the occasion of India's 80th Independence Day, I extend my heartfelt greetings and best wishes to PM Narendra Modi and the friendly people and Government of India,â the Office of the Prime Minister of Nepal said in a post on X.

Maldives

Maldives president Mohamed Muizzu also joined the global chorus of greetings, extending his âwarmest greetingsâ to the President and PM Modi on the countryâs 80th Independence Day. Muizzu said eight decades of independence reflected Indiaâs âaspirations, resilience and enduring spiritâ and reaffirmed Maleâs commitment to advancing the close partnership between the two countries, built on âmutual respect, shared prosperity and enduring friendshipâ.

Additionally, the former president, Ibrahim Mohamed Solih also greeted India, writing, âWarm felicitations to President Murmu, PM Narendra Modi, and our dear friends, the people of India, on the occasion of India's Independence Day." He described Indiaâs journey since 1947 as an inspiration and said, âMay the close ties of cooperation and friendship that exist between Maldives-India grow ever stronger.â

World.title: With nearly 40 mentions, ‘Mere pyare deshwasiyon’ dominates PM Modi’s Red Fort speech
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister

on Saturday addressed the nation from the ramparts of the iconic Red Fort in Delhi as the country celebrated its 80th

.

His 75-minute speech featured nearly 40 mentions of âMere pyare deshwasiyonâ (my beloved fellow citizens), making it the most-used phrase in his address.

âSaathiyonâ (friends) was the second-most used phrase, featuring 10 times in the speech.

He also used âmere pyare yuvaâ (my beloved youth) once while calling on young people to join the fight against drugs and other addictions.

The prime minister also used âdesh sevakâ (those who serve the nation) and âbhai behenoâ (brothers and sisters) once each.

Over the years, âdeshwashiyonâ (fellow citizens) has remained PM Modiâs go-to term for addressing the nation during his Independence Day speeches.

He used the term 50 times last year, around 30 times in 2024, nearly 15 times in 2023 and more than 40 times in 2022. In 2023, however, his preferred form of address was âparivaarjanâ (family member), which he used around 50 times.

âSaathiyonâ has also featured regularly in his Independence Day speeches. Modi used the term around 35 times in 2025, nearly 30 times in 2024, about five times in 2023 and approximately eight times in 2022.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines





Meanwhile, the prime ministerâs 2026 Independence Day speech was the fourth-shortest among his 13 consecutive August 15 addresses since his first in 2014. Saturdayâs address was also his shortest in four years.

His 2025 speech was his longest at 103 minutes, surpassing his previous record of 98 minutes in 2024. His shortest Independence Day address came in 2017, when he spoke for 56 minutes.

PM Modiâs first Independence Day address in 2014 lasted 65 minutes. Since then, his speeches have ranged from under an hour to more than 100 minutes. He spoke for 88 minutes in 2015, 96 minutes in 2016, 83 minutes in 2018 and nearly 92 minutes in 2019.

His address lasted 90 minutes in 2020, 88 minutes in 2021, 74 minutes in 2022 and 90 minutes in 2023.
