World.title: US to tell partners they must pick sides in AI race with China
World.content:
US-CHINA RIVALRY. US and Chinese flags are seen in this illustration created on April 10, 2025

'Signature of the Pax Silica Declaration is not merely a membership subscription, but a commitment,' a leaked draft letter from the US State Department says, urging countries to 'choose deliberately' on AI

WASHINGTON, US – The US is preparing to tell dozens of countries they must pick sides in the artificial intelligence race with China, warning they will be excluded from a US-led AI coalition if they also 

Washington last year launched the Pax Silica initiative aimed at securing supply chains for AI models, semiconductors and critical minerals, amid a fierce technology rivalry with Beijing.

About two dozen countries have joined, including Kazakhstan, a key potential source of critical minerals that has also joined China’s coalition, as well as close US allies such as Japan, Australia and South Korea.

The draft letter, prepared by the State Department, is addressed to the 35 signatories of a US “AI Opportunity Statement” signed in June, which includes members of the non-binding Pax Silica framework and other countries that have expressed a desire to align cooperation on AI with Washington.

By pressing countries to choose sides the US hopes to starve China of resources in a race to make the most sophisticated AI, which could be used for military or economic dominance.

In July, Chinese President ​Xi Jinping launched a rival “World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization,” promoting his country’s open-weight technology as a challenge to US influence over ‌the fast-moving sector.

Kazakhstan is the only country so far known to have joined both initiatives, setting off alarm bells in Washington.

“To be part of everything is to be part of nothing. Signature of the Pax Silica Declaration is not merely a membership subscription, but a commitment,” the letter says, urging countries to “choose deliberately” on AI.

“It cannot be held alongside membership in duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with our own,” the letter said, without specifically mentioning China.

Reuters could not determine when the US intends to send the letter or whether it might be amended before sending. The draft was undated.

The State Department told Reuters it would not comment on “purportedly leaked internal documents.”

The Chinese and Kazakh embassies in Washington did not respond immediately to requests for comment.

‘Can’t have it both ways’

The Pax Silica agreement aims to push US allies and partners toward joint projects and export controls, and ultimately reduce reliance on adversaries for critical minerals, AI models and the semiconductor chips that power them.

The race between the US and China for technological leadership has reached a pivotal moment, as Chinese open-weight AI models have made rapid gains against proprietary systems from US companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

The exponential growth of the technology’s capabilities, including the ability to hack autonomously, has forced a global reckoning over its power.

Beijing is weighing restrictions on overseas access to some ​of China’s leading AI models, highlighting the growing tension with its stringent national security agenda.

The US touted Kazakhstan in June as the first country in Central Asia to join Pax Silica, bringing significant reserves of critical minerals that fuel advanced technologies.

China has used its current near-monopolies over critical minerals as a retaliatory weapon in a tariff war launched last year by US President Donald Trump, who has ramped up US efforts to source the minerals domestically and from allies.

Members of Pax Silica have access to shared investment opportunities in AI-related projects while those who sign the AI Opportunity Statement have symbolically agreed on a “common purpose” and “shared vision” with the US, according to the statement posted on the State Department’s website.

US officials drafted the letter to make clear that “you can’t have it both ways,” the US official told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity given ongoing internal discussions on the issue.

“It’s difficult to see how a country can credibly position themselves as trusted partners in one technology ecosystem while simultaneously signing up for an initiative designed by China to advance a competing vision for AI,” the official said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Iran defiant on strait as Trump tells Americans to accept high gas prices
World.content:
Iran urges the US to accept defeat as Trump warns of high fuel prices amid ongoing conflict, with peace talks stalled and Strait of Hormuz traffic severely impacted

NEW YORK, US – Iran called on the US to accept defeat while President Donald Trump blasted Iran as “evil” and urged Americans to brace for continued high fuel prices.

The comments suggested the warring parties remained far apart, with progress toward peace talks and oil tanker traffic through the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway both halted.

“This strait will be opened and closed only under Iran’s command, and so long as you do not accept the reality of defeat and stop indulging in fantasies, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade,” Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a post on X early Saturday, showing little urgency toward restoring prewar trade.

“The Strait of Hormuz cannot be seized by a tweet or an aircraft carrier, by issuing an order or by delivering an election speech,” he said.

One out of every five barrels of the world’s oil exports passed through the strait before the US and Israel launched the war on February 28.

Trump on Friday urged Americans to accept slightly higher gasoline prices while the conflict with Iran continues.

At a political rally in Garden City, New York, Trump said paying “a tiny little bit more for your gasoline” is worth the cost of ensuring “a very evil country” could not have a nuclear weapon, one of the president’s stated rationales for the war.

In a trend that has fueled inflation and disappointed voters, the average U.S. price of a gallon of gasoline was about $4.08 on Friday, according to the American Automobile Association. That’s up 29% from $3.16 a year earlier.

Only two vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, according to analysis from ship-tracking firm Kpler: a grain ship entering Iranian waters and an empty dry bulk ship going the other direction. A separate empty liquefied petroleum products tanker was sailing into the Gulf via the strait, the data showed. There were no crude oil shipments visible.

Some ships may cross the strait undetected with their transponders off, but the figures are nowhere near the more than 130 ships that traversed it daily before the war.

Those that dare navigate the strait without Iranian permission risk missile or drone strikes. The United Arab Emirates’ Abu Dhabi National Oil Company said two of its vessels were attacked transiting the strait on Thursday evening, then the Emirati state news agency WAM reported another vessel came under attack on Friday.

Iran labels its enforcement of strait traffic a blockade, while the U.S. uses the same term for its threat against Iranian vessels leaving their ports.

“What we’re doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves … and we’re really doing a great job,” Trump said, adding that a 260-day deployment by a U.S. aircraft carrier supporting the war effort was “not nearly long enough.”

With a ⁠tentative June deal to end the war in tatters, there was no sign that the U.S. or Iran planned to resume peace talks.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said no decision has yet been made to restart negotiations with the United States, the ​Iranian Student News Agency reported on Saturday. Mediators Qatar and Pakistan were in contact with Iran and exchanging messages, but this did not amount to negotiations, the agency said.

Economic toll

Higher fuel prices have collided with a Trump campaign promise to lower energy costs, and Democrats are seeking to make economic fallout of the Iran war an issue in the November midterm elections.

The virtual closure of the strait helped raise crude oil futures another $1 a barrel on Friday. Benchmark Brent LCOc1 and West Texas Intermediate CLc1 futures were on track for weekly gains of 6.0% and 5.4%, respectively.

Gharibabadi said Tehran would not be intimidated by threats or a show of force. But there were signs of an economic toll on Iran.

In remarks broadcast on state television, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian blamed high inflation on a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and sanctions on Iran’s oil exports.

Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent each pledged to inflict more financial damage on Iran. Bessent told Newsmax’s “Rob Schmitt Tonight” program on Thursday that announcements of more measures against Iran were coming next week.

The latest attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis renewed concerns about a widening regional war. Yemen’s internationally recognized government said the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at the Red Sea port of Mocha on Friday, killing four civilians.

Separately, the Houthi-run SABA news agency cited a military source as saying the group had targeted an Aramco facility in the Saudi city of Najran with a drone. – Rappler.com

World.title: Japan’s record rains strand thousands at Narita airport, kill eight
World.content:
NARITA AIRPORT. Passengers queue to enter the train station after train lines and public transportation services were suspended due to heavy rain at the Narita International Airport in Narita, Chiba prefecture, Japan, August 14, 2026

Record rainfall — the highest over a 24-hour period since October 2013 — strands thousands at Narita airport, causing flooding and power outages in Chiba

CHIBA, Japan – Record rainfall in Japan stranded thousands of travellers at Tokyo’s Narita airport on Friday, bringing floods to the surrounding area that disrupted transport, knocked out power to 20,000 homes and killed eight.

During one of Japan’s busiest holiday weeks, more than 360 mm (14 inches) of rain fell in 24 hours in parts of the Chiba area adjoining Tokyo, inundating roads and railways, with soldiers sent to help with rescue efforts.

“This case was an extremely unusual situation,” Chiba Governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters. “I have responded to many disasters in the past, but I have never experienced a case like this.”

The eight dead included one person trapped in a submerged vehicle, public broadcaster NHK said, citing Chiba authorities and police.

At Narita, airport staff distributed sleeping bags, water and snacks to hundreds of passengers, many of whom had bedded down on Thursday after transport disruptions stranded about 7,000 people, causing widespread chaos.

“I queued for a taxi, but the wait was four hours,” said Minoru Yamasaki, a 48-year-old Chiba resident returning from holiday, who had booked a hotel only to be told it could not put him up. With nowhere else to go, he returned to the airport.

An airport spokesperson said most flights were expected to operate normally on Friday.

More than 20,000 homes were without power in the early hours of Friday, after rain flooded a power substation, utility Tokyo Electric Power said, while gas supply to nearly 13,000 was temporarily cut.

Local residents walk in a flooded area after heavy rain in Oamishirasato, Chiba Prefecture, Japan, August 14, 2026. Reuters/Issei Kato

In Chiba city, one of the worst-hit spots, hundreds of people spent the night under foil blankets at makeshift evacuation centers in government buildings.

Some major highways in Chiba were shut, forcing drivers to take alternative routes that clogged traffic, said highway operator NEXCO East.

Several rail services were also suspended on Friday, though some services from Narita to Tokyo resumed, easing congestion at the international transport hub.

Weather authorities said the 367 mm (14.5 inches) of rain over a 24-hour period in Chiba exceeded the previous record of 309 mm (12.17 inches) set in October 2013. – Rappler.com

World.title: Preparing for Economy That Doesn’t Yet Exist: Why Kazakhstan’s Experiment Is Worth Watching
World.content:
One of the things that has surprised me most over the past year is how rarely my conversations with futurists actually stay focused on artificial intelligence. We usually begin there. We talk about generative models, autonomous agents, the next version of ChatGPT, the speed at which these systems are evolving. Yet after twenty or thirty minutes, AI almost disappears from the conversation. We find ourselves talking instead about labor markets, education, political institutions, governance and, eventually, something much larger than technology itself: the possibility that we are approaching the end of an economic model that has shaped modern societies for generations.

AI isn’t the story

That shift in perspective has been difficult to ignore. We often compare AI to the internet or smartphones because it makes the transformation easier to understand. Those technologies undoubtedly changed our lives. But they never challenged one of the central assumptions underpinning modern economies: that human labor is the primary engine through which value is created and wealth is distributed. Artificial intelligence might.

During one of our interviews, futurist Brett King made an observation that has stayed with me ever since. The more automation we introduce into the economy, he said, the less the traditional mechanics of capitalism function in the way they were originally designed. As he put it, it will be the end of capitalism as we know it. Whether or not one agrees with his conclusion is almost secondary.

The more interesting question is what governments should do if he is even partially right. Because history suggests that institutions rarely have the luxury of waiting until structural change is complete before deciding how to respond. By then, the transition is usually far more painful than it needed to be.

Perhaps this is why I have gradually become less interested in AI itself and more interested in leadership. Not political leadership in the conventional sense, but the ability of governments to think beyond immediate political cycles and prepare societies for an economy that does not yet fully exist.

Brett challenged another assumption that many of us have taken for granted over the last four decades: that markets, left largely to themselves, will eventually solve most problems.

“The free market hasn’t solved climate change. The free market hasn’t solved poverty. It hasn’t solved homelessness. This is not something that the free market is going to solve. This is a function of coordinated governance,” he told me.

It is a provocative argument, particularly at a time when governments around the world are still trying to determine how much they should regulate artificial intelligence and how much they should simply allow innovation to unfold. Yet there is something compelling about the distinction he makes.

Artificial intelligence is not disrupting a single industry. It is beginning to influence healthcare, transportation, logistics, finance, manufacturing, education and public administration simultaneously. Unlike previous technological revolutions, it does not fit neatly within the responsibility of one ministry or one regulator. It cuts across virtually every institution that modern states have spent decades building.

If that is true, then leadership acquires a different meaning. It becomes less about managing today’s economy efficiently and more about preparing citizens for tomorrow’s economy before it fully arrives. This is perhaps why Kazakhstan has become an unexpectedly interesting case study.

Preparing before the future arrives

For years, discussions about Kazakhstan’s future largely revolved around energy, critical minerals, connectivity and its geopolitical position between major powers. Increasingly, however, another narrative has begun to emerge, one that places artificial intelligence at the center of the country’s long-term development strategy rather than treating it as another digital policy initiative.

Over the past two years, the government has launched the International AI Center Alem.ai, expanded the AI-Sana education initiative, invested in computing infrastructure and accelerated efforts to integrate artificial intelligence into public administration.

That shift is also evident in Kazakhstan’s official discourse. Speaking at the second meeting of the Council for the Development of Artificial Intelligence, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said that “traditional growth models based on resources and labour are losing effectiveness” and warned that unless Kazakhstan rapidly transitions to a fully integrated, AI-powered, data-driven economy, it risks falling behind in the global technological race.

Whether every initiative succeeds is, in some ways, beside the point. History offers very few examples of governments navigating technological revolutions perfectly. But there is a meaningful difference between preparing too early and preparing too late. One risks investing in ideas that will inevitably evolve. The other risks discovering that the rules of the global economy have already changed. This is precisely what Brett was referring to when he spoke not about technology, but about time.

Modern societies, he told me, have become trapped inside quarterly earnings reports, annual budgets and electoral cycles. Yet transformative projects have never been built that way. Cathedrals took generations. The Panama Canal took decades. The Apollo program demanded sustained political commitment that extended far beyond a single administration. AI, he believes, belongs in that same category of civilizational change.

Listening to him, I found myself wondering whether our biggest challenge is not AI at all. Perhaps it is our shrinking political imagination. Can democratic governments still think thirty years ahead? Can they justify investments whose returns may only become obvious long after today’s leaders leave office? Those questions feel increasingly relevant when looking at Kazakhstan.

President Tokayev has repeatedly noted that digital transformation is no longer optional but essential for maintaining competitiveness in a rapidly changing world. Speaking at the AI conference this July in Shanghai, he stressed that no country should remain merely a consumer of AI technologies and that every nation must develop its own human capital so technological progress serves society rather than deepening inequality.

“No country should remain merely a consumer of artificial intelligence. Every nation must have the opportunity to develop its own human capital, digital infrastructure and institutional capacity. At its core, this is a matter of fairness and equity,” he said.

The human side of an AI economy

What I find interesting is not the ambition itself. Many governments now speak enthusiastically about AI. What stands out is the attempt to connect AI with education, state capacity and long-term economic planning rather than viewing it simply as another technology sector. That connection surfaced repeatedly during my conversations with both futurists Brett King and Ron Immink.

Ron approached the issue from an entirely different direction. He was less concerned with algorithms than with culture. Most leading AI systems, he pointed out, continue to think primarily in English. Yet languages carry different ways of understanding the world, different historical experiences and different cultural contexts. If artificial intelligence is to become genuinely intelligent, it cannot simply translate languages; it must learn to understand them.

That observation gave me a different perspective on a seemingly minor piece of news: Kazakh has become one of the fastest-growing languages on ChatGPT. It is easy to dismiss that as an interesting statistic. But perhaps it represents something larger. In the age of AI, language is no longer only a question of identity. It increasingly becomes a question of participation. Cultures that exist inside AI systems will inevitably have a stronger voice in shaping how those systems understand humanity itself.

Education raises a similar challenge. Ron believes our schools are still largely organized around the needs of an industrial economy, preparing students for stable careers inside systems that may not exist in their current form within a generation. Brett goes even further. He says that philosophy, psychology, ethics and lifelong learning may become just as important as engineering because the defining skill of the AI era will not simply be coding. It will be adaptation.

After months of interviewing futurists, I have come to think that AI is asking governments a surprisingly old question. Not whether they can innovate faster than everyone else, but whether they are capable of imagining a future that does not yet exist and preparing for it anyway. No one knows what the AI economy will ultimately look like. Predictions differ, technologies evolve faster than policies, and history has a habit of humbling even the most confident forecasts. There is no guarantee that every initiative launched today will produce the intended outcome. But perhaps that is not the point. The point is that waiting for certainty may no longer be an option.

Looking at Kazakhstan today, what I find noteworthy is less the technology itself than the shift in thinking behind it. AI is no longer being discussed simply as another digital industry or another innovation agenda. Increasingly, it has become part of a broader conversation about education, institutions, public administration and the country’s long-term economic direction. Whether through AI-Sana, investments in computing infrastructure, the development of Alem.ai, or recent efforts to integrate AI across government, the common thread is an attempt to prepare before the transition becomes unavoidable.

Perhaps that is what leadership will increasingly mean in the age of AI: not the ability to predict every technological breakthrough, but the willingness to create the conditions for a country to adapt to profound uncertainty. Kazakhstan appears to be making that bet today, investing in institutions, education and digital capacity before anyone can say with confidence what the AI economy will ultimately look like.

World.title: Data Center Valley Is More Than AI: It’s Kazakhstan’s Economic Diversification Bet
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is advancing construction of the Data Center Valley in the Pavlodar Region, a large-scale computing infrastructure project intended to support artificial intelligence development, attract international technology companies and create a new export-oriented segment of the digital economy, as Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov reviewed progress on Aug. 13.

The first facility, with a planned capacity of 50 megawatts, is now under construction. Excavation work for the energy center and AI factory buildings is 90% complete, while foundation work and construction of administrative facilities are underway. Officials said the main buildings of the data center and power units are expected to be completed by the end of December 2026. Commissioning work is scheduled to finish in May 2027, with the facility expected to begin operations in June 2027.

Kazakhstan has also acquired a 215-megawatt substation to supply the site, and is developing water and telecommunications infrastructure. In the longer term, Data Center Valley is designed to expand in stages to a total capacity of up to 1 gigawatt. That would turn the project from a single data center into a large computing campus capable of hosting data centers, AI factories, GPU clusters and cloud platforms for international hyperscalers.

Why computing capacity is becoming strategic

As artificial intelligence requires large amounts of computing power, data centers are becoming an essential part of the infrastructure supporting the digital economy. For Kazakhstan, the potential opportunity is to move beyond being primarily a consumer of foreign digital services and develop the infrastructure needed to host computing capacity within the country.

“Data Center Valley is creating a new export potential for Kazakhstan. By locating computing capacity within the country, we are creating conditions for developing domestic AI solutions, attracting global companies and entering the international market for digital services,” Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said.

According to Kazakhtelecom Board Chairman Bagdat Mussin, the project’s expansion will depend on confirmed client demand.

“Our first priority is to complete construction of the first facility in June 2027. At the same time, we are creating the engineering foundation that will allow us to gradually increase the campus capacity in line with confirmed customer demand,” he said.

The project will therefore need to solve two parallel challenges: building enough infrastructure to attract major technology companies while avoiding capacity that significantly exceeds demand.

From infrastructure to a digital ecosystem

The project is also being developed with international partners. Firebird AI and NVIDIA are involved in building an ecosystem around artificial intelligence, cloud technologies and next-generation digital services.

Another proposal discussed during the meeting, the Cloud First Policy, or Data Embassy project, illustrates this ambition. The initiative could allow foreign states to store data in Kazakhstan while retaining full legal sovereignty over it.

Data Center Valley is being developed as countries across the region seek to position themselves in the rapidly expanding market for artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure. The first 50-megawatt facility, expected to open in June 2027, will therefore be an early test of a much larger strategy.

World.title: Kazakh Voters Increasingly Seek Concrete Policy Solutions, Experts Say
World.content:
ASTANA — Healthcare, education and social protection are emerging as key areas of competition in Kazakhstan’s election campaign, with experts saying voters are increasingly looking beyond broad promises to how seven political parties intend to deliver measurable improvements in quality of life.

Those issues were at the center of an Aug. 14 meeting of the Sarap Expert Club in Astana, where researchers, healthcare and education specialists and human-capital experts examined how social concerns are shaping party platforms and voter expectations ahead of the election.

The election to the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral Parliament, is scheduled for Aug. 23. Seven political parties are set to compete, with 545 candidates registered for the race. Campaigning will end at midnight on Aug. 21, followed by a campaign silence day on Aug. 22. More than 12.6 million people are eligible to vote on Aug. 23. As of Aug. 13, the Central Election Commission had accredited 656 observers representing foreign states and international organizations.

Experts said the parties largely agree on the problems across healthcare, education, employment and social protection but increasingly differ over who should provide the solutions, how they should be financed and how their effectiveness should be measured.

Zhuldyzai Iskakova, head of the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development, which organized the Sarap meeting, said the televised debates helped make those differences more visible to voters. Three nationally televised debates have already aired live on Qazaqstan TV, Channel 7 and Jibek Joly, while the final debate is scheduled for Aug. 19 on 24KZ.

The first two debates drew a combined audience of around two million viewers, according to experts at the meeting.

“They examined their programs in detail and challenged one another,” Iskakova said. “There is a common perception that the parties are broadly similar and that it is difficult to understand what distinguishes them. In reality, there are fundamental differences between them.”

From social promises to competing solutions

Zhanar Sankhayeva, head of the Department of Political Research at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, said political parties are placing greater emphasis on social protection, healthcare and education in their election programs.

“Healthcare is among the top three issues of greatest concern to citizens, while education ranks among the top six priorities affecting people’s everyday lives,” she said.

Sankhayeva said the substance of party platforms could play an important role in voters’ decisions. She cited a survey by the Institute of Public Policy in which 44.4% of respondents identified parties’ initiatives, policy proposals and campaign promises as one of the important factors influencing their choice.

The expert said public expectations in the social sphere are also evolving. While earlier demands focused largely on expanding access to education and healthcare, voters are increasingly concerned with the quality of the services they receive.

“I would describe the current competition between parties in the social sphere as a transition from a competition of social promises to a competition of concrete models for solving social problems,” she said.

Sankhayeva said the election campaign is now entering a “more mature phase.”

“Voters are also moving from a general interest in the election toward forming specific political preferences,” she said.

Long-term priorities

According to Nazarbayev University Vice President Gulmira Qanay, the quality of people’s lives is a clear indicator of how effective or ineffective state policies are. Health, education, safety, professional opportunities and confidence in the future are among the main factors shaping quality of life.

She highlighted the constitutional emphasis on developing human capital, science and education, which should be an important part of the agenda for the future members of the Kurultai.

“We can see major transformations taking place around the world. If we look at the achievements of leading countries over the past 50 years and examine how they reached their current level of development, much of what we see today is the result of investments made in science, education, medicine and the social sphere,” said Qanay.

However, she also stressed that improvements in quality of life require long-term investment rather than measures tied only to an election cycle.

“These are not achievements that appear in a day or two. (…) That is something future members of the Kurultai should also keep in mind,” she added.

After saying that government policy should ultimately be judged by whether it improves people’s quality of life, Qanay said the same principle should apply to higher education, with universities assessed less by formal credentials and more by what graduates are able to do afterward.

Qanay said Kazakhstan should place greater emphasis on developing intellectual capital and designing education policy around research, evidence and measurable outcomes, particularly as digitalization and artificial intelligence transform the skills and standards expected of universities and the wider education system.

Healthcare challenges

Healthcare illustrates the gap that can emerge between policy ambitions and the everyday delivery of public services. Bakytzhan Tazhibay, chair of the AQNIET Kazakhstan Sectoral Trade Union of Healthcare and Public Service Workers and a pediatric urologist, said his review of all seven party platforms showed broad agreement on the sector’s principal challenges.

These include unequal access to quality care between major cities and remote villages, a lack of transparency in the mandatory social health insurance system, shortages of medical personnel and the bureaucratic burden placed on healthcare workers.

“Any reform will remain on paper if we forget about the people responsible for putting it into practice,” Tazhibay said. “At the center of the healthcare system are doctors, nurses, paramedics and other medical workers.”

He identified staff shortages and professional burnout as direct threats to the quality and safety of patient care. Although healthcare salaries have increased, he said, many doctors and nurses still work more than one full-time position to provide an adequate income for their families. This problem is particularly acute outside major cities.

He described elections as a “moment of truth for society.”

“This is the time when the country’s course of development is set, determining what our social policies, labor laws, family support, and healthcare system will look like for years to come,” he added.

Tazhibay called for healthcare expenditure equivalent to at least 5%–6% of gross domestic product, more stable base salaries, workloads consistent with professional standards and greater public and trade-union oversight of the social health insurance system.

World.title: From Grain to Value Chains: Kazakhstan Seeks to Transform Its Agricultural Export Model
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has nearly doubled its agricultural exports over the past five years, reaching $7 billion in 2025 from $3.8 billion, according to an analysis published by the World Financial Review. The growth has strengthened Kazakhstan’s role as a food supplier to Central Asia and beyond. Still, it raises a broader question about the country’s agricultural future: can rising export volumes translate into a higher-value agri-food economy?

According to the World Financial Review, Kazakhstan’s growing agricultural capacity and location between major Eurasian markets are creating new opportunities for the country to play a larger role in regional food security. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization project that international trade will become increasingly important to global food systems, with around 22% of calories consumed worldwide expected to cross international borders by 2034.

For Kazakhstan, which borders or has close transport links to rapidly growing markets in Central Asia, China, the Caucasus and beyond, this creates an economic advantage. The country can supply regions with growing food demand while using its agricultural surplus to expand exports.

Kazakhstan’s agricultural products are already exported to more than 72 countries. Grain and flour remain among its most important exports, particularly to neighboring markets. Over the first 11 months of the latest marketing season, exports of grain and flour reached 13.5 million tons, according to figures cited in the World Financial Review.

Shipments increased particularly sharply to regional markets. Exports to Afghanistan rose by 59% to 2.2 million tons, while supplies to Uzbekistan increased by 37% to 5.6 million tons. Exports to the Kyrgyz Republic reached 504,000 tons, up around 40%, while shipments to Turkmenistan rose 34% to 210,000 tons.

These figures underline Kazakhstan’s importance as a regional supplier. But they also reveal the limits of an export model based primarily on increasing volumes of agricultural commodities.

From exporting more to creating more value

The more significant shift may now be taking place in food processing. According to official data, agricultural exports reached $7 billion in 2025, up 37% year-on-year. More than half of this amount, around $3.6 billion, came from processed agricultural products, whose exports grew by 35% compared with the previous year. The figures suggest that Kazakhstan is beginning to capture a larger share of the value generated from its agricultural production.

Vice Minister of Agriculture Yerbol Taszhurekov said processing is becoming one of the main drivers of growth in Kazakhstan’s agro-industrial complex. Speaking at a March 5 briefing at the Central Communications Service, he said the country’s strategy is not simply to increase agricultural output but to retain more of the economic value generated by it within Kazakhstan.

“Our strategic task is not only to increase the production of agricultural raw materials but also to ensure their processing within the country, including deep processing that creates products with high added value. Processing forms new production chains, creates jobs in the regions and strengthens Kazakhstan’s export potential,” Taszhurekov said.

But not all processing represents the same level of economic transformation. Turning wheat into flour is already a step beyond exporting raw grain. Deep processing, however, can create products such as starch, gluten, amino acids, syrups, vitamins and bioethanol, connecting agriculture to more complex industrial supply chains.

This distinction may become increasingly important for Kazakhstan. The country’s long-term agricultural strategy is therefore not simply about producing more grain, but about moving further along the value chain. The government aims to increase the share of processed agricultural products to 70%. New deep-processing facilities planned by 2028 are expected to have a combined capacity of 5.8 million tons per year and attract around 1.9 trillion tenge (US$3.9 billion) in investment.

Changing the fields to change the export model

The transformation is also evident in what Kazakhstan produces. In recent years, the area under wheat cultivation has declined by nearly 900,000 hectares. In comparison, oilseed acreage has increased by more than one million hectares and land used for pulse crops has expanded by 275,000 hectares, according to the World Financial Review.

This is more than a change in crop statistics. A broader crop mix creates a wider raw-material base for domestic processing industries. Oilseeds, for example, can support vegetable oil production, while pulses and grain can feed into increasingly sophisticated food and industrial processing. Kazakhstan produced a record 4.8 million tons of oilseeds in 2025, while food production rose 8.1% to 3.9 trillion tenge (US$8 billion).

The shift suggests that Kazakhstan’s agricultural diversification is becoming increasingly connected to its industrial policy. Diversification in the fields is intended to support diversification in factories, which in turn could change the composition of exports.

World.title: Experts: As Inflation Falls, Kazakhstan Faces New Monetary Policy Trade-Off
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s annual inflation slowed to 10.2% in July, extending its decline for a tenth consecutive month, while lending is increasingly shifting from consumer borrowing toward business financing, according to National Bank (NBK) Governor Timur Suleimenov’s report to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Aug. 13.

The figures point to a changing balance in Kazakhstan’s economy. Inflation is moving lower, and the NBK has already begun cautiously easing monetary policy, cutting the base rate to 16.75% in July. At the same time, stronger investment activity and continued quasi-fiscal stimulus are supporting faster economic growth, creating a potential limit on how quickly borrowing costs can decline further.

The National Bank’s next policy decision is scheduled for Sept. 4, when markets will be watching to see whether the regulator finds sufficient evidence that the slowdown in inflation is sustainable.

Inflation slows, creating room for cautious easing

According to Suleimenov, annual inflation declined to 10.2% in July. The slowdown follows a series of policy decisions that have gradually reduced the National Bank’s base rate. The regulator kept the rate at 18% in April, lowered it to 17% in June and then reduced it by another 25 basis points to 16.75% on July 24.

The latest reduction was significant because it marked a shift from maintaining restrictive conditions toward a cautious normalization of monetary policy. However, the National Bank has stressed that the decline in inflation does not mean the inflation problem has been resolved. In its July decision, the regulator noted that some underlying components of price growth remained elevated and inflation expectations continued to pose risks. The NBK therefore said that further decisions would depend on evidence that disinflation is sustainable, rather than on a predetermined path of rate cuts.

The central bank expects inflation to remain between 9% and 11% in 2026, then slow to 5.5%-7.5% in 2027 and approach its 5% target in 2028.

The key contradiction: growth is helping the economy but complicating inflation policy

One of the most important factors shaping the National Bank’s next steps is the strength of economic activity. According to the report, GDP growth reached 3% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, supported by stronger-than-expected investment activity.

Investment demand is expected to remain a major driver of growth, including through quasi-fiscal financing, subsidized loans, development institutions and guarantees supporting large projects. This creates a more complicated environment for monetary policy.

Normally, lower inflation would provide a stronger argument for cutting interest rates. But faster economic growth and continued investment stimulus can increase demand and liquidity, potentially adding new pressure to prices.

The National Bank has repeatedly identified the scale and parameters of quasi-fiscal stimulus as one of the major risks to the inflation outlook. In its monetary policy assessment, it warned that active quasi-fiscal financing can partly offset the effects of tighter monetary conditions and weaken the transmission of the base rate through the economy.

In other words, Kazakhstan is entering a phase in which monetary and quasi-fiscal policies will need to be more closely coordinated. The faster the government and quasi-public sector stimulate investment and demand, the more cautious the National Bank may need to be about reducing interest rates.

Credit growth shifts toward business

Suleimenov also reported a notable change in the structure of bank lending. As of July 1, business lending had increased 17.1% year-on-year, while lending to small and medium-sized enterprises accelerated to 29.6%. Meanwhile, consumer lending growth slowed from 21% at the beginning of the year to 13%, reflecting prudential measures and a gradual normalization of retail credit growth.

The shift is important for the broader economic strategy. Kazakhstan has long faced concerns about rapid growth in household borrowing and its potential contribution to consumption-driven demand. A slowdown in consumer lending combined with faster business financing could help redirect credit toward investment and production. Earlier National Bank data showed that SMEs were already the primary source of growth in corporate lending, while mortgage lending continued to expand, supported by preferential housing programs.

Whether this shift becomes sustainable will matter. Business lending can support productivity and supply capacity over the longer term, potentially reducing inflationary pressures if financing results in higher output. But in the short term, large-scale investment spending can also increase demand for imports, labor and construction materials.

A stronger tenge offers additional support

The strengthening of the tenge has also become an important part of the recent disinflation story. According to economist Ruslan Sultanov’s analysis of July currency market data, the rate on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange fell from 480.72 to 473.59 tenge per dollar during the month, while the weighted average rate on the over-the-counter market strengthened from approximately 486.2 to 471.4 tenge per dollar.

According to Sultanov, the strengthening occurred despite continued substantial demand for foreign currency. The Unified Accumulative Pension Fund purchased $375 million on the market in July, while the mandatory sale of part of quasi-public-sector foreign-currency revenues was suspended as of July 15.

At the same time, the National Bank did not conduct foreign exchange interventions, while sales from the National Fund totaled $200 million, and quasi-public-sector entities sold around $195 million.

“This is an interesting signal: even with significant counter‑demand from the fund and a reduction in one of the sources of the mandatory currency supply, the market still ended the month with a stronger tenge,” Sultanov wrote in his Telegram channel.

A stronger tenge can help slow inflation by reducing the cost of imported goods and limiting the pass-through of exchange-rate movements into consumer prices. The National Bank has identified the stronger currency as one of the factors supporting disinflation.

Markets expect another cut, but not a rapid easing cycle

Professional market participants surveyed by the Association of Financiers of Kazakhstan in August have become more optimistic about both inflation and the tenge. Their 12-month inflation forecast declined to 10.1%, while 60% of respondents expected the National Bank to lower the base rate to 16.5% at its Sept. 4 meeting. Another 28% expected the rate to remain unchanged at 16.75%, while 12% allowed for a rate increase.

Over a 12-month horizon, respondents expect the base rate to fall to 14.75%. Yet even this forecast points to gradual rather than aggressive easing. According to the AFK’s analytical center, the projected real interest rate would remain positive at around 4.65%, reflecting expectations that inflation risks will continue to constrain the speed of rate cuts.

That cautious outlook broadly corresponds with the National Bank’s position. The regulator has emphasized that the return to its 5% inflation target depends not only on interest rate policy, but also on fiscal consolidation, a narrowing of quasi-fiscal stimulus, stable inflation expectations and predictable tariff policies.

The Sept. 4 rate decision will therefore be about more than whether the base rate is reduced by another 25 basis points. It will provide a clearer indication of how the regulator views this trade-off: whether the recent decline in inflation is sufficient to justify a broader easing cycle, or whether Kazakhstan’s accelerating investment-driven economy will require monetary policy to remain restrictive for longer.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Higher Education Drive: From Importing Universities to Producing Knowledge at Home
World.content:
At a July 1 government session, Science and Higher Education Minister Sayasat Nurbek laid out a reform model built around five priorities: human capital, educational quality, science, innovation and artificial intelligence. The list shows how far the policy agenda has traveled since 2022, when the former Education and Science Ministry split into two ministries. Universities in Kazakhstan are no longer expected only to award degrees. They are being positioned as engines of technological development, economic diversification and the country’s regional influence.

Internationalization is the most visible part of that shift. Kazakhstan has built 40 strategic partnerships with foreign universities, including 33 branch campuses now operating on Kazakh soil. More than 35,000 international students were enrolled as of late 2025, and the government wants that figure at 100,000 by 2029. Kazakhstan also became the first Central Asian country to ratify UNESCO’s Tokyo Convention on the recognition of higher education qualifications, it took effect May 1, strengthening the legal basis for student mobility and cross-border recognition. These are real gains. But they are inputs, not outcomes. The next phase of reform should be measured less by the number of foreign campuses, partnerships or international students, and more by what Kazakhstan keeps from this expansion.

A foreign university branch builds lasting value only when it trains local faculty, staffs joint research teams, supervises doctoral students and grows laboratories and future academic leaders at home. Each major partnership should carry measurable commitments on skills transfer, local leadership and research infrastructure along with protections for students if a foreign partner changes course or leaves. Internationalization should make Kazakhstan more capable, not more dependent.

The same principle should guide regional university policy. Not every institution needs to chase Nazarbayev University’s global ranking strategy. Universities should be funded and judged against missions tied to their own regions, an agricultural university leading on food systems and water security, an institution in an industrial region specializing in mining safety and the energy transition, others focused on teacher training, public health, logistics or Kazakh-language technology. National importance does not require one university model.

Science policy faces the same test. Kazakhstan’s Concept for the Development of Higher Education and Science for 2023-2029 aims to lift research spending to the global benchmark of 1% of GDP, a serious climb from the roughly 0.16% the country spends today. Public grants alone will not close that gap. Companies need to become active users and co-funders of university research, not just recipients of its graduates.

Artificial intelligence raises the stakes further. Kazakhstan has declared 2026 the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence, and the national AI-Sana program has already introduced roughly 650,000 students to AI fundamentals, with 100,000 now moving into advanced, project-based training. Universities must prepare specialists and produce research at the same speed the technology moves. That means confronting harder questions early, who owns student data? How should AI-assisted assessment be governed? Will Kazakh-language resources keep pace with imported platforms? Answering them now will determine whether technological modernization narrows Kazakhstan’s gaps or opens new ones.

Nazarbayev University’s own new strategy offers the clearest articulation of what should guide the whole system: A World-Class- made in Kazakhstan. World-class means strong research, credible teaching and real international engagement. Made in Kazakhstan means the people, institutions and intellectual capacity to sustain those standards without outside help.

That distinction should frame the next phase nationally. Kazakhstan has already shown it can attract respected universities and build flagship institutions of its own. Its next task is to carry that capacity beyond a handful of campuses, connect research to problems that matter at home, and build educational models other countries will eventually want to study.

The measure of success is no longer how much international education Kazakhstan can import. It is how much world-class knowledge the country can produce, retain and share.

The author is Saqib Raza, a PhD scholar in education and an MSc graduate in Educational Leadership in Higher Education from Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Education, Kazakhstan.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: UAE Coal Deal Highlights Why Foreign Investors Are Betting on Kazakh Coal Industry
World.content:
ASTANA – A United Arab Emirates company has secured a 25-year license to develop the Kenderlyk coal deposit in eastern Kazakhstan, expanding foreign investment in the country’s mining sector.

According to documents released ahead of public hearings in early August, MQ Emirates Group Ltd will develop Coal-Shale Field No. 1 of the Kenderlyk deposit using open-pit mining methods.

Coal production is scheduled to begin in 2028, following geological exploration and preparatory work planned for 2026 and 2027. Initial output is projected at 10,000 metric tons, increasing to the mine’s planned annual capacity of 50,000 metric tons by 2034. Recoverable reserves are estimated at 940,000 metric tons.

The Kenderlyk deposit is located around 70 kilometers from the town of Zaisan in the East Kazakhstan Region. It has been known since the late 19th century, when coal and oil shale were extracted through small surface mines. During the Soviet era, the area underwent extensive geological exploration for coal, shale, and hydrocarbons.

Several years ago, the Kazakh Industry Ministry offered parts of the Kenderlyk deposit for auction. According to the National Geological Service, the broader deposit contains 11.3 million metric tons of coal reserves across three coal-bearing formations. Coal at Field No. 1 has a relatively high ash content of 35% to 40%.

Coal remains key to energy security

Although many countries are accelerating the shift toward renewable energy, coal remains one of the world’s primary sources of electricity. It generates roughly one-third of global power. Demand continues to be driven largely by China and India. According to the Energy Ministry, Kazakhstan ranks 10th globally in proven coal reserves, with an estimated 33.6 billion metric tons, enough to sustain current production levels for more than three centuries.

The country’s largest coal-producing regions include the Karagandy and Turgai coal basins in central Kazakhstan and the Ekibastuz, Maikuben and Karazhyra deposits in the northeast. Kazakhstan exports coal primarily to Russia, Poland, Uzbekistan, Türkiye, India and Malaysia.

To support future growth, the Energy Ministry plans to auction 10 additional coal exploration blocks by the end of the year. The government has also approved the Coal Power Development national project, which includes investment projects with a combined installed capacity of around 7.8 gigawatts.

Investment in the sector continues to rise. Mining companies invested 305 billion tenge (US$654 million) in 2025, while investment is projected to increase to 553 billion tenge (US$1.2 billion) this year.

Kazakhstan is also expanding investment in its broader mining sector. The government plans to develop the Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty deposits, among the world’s largest undeveloped tungsten reserves, into the country’s first full-cycle tungsten operation.

Highly concentrated market

While Kazakhstan is expanding coal production, a new report from the Agency for the Protection and Development of Competition (APDC) found that the country’s primary wholesale coal market remains highly concentrated.

The agency’s review of the 2024-25 market concluded that the sector continues to be dominated by a small number of producers operating in an essentially unchanged oligopolistic market. For coal supplied to households and municipal utilities, the ERG Group and Karazhyra company controlled a combined market share of 74.8% in 2024 and 67.9% in 2025.

In the power generation segment, Bogatyr Komir and Kazakhmys Coal accounted for 84.1% of the market in 2024 and 81.6% in 2025. For industrial coal, the ERG Group held a market share of 62.3% in 2024, increasing to 69.1% in 2025. The agency said Kazakhstan’s oligopolistic market structure has contributed to sustained price increases.

According to APDC, wholesale prices for coal supplied to households increased 30% to 35% between 2022 and 2025, while thermal coal prices rose approximately 45% over the same period.

To improve competition, the agency proposed introducing price regulation for household and thermal coal, increasing the share of coal sold through commodity exchanges to 52%, and moving off-exchange transactions to digital trading platforms.

The report also identified several structural barriers to competition, including differences in mining contract terms and limited transparency in granting exclusive coal export rights. It further highlighted concerns over the allocation of rail capacity by the national railway operator, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy.

APDC recommended establishing transparent criteria for coal export permits, ensuring equal treatment for producers and improving disclosure of available railway capacity.

The agency also identified companies that qualify as holders of key capacity in the coal market, including Shubarkol Komir, Karazhyra, Bogatyr Komir, Kazakhmys Coal and the Eurasian Energy Corporation. Once these companies are formally recognized as holders of key capacity, they will be required to sell coal under Kazakhstan’s Rules on Equal Access to Key Capacity, which are intended to promote fair competition and equal market access.

World.title: More than 32,000 applications for Armenian citizenship in a year: who is applying and why
World.content:
Rise in applications for Armenian citizenship

“There has been a sharp increase in the number of applications for Armenian citizenship. In 2025, the number exceeded 32,000, a historic high for the entire history of the Republic of Armenia,” said Armen Kazaryan, acting deputy interior minister.

According to him, the number of citizenship applications exceeded 20,000 in each of the previous two years, compared with 7,000-8,000 in earlier years.

Kazaryan believes the main goal of applicants is to obtain a document that allows them to travel:

“We have seen certain developments, in particular the outbreak of hostilities in Ukraine and restrictions on travel for Russian citizens. After that, we saw an increase in applications for Armenian citizenship. By the way, most Russian citizens applying for Armenian citizenship are ethnic Armenians.”

He rejected claims that obtaining Armenian citizenship is a complicated process:

“The requirements for ethnic Armenians are ‘zero’. People may face administrative difficulties. For example, some may lack the necessary documents proving their ethnicity, or their records may contain errors. In such cases, we need to compare the information with other records and verify it. Essentially, Armenia imposes no requirements on ethnic Armenians.”

Kazaryan himself considers the lack of requirements for ethnic Armenians problematic. In his view, this devalues the institution of citizenship itself.

“We will soon present a draft of the relevant legislative amendments addressing these issues,” he said, without specifying what changes the amendments would introduce.

Border crossings: more people entered than left

Nelli Davtyan, acting head of the Migration and Citizenship Service, also spoke to journalists. She recalled that last year Armenia recorded a “significant positive figure” in the difference between the number of citizens entering and leaving the country. The figure stood at 8,660.

In the first half of this year, the difference between entries and exits stood at 1,347.

“There were 871,409 entries and 870,062 exits. If we compare this with figures for the first half of previous years, last year’s figure was -20,065, while in 2024 it was -22,893,” Davtyan noted.

She stressed that the figure usually rises in the second half of the year. This happens because seasonal migrant workers return home after leaving the country for temporary work. They usually leave in early spring and return in autumn. Davtyan therefore described a positive figure already in the first half of the year as “exceptional”.

More than 6,000 people granted temporary residence permits

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia had transformed from a country that “sends” migrants abroad into a country that receives migrants. “The second major trend is the growing interest in Armenia among foreign nationals,” he noted.

Nelli Davtyan said the Migration and Citizenship Service had received 9,534 applications for one-year temporary residence permits: “Of these, 6,059 were approved. Compared with previous years, the number of applications has almost tripled. The proportion of approved applications has also nearly tripled.”

According to Davtyan, the number of applications for three-year residence permits has also increased, although more modestly: “In previous years, the figure stood at 1,500-1,700, while in the first half of this year it had already reached 2,085.”

Armenia implementing 53 EU recommendations on visa liberalisation

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia was actively cooperating with the European Union on visa liberalisation. He recalled that Armenia received its first report on the implementation of the action plan in May 2026. The report gave a fairly positive assessment of the steps taken by the Armenian government.

“The EU presented us with 53 recommendations. To complete our work, we divided them into specific actions. We broke down the recommendations so that we could clearly identify the steps we need to take to implement them,” Kazaryan explained.

Based on the 53 recommendations, an Armenian working group drew up a list of 117 actions. More than half of them have already been completed.

The recommendations form part of the first stage of the visa liberalisation action plan. This stage covers legislation and policy development only. The authorities expect to assess how effectively Armenia has implemented the first stage by early 2027 or during the first half of the year. If the results prove positive, work on the second stage will begin.

Rise in applications for Armenian citizenship

World.title: Myth Detector: 230 fake social media accounts created to create illusion of support for Georgian PM’s statements
World.content:
Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

1On 2 August, marking the 18th anniversary of the 2008 August War, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze held a briefing. He focused in particular on what he described as the spread of “Russophobia” in Georgia and the role of the so-called “deep state” in this process.

After the briefing, pro-government messages began circulating widely on social media. Various media outlets also published visual materials promoting these messages.

According to a study by Myth Detector, 230 fake accounts took part in the campaign. The organisation analysed likes on social media posts, as well as the photos and activity of the profiles that shared them. It identified signs of coordinated and suspicious behaviour that, according to the study, aimed to increase support for specific government narratives.

The study also says the profiles were designed to appear as if they belonged to different socio-demographic groups. Some accounts used photographs depicting idyllic family life to make themselves appear more trustworthy.

Profile photos were generated using artificial intelligence (AI)

According to Hive Moderation, a tool for detecting AI-generated images, there was more than a 90% probability that all 230 profile photos had been generated using AI. In some cases, the probability reached 100%. A visual inspection also identified features typical of AI-generated images, including unnatural shapes of hands and fingers, as well as certain distortions.

The photos repeat the same settings and compositions

Some accounts use identical or very similar photos, including the same images with minor changes. The visual design of different accounts also repeats similar photography styles and details. These include photos with a consistent aesthetic, featuring Tbilisi in the background, a glass of wine or a cup of coffee, a hand touching the head, or similar compositional choices. The accounts also use images showing people having fun, relaxing or taking part in sports to create an impression of authenticity. In some cases, different accounts use the same first and last names.

An illusion of broad support is created through artificially diverse social and demographic profiles

The campaign creates the impression that it brings together people of different ages, appearances and interests. The profiles include young and older people, supporters of conservative and alternative views, as well as religious people, family-oriented users, sports enthusiasts and people who enjoy outdoor activities.

AI-generated accounts use real workplaces and educational institutions to make their profiles appear more credible

Most profiles list places of education and employment, including the Tbilisi Transport Company, various Georgian insurance companies, commercial banks, microfinance organisations, government agencies and municipal services.

Different accounts show identical behaviour

Most profiles list a date between 20 and 24 July 2026 as the date they began living in Georgian cities, although some accounts appear to have been created earlier.

Profile activity focuses on the same messages

The activity of the suspicious accounts, particularly their likes, is concentrated on posts featuring conspiracy claims by the ruling party’s chairman about the “party of global war”, the “deep state’s plan” and the “opening of a second front”. They also engage with the narrative about “Russophobia”, suggesting an artificial increase in the level of support.

Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

World.title: Russia no longer attracts Armenian migrant workers as they look for new opportunities in Europe
World.content:
Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

The geography of labour migration from Armenia is changing. Russia, which until recently remained the main destination, has become less attractive. The main reasons are Russia’s economic downturn, driven by the war in Ukraine, and the depreciation of the rouble.

Many migrants are now returning from Russia to Armenia. Some are trying to find work in their home villages or in the capital, while others are looking for new opportunities, particularly in Europe. The direction of labour migration is changing, with European countries becoming increasingly popular.

Work visa for Poland

After two years working at a meat-processing plant in Poland, 40-year-old Serob (name changed) returned to Armenia for a month. He came to prepare all the necessary documents and take his wife and children with him to Warsaw.

“I received a three-year residence permit and the right to work. Living away from my family is difficult. I decided that we should be together. I should also say that Poland has become one of the first steps towards the European labour market for many people. Many of my friends work in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and other countries on legal work visas. I was also offered a job in the Netherlands, but I decided to stay in Poland,” he says.

Serob is a butcher. He was also in demand in Armenia. However, he says his salary there was not enough to support his family:

“I had friends who worked as butchers in Europe. They told me that the profession was in demand there and well paid. Gradually, I started thinking: why not try going to Europe and working there? I also had a lot of debts and loans. I went to Poland on a work visa. The process moved slowly. The Polish embassy invited me for an interview a year after I submitted my application.”

A recruitment agency then sent his details to a meat-processing company. Representatives of the company interviewed Serob online. During the video call, he demonstrated his professional skills to the employer, including how he deboned meat.

“The employer liked my work and sent me a contract and the necessary documents. The embassy then approved my work visa. At first, I lived in a house in Poland with people of different nationalities. They all worked for the same company and lived in separate rooms. Later, when my financial situation improved, I moved into a separate flat with a friend from Armenia. I sent most of my earnings to my family to help resolve our financial problems. I did not work in a shop or at a market. I worked at a specialised meat-processing plant with refrigerated storage facilities. It is physically demanding work,” the butcher says.

He notes a shortage of butchers in the European labour market, which creates demand for migrants with the necessary skills. Meat-processing plants employ workers from Ukraine, Argentina, Azerbaijan and Armenia.

“Many Armenians are now going to European countries for work. And not only to meat-processing plants. When I flew to Poland, I met some women who worked as pastry chefs on the plane. They were also travelling to Poland under legal employment contracts. Many Armenians also work in shops. These are people who speak foreign languages. In any case, I am happy. I will return to work in a month, this time with my family,” Serob says.

Working at a German medical clinic with an Armenian degree

Doctors, teachers and highly skilled professionals in various fields are also in demand on the European labour market. Dentist Edgar Mirzoyan has been living and working in Germany for nine months.

Edgar Mirzoyan

“One day, my nurse told me that her friend worked in Germany and that they might need a dentist. I simply gave her my contact details and forgot about it. Some time later, they contacted me. At the same time, I started learning German. The whole process took two years: learning the language, preparing documents and taking exams. Finally, I moved to Germany. By the way, getting my Armenian degree recognised in Germany seemed more realistic and achievable than in other European countries,” Edgar says.

At the same time, the 30-year-old dentist studied not only the professional requirements but also the overall situation in the country, including its economy, level of safety and even happiness index.

“Geography also influenced my final decision. It was important for me to stay connected to Armenia. You can get from Germany to Armenia in just a few hours. In this sense, Europe was a much more convenient destination for me than, for example, Canada. Before moving to Germany, I had a completely different idea of what it would be like. Of course, everyone’s experience is different. Some doctors who arrived at the same time as me had a much harder journey. A lot depends on which city you move to, who your employer is and who you interact with. Everyone has their own experience,” he says.

Edgar started working two days after arriving in Germany. Some time later, his wife also joined him.

“Before moving to Germany, I registered in advance to take a language exam. They tested my knowledge of medical German. I passed the exam successfully. After that, I received a temporary licence valid for two years. I can work during this period, but I must work under the supervision of an experienced doctor.

However, the process of having my degree fully recognised is still under way. The authorities compare my entire university curriculum, the number of hours I completed and the subjects I studied with the German curriculum. I applied for this process while I was still in Armenia. They only started reviewing my documents after two years of waiting. If they find differences between the curricula, I will have to make up the gaps. It is not yet clear how significant those differences will be,” the doctor says.

According to Edgar, working in Germany has its own particularities. Berlin is a multicultural city, and his patients include not only Germans. About 30 per cent are Armenians and Yazidis, while another 30 per cent are Russians and Ukrainians.

Edgar continues to practise in Armenia as well:

“I can take leave twice a year. I come to Armenia, mainly perform implant procedures and surgeries, and then return to Germany. I have many patients who wait for me to come back. They book appointments in advance, I come and perform the surgery, and the next stage of treatment takes place three to six months later, when I can return again.”

When labour migration is a family choice

For many people who move to Europe, leaving is a decision about their family’s future, improving their living conditions and trying to build a new life in a different environment.

Vergine (name changed) chose this path. She has lived in the Czech Republic with her husband for seven years and now has two children.

“First, my husband moved to Prague on a work visa. He started working in the security department of a shopping centre. Two years later, I joined him. We made the decision consciously, after carefully considering everything. We wanted to settle down and continue our lives in a European country. In this sense, the Czech Republic seemed like a suitable option, and we are very happy with our choice,” Vergine says.

Before moving to the Czech Republic, the couple worked at Zvartnots Airport.

“At first, I worked at a language centre as an English teacher. Then my second child was born here. Of course, there were many difficulties. We lived in a foreign country without support from relatives and with a small child, but we managed. I now work as an English teacher at a school,” she says.

The young family does not plan to return to Armenia for now, but they regularly visit their relatives.

“We have the right to live and work here, but I am sure that one day we will definitely return,” Vergine says.

Changing migration patterns

According to Tatevik Bezhanian, an expert with the migration programme of the charitable organisation Armenian Caritas, Armenia currently has no statistics showing how many people leave for European countries to work.

One reason is that Armenia has no intergovernmental labour migration agreements with EU countries. Bulgaria is the only exception. In addition, most people who leave for Europe find jobs through private recruitment agencies, and the state does not register this process.

“You will not find this data in official statistics. On the other hand, we also do not have a migration card system under which people have to state when entering or leaving the country that they are going abroad to work. They may not indicate the purpose of their departure at all,” Bezhanian says.

She says this problem is not unique to Armenia. Internationally, governments mainly register migrant workers arriving in their countries because they can manage these migration flows. Countries that pursue targeted labour migration policies, sign bilateral agreements and organise the recruitment of their citizens abroad usually have comprehensive data on those who leave. The Philippines and Uzbekistan are among them, for example.

Tatevik Bezhanian notes that even when Armenian authorities want information about labour migrants leaving for Russia, they have to rely on official Russian statistics:

“If the geography of labour migration expands, we will have to approach the relevant authorities in countries such as Poland, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. We will need to obtain data and determine how many Armenian citizens work there.”

Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

World.title: Opinion on Georgian petrol in Abkhazia: ‘If needed, it’s possible’
World.content:
The indirect consequence of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries has been a fuel crisis in Abkhazia, which in recent years has been buying petrol from Russia.

After struggling with shortages for two weeks, Abkhazia decided to buy petrol from Georgia. Given the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, this was a rather “unorthodox” move, but at the same time the only viable way out of the situation.

In a blog post, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz outlet Chegemskaya Pravda, discusses whether Abkhazia can trade with Georgia.

Inal Khashig: “Abkhazia has been grappling with a petrol shortage for the past two weeks. There is virtually no fuel left in the country. Government assurances that the situation is under control and that a new shipment of petrol is about to arrive have done little to reassure people — if anything, they have only deepened the pessimism. Queues at petrol stations stretch as far as the eye can see.

And then petrol arrived from an unexpected source — Georgia.

Tbilisi says the government has nothing to do with it and that it is entirely a private business matter. Sukhumi, for its part, says that when the country is facing a fuel shortage, it will not prevent petrol tankers from entering from Georgia. After all, there is precedent for this kind of economic contact: during the difficult 1990s, we supplied Georgians with relatively cheap fuel.

This particular fuel crisis has once again brought an enduring Abkhaz question to the fore: should we trade with an enemy state or not?”

To me, it is quite straightforward: if this kind of cooperation is vital for the country as a whole, its economy and the well-being of its people, then it is justified. Sukhumi has, after all, cooperated with Tbilisi in the energy sector throughout the post-war years, and no one objects because there is no alternative. This cooperation is vital to both Abkhazia and Georgia.

And now, when the whole of Abkhazia — and with it the country’s economy — has ground to a halt because of the lack of petrol, refusing to buy fuel from the Georgians looks like outright posturing.

Incidentally, I think the government’s argument that Abkhazia actively sold petrol to Georgia in the 1990s is a very good one. At the time, war-ravaged Abkhazia was under a severe blockade: Russia under Boris Yeltsin had effectively sealed us off on all sides. Nothing could be brought in or taken out. About the only thing permitted was taking mandarins across the border in handcarts, with Abkhaz women effectively serving as beasts of burden.

Abkhazia’s tiny budget was funded by selling timber and scrap metal to Turkey, as well as by smuggling fuel into Georgia.

The latter involved considerable risk and loss of life, as fuel tankers had to travel towards the Georgian border through the Gali district, which was unstable at the time. But there was effectively no other way of bringing even a little money into the state coffers. Whatever anyone may say, those modest revenues helped Abkhazia survive at the time.

And yes, we traded with Georgia then because we had to.

And we need to do so now to protect the country from a fuel crisis.

And in future, we need to take similarly responsible steps, even if they run counter to established dogmas. Rigid dogma is not the best guide to action in crises like the one we are facing now.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Analysts say Ukraine is preparing a large-scale offensive
World.content:
Ukraine Launches Large-Scale Offensive

Based on reporting by Novosti Donbassa

Ukrainian defense forces have liberated 19 settlements across several sectors of the front, according to DeepState, a Ukrainian battlefield monitoring project, which reported the advances after updating its combat map.

According to the analysts, Ukrainian forces have regained control of Zelenyi Hai, Novokhatske, Hrushevske, Tolstoi, Zirka, Yalta, Piddubne, Myrne, Voskresenka, Sichneve, Vorone, Ternove, Berezove, Stepne, Kalynovske, Pryvillia, Zlahoda, Rybne and Krasnohorske.

In addition, Ukrainian troops pushed Russian forces back in six other settlements: Novopavlivka, Novoheorhiivka, Novomykolaivka, Novohryhorivka, Zaporizke and Pryvilne.

The Ukrainian military also released video footage from settlements it said had been liberated in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions.
