World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: Sharks stumble as Dolphins stay in NRL's vital top four
World.content:
Cronulla have blown a huge opportunity to move back into the NRL's top four with a painful and potentially fatal 24-20 loss to lowly Canberra.

Star Sharks playmaker Braydon Trindall also suffered a dislocated shoulder as the Dolphins held on to the all-important fourth spot with three rounds remaining before the finals.

Cronulla will rue not finding a match-winner despite being camped on Canberra's line, set after set, for the final 10 minutes.

But the Sharks' mounting injury toll will be of equal concern for coach Craig Fitzgibbon, who has now watched his faltering side fumble and bumble their way to consecutive losses to sides well out of finals contention.

Trindall lasted less than 10 minutes before trudging off.

Initial reports were promising, with the shoulder quickly put back in.

But with the Sharks leading 8-0 and looking strong, Fitzgibbon opted not to risk their key playmaker any longer.

It may have been the wrong move as the Raiders wrestled back control and momentum.

Already without suspended forward enforcer Addin Fonua-Blake and injured centre Jesse Ramien, suddenly the Sharks were looking significantly understrength and vulnerable.

The afternoon had started brightly enough for Cronulla, with a Nicho Hynes penalty preceding a lovely chip-and-regather try for Trindall in the fifth minute.

But from 8-0 up, the Sharks lost their way after Trindall was forced off.

First, winger Xavier Savage steamed on to a beautiful long ball from Kaeo Weekes, then Owen Pattie wriggled his way over to suddenly put Canberra ahead 12-8 after 15 minutes.

Things were looking grim for the Sharks when winger Jed Stuart collected a double cut-out pass from Ethan Strange to stroll over and extend the Raiders' lead to 10 points.

But with their top-four hopes — and history would suggest — title prospects on the line, the Sharks regrouped with a much-needed reply from Teig Wilton off a short ball from Nicho Hynes.

The hosts should have snatched the lead after the half-time siren, only for Briton Nikora to ignore a three-on-one overlap on the right edge.

The Sharks, though, were first to score after the break when Will Kennedy swooped to score, before handing the momentum back to Canberra through a soft Joseph Tapine try under the sticks.

There was a huge moment with seven minutes remaining when video replays looked to have shown Ronaldo Mulitalo contorting his body and planting the ball down for a match-levelling try.

But The Bunker went with referee Gerard Sutton's on-field "no try" call.

The near-miss proved Cronulla's last chance as consecutive defeats to last-placed St George Illawarra and now Canberra leave the Sharks likely needing to beat Gold Coast, Parramatta and Melbourne to earn a double-chance in the play-offs.

No team has ever won the premiership in the NRL era from outside the top four.

AAP

World.title: Quick hits: Smith sets review record after horror drop, Warner jinxes Marnus
World.content:
Steve Smith reviews a decision before he's given out, Marnus Labuschagne gets desperate and then jinxed, while Josh Hazlewood provides a bright spot in an otherwise pitch-black day for Australia.

As it happened: Australia fighting to save first Test as Bangladesh claim top order wickets

Here are the quick hits from day three of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Marnus's desperate, ugly appeal

The ball clearly bounced before reaching Labuschagne. (Fox Cricket)

Marnus Labsuchagne is rarely shy in making an appeal.

But even he seemed a little sheepish about this one.

With Josh Hazlewood having snared the crucial early wicket of Hasan Mahmud, the Australians, already well behind in the game, were hopeful of wrapping up the Bangladeshi innings quickly.

But tailender Taijul Islam was finding some sweet timing in the middle, and was profiting with some quick, elegant runs.

In the 117th over, he creamed one straight into the ground and then into the covers, where Labuschagne made a fine diving stop.

But the inner-ring livewire came up holding the ball like he'd claimed a prize at the Easter Show.

Labuschagne made a desperate appeal early on day three. (Fox Cricket)

No-one seemed particularly convinced by the appeal, but umpire Kumar Dharmasena decided to send the decision upstairs.

And sure enough, the television replays confirmed what even Marnus surely must have known — the ball had clearly bounced between the batter and fielder.

Desperate, ugly stuff from the Australians.

2. Smith's inconceivable drop

Smith dropped a sitter in the morning session. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

In a morning of serious lows for Australia, this was surely the nadir.

Steve Smith, just one take away from becoming Test cricket's all-time leading catcher, settled underneath a Taskin top edge.

The Bangladeshi tailender took his eye of the ball as he played his pull shot, and the Australian vice-captain seemed destined to carve out another piece of history.

But the ball was in and then out of Smith's usually so-reliable hands, leaving the best since Bradman looking to the heavens for some sort of explanation.

Only a matter of balls later, it was Travis Head's turn to put one down.

Head's chance was a lot more difficult, retreating at full pelt, but it was the kind of catch we've seen him take in the past.

Australia was forced to wait until after lunch to belatedly see the back of the fighting Bangladeshi tail, which added another 24 runs after those fumbles, with the tourists taking an enormous 228-run lead into the second innings of the match.

3. Hazlewood passes 300

Hazlewood became the ninth Australian to pass 300 Test wickets on day three. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

A bright spot for the Australians in an otherwise pitch-black morning was Josh Hazlewood.

Playing his first international cricket since October last year, the big fast bowler ran in admirably all innings, looking amongst the fittest and most disciplined of his teammates as he returned figures of 6-89.

His fifth wicket of the innings, which was earnt by nicking off the excellent Mehidy, was his 300th in Test cricket.

He was the ninth Australian to reach the milestone, and after picking up the wicket of Ebadot Hossain to finish off the Bangladeshi innings, moved within nine wickets of Brett Lee on Australia's all-time leaderboard.

How high can Hazlewood get?

Well, Lee (310) is certainly in his crosshairs, as is Mitchell Johnson, who took 313 wickets during his Test career.

Then it's captain Cummins on 316 and the great DK Lillee on 355, which you'd imagine, given Hazlewood's injury record, may be a step too far.

Regardless, Hazlewood will finish his career of one of Australia's finest.

Not that that will be of any consolation to the Australian today.

4. Jake's horror homecoming

With 23 runs, Jake Weatherald was Australia's second-highest run scorer in the first innings, an accolade that carries as much credibility as being the English bowler with the best economy rate during the last Ashes.

But through almost all of his 37-ball, 56-minute stay at the crease, he looked skittish and nervous and wholly unsuited to opening the batting at Test level.

It made his second innings all the more crucial personally, even without accounting for the perilous situation Australia found themselves in, over 200 runs in arrears.

How disappointing then, that Weatherald seemingly learned nothing from his first-innings failure, playing with an angled bat outside off with minimal foot movement to be dismissed bowled off the inside edge by Hasan Mahmud.

The ball was too close to play a cut to, he still attempted it and was on his way.

The dismissal raises more uncomfortable questions for Australia's selectors, about whether they stick or twist ahead of a very busy 12 months.

5. Smith reviews before being given out

Smith surely set a new record for the fastest review on day three. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Steve Smith might have got away with one in the first innings, admitting that he hit the ball on its way through to Litton Das.

He got away with that one, but he was going to make doubly sure that he wouldn't be dismissed when a similar event happened when he was on just three runs in the second innings.

The ball beat the outside edge from a superb Ebadot delivery, and umpire Kumar Dharmasena wasted no time in raising the finger after hearing an edge.

Not quick enough for Smith though, who was shaking his head and reviewing before the umpire even put his finger up.

Dharmasena did nod at Smith, in his defence, but even so, it was an odd and extraordinarily self-consciously performative action.

It was not necessarily a surprise that Smith, never one to go willingly from the middle, was so quick to review, but he was proven to be vindicated, the sound coming from hitting the ground with his bat.

6. Warner puts the mockers on 'the Marnus of old'

Labuschagne departed after prematurely glowing praise from a former teammate in the commentary box. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

One of the Australians in desperate need of a big score, Marnus Labuschagne began his innings like he was cripplingly aware of just that, scratchy and anxious, struggling for any sort of rhythm.

But things were slowly improving, with the idiosyncratic first drop playing a few nice drives through the covers and finding some stability in his stance.

On commentary for Fox Cricket, David Warner was glowing in his praise for Labuschagne.

Even at the time, it felt like the former Australia opener was both jumping the gun and tempting fate.

“He’s confident in his game, he’s hitting the ball well ... now he’s in, he looks like the Marnus of old," Warner said while comparing images of Labuschagne's stance early in his innings against footage from after he had found some form.

"He’s confident, he’s got his whole rhythm back. And it’s exciting to see, and I’m happy for him.

" I really hope he goes on with it, and he'll be able to go back today and say 'I feel good, what was it?' And hopefully he can identify that. "

Labuschagne added just one more run after Warner's glowing review, being promptly yorked by spinner Taijul, the Australian playing all around a straight one and departing for 31.

World.title: Resources Minister King weighs in on WA GST furore
World.content:
Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King has slammed as "unbalanced, highly speculative and clearly incorrect" an interim report that recommended a cut to Western Australia's share of the GST, reassuring voters that the Labor government was committed to supporting the resource-rich state.

Minister King was speaking a day after state Premier Roger Cook called the Productivity Commission report on GST distribution an "attack on Western Australians", and dubbed its authors "east-coast clowns".

"I want to make it clear to all Western Australians that the Albanese Labor government has your back," she said today as Labor officially launched its campaign for the hotly contested suburban seat of Secret Harbour, south of Perth.

" We will always ensure Western Australia gets its fair share of the GST, we will always support Western Australia's ambitions to be the resources capital. "

The explosive report, which was released on Friday, recommended the government scrap 2018 changes to how the goods and services tax was carved up among the states, saying Western Australia was the only state or territory to benefit from it and that it was a "costly mistake".

GST alarm bells ringing in the west Premier Roger Cook said "east coast clowns" attacked Western Australia's federal GST deal. It set alarm bells ringing in WA government offices, literally, as state political reporter Keane Bourke witnessed.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose government has endorsed and extended the deal to at least 2029, has said that WA would "get [its] fair share" of GST but signalled he would wait for the final report in December to comment on specifics.

Cook says he has PM's assurances

Minister King said Mr Albanese had assured Mr Cook that there would be no change to the current arrangements.

Minister King said the Productivity Commission's report was speculating about things "that won't happen". (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"The report itself is not only unbalanced, it is highly speculative and is clearly incorrect. It fails to take account of the enormous contribution Western Australia and Western Australia's resources industry provides to the whole of the nation," she said.

At the same Secret Harbour event, Mr Cook also said he had the prime minister's assurances that the GST deal would remain.

Mr Cook says he has assurances from the prime minister about the GST deal. (ABC News: Lauren Smith )

"He knows that Western Australia is the engine room of the national economy," Mr Cook said.

" And that's why he's backing our team and he's back in our state and he's backing our situation when it comes to the GST. "

The deal struck by then-treasurer Scott Morrison ensures WA gets a bigger slice of GST revenue every year than it would under the national formula, which is meant to give more money per person to states with the highest need and lowest financial means.

The formula has always been contentious, but became particularly so in WA when successive mining booms made it by far the richest state in the federation, resulting in very low GST relativities because the formula assessed the state as very high means.

Mr Cook's government, however, has maintained that changing the GST distribution would unfairly punish WA for its success, with state Treasurer Rita Saffioti saying that unravelling the deal would unfairly disadvantage the state.

World.title: Charity drive charges on despite boggy conditions
World.content:
Torrential rains and flooded roads have not deterred more than 70 cars from taking part in this year's Variety Bash — though the wet did cause a major detour.

The annual event, which raises money for children's charity Variety SA, was originally set for a route from Mildura to Gawler, via Queensland and far north South Australia.

But with outback roads still underwater after record-breaking rains in May, the route was changed to be entirely in SA — what the charity called a "pivot to Pirie".

Bash entrants have been raising money for children experiencing sickness, disadvantage, or living with disability. (Supplied: Variety/Keryn Stevens)

Kicking off at Gawler on August 8, the drivers turned the usually 200-kilometre trip to Port Pirie into a 2,304km trek, via Kimba, Streaky Bay, Port Lincoln, and more.

The change took a "monumental effort", said event chair Darren Greatrex.

"This wasn't supposed to happen this year. We were always going to come to the West Coast next year," he said.

The cars will need to visit an industrial car wash once the bash is over. (Supplied: Variety/Keryn Stevens)

"But 12 weeks ago, we realised we couldn't get to our original destination, which was Birdsville, just because of the volume of water up there.

"Not easy to do with 300 crazy people behind me and rolling into these small towns, and so it's been a monumental effort to do a total flip of the bash.

"[But] we got there and we've had an absolute ball."

A wet road ahead

Despite the bash kicking off just as a major weather event reached the state, Mr Greatrex said the drivers held up "surprisingly well".

Travelling along a diverted route due to flooding on the Birdsville track, rally entrants still found plenty of mud. (Supplied: Variety/Keryn Stevens)

"When we started and left Gawler, the clouds opened up and didn't stop for about 72 hours," he said.

" It threw us into a little bit of disarray, but the farmers out there loved it. But not so good for our bashers who've been swagging for the last seven nights. "

With some particularly soft — and underwater — roads along the way, there is a car wash or two in the future of the 72 cars taking part.

Late August rains provided some particularly soft roads. (Supplied: Variety/Keryn Stevens)

Over the past 12 months, the 231 bash entrants have been raising money for children experiencing sickness, disadvantage, or living with disability, funding more than $480,000 in grants delivered during the eight-day drive.

"They get the opportunity to let their hair down and have a week away and celebrate all the hard work, but also then they get to see the impact of that hard work and where that money goes," Mr Greatrex said.

These colourful characters travelled more than $2,000km on a charity run that raised over $2 million. (Supplied: Variety/Keryn Stevens)

"Some of the grants have been substantial, and it just makes a huge difference to people with disabilities and special needs to just have a much better life."

Grants delivered include $150,000 each for all-abilities playgrounds at Penong Primary School and Port Lincoln Primary School, and funding for sensory equipment, scholarships, and sports facilities in several towns.

Port Lincoln Primary School received a grant to fund an all-abilities playground. (ABC News: Luke Lay)

Port Lincoln Primary School principal Kathy Davison said the grant was "incredible" for the community.

"We had a playground removed and now we can reinstate one for students with disabilities and all abled students. It's great," she said.

South Australian Variety Bash rally driver Sandra Lukin has been taking part in the annual run for 20 years. (Jodie Hamilton)

This year the SA Bash was able to raise just over $2 million, and seeing that money bring joy to kid's faces is what keeps rally goers coming back.

"This is my 20th bash and including this year of fundraising, it's just over $1.3 million [we've raised]," Sandra Lukin said.

"This year, to see how much has come back onto Eyre Peninsula in the way of grants and helping kids and schools and everything, that's what warms all our hearts and keeps us going for next year."

World.title: Fraud officials charge another over alleged $5 million NDIS dishonesty plot
World.content:
A 38-year-old Adelaide man has been charged over an alleged $5 million dishonesty plot against the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS).

The man, who is a director of a registered NDIS provider, was arrested and charged by Australian Federal Police (AFP) officers at Adelaide Airport on Friday as he prepared to leave the country.

It follows an investigation by the federal government's Fraud Fusion Taskforce (FFT), which began in March in response to the NDIA's finding that unauthorised access to protected records of NDIS participants had taken place.

In June, a 48-year-old woman was the first person to face charges over the same alleged plot after FFT investigators searched premises in Adelaide's northern suburbs, including a business in Prospect and homes in Mawson Lakes and Blakeview.

The AFP charged the man with one count of dealing with the proceeds of crime, fraudulently claimed from the NDIS.

He was also charged with one count of soliciting protected agency information from a National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) staff member.

The offences carry maximum penalties of 25 years's and 2 years's imprisonment, respectively, according to the AFP.

The man has been remanded in custody and is expected to appear before the Adelaide Magistrates Court on Monday.

World.title: First H5N1 bird flu death recorded in Phillip Island penguins
World.content:
A Phillip Island penguin has died from H5N1 bird flu in the first detection among the island's little penguin colony.

The new detection is one of three announced by Victoria's chief veterinary officer, Graeme Cooke, on Saturday.

It comes ahead of plans to begin vaccinating the Phillip Island penguins against the virus on Monday.

The Phillip Island penguin parade is a major attraction that draws national and international visitors.

Authorities found the dead penguin away from the area where the penguin parade takes place.

A great crested tern found in Lakes Entrance in East Gippsland and another in Dromana, on the Victorian Mornington Peninsula, also died of bird flu.

It brings the total number of bird flu cases in Victoria to 74, but Dr Cooke said there were likely more birds sick or dead in the state.

"We … recognise that this is distressing for Victorians to see and to hear," he said.

Dr James Todd says the latest bird flu detections could lead to large losses of wildlife. (ABC News)

Victoria's chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said the latest cases were significant because the areas hosted several at-risk bird species that would congregate for the upcoming spring breeding season.

"It's highly likely the conditions are conducive for H5N1 spread in those areas that would lead to large losses of wildlife," Mr Cooke said.

"There's little we can do to minimise that impact.

"Having said that, we are working as hard as we can to protect at-risk species and to continue to respond to detections as they come on hand."

The vaccination of Phillip Island's penguins against bird flu will continue as planned. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

No halt to vaccinations

He said the recently announced vaccination program of the little penguin colonies on Phillip Island and St Kilda will begin on Monday despite the detection there.

"We know that little penguins are iconic and highly valued by Victorians, and for that reason, we are working as a priority to protect those communities," he said.

Phillip Island Nature Park, which operates the penguin parade, will also remain open while the vaccination program is rolled out.

"We are rolling out the vaccination program as quickly and urgently as was possible after the federal authorities released the permits and released the vaccines to the jurisdictions," Dr Cooke said.

"We are very concerned … about this detection, but it does represent early surveillance and early vigilance."

He said large groupings of penguins were historically more susceptible to infection.

"At this time of year, the penguins are not at their full capacity in terms of numbers, so it's a good time to start vaccinating," Dr Cooke said.

World.title: Shoppers payments declined due to 'global' Mastercard outage
World.content:
Card payments have been declined for shoppers around Australia due to a Mastercard system update, the multinational card provider says.

"A scheduled system update caused Mastercard transactions to be declined for a period of time earlier today. The situation has been resolved and all systems are working as normal," Mastercard told the ABC in a statement.

Shoppers across several Australian states reached out to the ABC to report issues with card payments, including using Apple pay, making cash withdrawals and using Mastercard travel cards.

Commbank said the problems were due to a "global Mastercard issue," which had been resolved.

Jackie Wells from Bayside, Victoria, was trying to pay for her shopping at Aldi when two of her cards were declined.

"I had a trolley full of all sorts of goods, $208 altogether, so a fair bit," she said.

"I tried one card and it was declined, tried another card and it was declined, so we went to another POS station and they were both declined again."

Ms Wells then called her husband to bring a different card, which was also declined.

When the couple wasn't able to withdraw cash with their cards, they decided to leave the shopping cart behind in the shop's cool storage area and go home to pick up cash.

She said she saw others shoppers exiting shops "disgruntled" because they weren't able to pay for their shopping.

By the time she returned to the shops, the payment issue had been resolved.

Downdetector, a website where users are able to report service outages, had more than 1,700 reports of Mastercard issues at 3pm on Saturday.

Those reports were down to 173 two hours later.

The most common issues reported on Downdetector involved funds transfers and mobile banking.

World.title: Fraud charges added to fatal hit-and-run accused
World.content:
A former Nationals WA candidate already facing charges over an alleged fatal hit-and-run is now facing additional fraud charges.

Benjamin Thomas Simpkins, 26, was arrested in May after the death of a 49-year-old man in Katanning.

He is facing three serious driving charges in relation to that incident and the matters are proceeding through court.

Today police have charged Mr Simpkins with attempting to pervert the course of justice, gaining benefit by fraud and using a forged record with intent to defraud.

In a statement, WA Police said further inquiries as a result of the driving charges allegedly identified he had falsely claimed to hold a university degree.

Police will allege he used falsified academic records to obtain employment in June 2023 as a cardiac scientific officer at a Western Australian hospital.

It will also be alleged he provided false information regarding his volunteer work within the local community and that this information was supplied to the Supreme Court.

Police also allege that in October 2023, he used falsified documentation in an attempt to gain admission to other universities for further education purposes.

He is also facing two further counts of driving with a suspended licence in May of this year.

Mr Simpkins will face court on the new charges next month.

World.title: Late drama as Eels pip Cowboys to keep rivals’ finals hopes alive
World.content:
Parramatta 32 North Queensland 30 SportNRLNRL 2026 Late drama as Eels pip Cowboys to keep rivals’ finals hopes alive Scott Bailey August 15, 2026 — 8:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The race for the NRL’s top eight is still alive after a controversial late penalty consigned North Queensland to a 32-30 loss to Parramatta at CommBank Stadium. With a chance to lock in a finals spot beckoning, the Cowboys’ defence crumbled on Saturday night as they let in six Eels tries. Loading The defining moment then came with four minutes to play, when Mitch Moses set up for a Parramatta field goal with scores locked at 30-30. The Eels halfback eventually ran it on the last, was ankle-tapped by Heilum Luki and spilled the ball forward while falling.



But Moses reviewed the call, and the bunker found he had been collected in the head by Tom Chester while just inches above the ground. The result means Canterbury are still alive in the race for the finals, albeit still two points behind the Cowboys and with North Queensland having a bye next week. Loading Manly also remain in the hunt, but would need to win their last three and have the Cowboys drop their final two games at home against Wests Tigers and Canberra. As tough as the late penalty may have been for North Queensland, their defence remains a massive issue just weeks out from the finals.



A fortnight after leaking 82 points to the Sydney Roosters, it was poor again on Saturday night. The tone was set when Parramatta winger Brian Kelly went 60 metres from the opening kick-off, while the Cowboys also conceded six first-half penalties. The Eels celebrate a try against North Queensland. Getty Images Luki could also find himself in trouble with the match review committee, after being sin-binned in the opening half for a high shot on Luca Moretti. There is no doubt North Queensland’s attack has the spark to put points on, with halfback Jaxon Purdue again impressing.



He put on a long cut-out ball for a Braidon Burns try in the first half, then stepped Teancum Brown and fullback Apa Twidle for a second-half try of his own. Related Article Cronulla 20 Canberra 24

NRL 2026 Trindall injured as Raiders bump Sharks out of NRL’s top four Reed Mahoney also starred out of dummy-half, burrowing over for the night’s first try, before going short to Reuben Cotter and putting him over after the break. The Cowboys also put on one of the tries of the year with scores locked at 24-24, with the ball going from right to left and back to the right through five passes and two kicks before Chester crossed. Not to be outdone, Parramatta also had plenty of attacking flair.



It was big prop Junior Paulo who responded to level the scores at 30-30, with a lofted 35-metre cut-out ball in the lead-up to a Jordan Samrani try. Moses also had three try assists and broke through the line in the lead-up to a Tallyn Da Silva penalty try. And his off-contract halves partner Ronald Volkman again pushed his case for another deal, scoring one try and putting a grubber-kick in for a Josh Addo-Carr four-pointer.

World.title: ‘We just didn’t have the answers’: The lifesaving disability teams keeping families afloat
World.content:
NationalNSWFamily ‘We just didn’t have the answers’: The lifesaving disability teams keeping families afloat Rachel Rasker August 15, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Rose Mitchell was 10, she felt like she became a parent. “The minute he was born, something shifted within me,” she said of her brother Daniel Rata. From that day on, for decades, the pair were inseparable. Now, no matter how often she visits her brother, it never feels like enough. “I carry a lot of guilt with having my own independent life away from him,” she said. “I struggle with balancing being that caretaker for him ... with trying to find my own identity outside of being his sister.” Rose Mitchell said her brother Daniel Rata has enriched her life. STEVEN SIEWERT



For the carers and families of the approximately 117,000 people with an intellectual disability in NSW, finding and accessing support in a fragmented system is “exceptionally hard,” said Dr Alexis Berry, vice president of the Australian Association of Developmental Disability Medicine. Previously, she said people with intellectual disabilities would be known to their local government service, which acted as a “one-stop shop”, with a case manager assigned. “With the introduction of the NDIS, it’s become a much more individualistic approach, so it’s up to the individual to navigate the system – there’s nobody there helping them do that,” Berry said. Rata needed to be frequently hospitalised due to seizures, and his frustrated, violent meltdowns became difficult for his family to manage as he aged into a fully grown adult who didn’t know his own strength. “There was a lot of fear around taking him outside, which would have helped him because he needs that stimulation,” Mitchell, who is based in Sydney’s inner-west, said. “We felt like we had to control his environment at all times, just in case, because we just didn’t have the answers.”



Rose Mitchell and her brother have been inseparable since “the minute he was born”. STEVEN SIEWERT It wasn’t until Mitchell’s family was connected with the Sydney Local Health District’s Specialist Intellectual Disability Health Team (SIDHT) that she realised she wouldn’t have to spend her whole life as the primary carer for her brother. Without their support, “I have no idea where we would be”. Related Article Healthcare ‘Why are you letting them do this?’ The terror these mothers have for ‘unseen’ children There are just seven SIDHTs teams across the state’s 15 local health districts. Each small team is made up of a doctor, nurse and other health professionals, and aims to address the complex health needs of people with an intellectual disability. “Only a small proportion of the people who really could benefit from these teams are able to access them and get that benefit,” Jim Simpson, senior advocate for the Council for Intellectual Disability (CID) said.



Funding for existing teams was not determined by local population need, but instead by which LHDs had the organisation and infrastructure in place to put in a funding bid at their inception in 2019, according to advocates. Simpson said this has created a funding inequity, and the CID is now calling on the government to boost services in the areas with the highest need, and expand to 15 teams: “In other words, a team in every local health district”. Health outcomes for people with an intellectual disability remain “unconscionable,” Simpson said. Compared to the general population, they are more than twice as likely to die potentially avoidable deaths, and die an average 27 years earlier. They are also over-represented in the healthcare system, with hospitalisation and emergency presentation rates twice as high, and admissions also twice as long, and twice and expensive. A 2025 evaluation of the existing SIDHTs commissioned by NSW Health found the teams improved short-term and intermediate outcomes for clients. Simpson said expansion of the teams has the potential to save the health system overall through preventative healthcare and reduced hospitalisations.



In a statement, NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said since 2020, the SIDHTs have assessed more than 3700 people, and his government would continue to engage closely with the CID on their funding. He said the government invested over $6 million to operate the NSW Intellectual Disability Health Service each year. Daniel Rata is now thriving, and loves playing basketball. STEVEN SIEWERT When clinicians in Rata’s SIDHT linked his behaviour to anxiety and put him on new medication, Mitchell said everything changed for their family, as the fear of taking him outside dissipated. “It just completely levelled out the frequency of the meltdowns, and it meant that he could start integrating into social groups again,” she said, allowing the siblings to return to their favourite activities. “We would go to the local basketball courts and he would play for hours ... he would make friends in the park,” she said. “I could go and chill on the sidelines, and he would just be feeding his soul because he’s socialising and he’s playing basketball and doing all the things that he loves.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The two species NSW is racing to protect after fifth case of deadly virus
World.content:
NationalNSWBird flu The two species NSW is racing to protect after fifth case of deadly virus Angus Dalton August 15, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NSW government has identified little penguins and critically endangered regent honeyeaters as priority species for bird flu vaccination, after the state’s fifth case of the deadly virus was confirmed on Saturday in a greater crested tern found dead near Eden on the South Coast. At least 50 birds of the same species died in a mass mortality event in South Australia earlier this month. Little penguins are a priority species for vaccination, the NSW government said. A Victorian little penguin has died from the disease. Sitthixay Ditthavong With increasing deaths and the detection of the virus in a “Typhoid Mary” superspreader species, attention is starting to shift from individual sick or dead birds to monitoring for mass die-offs and detecting shifts in the virus’s genetics. A Victorian plan to vaccinate 5000 little penguins on Phillip Island did not move fast enough, with news of a penguin dying from the disease breaking on Saturday.



The NSW government said plans to inoculate captive little penguins and regent honeyeaters in the state were on track but awaiting approval from the national Animal Health Committee. The government is working with organisations including Taronga Zoo, which breeds regent honeyeaters for wild release. Fewer than 400 exist in the wild. Between 200 and 400 regent honeyeaters exist in the wild. Getty Images While the vaccine can reduce mortality, it’s not known exactly how well it protects native birds, and experts warn vaccines alone can’t stop ecological catastrophe. The government has acknowledged there is little data about the vaccine’s effectiveness outside of poultry. “It is not a silver bullet. The vaccine cannot be the only weapon to control the virus and containment of outbreaks. It’s a supplementary tool,” bird flu expert Dr Ariful Islam from Charles Sturt University said.



Last year, the government commissioned trials at CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness to establish dose rates for small native bird species. Further pilot studies tested the safety of the vaccine – which was developed for poultry – in other captive natives including penguins, ratites (emus and cassowaries), raptors, owls, shorebirds, ducks, cockatoos and other parrots. When asked for efficacy data, a spokesperson from the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry said “results to date have been encouraging and have informed regulatory assessments and emergency use arrangements for the vaccine”. The spread of the virus into silver gulls in South Australia has sparked fears of widespread infection among native birds.



Bird ecologist Professor Anne Peters, from Monash University, dubbed the notorious fish-and-chip thieves the “Typhoid Mary” superspreaders of bird flu because they range widely between cities, the coast and inland areas. Infected ducks, meanwhile, can carry the virus far without falling ill. “Finding active viruses in birds that aren’t sick at all would also be extremely worrying,” Peters said. NSW’s fifth bird flu case has been confirmed in a greater crested tern, a species which suffered a mass die-off in South Australia. Neil Bowman “Unfortunately, very many of our birds but also mammals, for example seals and sea lions, but also dolphins, are known to be at great risk of mass mortalities.” Experts have called for greater action to protect marine mammals, including the endangered Australian sea lion.



A trial in the US showed a vaccine developed for cows safely generated antibodies in elephant seals, suggesting existing vaccines might be adapted to protect pinnipeds. Australian authorities are monitoring those trials. Professor Euan Ritchie, an ecologist at Deakin University, questioned why the government hadn’t capitalised on the five-year head start Australia had before the virus arrived to invest in developing our own vaccine to protect the nation’s globally unique mammals. An Australian sea lion pup at Taronga Zoo. The endangered species is at dire risk of bird flu. Louise Kennerley “If [a mammal vaccination] is possible, and it’s only been limited by investment, then the government would need to answer to Australians why that hasn’t been a priority,” he said. Delivering the two required vaccine doses to many wild species is not feasible, but it’s theoretically possible to target some threatened animal populations such as sea lions, Ritchie said.



“In some cases, like the Tasmanian devil, they have small populations and they’re range-restricted, so it’s not outside the realm of possibility to entertain a vaccination program.” Related Article Bird flu ‘List of doom’: Bird flu puts one in five Australian bird and mammal species at risk The genotype of H5 bird flu hitting Australia, called B3.2, ripped down the entire west coast of South America in just six months before jumping into the sub-Antarctic, according to CSIRO. “[It caused] great impact to South American poultry industries as well as to wild bird life and to marine mammals, so that’s why we’re concerned about the introduction of this virus to Australia,” Dr Frank Wong from the agency’s Australian Animal Health Laboratory said. The genotype is different to the strain of the virus that has circulated in dairy cows and sickened humans in the US.



CSIRO released a pre-print paper last week using genomic data to track how the virus spread from South America across the sub-Antarctic to Australia. The agency is now monitoring the virus for changes, including re-assortment with local low-pathogenic bird flu, which could increase infectiousness, and mutations in a gene called PB2. “In other parts of the world, when this virus has got into mammals, there’s certain particular nucleotides in the gene which change and allow that virus to infect mammals more readily,” Dr Matthew Neave from CSIRO said. World.title: AFL LIVE: Hawks, Pies off to a fast start under lights at the ’G; Cats storm back to leave North stunned
World.content:

World.title: Two billy goats boarded a bus in Portland. They did not have tickets
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAnimals Two billy goats boarded a bus in Portland. They did not have tickets Neil Vigdor August 15, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was not a moment to spare. The doors to the TriMet bus, which was heading west on Tuesday morning towards downtown Portland, Oregon, had started to close when they opened for two stragglers. Loading Neither paid the fare. Kids ride free – or so they thought.



Not in the case of these two juvenile goats, which transit officials and police said had escaped from their enclosure and ventured onto a lime green FX2-Division bus. Security camera footage chronicled their strange escapade, showing some other passengers doing a double take before shooing the goats off the bus after the driver reopened the doors. Their jaunt prompted 911 calls and drew comparisons in Portland to the famous 2002 foray of a coyote that wandered onto a light rail MAX train, which was not in service at the time, and inspired a music video and another song. “They don’t have a valid pass,” the driver playfully told the other passengers as the goats exited the bus. The goats belong to a family that lives less than two blocks from the bus stop and are named Billy the Kid and Billy the Goat, Lrae Anderson, who identified himself as the owner, said on Friday.



“I couldn’t believe that they actually went across the busy street and tried to get on the bus and all that,” Anderson said. “They got on like they’ve done it before.” Related Article MIFF Love watching Neil the seal? This doco unearths the truth about ‘nuisance’ animals Anderson, 48, a rapper who also goes by the name Copper Loc, said his children — he has four sons — sometimes forgot to close the gate of the goats’ enclosure. A neighbour brought the goats back to their home the same day, Anderson said, noting that he had since installed a lock and improved the fencing.



Anderson said the family had acquired the goats about three months ago after moving to the property at the suggestion of a friend, who told him they would feed on plentiful blackberries from sticker bushes on the property. Since their escape he had learnt that they were pygmy goats, he said. Footage of the horned interlopers, which TriMet posted last week to Instagram, had amassed more than 5.4 million views, according to the transit agency. “The video of them boarding the bus has definitely sparked something in people’s imaginations,” Tyler Graf, a spokesperson for TriMet, said in an email on Friday. But not every passenger paid much attention to the escapees, video footage from inside the bus showed.



“I see the one lady,” Anderson said. “She’s sitting there, and she’s on her phone and she didn’t even notice the goats on the bus. I was like, ‘What are they doing?’” Two loose pygmy goats unexpectedly wandered onto a bus in Portland, Oregon. TRIMET As he was preparing for a hip-hop show in Seattle scheduled for Saturday, Anderson said the episode had provided musical inspiration. “I’ve already started making a song about the goats,” he said. World.title: Death toll rises in Indonesia after powerful earthquake
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaIndonesia Death toll rises in Indonesia after powerful earthquake Updated August 15, 2026 — 7:39pm ,first published 10:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Maumere, Indonesia: A powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early on Saturday, killing at least 38 people, collapsing buildings and homes as well as causing panic in a region prone to deadly quakes. Authorities said more than a dozen residents were injured. Authorities issued a tsunami warning and urged coastal residents to move to higher ground, but later lifted the warning when Indonesia’s Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency said monitoring showed no significant sea-level changes that would pose a threat to coastal communities. Loading The US Geological Survey said the quake hit Indonesia’s Flores region with a depth of 10 kilometres at 5:58am, local time. Its epicentre was 68 km north-northwest of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province. The initial quake was followed by several aftershocks. The head of the National Disaster Management Agency, Suharyanto, said rescuers have recovered at least 38 bodies, mostly in the three devastated regencies of Sikka, Manggarai and East Manggarai, including 16 bodies that were pulled from a landslide in the village of Reok in Manggarai. At least 13 people were rushed to nearby hospitals, including two with serious injuries.



Suharyanto said three helicopters and a rescue vessel were deployed to assist with logistics and support emergency response operations, including possible evacuations if needed, given East Nusa Tenggara’s geography, which consists of numerous islands and presents significant transportation and access challenges. He said about 2000 villagers in Nagekeo regency fled their homes to temporary shelters. Damaged houses following a 7.7-magnitude earthquake in Ruteng, Indonesia. AFP People clear up the rubble from a house damaged in an earthquake in East Manggarai, East Nusa Tenggara province. AP East Nusa Tenggara Police Chief Rudi Darmoko said the earthquake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings. He said power outages in cities and villages have hampered the flow of information and complicated search and rescue efforts.



“We are continuing to collect reports of damage and casualties, but there are communication disruptions,” Darmoko said. He said that landslides in Ende regency triggered by the earthquake also cut off the Trans-Flores highway, a roughly 700-kilometre paved mountain road spanning Flores Island, from Labuan Bajo to Larantuka. Footage on local television showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution following the quake. Hospital staff moved equipment outdoors, including beds, IV stands and oxygen cylinders, and set up temporary treatment areas to adapt to emergency conditions. Rescuers search for victims at a damaged building in Maumere, East Nusa Tenggara Province, Indonesia, following the earthquake, BASARNAS via AP Quake felt on Flores island and other areas The quake was felt across much of Flores island with initial reports indicating heavy damage.



Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka regency, said a number of buildings were damaged by the strong shaking and panicked people ran to higher ground. “Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the port terminal in Maumere had collapsed,” she said. Students at St. Peter Major Seminary in Sikka who were attending morning Mass fled in panic when the roof of an assembly hall collapsed, said Reverend Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of the seminary, which is known locally as Ritapiret Seminary on the predominantly Catholic island of Flores. A damaged building in Ruteng on Flores Island, Indonesia. AFP “Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof,” Tanga said. “At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake.”



The quake also reportedly caused panic in Labuan Bajo, a gateway town to eastern Indonesia’s Komodo National Park, one of the country’s best-known attractions. Damage was also reported in Bima, a city in neighboring West Nusa Tenggara province, and in some parts of southern Sulawesi island. Indonesian authorities initially issued a tsunami warning for parts of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, and urged residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks. The agency located the shallow undersea quake near Flores island. Indonesia prone to earthquakes Indonesia, a vast archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the “Ring of Fire,” an arc of volcanoes and fault lines in the Pacific Basin. A powerful earthquake caused a tsunami in 1992 that killed about 2500 people on Flores, part of a group of islands in the eastern half of Indonesia.



Editor's pick Myanmar coup On the front line of a forgotten war, you can’t see your enemy – but you can hear him In 2018, a magnitude 7.5 quake spawned a large localised tsunami that wiped out coastal areas, while liquefaction caused by the shaking turned entire neighbourhoods into rivers of sludge in the eastern Indonesian city of Palu, on the Palu-Koro Fault. The disaster killed more than 4,400 people. In 2010, a three-metre wave struck the Mentawai Islands, off the western coast of Sumatra in Indonesia, just minutes after a massive offshore earthquake. More than 400 people were killed and hundreds of homes were destroyed. In December 2004, a massive magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra in western Indonesia triggered a tsunami that killed 230,000 people in a dozen countries.
