World.title: Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan Iain Payten August 15, 2026 — 7:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

How Australia’s players performed in Saturday’s 56-17 win over Japan in Townsville. Tom Wright – 6 Had a first half to mostly forget, with decent attacking involvements offset by some clunky ones, and an ill-judged decision to run from his own half which saw him get isolated and give Japan entry, which they turned into a try. Easily the most instinctive of all Wallabies attackers but that can be a double-edged sword. Max Jorgensen – 7.5 A nice run lead to Australia’s first try, and some superb aerial work from Jorgensen in the middle of the game was one of the big reasons why the Wallabies started to get on top. Such a dangerous runner when given a sniff of space. More please.



Loading Isaac Henry – 7.5 Ewen McKenzie described Henry as Jesse Kriel-like during the week, and that’s a good call. Henry is a ball of muscle who is not only hard to bring down, he’s a solid hitter in defence, too. His hole run for Ryan Lonergan’s disallowed try was ‘chef’s kiss’. Backing Henry is one of Les Kiss’ best calls so far. Hunter Paisami – 8 Paisami is making the most of these rare starts for the Wallabies, and he’s given Kiss a headache, with Len Ikitau due back for the next Tests against Argentina. Powerful, skilful and smart – on both sides of the ball – Paisami set the tone for the whole Wallabies side, as far as the direct footy required to punch through Japan.



Hunter Paisami runs the ball in Townsville. Getty Images Harry Potter – 6 It wasn’t really a day to be a winger, given the Wallabies learned their best way to score was using the big boys at the other end of the team sheet. Potter was busy, as ever, but didn’t make a huge impact; his one long run across the field, that avoided six defenders but didn’t make a metre, probably summed things up. Carter Gordon – 7 There was inevitable rustiness from Carter, who hasn’t played in several weeks. And the Wallabies’ flow and confused attack in the first half probably suffered from that. But Gordon was solid and grew into the game. He was one of the stronger defenders, too.



Carter Gordon runs the ball during the match against Japan Getty Images Ryan Lonergan – 7 Marshalled the Wallaby forward runners nicely and kept the home team’s attack on top of Japan when they had the pill. Also kicked all his goals – have Australia finally found a reliable goalkicker? Marks off for conceding a try when he kicked a clearance straight into the Japanese eclipse – 206cm lock Harry Hockings. Harry Wilson (c) – 6.5 Industrious performance, as usual, that saw the skipper stick his hand up for some tough carries. Rewarded with a late try.



Carlo Tizzano was superb in Townsville. Getty Images Carlo Tizzano – 9 Yet again the Wallabies are blessed with two world-class opensides at the same time. Can we toss a bit of that magic flanker water over the five-eighths when they stand together please? Tizzano was simply outstanding, and his three steals in the second half all but snuffed out any hope of Japan staying in this game. Charlie Cale – 7 Cale produces his fair share of highlight-reel moments but you can be sure coaches love seeing head-down, bum-up efforts like this just as much. Not flashy but plenty productive. Equal top tackler for the Wallabies, and equal second-highest carrier. Grabbed some lineout steals, too.



Lukhan Salakaia-Loto – 6.5 Has embraced being a big enforcer and we saw that in his return to the Test team. Charged into the defence several times. Looked a bit cooked towards the end of his stint but that’s probably understandable Lachlan Shaw – 6.5 Had a bumpy entry into Test rugby off the bench in July but this was a much steadier day out for Shaw, in the starting pack. Contributed across the park with his trademark high workrate, and threw himself into defence. Loading



Taniela Tupou – 8.5 There are days when Taniela seems like he is everywhere, and on those days, the Wallabies rarely lose. Charged like a rhino near the line and scored two unstoppable tries, defended with starch and (mostly) handled the ball with aplomb. Confidence is sky-high. Josh Nasser – 6.5 Scored a nice try after a supporting chase, and threw well at the lineout again. But also seemed hampered with a leg injury in the first half, and was replaced by Brandon Paenga-Amosa at half-time. Angus Bell – 8



When it comes to ratings, Bell can suffer from the same problem as a Michael Hooper or a Rob Valetini. Their bar is so consistently high, you can overlook how good an “average” night at the office is. The Waratahs prop topped the tackle count, scored a try, hit bulk rucks, carried powerfully and was part of a dominant scrum. Angus Bell of the Wallabies scores a try. Getty Images RESERVES Brandon Paenga-Amosa – 8 Having missed the team in Osaka, BPA looked keen to make an impression on Les Kiss. And boy oh boy, did he make an impression. Outstanding and energetic 40-minute effort from the bench hooker, who seemed almost magnetically connected to the ball.



Aidan Ross – 6 Tidy cameo from the bench was part of the Wallabies’ pushover try in the second half. Massimo De Lutiis – 7 Some Wallabies debutants get minutes at the end of a thrashing, and carry a dusty memory. Not Wallaby No.1000, who scored a try within minutes of getting on, was part of a pushover and saw his side post 50 points. Not bad. Jeremy Williams – 7



Related Article Opinion

Wallabies Pigs in muck: Wallabies forwards have a field day against Japan Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author High quality from the bench, and you do wonder if Kiss will bring Williams back into the starting side when the dust has settled. Fraser McReight – 6.5 Limited minutes – Kiss said they’d planned to bring him on earlier – but McReight still did his thing, grabbing one steal and attacking in open space. Interesting question: will the Wallabies play McReight and Tizzano together against a bigger opponent? Tate McDermott – 6.5



Probably the smoothest performance from McDermott off the bench this year. Starting to get that deadly attacking threat back, after a long layoff. Ben Donaldson – 6 Solid effort from the bench, with some nice kicking and awareness of space out wide. Filipo Daugunu – 6 Looked like he wanted to get 30 touches with his limited game time, and may have got close.

World.title: A target of arsonists and gunmen, popular South Yarra nightclub faces financial collapse
World.content:
NationalVictoriaInsolvency A target of arsonists and gunmen, popular South Yarra nightclub faces financial collapse Cameron Houston and Carla Jaeger August 15, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A popular South Yarra nightclub that was recently the target of two firebombings and a drive-by shooting has been placed into external administration. The owners of The Emerson Rooftop Bar and Club filed documents with the corporate regulator on August 13 and declared that insolvency firm Mackay Goodwin had been appointed to oversee the embattled venue on Commercial Road. Shipping containers were put outside The Emerson following a drive-by shooting in May. Luis Enrique Ascui A spokesman for Emerson Holdings (Aus) Pty Ltd said the recent campaign of arson attacks, shootings and kidnappings involving licensed venues across Melbourne had taken a significant toll on the business. “The impact has extended well beyond the immediate physical damage, resulting in substantial recovery costs, operational disruption and sustained financial pressure on the business,” a company spokesman said.



However, he insisted The Emerson would remain open and trade as normal. Related Article Exclusive

Organised crime Alleged ‘bar wars’ shot caller was released early from youth detention “Voluntary administration provides an independent framework to preserve value, assess the options available to the company and pursue the best possible outcome for creditors,” he said. “The directors believe it offers the clearest path to address the impact of this exceptionally difficult period.” The collapse of The Emerson last week follows the voluntary administration of six other venues in Prahran and South Yarra also owned by the Good Company Bar Group, including Circus Bar, Electric Ladyland, Holy Grail, La La Land and Somewhere Bar.



Despite owing unsecured creditors more than $4 million when administrators were appointed in December 2025, the six venues have continued to operate following a deed of company arrangement with creditors in February. Related Article Analysis

Naked City Bar wars, carjackings, home invasions: Why I grieve for my city At the time, the owners blamed the debts on challenging trading conditions and rising security costs caused by a surge in crime. However, the administrators pointed to poor strategic management and the use of cash to fund a web of related-party loans, according to a report from January. The administrators also found companies linked to the venues were involved in the acquisition of several luxury assets, including a $520,000 party boat docked at a marina on Hamilton Island, two Mercedes-Benz wagons and a 2017 black Bentley coupe.



The future of The Emerson remains uncertain, after six turbulent months for the venue and its owners. In February, the nightclub was forced to temporarily close after it was the target of a ram raid and arson attack. CCTV footage obtained by this masthead captured three hooded figures driving a white utility vehicle through the venue’s entrance. They doused the area with fuel from jerry cans and set it alight. The venue was again firebombed in April, when a loading dock at the rear of the premises was torched. Just days later, the club was sprayed with bullets while patrons were inside.



The owners responded to the violence by parking two shipping containers in front of the club, which have since been removed. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Late drama as Eels pip Cowboys to keep rivals’ finals hopes alive
World.content:
Parramatta 32 North Queensland 30 SportNRLNRL 2026 Late drama as Eels pip Cowboys to keep rivals’ finals hopes alive Scott Bailey August 15, 2026 — 8:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The race for the NRL’s top eight is still alive after a controversial late penalty consigned North Queensland to a 32-30 loss to Parramatta at CommBank Stadium. With a chance to lock in a finals spot beckoning, the Cowboys’ defence crumbled on Saturday night as they let in six Eels tries. Loading The defining moment then came with four minutes to play, when Mitch Moses set up for a Parramatta field goal with scores locked at 30-30. The Eels halfback eventually ran it on the last, was ankle-tapped by Heilum Luki and spilled the ball forward while falling.



But Moses reviewed the call, and the bunker found he had been collected in the head by Tom Chester while just inches above the ground. The result means Canterbury are still alive in the race for the finals, albeit still two points behind the Cowboys and with North Queensland having a bye next week. Loading Manly also remain in the hunt, but would need to win their last three and have the Cowboys drop their final two games at home against Wests Tigers and Canberra. As tough as the late penalty may have been for North Queensland, their defence remains a massive issue just weeks out from the finals.



A fortnight after leaking 82 points to the Sydney Roosters, it was poor again on Saturday night. The tone was set when Parramatta winger Brian Kelly went 60 metres from the opening kick-off, while the Cowboys also conceded six first-half penalties. The Eels celebrate a try against North Queensland. Getty Images Luki could also find himself in trouble with the match review committee, after being sin-binned in the opening half for a high shot on Luca Moretti. There is no doubt North Queensland’s attack has the spark to put points on, with halfback Jaxon Purdue again impressing.



He put on a long cut-out ball for a Braidon Burns try in the first half, then stepped Teancum Brown and fullback Apa Twidle for a second-half try of his own. Related Article Cronulla 20 Canberra 24

NRL 2026 Trindall injured as Raiders bump Sharks out of NRL’s top four Reed Mahoney also starred out of dummy-half, burrowing over for the night’s first try, before going short to Reuben Cotter and putting him over after the break. The Cowboys also put on one of the tries of the year with scores locked at 24-24, with the ball going from right to left and back to the right through five passes and two kicks before Chester crossed. Not to be outdone, Parramatta also had plenty of attacking flair.



It was big prop Junior Paulo who responded to level the scores at 30-30, with a lofted 35-metre cut-out ball in the lead-up to a Jordan Samrani try. Moses also had three try assists and broke through the line in the lead-up to a Tallyn Da Silva penalty try. And his off-contract halves partner Ronald Volkman again pushed his case for another deal, scoring one try and putting a grubber-kick in for a Josh Addo-Carr four-pointer.

World.title: ‘We just didn’t have the answers’: The lifesaving disability teams keeping families afloat
World.content:
NationalNSWFamily ‘We just didn’t have the answers’: The lifesaving disability teams keeping families afloat Rachel Rasker August 15, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Rose Mitchell was 10, she felt like she became a parent. “The minute he was born, something shifted within me,” she said of her brother Daniel Rata. From that day on, for decades, the pair were inseparable. Now, no matter how often she visits her brother, it never feels like enough. “I carry a lot of guilt with having my own independent life away from him,” she said. “I struggle with balancing being that caretaker for him ... with trying to find my own identity outside of being his sister.” Rose Mitchell said her brother Daniel Rata has enriched her life. STEVEN SIEWERT



For the carers and families of the approximately 117,000 people with an intellectual disability in NSW, finding and accessing support in a fragmented system is “exceptionally hard,” said Dr Alexis Berry, vice president of the Australian Association of Developmental Disability Medicine. Previously, she said people with intellectual disabilities would be known to their local government service, which acted as a “one-stop shop”, with a case manager assigned. “With the introduction of the NDIS, it’s become a much more individualistic approach, so it’s up to the individual to navigate the system – there’s nobody there helping them do that,” Berry said. Rata needed to be frequently hospitalised due to seizures, and his frustrated, violent meltdowns became difficult for his family to manage as he aged into a fully grown adult who didn’t know his own strength. “There was a lot of fear around taking him outside, which would have helped him because he needs that stimulation,” Mitchell, who is based in Sydney’s inner-west, said. “We felt like we had to control his environment at all times, just in case, because we just didn’t have the answers.”



Rose Mitchell and her brother have been inseparable since “the minute he was born”. STEVEN SIEWERT It wasn’t until Mitchell’s family was connected with the Sydney Local Health District’s Specialist Intellectual Disability Health Team (SIDHT) that she realised she wouldn’t have to spend her whole life as the primary carer for her brother. Without their support, “I have no idea where we would be”. Related Article Healthcare ‘Why are you letting them do this?’ The terror these mothers have for ‘unseen’ children There are just seven SIDHTs teams across the state’s 15 local health districts. Each small team is made up of a doctor, nurse and other health professionals, and aims to address the complex health needs of people with an intellectual disability. “Only a small proportion of the people who really could benefit from these teams are able to access them and get that benefit,” Jim Simpson, senior advocate for the Council for Intellectual Disability (CID) said.



Funding for existing teams was not determined by local population need, but instead by which LHDs had the organisation and infrastructure in place to put in a funding bid at their inception in 2019, according to advocates. Simpson said this has created a funding inequity, and the CID is now calling on the government to boost services in the areas with the highest need, and expand to 15 teams: “In other words, a team in every local health district”. Health outcomes for people with an intellectual disability remain “unconscionable,” Simpson said. Compared to the general population, they are more than twice as likely to die potentially avoidable deaths, and die an average 27 years earlier. They are also over-represented in the healthcare system, with hospitalisation and emergency presentation rates twice as high, and admissions also twice as long, and twice and expensive. A 2025 evaluation of the existing SIDHTs commissioned by NSW Health found the teams improved short-term and intermediate outcomes for clients. Simpson said expansion of the teams has the potential to save the health system overall through preventative healthcare and reduced hospitalisations.



In a statement, NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said since 2020, the SIDHTs have assessed more than 3700 people, and his government would continue to engage closely with the CID on their funding. He said the government invested over $6 million to operate the NSW Intellectual Disability Health Service each year. Daniel Rata is now thriving, and loves playing basketball. STEVEN SIEWERT When clinicians in Rata’s SIDHT linked his behaviour to anxiety and put him on new medication, Mitchell said everything changed for their family, as the fear of taking him outside dissipated. “It just completely levelled out the frequency of the meltdowns, and it meant that he could start integrating into social groups again,” she said, allowing the siblings to return to their favourite activities. “We would go to the local basketball courts and he would play for hours ... he would make friends in the park,” she said. “I could go and chill on the sidelines, and he would just be feeding his soul because he’s socialising and he’s playing basketball and doing all the things that he loves.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The two species NSW is racing to protect after fifth case of deadly virus
World.content:
NationalNSWBird flu The two species NSW is racing to protect after fifth case of deadly virus Angus Dalton August 15, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NSW government has identified little penguins and critically endangered regent honeyeaters as priority species for bird flu vaccination, after the state’s fifth case of the deadly virus was confirmed on Saturday in a greater crested tern found dead near Eden on the South Coast. At least 50 birds of the same species died in a mass mortality event in South Australia earlier this month. Little penguins are a priority species for vaccination, the NSW government said. A Victorian little penguin has died from the disease. Sitthixay Ditthavong With increasing deaths and the detection of the virus in a “Typhoid Mary” superspreader species, attention is starting to shift from individual sick or dead birds to monitoring for mass die-offs and detecting shifts in the virus’s genetics. A Victorian plan to vaccinate 5000 little penguins on Phillip Island did not move fast enough, with news of a penguin dying from the disease breaking on Saturday.



The NSW government said plans to inoculate captive little penguins and regent honeyeaters in the state were on track but awaiting approval from the national Animal Health Committee. The government is working with organisations including Taronga Zoo, which breeds regent honeyeaters for wild release. Fewer than 400 exist in the wild. Between 200 and 400 regent honeyeaters exist in the wild. Getty Images While the vaccine can reduce mortality, it’s not known exactly how well it protects native birds, and experts warn vaccines alone can’t stop ecological catastrophe. The government has acknowledged there is little data about the vaccine’s effectiveness outside of poultry. “It is not a silver bullet. The vaccine cannot be the only weapon to control the virus and containment of outbreaks. It’s a supplementary tool,” bird flu expert Dr Ariful Islam from Charles Sturt University said.



Last year, the government commissioned trials at CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness to establish dose rates for small native bird species. Further pilot studies tested the safety of the vaccine – which was developed for poultry – in other captive natives including penguins, ratites (emus and cassowaries), raptors, owls, shorebirds, ducks, cockatoos and other parrots. When asked for efficacy data, a spokesperson from the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry said “results to date have been encouraging and have informed regulatory assessments and emergency use arrangements for the vaccine”. The spread of the virus into silver gulls in South Australia has sparked fears of widespread infection among native birds.



Bird ecologist Professor Anne Peters, from Monash University, dubbed the notorious fish-and-chip thieves the “Typhoid Mary” superspreaders of bird flu because they range widely between cities, the coast and inland areas. Infected ducks, meanwhile, can carry the virus far without falling ill. “Finding active viruses in birds that aren’t sick at all would also be extremely worrying,” Peters said. NSW’s fifth bird flu case has been confirmed in a greater crested tern, a species which suffered a mass die-off in South Australia. Neil Bowman “Unfortunately, very many of our birds but also mammals, for example seals and sea lions, but also dolphins, are known to be at great risk of mass mortalities.” Experts have called for greater action to protect marine mammals, including the endangered Australian sea lion.



A trial in the US showed a vaccine developed for cows safely generated antibodies in elephant seals, suggesting existing vaccines might be adapted to protect pinnipeds. Australian authorities are monitoring those trials. Professor Euan Ritchie, an ecologist at Deakin University, questioned why the government hadn’t capitalised on the five-year head start Australia had before the virus arrived to invest in developing our own vaccine to protect the nation’s globally unique mammals. An Australian sea lion pup at Taronga Zoo. The endangered species is at dire risk of bird flu. Louise Kennerley “If [a mammal vaccination] is possible, and it’s only been limited by investment, then the government would need to answer to Australians why that hasn’t been a priority,” he said. Delivering the two required vaccine doses to many wild species is not feasible, but it’s theoretically possible to target some threatened animal populations such as sea lions, Ritchie said.



“In some cases, like the Tasmanian devil, they have small populations and they’re range-restricted, so it’s not outside the realm of possibility to entertain a vaccination program.” Related Article Bird flu ‘List of doom’: Bird flu puts one in five Australian bird and mammal species at risk The genotype of H5 bird flu hitting Australia, called B3.2, ripped down the entire west coast of South America in just six months before jumping into the sub-Antarctic, according to CSIRO. “[It caused] great impact to South American poultry industries as well as to wild bird life and to marine mammals, so that’s why we’re concerned about the introduction of this virus to Australia,” Dr Frank Wong from the agency’s Australian Animal Health Laboratory said. The genotype is different to the strain of the virus that has circulated in dairy cows and sickened humans in the US.



CSIRO released a pre-print paper last week using genomic data to track how the virus spread from South America across the sub-Antarctic to Australia. The agency is now monitoring the virus for changes, including re-assortment with local low-pathogenic bird flu, which could increase infectiousness, and mutations in a gene called PB2. “In other parts of the world, when this virus has got into mammals, there’s certain particular nucleotides in the gene which change and allow that virus to infect mammals more readily,” Dr Matthew Neave from CSIRO said. The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

World.title: Residents need waste education, not more bin nights
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Residents need waste education, not more bin nights August 15, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Waste education key

The state Liberals propose weekly rubbish bin collection. But what about when we run out of landfill sites? Instead of encouraging more rubbish, why not educate people on how to reduce waste? This would be a longer-term and more environmental solution.

Our family was inspired by a couple who went a year without putting their landfill bin out. We composted all our food scraps, tissues and paper towels in a worm farm and composting bays, which Imade from pallets . I covered them up with chook-wire to keep the rats and possums out. (Dog poo’s OK too, as long as you don’t put it on your veggies.) We bought a set of washable nappies, refilled containers with shampoo, laundry powder and honey from the local wholefoods store. And tried to buy products that had minimal or recyclable packaging. All the soft plastics, we bagged and took to Woolies.

After six months of not putting our bin out, a tatty old pillow tipped us over the edge. That was a couple of years ago. But now, thanks to Liberals leader Jess Wilson, we’re fired up to see if we can beat our PB.

Grant Morgan, Hurstbridge Priorities amiss

Angus Taylor, Andrew Bragg and Tim Wilson have done no favours to ordinary Australians with their plans to gut the National Construction Code. Wilson says lower income earners should just “put on a jumper” in colder weather. They propose reducing regulation including energy efficiency. Wow. They (say they) will make housing cheaper and make owners (and renters) pay for it with increased energy use for the life of the building. They decry the cost of energy on the one hand but on the other hand they will make us all use more of it. If people should just get used to the weather, they could start by turning off the heating and cooling in Parliament House.

Chris Curnow, Skye Outrageous spending

For the Bayside Council to propose spending $40,000 to forensically research how the endangered Growling Grass Frogs first arrived at the site of the Yalukit William Nature Reserve, in Brighton, is outrageous (″⁣How did frogs get to Brighton? For council, it’s a $40,000 question″⁣, 13/8). Our rates should be spent on protecting and preserving endangered species, including frogs, not a witch-hunt. The volunteers for the Yalukit William Nature Reserve Association, who care for this site, should be applauded and encouraged by the council, for their work.

Caroline Shepard, Brighton



Look to the birds

Growling Grass Frogs used to be common in the eastern suburbs of Melbourne, although their presence has no doubt been affected by the recent worldwide decline in frog populations due to a fungal disease

While it is comforting to learn that this frog species is once again thriving in a Brighton nature reserve, it is also laughable to learn that Bayside Council is considering spending $40,000 to dispel a claim that they were illegally transported from Melbourne’s west. If indeed the species has only recently arrived at the reserve it is more likely that the frog eggs were transported there by water birds, which is a common method of distribution.

John Lambrick, Malvern Heat problems

They are shutting down nuclear sites in Europe because of the heatwaves causing lack of water. What say those who want them here in our climate?

Ross Hosking, Blackwood, SA Power of policies

Sussan Ley says her bus trip through America was to try to find ″⁣clarity″⁣. She has talked about people whose lives were in transition and disarray, and people who are disconnected from politics and the ways of government, and those whose lives are characterised by a lifetime of being overlooked.

It is somewhat disingenuous to speak of people as being ″⁣overlooked″⁣ without acknowledging the structural conditions that leave people overlooked in the first place. Chronic, grinding poverty, insecure housing, inadequate access to health and social services, and persistent economic exclusion are not incidental to people’s disconnection from government.

These are not simply personal circumstances. Disconnection is shaped by policy choices, the distribution of resources and access to opportunity. If we are serious about understanding people who feel overlooked, we need to look beyond their disconnection and examine the structural conditions that produce it. Clarify is what governments must do: to make the connections between people’s lived experiences and the policies that shape them and allocating resources to address disadvantage rather than simply describing its consequences. Every government has a responsibility to improve the lives of its citizens, particularly those who do not have the income and resources necessary to live a decent and secure life.

Dr Helen Keleher, Professor (Adj) Monash University The correct usage

Not to sound pedantic, but Nikki Barrowclough’s piece (“About time we got our heads around correct grammar”, 14/08) wasn’t about grammar at all. It was about usage. She has noticed the relentless rise in the popularity of around in place of alternative prepositions such as concerning or regarding. She has put her finger on a trend that she finds annoying, and many of us would agree with her. But none of her examples seem to be ungrammatical; they are just questions of usage or style.

By contrast, it would be very bad grammar to say “I’m sick of him hanging around I”, instead of “around me”. In English, prepositions are followed by nouns or pronouns in the objective or accusative case, like him or me.

Justin McDermott, West Brunswick Sides of a coin

Your correspondent (Letters, 15/8) argues that private school funding alleviates strain on state schools, but how do we justify a system where 98 per cent of our private schools are funded above the School Resourcing Standard and 98 per cent of public schools below this standard?

Productivity Commission data shows that over the 2023-24 period non-government school spending per student grew 27.5 per cent versus 5 per cent for government schools. A UNICEF report has described the Australian education system as one of the most unequal in the developed world.

In the end, it is not about who pays for what, but about the sort ofsociety we want, and we are accepting a divided educational system that would not be tolerated by any other visionary country.

Bryan Long, Balwyn



A hipster the PM is not

Can we just move on from the PM’s stupid remark about melons? He was trying to be hip and failed miserably. Surely there must be more important things on the agenda.

Ian Anderson, Ascot Vale Fruits of sadness

Ditch the influencers prime minister, we would rather not know their opinion – it only leads to melancholia.

Greg Curtin, Nunawading Spoils of war

So now we need to buy a missile system to protect the AUKUS submarines we may never see. MAGA has become MARA – Make Americans Richer Again.

Pete Garfield, Echuca Bin, and gone

Following his defeat in the Clacton byelection in the UK, I guess the Count is now, sadly, a bit of a has-bin.

Paul Sands, Sunbury The real thing

The country sends all its loving to you, Johnny. Young Talent Time was such good fun. Smiley is a great anti-war song. You were the real thing. Tomorrow, we’ll miss you.

Ann Rennie, Surrey Hills

World.title: Two billy goats boarded a bus in Portland. They did not have tickets
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAnimals Two billy goats boarded a bus in Portland. They did not have tickets Neil Vigdor August 15, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was not a moment to spare. The doors to the TriMet bus, which was heading west on Tuesday morning towards downtown Portland, Oregon, had started to close when they opened for two stragglers. Loading Neither paid the fare. Kids ride free – or so they thought.



Not in the case of these two juvenile goats, which transit officials and police said had escaped from their enclosure and ventured onto a lime green FX2-Division bus. Security camera footage chronicled their strange escapade, showing some other passengers doing a double take before shooing the goats off the bus after the driver reopened the doors. Their jaunt prompted 911 calls and drew comparisons in Portland to the famous 2002 foray of a coyote that wandered onto a light rail MAX train, which was not in service at the time, and inspired a music video and another song. “They don’t have a valid pass,” the driver playfully told the other passengers as the goats exited the bus. The goats belong to a family that lives less than two blocks from the bus stop and are named Billy the Kid and Billy the Goat, Lrae Anderson, who identified himself as the owner, said on Friday.



“I couldn’t believe that they actually went across the busy street and tried to get on the bus and all that,” Anderson said. “They got on like they’ve done it before.” Related Article MIFF Love watching Neil the seal? This doco unearths the truth about ‘nuisance’ animals Anderson, 48, a rapper who also goes by the name Copper Loc, said his children — he has four sons — sometimes forgot to close the gate of the goats’ enclosure. A neighbour brought the goats back to their home the same day, Anderson said, noting that he had since installed a lock and improved the fencing.



Anderson said the family had acquired the goats about three months ago after moving to the property at the suggestion of a friend, who told him they would feed on plentiful blackberries from sticker bushes on the property. Since their escape he had learnt that they were pygmy goats, he said. Footage of the horned interlopers, which TriMet posted last week to Instagram, had amassed more than 5.4 million views, according to the transit agency. “The video of them boarding the bus has definitely sparked something in people’s imaginations,” Tyler Graf, a spokesperson for TriMet, said in an email on Friday. But not every passenger paid much attention to the escapees, video footage from inside the bus showed.



“I see the one lady,” Anderson said. “She’s sitting there, and she’s on her phone and she didn’t even notice the goats on the bus. I was like, ‘What are they doing?’” Two loose pygmy goats unexpectedly wandered onto a bus in Portland, Oregon. TRIMET As he was preparing for a hip-hop show in Seattle scheduled for Saturday, Anderson said the episode had provided musical inspiration. “I’ve already started making a song about the goats,” he said. World.title: Death toll rises in Indonesia after powerful earthquake
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaIndonesia Death toll rises in Indonesia after powerful earthquake Updated August 15, 2026 — 7:39pm ,first published 10:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Maumere, Indonesia: A powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early on Saturday, killing at least 38 people, collapsing buildings and homes as well as causing panic in a region prone to deadly quakes. Authorities said more than a dozen residents were injured. Authorities issued a tsunami warning and urged coastal residents to move to higher ground, but later lifted the warning when Indonesia’s Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency said monitoring showed no significant sea-level changes that would pose a threat to coastal communities. Loading The US Geological Survey said the quake hit Indonesia’s Flores region with a depth of 10 kilometres at 5:58am, local time. Its epicentre was 68 km north-northwest of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province. The initial quake was followed by several aftershocks. The head of the National Disaster Management Agency, Suharyanto, said rescuers have recovered at least 38 bodies, mostly in the three devastated regencies of Sikka, Manggarai and East Manggarai, including 16 bodies that were pulled from a landslide in the village of Reok in Manggarai. At least 13 people were rushed to nearby hospitals, including two with serious injuries.



Suharyanto said three helicopters and a rescue vessel were deployed to assist with logistics and support emergency response operations, including possible evacuations if needed, given East Nusa Tenggara’s geography, which consists of numerous islands and presents significant transportation and access challenges. He said about 2000 villagers in Nagekeo regency fled their homes to temporary shelters. Damaged houses following a 7.7-magnitude earthquake in Ruteng, Indonesia. AFP People clear up the rubble from a house damaged in an earthquake in East Manggarai, East Nusa Tenggara province. AP East Nusa Tenggara Police Chief Rudi Darmoko said the earthquake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings. He said power outages in cities and villages have hampered the flow of information and complicated search and rescue efforts.



“We are continuing to collect reports of damage and casualties, but there are communication disruptions,” Darmoko said. He said that landslides in Ende regency triggered by the earthquake also cut off the Trans-Flores highway, a roughly 700-kilometre paved mountain road spanning Flores Island, from Labuan Bajo to Larantuka. Footage on local television showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution following the quake. Hospital staff moved equipment outdoors, including beds, IV stands and oxygen cylinders, and set up temporary treatment areas to adapt to emergency conditions. Rescuers search for victims at a damaged building in Maumere, East Nusa Tenggara Province, Indonesia, following the earthquake, BASARNAS via AP Quake felt on Flores island and other areas The quake was felt across much of Flores island with initial reports indicating heavy damage.



Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka regency, said a number of buildings were damaged by the strong shaking and panicked people ran to higher ground. “Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the port terminal in Maumere had collapsed,” she said. Students at St. Peter Major Seminary in Sikka who were attending morning Mass fled in panic when the roof of an assembly hall collapsed, said Reverend Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of the seminary, which is known locally as Ritapiret Seminary on the predominantly Catholic island of Flores. A damaged building in Ruteng on Flores Island, Indonesia. AFP “Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof,” Tanga said. “At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake.”



The quake also reportedly caused panic in Labuan Bajo, a gateway town to eastern Indonesia’s Komodo National Park, one of the country’s best-known attractions. Damage was also reported in Bima, a city in neighboring West Nusa Tenggara province, and in some parts of southern Sulawesi island. Indonesian authorities initially issued a tsunami warning for parts of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, and urged residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks. The agency located the shallow undersea quake near Flores island. Indonesia prone to earthquakes Indonesia, a vast archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the “Ring of Fire,” an arc of volcanoes and fault lines in the Pacific Basin. A powerful earthquake caused a tsunami in 1992 that killed about 2500 people on Flores, part of a group of islands in the eastern half of Indonesia.



Editor's pick Myanmar coup On the front line of a forgotten war, you can’t see your enemy – but you can hear him In 2018, a magnitude 7.5 quake spawned a large localised tsunami that wiped out coastal areas, while liquefaction caused by the shaking turned entire neighbourhoods into rivers of sludge in the eastern Indonesian city of Palu, on the Palu-Koro Fault. The disaster killed more than 4,400 people. In 2010, a three-metre wave struck the Mentawai Islands, off the western coast of Sumatra in Indonesia, just minutes after a massive offshore earthquake. More than 400 people were killed and hundreds of homes were destroyed. In December 2004, a massive magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra in western Indonesia triggered a tsunami that killed 230,000 people in a dozen countries. World.title: Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan Iain Payten August 15, 2026 — 7:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

How Australia’s players performed in Saturday’s 56-17 win over Japan in Townsville. Tom Wright – 6 Had a first half to mostly forget, with decent attacking involvements offset by some clunky ones, and an ill-judged decision to run from his own half which saw him get isolated and give Japan entry, which they turned into a try. Easily the most instinctive of all Wallabies attackers but that can be a double-edged sword. Max Jorgensen – 7.5 A nice run lead to Australia’s first try, and some superb aerial work from Jorgensen in the middle of the game was one of the big reasons why the Wallabies started to get on top. Such a dangerous runner when given a sniff of space. More please.



Loading Isaac Henry – 7.5 Ewen McKenzie described Henry as Jesse Kriel-like during the week, and that’s a good call. Henry is a ball of muscle who is not only hard to bring down, he’s a solid hitter in defence, too. His hole run for Ryan Lonergan’s disallowed try was ‘chef’s kiss’. Backing Henry is one of Les Kiss’ best calls so far. Hunter Paisami – 8 Paisami is making the most of these rare starts for the Wallabies, and he’s given Kiss a headache, with Len Ikitau due back for the next Tests against Argentina. Powerful, skilful and smart – on both sides of the ball – Paisami set the tone for the whole Wallabies side, as far as the direct footy required to punch through Japan.



Hunter Paisami runs the ball in Townsville. Getty Images Harry Potter – 6 It wasn’t really a day to be a winger, given the Wallabies learned their best way to score was using the big boys at the other end of the team sheet. Potter was busy, as ever, but didn’t make a huge impact; his one long run across the field, that avoided six defenders but didn’t make a metre, probably summed things up. Carter Gordon – 7 There was inevitable rustiness from Carter, who hasn’t played in several weeks. And the Wallabies’ flow and confused attack in the first half probably suffered from that. But Gordon was solid and grew into the game. He was one of the stronger defenders, too.



Carter Gordon runs the ball during the match against Japan Getty Images Ryan Lonergan – 7 Marshalled the Wallaby forward runners nicely and kept the home team’s attack on top of Japan when they had the pill. Also kicked all his goals – have Australia finally found a reliable goalkicker? Marks off for conceding a try when he kicked a clearance straight into the Japanese eclipse – 206cm lock Harry Hockings. Harry Wilson (c) – 6.5 Industrious performance, as usual, that saw the skipper stick his hand up for some tough carries. Rewarded with a late try.



Carlo Tizzano was superb in Townsville. Getty Images Carlo Tizzano – 9 Yet again the Wallabies are blessed with two world-class opensides at the same time. Can we toss a bit of that magic flanker water over the five-eighths when they stand together please? Tizzano was simply outstanding, and his three steals in the second half all but snuffed out any hope of Japan staying in this game. Charlie Cale – 7 Cale produces his fair share of highlight-reel moments but you can be sure coaches love seeing head-down, bum-up efforts like this just as much. Not flashy but plenty productive. Equal top tackler for the Wallabies, and equal second-highest carrier. Grabbed some lineout steals, too.



Lukhan Salakaia-Loto – 6.5 Has embraced being a big enforcer and we saw that in his return to the Test team. Charged into the defence several times. Looked a bit cooked towards the end of his stint but that’s probably understandable Lachlan Shaw – 6.5 Had a bumpy entry into Test rugby off the bench in July but this was a much steadier day out for Shaw, in the starting pack. Contributed across the park with his trademark high workrate, and threw himself into defence. Loading



Taniela Tupou – 8.5 There are days when Taniela seems like he is everywhere, and on those days, the Wallabies rarely lose. Charged like a rhino near the line and scored two unstoppable tries, defended with starch and (mostly) handled the ball with aplomb. Confidence is sky-high. Josh Nasser – 6.5 Scored a nice try after a supporting chase, and threw well at the lineout again. But also seemed hampered with a leg injury in the first half, and was replaced by Brandon Paenga-Amosa at half-time. Angus Bell – 8



When it comes to ratings, Bell can suffer from the same problem as a Michael Hooper or a Rob Valetini. Their bar is so consistently high, you can overlook how good an “average” night at the office is. The Waratahs prop topped the tackle count, scored a try, hit bulk rucks, carried powerfully and was part of a dominant scrum. Angus Bell of the Wallabies scores a try. Getty Images RESERVES Brandon Paenga-Amosa – 8 Having missed the team in Osaka, BPA looked keen to make an impression on Les Kiss. And boy oh boy, did he make an impression. Outstanding and energetic 40-minute effort from the bench hooker, who seemed almost magnetically connected to the ball.



Aidan Ross – 6 Tidy cameo from the bench was part of the Wallabies’ pushover try in the second half. Massimo De Lutiis – 7 Some Wallabies debutants get minutes at the end of a thrashing, and carry a dusty memory. Not Wallaby No.1000, who scored a try within minutes of getting on, was part of a pushover and saw his side post 50 points. Not bad. Jeremy Williams – 7



Related Article Opinion

Wallabies Pigs in muck: Wallabies forwards have a field day against Japan Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author High quality from the bench, and you do wonder if Kiss will bring Williams back into the starting side when the dust has settled. Fraser McReight – 6.5 Limited minutes – Kiss said they’d planned to bring him on earlier – but McReight still did his thing, grabbing one steal and attacking in open space. Interesting question: will the Wallabies play McReight and Tizzano together against a bigger opponent? Tate McDermott – 6.5



Probably the smoothest performance from McDermott off the bench this year. Starting to get that deadly attacking threat back, after a long layoff. Ben Donaldson – 6 Solid effort from the bench, with some nice kicking and awareness of space out wide. Filipo Daugunu – 6 Looked like he wanted to get 30 touches with his limited game time, and may have got close.

World.title: Water main bursts in Porirua, causing hours of disruption
World.content:
A burst water main in Porirua was being repaired on Saturday night, with water outages expected to end around 10.30pm.

A 300mm main burst on Mepham Place around 2:20pm on Saturday, causing asphalt on the road to crack.

That led to outages for the city centre, Rānui, and Elsdon.

"It is anticipated that service will be interrupted for at least eight hours," mayor Anita Baker said on Saturday afternoon.

Pātaka Art + Museum, Café Kaizen, Porirua Library, and Te Rauparaha Arena and Aquatic Centre all closed as a result of the burst water main.

A water tank was ordered for affected residents.

In the following hours, Tiaki Wai confirmed the outages had been contained to numbers 1-16 on Champion Street and all of Mepham Place.

World.title: Auckland Airport enters next phase of international terminal redevelopment
World.content:
Auckland Airport is moving into the next phase of its international terminal redevelopment, with retail and duty-free areas being refurbished for departing and arriving travellers.

The airport said the retail upgrade is its most significant airside refurbishment in a decade.

Work is underway on duty-free areas at international departures and arrivals, including two stores near departure gates.

The airport said the refurbished areas will have new layouts and a wider range of products, with beauty and fragrance at the centre of the changes.

Auckland Airport Chief Commercial Officer Mark Thomson said the changes are aimed at giving travellers a more engaging experience and greater choice.

"This is a deliberate move to strengthen our retail mix, provide an enhanced customer proposition, and modernise the space."

The redevelopment will also include new standalone retail stores, while the airport said further improvements to food and beverage areas are planned later this year.

Two standalone stores due to open later this year are skincare and bodycare brand Aesop and French fragrance brand Le Labo.

Some of the refurbished duty-free areas have already reopened, with the remaining retail refurbishment expected to be completed by December.

The airport said the overall footprint of its duty-free area will not increase as part of the redevelopment.

The international terminal transformation has been underway since January, with the work being carried out in stages while the terminal remains operational.

World.title: Nurse who cared for student who died at mental health unit can be named
World.content:
A name suppression order for one of the nurses responsible for the care of a 21-year-old student who died by suicide at a mental health ward has lapsed.

Erica Hume died in May 2014 at Palmerston North Hospital, a death Coroner Matthew Bates ruled was preventable and could have been avoided if staff had correctly followed policies and procedures.

He also found staff were under pressure due to the high number of patients and that the ward's physical environment wasn't fit for purpose. A replacement ward opened last year.

During an inquest into the death in 2022, temporary name suppression orders covered healthcare workers. When the coroner's ruling was released in June these orders lifted, except for one covering registered nurse Donna Jo-Anne Jones.

She was granted temporary suppression to allow her to consider an appeal against the coroner's ruling against her application for suppression.

She had until 31 July to do this, but the Coroner's Court and the High Court have confirmed no application was received.

Erica Hume's parents, Carey and Owen, said they were pleased to see the order lapse.

"Open justice does require people to be named and applications for a permanent non-disclosure order should be declined if there is truly to be embedded change in mental healthcare within New Zealand," they told RNZ in a statement.

Erica's father Owen Hume at his daughter's inquest. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Nurse's role among widespread systemic failures - coroner

Coroner Bates' ruling declining Jones' application for suppression said she cited interests of justice and personal privacy in arguing her name should remain secret. The coroner has ruled the specifics of her argument are suppressed.

Jones, who could not be contacted, managed Erica Hume's admission to the Palmerston North Hospital mental health ward, known as ward 21, on 6 May 2014 and nursed her that evening. Erica Hume died the next day.

The coroner found that despite Erica Hume's care worker giving a "detailed and diligent verbal handover", Jones did not take on board the heightened risk of suicide.

She also failed to adequately review admission information in Erica Hume's clinical file and record that information on admission documentation.

"These failures meant that from the time of admission to ward 21, Erica's heightened risk of suicide... went either unrecognised on the ward or, at the very least, the severity of her risk was not appreciated."

Coroner Matthew Bates at Erica Hume's inquest. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Coroner Bates said this affected the care Erica Hume received, including the levels of observation she was under, and the following shift wasn't fully appraised of the situation.

The coroner said Jones believed she did the best she could in the time available, writing in Erica Hume's file: "Admission paperwork to complete. Due to ward activity, unable to do."

Jones did not alone bear responsibility for Erica Hume's death and no individual was singled out for criticism in his findings, the coroner said.

"The role she played occurred in the context of widespread systemic failings and resourcing shortfalls at ward 21, including prolonged staff shortages."

Jones has been a registered nurse for almost 20 years and still works at Palmerston North Hospital.

Public interest in naming - Hume family

Carey and Owen Hume said after Erica's death they encountered a hospital system "embedded with non disclosure" and a "deep-seated expectation of non accountability".

"It is our opinion that accountability is a major factor in the examination of the care of Erica, and this includes the actions or inactions of all parties, staff and management.

"It is also our opinion that the purpose of having an inquest is to determine what happened and try to ensure that there is no repeat of the circumstances that allowed it to happen.

"This means, too, that individual as well as collective responsibility and accountability must occur."

Erica Hume in her Year 12 ball dress, taken several years before she died by suicide at Palmerston North Hospital aged 21. RNZ / Supplied

Carey and Owen Hume said for too long it was assumed healthcare workers would receive name suppression because it would harm their therapeutic relationship with patients, which was a a poor excuse.

"We firmly believe patients and families have the right to informed consent and knowledge of whom they are entrusting their care to," they said.

There was public interest in naming Jones and her not seeking to appeal against the coroner's ruling could be a sign she was taking responsibility for her role in what happened, which they said wasn't minor.

World.title: 38 dead after 7.7 magnitude earthquake strikes off coast of Indonesia
World.content:
A 7.7-magnitude earthquake that struck eastern Indonesia on Saturday killed at least 38 people, a disaster management official said, revising an earlier toll.

"Thirty-eight people have been confirmed dead, two were seriously injured, 11 sustained minor injuries, and approximately 2000 people have evacuated on their own," National Disaster Mitigation Agency chief Suharyanto told a news conference.

Dozens of aftershocks struck off eastern Indonesia after the main quake.

Tsunami waves of less than 1 metre were recorded in several areas of the Southeast Asian nation after the early morning tremor. The tsunami warning was lifted about three hours after the quake.

Rescuers around the port town of Maumere found 20 dead, six injured and two trapped under the rubble, said Fathur Rahman, head of the city's rescue agency. Maumere is the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in the east of Indonesia's vast archipelago.

Teams were yet to reach Nagekeo, the region closest to the epicentre, and communications signals there had been affected, Fathur told Reuters. Attempts to reach Nagekeo by car were blocked by landslides, while another team was attempting to go by ferry, he said.

Rescuers working amid the rubble of a damaged building after an earthquake in Maumere, East Nusa Tenggara. AFP PHOTO / INDONESIA'S NATIONAL SEARCH AND RESCUE AGENCY (BASARNAS)

About 2000 residents in Nagekeo evacuated, and damage was reported to a number of houses, warehouses and government facilities, national disaster mitigation agency BNPB said. Authorities also reported traffic congestion and power outages affecting parts of the regency, it said.

The governor of East Nusa Tenggara Province, Emanuel Melkiades Laka Lena, told a press conference at least five people died from collapsing rubble as they slept.

The BNPB, which put the quake's toll at one dead and four injured, said it was still gathering data.

"I have never felt an earthquake this big," Yulian Juita Ekalia, who lives in Ruteng city more than 100km west of the epicentre, told AFP by telephone.

"It felt like we were on a trampoline; it was really scary," said the 37-year-old university lecturer, who jolted awake at around 5:30am local time.

"As I rushed to get outside, everything in the house fell down: the television, my son's trophies, the dish racks, suitcases on top of the wardrobes. When I got outside, my son and neighbours were already there, screaming in fear."

Parts of a building collapsed into dust and rubble as people screamed and ran in the street, a video on Facebook, verified by Reuters as being at a port in Maumere, showed.

"The quake was massive, the shock was so strong, we were resting at home with family," said Nona, a 51-year-old resident of Talibura, a village in East Nusa Tenggara. "There were 13 of us inside the house and we all ran to save ourselves."

Strong shaking was felt across East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara and parts of South Sulawesi, and residents in several areas reported shaking lasting about one minute, BNPB said in a statement.

Damaged houses in Ruteng, Manggarai, East Nusa Tenggara. AFP / Selo

"Most of the people felt the shock and scattered out of their homes," it said.

A hospital in the district of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara Province was moving patients outside, Kompas TV footage showed, and Kompas.com reported at least one landslide.

Indonesian geophysics agency BMKG recorded the first quake at 4:58am at a depth of 15 km, followed by several aftershocks.

In 1992 the same area was hit by a magnitude-7.5 quake, causing extensive destruction at that time, the agency said.

No threat to NZ

There was no tsunami threat to New Zealand or Australia following the quake.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade was monitoring the situation and working with Indonesian authorities to assess the earthquake's impact, an MFAT spokesperson said.

There are 277 people from New Zealand registered on SafeTravel as being in Indonesia and 22 in Timor-Leste.

A damaged buildingin Ruteng, Manggarai, East Nusa Tenggara. AFP / Selo

MFAT was not aware of any New Zealanders who had requested assistance, the spokesperson said.

New Zealanders who require urgent consular assistance can contact the 24/7 consular emergency line on +64 99 20 20 20 or 0800 30 10 30.

Those in the affected areas should follow the advice of local authorities at all times. New Zealanders should also register on SafeTravel and, when they are able, let their family and friends in NZ know that they are safe, MFAT said.

World.title: Best-selling writer Meg Mason loved growing up Exclusive Brethren, but it left her feeling 'permanently othered'
World.content: "Everybody thinks that you race out and do all the things that you weren't allowed to do, but that's not true because you've had this fear ingrained in you that, you know, drinking is evil and horoscopes are evil… I'm 48, and I could not read a horoscope with a gun to my head. I don't even know what star sign I am," Mason tells RNZ's Saturday Morning .

World.title: MPs shocked by fatal Aranui dog attack
World.content:
The local MP says he was distressed to hear that a young child had died after a dog attack in the Christchurch suburb of Aranui.

Police found the child in a critical condition after being called to a house on Basingstoke Street just before 5pm on Friday. They later died at the scene.

MP for the Christchurch East electorate, Reuben Davidson, said it was a tragedy for the family and the wider community.

Local Burwood Ward councillor Kelly Barber said his first thoughts were with the child's family.

"It's a very sad situation, and my first thoughts were with the family and how devastated they must be at the loss of their child. I also hope there is something we can learn from the ongoing police investigation that reduces the likelihood of this ever happening again," he said.

Police investigators have left the scene.

The dog, which lived at the house, was removed by Animal Control, and police were speaking with the residents and providing support.

"Upon arrival, emergency services located a young child in a critical condition," Senior Sergeant Dan Overend said.

Basingstoke Street, Christchurch, 15 August. Tim Brown / RNZ

"Despite the immediate efforts of first responders and a member of the household, the child sadly died at the scene."

Overend said the dog involved was known to the occupants of the address and lived at the property.

"Occupants of the address are assisting police with enquiries."

St John said two ambulances, two rapid response units and one operations manager attended.

Govt weighs stronger dog control penalties, greater council powers

Local Government Minister Simon Watts said the Government was reviewing the Dog Control Act to ensure councils had the tools to manage dangerous dogs and protect communities.

"The news of this dog attack is devastating, and my thoughts are with the child's family, and everyone affected," he said.

"Every New Zealander should be able to feel safe in their community and not fear being attacked by a dangerous and uncontrolled dog."

Watts said stronger penalties and greater powers for council officers were among the options being considered as part of the review.

He said the Government had also released updated Dog Control and Enforcement Guidelines, giving councils clearer and more consistent guidance under the current framework.

Officials were working with councils, animal control officers and other stakeholders to identify further changes that might be needed, he said.

World.title: Tibetan community harassed over opposition to China's ethnic unity law, local man says
World.content:
A Tibetan man living in New Zealand says his community is being spied on and harassed for protesting against China's law on promoting ethnic unity and progress.

The man, Gaden, told RNZ he knew of a few incidents where people had faced pressure from Chinese nationals.

"They don't come ... straight to us, they just take the photo from a distance," he said.

He did not know if they would attempt to take any further action, but said "to be honest, as a Tibetan, I don't care".

In its latest threat assessment, the SIS said diaspora community groups living in this country were being unfairly targeted by foreign states and proxies seeking to limit their democratic rights and freedoms.

Academics warn of reach of China's new ethnic unity law Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Gaden said the ethnic unity law was an attempt to wipe Tibetan culture from the world.

"In Tibet, you cannot hoist a Tibetan national flag. However, we do still have the prayer flags in front of the monastery, or people's house or anywhere. Now, they have started to take it down, burn it down, stamp it on it," he said.

Some Tibetans were setting themselves on fire in response to the law, he said, with one such incident occuring in July in front of United Nations headquarters in New York, US.

"He burned himself for the just cause of Tibetans, because we are all very frustrated," Gaden said.

"We are very peaceful people. We don't want to take up or cause any harm inside of China. We just need our own identity preserved."

World.title: Wallaby 1,000 has 'dream come true' as Australia thrash Japan
World.content:
Massimo De Lutiis has enjoyed a dream debut for Australia, as the 1,000th Wallaby scored a try in his country's commanding 56-17 win over Japan in the second Test.

De Lutiis came on in the 50th minute of the Test match in Townsville with the match delicately poised at 21-17, the half-time score.

But the introduction of the hulking 22-year-old began the start of Australia's dominance in the Test match, as fellow prop Angus Bell scored the first of five second-half tries.

De Lutiis, with the descendants of the very first Wallaby Patrick Carew in attendance, scored minutes later to send his teammates, and the crowd, into a frenzy.

"One thousand is awesome. But just to be a Wallaby in general is crazy to me. It's a dream come true," De Lutiis told the Nine Network post-match.

"When I scored, I was just over the moon. I couldn't believe it."

After a difficult first half, the Wallabies improved in attack and defence to earn the win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Despite the impressive scoreline, the Wallabies were tested in the opening 50 minutes, with the Japanese taking the lead late in the first half.

At three tries apiece after 40 minutes, the Brave Blossoms had every right to believe a maiden win over the Wallabies was there for the taking.

But Australia showed the polish which eluded them in the first half, and the first Test in Osaka last weekend.

New coach Les Kiss, in his second match in charge, provided the right team talk at half-time to wrestle momentum from Japan.

"We got challenged by Les [Kiss] at half-time," captain Harry Wilson told the Nine Network.

"A team like Japan, if you're not up for it, they really make you pay.

"I was really proud of the group in the second half. We stepped it up and put on a great performance."

The win is Australia's third in a row, the first time the Wallabies have strung together a trio of triumphs since 2024.

The challenge for Australia gets harder, with two Tests in Argentina followed by one Test against South Africa, and two Bledisloe Cup matches against the All Blacks.

Relive all the action from the second Test between Australia and Japan in the blog below.

World.title: Live: Daicos running hot early as Hawks and Pies face off, Port hosts Dees
World.content:
Logan Morris kicked four goals for Brisbane as the Lions beat Gold Coast in the Q-Clash (Getty Images/AFL Photos)

The Brisbane Lions have tightened their grip on a top-four finish on the AFL ladder with a hard-fought 42-point win over the Gold Coast Suns.

In a high-pressure contest, the Suns fought valiantly to limit the Lions for three quarters, before the home side finally broke free, running away with the game in the last term for a 14.11 (95) to 6.17 (53) victory.

Terrible finishing in front of goal and two critical errors in the third quarter sabotaged the Suns' efforts.

First, stopper Sam Collins shanked a kick out of defence that was pounced on by Charlie Cameron, leading directly to a goal by Collins' opponent, Logan Morris.

A few minutes later, Beau Addinsall gave away a silly 50-metre penalty to Dayne Zorko at half-back. With no one on the mark, Zorko waltzed through middle and rifled the ball through an unguarded goal square.

The Lions had most of the dominant players on the ground, with the Ashcroft brothers Will and Levi having 57 disposals between them, Zorko finishing with 25 possessions, and Morris continuing his hot run of form with four goals.

Cameron was also lively from the start, working hard well up the ground and finally being rewarded with two late goals that led to John Denver's Take Me Home, Country Roads ringing around the Gabba.

Will Ashcroft — son of Lions legend and former Suns administrator Marcus — finished with his second medal struck in his father's name, adding to an already impressive list of individual honours.

It was also a sweet result for the Lions' Chris Fagan, who was coaching a club-record 248th game, surpassing triple-premiership coach Leigh Matthews.

Fagan has a real chance of joining Matthews in that ultra-elite club in September.

For the Suns, Matt Rowell dug in without hitting the heights of his efforts against GWS last week, and Ned Moyle competed manfully in the ruck with 41 hit-outs.

But effort wasn't the issue for the Suns. Collectively, they won many key indicators on the stats sheet — inside-50 entries, centre clearances and contested possessions were all in their favour.

It was their failure to execute and lack of composure at key moments that undid them.

They also experimented again with playing blue-chip import Christian Petracca in attack for minimal return, with the former Demon finishing with just 12 disposals and failing to have an impact on the game.

The result keeps Brisbane a game clear of fifth-placed Geelong with one round to go, with the Cats having a slightly superior percentage.

The Lions will need to beat Collingwood at the MCG in the final round of the home-and-away season on Friday to ensure a top-four finish.

AAP

World.title: Cyclist, 19, dies during Volta a Portugal after collision with vehicle
World.content:
A 19-year-old British cyclist has been killed in an accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

Welsh rider Finlay Tarling died after "a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle", Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said in a statement.

An investigation is underway, according to local authorities.

Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany-Ineos rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on the road and track.

He was competing for the NSN Development Team when the incident occurred on the 166.8-kilometre route from Melgaco to Fafe.

Riders are seen in Fafe, Portugal, reacting to the news that Finlay Tarling had died. (Getty Images: Miguel Lemos/NurPhoto)

In a statement, NSN said the team was heartbroken to announce Tarling's passing.

"Fin was a much-loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend."

The intrinsic failings and risks of cycling laid bare with another premature death Cycling has lost another rider due to a downhill crash, with teenager Muriel Furrer killed on a descent at the World Championships in Zurich. So where does the responsibility lie?

In a post on X, the race organisers and the Portuguese Cycling Federation also expressed their "most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones".

It added that the racing was stopped and the scheduled podium ceremony would not take place as a sign of "respect and mourning".

Portuguese president António José Seguro said that Tarling's death had "plunged the peloton, the tournament and the host nation into mourning".

British Cycling's performance director Stephen Park added: "All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal.

"Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man.

"Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh, at this tragic time."

World.title: Australia fighting to save first Test as Bangladesh claim top order wickets
World.content:
Australia has closed day three of the first Test against Bangladesh on 4-161, still 67 runs behind the tourists on another chastening day in Darwin.

Alex Carey (19) and Cameron Green (43) are the not out batters, combining for a valuable 39-run partnership late in the day that will prove crucial for Australia's chances of saving, or perhaps even winning the Test.

Australia will back itself to make Bangladesh bat again but, on an increasingly placid pitch, will have to bat very well to set a challenging target to the tourists, a scenario almost inconceivable for supporters of the world's number one side prior to the match getting underway.

With Bangladesh resuming on 6-351, Australia once again struggled to make inroads, extending their already gruelling labours in the field.

Josh Hazlewood thought he had made the breakthrough when umpire Richard Illingworth fired out Mehidy Hasan LBW, only for the DRS to show the ball was missing the leg stump.

The veteran quick was frustrated then, but soon was celebrating when Hasan Mahmud was trapped bang in front to depart for 14.

Hazlewood became the ninth Australian to pass 300 Test wickets on day three. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Hazlewood then claimed another, having Taijul Islam caught sharply by Cam Green, whose self-preservation instincts came to the fore to stop the ball flying into his face at gully.

If those two wickets had Australia thinking they'd soon be batting, the discipline of the Bangladeshi batters made sure they had to stay out even longer, coupled with a shocking drop from Steve Smith.

Taskin Ahmed top edged a pull shot out to Smith, who settled under the ball and let it through his finger tips.

A few balls later, Travis Head dropped a far harder chance, racing around from close to the wicket as Bangladesh reached 8-417 at lunch.

Smith dropped a sitter in the morning session. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

The mounting frustration eased somewhat by two more Hazlewood wickets, as he claimed Mehidy Hasan Miraz and Ebadot Hossain, both caught behind, to secure a 14th Test five-fa and his 300th Test wicket, becoming the ninth Australian to reach that particular milestone.

Australia needed a good start, but under-pressure home-town favourite Jake Weatherald departed second over for a duck, chopping on after playing with an angled bat to Hasan Mahmud.

Failing to learn from his first innings dismissal and that of his opening partner, Travis Head followed in near identical fashion to leave Australia 2-37 and in desperate trouble.

Marnus Labuschagne and Steve Smith came to the crease and both survived big Bangladeshi appeals, with Smith forced to review a caught behind decision when he was on three, the replay showing that he hit the ground with his bat instead of the ball.

Labuschagne departed after prematurely glowing praise from a former teammate in the commentary box. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

That pair looked set, with Labuschagne seemingly playing with am encouragingly positive intent that was desperately lacking in his first innings effort.

However, the Queenslander was next to depart, playing all around a Taijul Islam fuller ball and yorking himself against the spinner to be out for 31.

Smith and Cameron Green rebuilt with a patient and untroubled 49-run partnership on an increasingly docile pitch, right up until Smith flat-batted a return catch to Bangladesh's other spinner, Mehidy Hasan for 44.

Australia still trailed by over 100 runs at that stage, with Alex Carey joining Green, who incredibly survived an inside edge that clipped his leg stump without dislodging the bail early in the evening session.

They batted out the remainder of the day without too much alarm, but know they will have to fight just as hard to save this Test match over the next two days.
