World.title: Bezos consortium enters 'definitive agreement' to buy Liverpool stake
World.content:
A consortium containing Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is buying a minority stake in Premier League club Liverpool, the English soccer giant says.

Club owner Fenway Sports Group (FSG) said in a statement it entered into a "definitive agreement" for the sale to 1892 Holdings.

The investor group is led by Amit Bhatia, who is married to a daughter of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, and has taken a stake of more than 30 per cent in the 20-time English champion. The deal reportedly values Liverpool at around $US6 billion ($8.4 billion).

Boston-based FSG paid $US400 million to take over Liverpool in 2010 and also owns the Boston Red Sox. FSG said in July that it had been approached by the Bhatia-led consortium regarding a "strategic minority investment" in the club.

Eduardo Saverin is part of the investment group with Jeff Bezos. (Getty Images: Sam Barnes/Sportsfile)

"As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special," FSG president Mike Gordon said in the statement.

It marks the first foray into soccer by Bezos, who, according to Forbes, is the fourth-richest person in the world with a net worth of about $US280 billion. He founded Amazon in 1994 and has been executive chairman since 2021.

Saverin is a Brazilian businessman worth about $US36 billion, according to Forbes.

Bhatia, a British-Indian entrepreneur, was the co-owner of second-tier English team Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before stepping down recently.

Amit Bhatia during his time as the chairman of Queens Park Rangers. (Getty Images: Steven Paston/PA Images)

"We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club's continued success for years to come," Bhatia said in the statement.

Under the leadership of FSG and its principal owner John Henry, Liverpool ended a 30-year wait to be English champion in 2020 and added another Premier League title last year. That tied Manchester United on 20 English top-flight league championships.

The club was European champion for a sixth time — a record for an English team — in 2019.

The Premier League is one of the biggest competitions in sports, with its teams now largely owned by oil-rich Gulf states or private equity.

Liverpool sack manager Arne Slot after underwhelming season The Dutchman won the Premier League title in his first season, but failed to live up to expectations the following year as Liverpool finished fifth.

Liverpool now has three of the richest people in the world as minority owners.

That does not mean, however, that the club can simply start spending recklessly in the transfer market on new players.

That is because the Premier League has financial rules in place to protect the competitive balance of the competition and ensure the financial sustainability of clubs.

In broad terms, a club's on-pitch spending is related to 85 per cent of its "football-related revenue and net profit/loss from player sales," the Premier League says.

Instead, the difference will come in how Liverpool — already one of the top teams in world soccer — is marketed more around the world under Bezos and Saverin, especially.

The deal is likely to bring more commercial revenue into the club, thereby improving its profits.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Hockeyroos and Kookaburras tackle World Cup with fresh perspectives
World.content:
Kookaburras midfielder Liam Henderson has the attitude of a winner.

It is a confidence that comes with being part of a team used to sustained excellence, backed by a growing reputation as one of hockey's global rising stars.

And in his second year on the national team, the 22-year-old is ready to deliver at the World Cup which begins this weekend.

"We think we can win it. And if other teams don't think we can, we'll just prove them wrong," he told ABC Sport from the team's base in Belgium.

Liam Henderson (right) is heading to his first World Cup. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

The Kookaburras are ranked fourth in the world, and won the last of their three World Cup titles in 2014.

Recent FIH Pro League victories over the top two ranked teams, Belgium and Netherlands, mean Henderson's confidence is justified.

"Everyone brings their natural game. We're a force to be reckoned with," he said.

"The last two games we played against the two world's best, we had two wins and two losses. We can beat them. And if it's our day, anything can happen."

The Kookaburras have won the World Cup three times. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

The team's last major tournament was the Paris 2024 Olympics, which ended in an uncharacteristic quarter-final exit.

There has been significant change since then with a new coach, Mark Hager, and the retirements of some of their longest serving players including Eddie Ockenden, Aran Zalewski, and Andrew Charter.

But a hallmark of the Kookaburras throughout their history has been a constant ability to regenerate and maintain their position amongst the world's top teams.

"As a hockey community, we're always watching our national teams. And when you watch them, something you aspire to do is just be in that team," Henderson said.

The Kookaburras are ranked fourth in the world. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"And once you're there, I think every chance you get, you just want to work as hard as possible.

"I think another piece of that is the group that we have at the moment are all so close.

"We're such good mates, all of us, and such a welcoming team that you just want to play for each other. It's something you really want to be a part of."

Hockeyroos to rise up

The men's tournament will be played in Wavre, just outside of Brussels, played concurrently with the women's event in Amstelveen, Netherlands.

That is where the Hockeyroos are based, led by the most experienced player in the team, co-captain Kaitlin Nobbs, heading to her third World Cup.

She is part of one of the sport's most illustrious dynasties, with both parents having represented Australia, alongside her grandmother, aunty, and uncle — the Kookaburras coach.

Kaitlin Nobbs is playing at her third World Cup. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

"Coming into this one it marks the 40th anniversary from when my mum went to a World Cup as well representing the Hockeyroos," Nobbs told ABC Sport.

"So looking at the past and reflecting and seeing where we've come from, where the Hockeyroos have come from until now, it means the world to be able to go out and represent the team and captain them."

Her dad, Michael Nobbs, died earlier this year, and has provided her with extra motivation to excel.

"I think he would be so chuffed that I'm playing and enjoying the game and trying to take the most out of it that I can," she said.

"He loved hockey more than anyone and loved watching me play. So I'm sure he'll be watching and following along from wherever he is."

The Hockeyroos are ranked eighth in the world, and after winning the last of their three Olympic golds in 2000, have not managed to reach those heights again, although bronze at the 2022 World Cup was a highlight.

Katrina Powell took over as coach just before the Tokyo Olympics in the wake of systemic cultural issues in the women's program, and after stepping down last year, she was replaced by former South Africa men's international Rhett Halkett.

The Hockeyroos have had a period of change over the past two years. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"I think we are more than capable of playing in the finals for a medal," Nobbs said.

"Rhett comes from a bit of a European background, so we've changed up how we've played in the past year.

"This year in itself has been enough stress for the next four years or the last four years because we've had to play Pro League, qualify for this World Cup, change our structure, change our way of play.

The Hockeyroos celebrate a penalty shootout win over the Netherlands, to secure a spot in next year's FIH Pro League. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"So it has been a crazy journey, but I think all of those things give you experience and evidence leading into big tournaments like this that you can lean on."

Growing the game

The interest in hockey is at a different level in Europe, particularly in Belgium and the Netherlands, and it is something Henderson is embracing.

"Just walking around the streets, you're seeing billboards, you're seeing [players] on bus stops," Henderson said.

"I think the general population know more about the game."

Henderson has also started to make a name for himself in India, another hockey hotbed, after fetching the highest price at the Hockey India League auction last year — around $71,500.

While not in the same ballpark as the IPL, it is a lucrative league for Australians, who usually juggle studying or work alongside playing.

"I was actually in the gym with a few of my teammates when [the auction] was going down," Henderson said.

"It was more just shock. I'd only played 11 international games at that stage. And I think just showed potentially what people think I can do.

"The team obviously were very successful, we won a tournament. It was such a valuable experience for me. You can't put a price tag on that."

Henderson and Nobbs also play in Australia's domestic league, Hockey One, and hope to see its continued growth.

"It's finally a competition that gets talked about, I think, internationally and really good players from abroad wanting to come over and be part of that competition," Nobbs said.

"We obviously compete with a lot of sports in Australia, cricket, soccer, netball, everything.

"So to have a product like that growing and something exciting that young kids can come and watch is definitely a good thing."

World.title: What went wrong for the Suns this year and how 2027 can be much better
World.content:
Sometimes an essay is needed to describe what has happened on the footy field. Sometimes a book will only start to scratch the surface.

But sometimes a single word will do it best. As the Gold Coast Suns filtered off a frigid Manuka Oval after beating GWS, one word seemed to sum up the mood in a nutshell: Finally.

For the first time since May 15, the Suns had entered the winner's circle. At the time of their last win, the Suns sat fourth on the ladder, with many believing they were poised for a real shot at a deep finals run.

But as the weeks drew shorter and the nights colder, their hopes faded.

By the start of July, the hopes of a top-four finish had effectively vanished. Two weeks later, their finals hopes were on life support. By the end of the month, even the wildcard spots were taken off the table.

Damien Hardwick summed up the year via the slightly misheard words of one of the big four of American thrash metal.

"There's a great line by Metallica that I'm going to butcher, where 'sometimes you can see the light at the end of the tunnel, but it's a freight train coming the other way'. That's how it's felt this year. That's the reality of it," he said.

Despite the season being lost, both Hardwick and his playing staff were overjoyed with the win.

"It's been … it's been a while. The boys were really hungry for a win today and I thought we brought the spirit and it was great to sing that song again," Suns star Matt Rowell told ABC Sport after the win over GWS.

For one week, everything worked as it should for the side many thought to be a premiership contender. The win wasn't just one in isolation; it also practically ended the season for their Expansion Cup rivals, the Giants.

For both sides, the hope is that a small slice of pain in 2026 will set them up for success in 2027. But to do so, there has to be an understanding of what exactly went wrong.

Hardwick's hard year with Gold Coast

Of all the jobs in elite football, that of the senior club coach may be the most coveted and the most stressful. The coach operates as not only a leader to the players but also a figurehead for the club.

It's a job that many, if not most, of the league's assistant coaches and football staffers aspire to. But for roughly every 10 aspirants to the ranks, there's only ever one opening. Those lucky enough to sit in the big chair often do so after mentoring by a few others.

Few coaches have been more highly credentialed in recent years than Hardwick. Beyond the three flags the Tigers won under his guidance, his impact across the league is clear.

While Hardwick served an apprenticeship under a more kick-mark style operator in Alistair Clarkson, his own method differed to that of former co-worker Chris Fagan. Instead, the influence of Hardwick is best seen through the defensive-first-yet-free-flowing styles exhibited by Collingwood and GWS under former Hardwick assistants Craig McRae and Adam Kingsley.

Hardwick's teams have an idiosyncratic stylistic footprint. Under his reign at Richmond, the Tigers overhauled teams with chaos, not control. The side often lost the marking battle but played surge football, running on adrenaline and enthusiasm. Instead of a side built on winning and scoring from clearances, their drive came from scoring on the intercept.

McRae and Kingsley, alongside West Coast's Andrew McQualter, have regularly influenced proceedings in September. The Hardwick school sits as a counterbalance to the way that sides such as Brisbane pick through defences by controlling the ball.

Despite being so influential to how football is played in 2026, Hardwick is quick to note that this may not have been his finest year.

"I feel I haven't had my best year as a coach with regard to bending a little bit of my system of how we want to play," he said. "So those realisations are very, very important. And these are the things that actually your greatest growth comes from."

In the wake of teams inspired by the control-heavy game styles influenced by Alistair Clarkson's Hawthorn sides, Tigerball was risky, dangerous and exciting.

All good coaches evolve. And all good "brands" are strategised against and countered. Football is not a solved game with a perfect way to play.

The developing Suns Hardwick inherited were quite different from the Tigers he left. Instead of building from a rock-solid counterattacking defensive unit, they led with the contested, stoppage game the premiership Tigers largely eschewed.

In 2025, Hardwick bent to accommodate both strands, leaning on rising stars Anderson, Rowell, Miller and Humphries to dominate in the middle and using Noble, Rioli and Jeffrey to provide drive on the counterattack.

There were clear parts of the game plan that held strong across both seasons. Gold Coast continued to lean on handball more than most and played into chaotic situations.

But the other part of the balance, that of the stoppage game, fell away.

Last year, the Suns finished +3.3 in clearance differential and third in the league for scoring differential from stoppages.

This year — with a group in flux with early season injuries to Matt Rowell and the incorporation of Christian Petracca — the Suns sit last for clearance differential and fourth-worst for stoppage scoring differential.

Notably, the win in Canberra came in one of the hardest, most contested games of the season. The game was cold, wet and physical and played largely at ground level. The sides combined for just 96 marks all day — about half of the average game this year.

"We love the wet weather footy, as you can tell, and I think it really suited us today," midfielder Bodhi Uwland told ABC Sport post-game.

ABC AFL Daily podcast Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron are joined by a rotating cast of AFL legends, including some of the sharpest minds in the game, to pull apart the biggest stories in Aussie Rules.

"We like being a contested team, that surge mentality, like getting the ball forward. And I think we really showed that today and we're able to really adapt to the conditions."

The Suns played for territory first and results later in Canberra. Despite dominating hit-outs and clearances, the Giants still scored more from stoppage. But the high defensive wall that the Suns were able to establish helped the Suns re-enter the winner's circle.

Reigning Brownlow Medallist Rowell led the way for the Suns with one of the finest games imaginable in tough conditions. Despite the number of accolades he has already accumulated in his short career, the game may have been one of his best yet.

"That's one of the best performances I've seen from Rowell, to be honest, like, especially from behind the ball. Seeing him u-turning out of stoppage, shrugging tackles and just getting it forward … and he did it so consistently throughout the game. It was an amazing performance." Uwland said.

It wasn't just his teammates who were effusive about his effort.

"Yeah, he's a difference maker. It's a pleasure to have a guy like that in our footy club who, you see, the way the game plays today." Hardwick added.

"You know, it's 40-odd possessions, 22 contested, I think 18 tackles and 12 clearances as well. It's just one of those games you go, 'Wow'.

"You know, they're video game numbers, but he revels in those conditions. You know, that's the way he plays the game and it's such a pleasure to watch those players that give absolutely everything."

Rowell's preseason Origin injury threw the Suns' midfield balance off at the start of the season and left the side looking for what was their best look through the middle as the season developed. The Suns are blessed with highly capable players at the contest, with more bodies than opportunities most weeks.

The game in Canberra was a hint of what it could look like when it worked for the Suns.

Despite reports in the media of a loss of connection in recent weeks, at least in the wake of the win, the connection between coach and group seemed to be growing and evolving through the adversity.

"We haven't had the year we've wanted, but I think he's been really impressed by the way we've kept our spirit as a group," Rowell said.

"Even though we can't make finals, we've still got a lot of pride as a group. I think that really showed today. Yeah, Dimma's (Hardwick's) connection with the group is growing each game."

Suns keen to rise in 2027

In the wake of the Canberra game, attention for both sides turned, at least a little, to next season. The balance between running out a season where a premiership is an impossible task and preparing for the next one is a tough balance to strike for all teams.

"Yeah (2027 starts now). We have spoken about that. You look at Sydney — a great example from last year. You know, they had a disappointing year, much like we have this year, and they sort of went to work on some things. Look where they are now." Hardwick said after the game.

"That was our challenge. We spoke to the players about it. Noah and his leaders have just been absolutely leading the charge in that space."

Given how few competitive games there are each year, not a single one needs to be wasted. A flag is always the goal for each of the league's 18 clubs, even if it's not this year's.

Having shown the quality to win a final last year, Gold Coast's prospects of recovery look reasonably bright. Roughly half of the teams in the 18-team era to win a final then dip to double-digit ladder placings returned to finals the following year.

Most of the rest took two years to get back, with Melbourne and Collingwood grabbing the 2021 and 2023 flags. Most encouragingly, only three times since 2012 has a finals-winning team immediately crashed down the ladder and failed to recover at all.

These gap years have almost become routine as footy becomes ever more even and competitive. Almost every year since 2020, at least one side has found itself dipping and another recovering from such a dip.

The one slight pause for both the Suns and Giants is the relatively low placement of all four of the Hardwick-styled teams in 2026. Of the four, only McRae's Pies will play finals, entering via the wildcard round. As always, the question will be whether that style of play is conducive to winning football in 2026 and beyond, or whether the next evolution is upon us already.

Still, the Gold Coast list might be the most talented in the league. If they can get the strategic balance right, and a little luck to fall their way, the sky is the limit for this Suns group.

World.title: Freo locks up minor premiership after downing Crows in thriller
World.content:
Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Caleb Serong played a starring role as Fremantle snared just the second minor premiership in the club's history with a 24-point win over Adelaide in Perth.

Scores were level early in the final quarter of Friday night's blockbuster following Crows forward Riley Thilthorpe's second goal of the night.

But buoyed by a thundering 55,010-strong crowd, Fremantle did what it has done all season — blowing its rival off the park with a devastating burst.

Michael Frederick started the run when he nailed a tough set shot after being tackled high.

Jye Amiss (centre) kicked 5.1 in the win while Josh Treacy (right) took six contested marks. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Although Josh Treacy, Luke Jackson and Andrew Brayshaw missed their shots after that, Amiss bobbed up for his fifth goal of the night by snapping from the goalsquare.

And when Isaiah Dudley dodged and weaved his way through three Crows players before unleashing a successful snap, the margin was 22 points and it was game over.

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox rubbed it in by roughing up an opponent and then pointing to the scoreboard after kicking a goal in the dying minutes of the 16.16 (112) to 13.10 (88) win.

The triumph boosted Fremantle's record to 19-3, securing the club a second minor premiership to go with their 2013 efforts.

It also meant Fremantle will end the home-and-away season with a perfect 12-0 record at Perth Stadium.

Adelaide (14-8) now faces a huge battle to snare a top-four berth, with the loss even leaving them vulnerable to slipping into the dreaded wildcard spots from seventh to 10th.

Amiss finished with 5.1 in a powerful display, Josh Treacy was huge with six contested marks but a wayward 1.4, Dudley kicked three goals, while Serong was influential with 29 disposals, 12 clearances, 536m gained and two goals.

Crows playmaker Izak Rankine racked up a monster 14 disposals in the opening term on the way to 39 possessions, 10 clearances, 717m gained and one goal.

Adelaide star Izak Rankine finished the match with a game-high 39 disposals. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Adelaide had an interesting lead-in to the match, with players forced to evacuate their hotel just hours before bounce down due to a fire alarm going off in their hotel.

Amiss missed an early set shot sitter from 15m out as Adelaide skipped out to a two-goal lead.

But Amiss soon made amends, nailing three other set shots for the term — from 50m, 40m and 35m — to give Fremantle a 13-point edge by quarter time.

Fremantle led by just five points at half-time, and the third quarter was a rollercoaster ride featuring four lead changes and five occasions when the scores were even.

Fremantle skipper Alex Pearce suffered a huge scare when his heavily-strapped left knee hyper-extend during a collision, leaving him hobbled for the next couple of minutes.

The action was fierce and fast, but it was Fremantle who produced more of the memorable moments.

Treacy hurt himself while completing a team-lifting tackle on Max Michalanney.

The Fremantle powerhouse dusted himself off after a few deep breaths and kicked a goal moments later.

Serong nailed a goal from just inside the centre square following a dazzling series of handballs from the Dockers.

And when Brayshaw dribbled one through with the outside of his right boot, Fremantle turned for home with a seven-point edge.

The Dockers kicked five goals to three in a powerful final term to wrap up top spot on the ladder with one round to spare.

AAP

Tech.title: Samsung has new Galaxy headphones in the works
Tech.content:
Strings of code in Samsung’s Galaxy Wearable app hint at an upcoming pair of over-ear headphones that could compete with the AirPods Max, SamMobile reports. Samsung’s reportedly referring to the headphones as the “Galaxy H1,” and SamMobile says they could launch sometime in 2027. That would make these the company’s first pair of over-ear headphones since the Level On in 2015, which was released well before Samsung acquired Harman and a number of other audio brands.

Connection status icons in the app standard show the design of over-ear, wireless Bluetooth headphones, but not necessarily exactly what these will look like in the end. Samsung’s main audio device right now is its Galaxy Buds line, but it doesn’t have high-end headphones similar to the AirPods Max or Sony XM series.

Apple released a revised AirPods Max 2 model earlier this year, which looked the same but added a new chip to power more features like adaptive audio and live translation. When the Galaxy H1 launches, as SamMobile points out, we would expect it to include the Samsung Seamless Codec Ultra High Quality (SSC UHQ) codec that works exclusively with 2023 and newer Galaxy phones and tablets, as well as support for AI assistants like Gemini and Bixby that’s similar to what we saw in the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro.

Tech.title: A RAMageddon guide to back-to-school laptop shopping
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

If you’re a student looking for an affordable laptop, I have bad news and I have good news. The bad news is that computer prices are out of whack due to the ongoing RAM and storage crunch, making some a little pricier than they used to be and others wildly more expensive.

The good news? Despite that, there are still many great options, including the selection we’ve tested and highlighted below.

Before you go for the cheapest option you can still find, consider biting the bullet on a more powerful laptop, especially if you’re buying for a college student. Prices are likely to continue rising well into next year — especially since all the memory being made through 2027 is already allocated. You can get a mostly tolerable laptop for under $500 and a good one for around $700, but spending more to get something like a MacBook Air gets you better build quality and enough performance headroom to last through four years of college and well beyond. (Many Verge writers and editors are still using M1 MacBook Airs from 2020). But even the modest options below (new or refurbished) should easily be good for more than a few years. The key is to avoid something that feels slow or janky on day one, if you can. It’ll only get worse from there.

If your school or curriculum recommends certain laptops or minimum specs, then you already know what to aim for. If not, our rule of thumb is to go with a Mac running Apple silicon or a Windows laptop running Intel or AMD chips released in the last few years. (For Windows machines, don’t go any older than 2022 or 2023 — Intel’s 13th-gen “Raptor Lake” or AMD’s Ryzen 7000 series.) Snapdragon X chips are also great options unless you’re a college student who needs to run specialized software not compatible with Windows on Arm (or if you want to play games).

But try to get 16GB of memory and 512GB of storage or more if you can — especially for college students. Eight GB of RAM is workable on macOS with the MacBook Neo, but Windows laptops struggle a bit with it. And for the most budget-conscious or anyone shopping for younger kids, a quality Chromebook is still great.

The best cheap laptop

The MacBook Neo is the easy pick for students from middle school to high school who need a laptop. There’s still no beating its balance of build quality and good-enough performance at this price. Students and teachers can get it starting at $599, and Apple offers refurbished models for $599 for the rest of us as well. If you can justify spending an additional $100, it’s worth getting the model with twice the storage and a Touch ID fingerprint sensor, which makes logging in and entering passwords much less of a hassle.

The A18 Pro chip is powerful enough for most high school students (and adults), and everything from its trackpad to its speakers and screen range from good to great, which is not the case for Windows laptops in this price range. Its only shortcoming by comparison is having just two USB-C ports. The 8GB of RAM and 256GB of base storage mean a student eventually pushes the limits of what this laptop can do sooner than a more powerful MacBook Air, but the Neo is still significantly cheaper.

The best laptop for college

The Neo is the best cheap laptop, but the MacBook Air is still the best laptop for most people, and the standard recommendation for college students. Every part of it is a step up from the Neo: It has a much more powerful processor, and it starts with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of much faster storage. And few laptops can match the Air’s overall build quality. It also means spending $1,299 (or $1,199 for students) on a 13-inch model, or $1,499 for the 15-inch. It’s a shame the Air no longer starts at $999 like it did just last year, but it’s still worth springing for if you’re buying for the long term.

The Airs have been so good for so many years now, you don’t miss out on much by buying a refurbished model if it’s substantially cheaper. Keep an eye on Apple’s refurb store, and retailers like Best Buy sometimes have great deals too.

A Windows laptop nearly as nice as a MacBook Air

Asus Zenbook A14 $ 700 $ 1000 30 % off $ 700 Asus’s Zenbook A14 is a bit of a MacBook Air wannabe, but it’s a compelling alternative if you value a superlight Windows laptop with long battery life. The 2025 model sports an Arm-based Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus chip, a nice 14-inch OLED display, and a sleek textured beige finish. Read More $700 at Best Buy

Asus Zenbooks are some of the sleeker, better-looking Windows laptops, and the Zenbook A14 is Asus’ wannabe MacBook Air. It has a good Snapdragon X Plus chip, 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a lovely OLED display in an ultra-light chassis (it’s just 2.4 pounds / 1.09kg), all for $1,000 or as low as $700 on sale. It even has a solid port selection, with one USB-A, two speedy USB4, and HDMI 2.1. I really enjoyed the larger Zenbook A16 version when I reviewed it, but the A14 is even lighter and significantly cheaper. Like its larger sibling, the A14 is coated in Asus’ Ceraluminum finish that gives it a nice textured feel and unique look. (It’s a beige laptop!)

A cheap laptop with a great processor

Acer’s Aspire 14 AI didn’t impress me with its screen, speakers, or build quality when I tested it against the Neo, but for $500 or $600 on sale, which it often is, it’s hard to beat. It has a solid Intel Lunar Lake processor, 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a bunch of speedy ports. Getting two USB-A, two Thunderbolt 4, and HDMI 2.1 on a $600 laptop? Hell yeah.

A Lunar Lake chip means you get great battery life, and you can even do some light gaming. Its screen isn’t pretty and everything creaks, but with the money you save you can overcome some of its shortcomings with a mouse and monitor. Just keep in mind that the appeal of this laptop is what you’re getting for the price. If the deal winds change and Aspire 14 AIs are selling for $700 or more, consider something else.

A formidable 16-incher for about $500

I’m still testing the HP OmniBook 3 for a full review, but I’ve used it enough and I like it enough at around $500 to give it a nod. Its speakers and screen are not good quality, but they’re slightly better than the Acer Aspire above — just don’t look too close, or you’ll notice that its 1920 x 1200 resolution isn’t very sharp at this scale. At 16 inches you’re getting a big screen for cheap, but this laptop doesn’t feel large, as it weighs only 3.65 pounds / 1.66kg and is about 0.63 inches / 16mm thick (at its hinge, where it’s slightly thicker). And its sizable battery and efficient Snapdragon X chip allow it to last long on a charge. Plus, it’s got an ample-sized numpad for you numbers people.

Consider a refurbished ThinkPad

ThinkPads are awesome. They have great keyboards and trackpads, sturdy builds, lots of ports, and even a TrackPoint. They’re typically very expensive when bought new, and they have a reputation for lasting a long time. They’re Lenovo’s business line, so there’s a constant stream of used ThinkPads entering the secondhand market when companies refresh their fleets. That makes them a great candidate for buying refurbished or used. Lenovo sells many refurb units directly, so you know you should be getting something in good shape. Many of them are still expensive, but this ThinkPad T14 is an attractive example, offering a 13th-gen Intel chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage for around $700. Or for a bit more you can get this ThinkPad L14 Gen 5 with a newer Intel Meteor Lake chip for around $1,000.

And for the more adventurous folks out there, you can pick up an even older ThinkPad on the cheap and install Linux to give it new life.

Our go-to pick for a cheap Chromebook

A Chromebook is good for web browsing, doing homework, and nailing the basics of browser-first computer use — when done well. The Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 is a mainstay of The Verge’s laptop recommendations, despite being a few years old. It’s very affordable at just $350, and even with its 12th-gen Intel chip and 8GB of RAM it’s more than serviceable for ChromeOS. Google’s new Googlebooks are coming in the fall, but some early leaks are pointing at those potentially being pricier laptops (making me wonder what exactly their appeal will be).

A great convertible Chromebook

If you can afford a slightly pricier, newer, and better Chromebook than the Asus, check out the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514. Its full price of $749 is a bit much, but when discounted to $600 like it is at the time of this writing it can be worth it. The Arm-based MediaTek Kompanio Ultra in this Chromebook paired with 12GB of RAM gives it very good performance and excellent battery life. And since it’s a convertible, it’s also great to use with an optional stylus for note-taking, drawing, and sketching.

Tech.title: Lamborghini’s flagship Revuelto levels up with SV trim
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

A lot of automakers talk about wanting to minimize or eliminate driver distractions so as to make the experience of driving more rewarding and safer overall. Lamborghini has a different strategy; it wants the driver to become one with their vehicle. This helps explain the storied super car maker’s tagline for the new Revuelto SV: the quantum of driving.

“For us, quantum of driving is the moment when you get into the car, you start driving the car, and the car and you become one piece,” said Alessandro Farmeschi, product line director for the Revuelto, the Italian brand’s top V12 powered model. “And you start just thinking about your drive, feeling the adrenaline of the acceleration, braking, the G-forces, you know. You feel everything and you basically forget about the rest because you are so concentrated and you enjoy so much this experience.”

Be the car! What better way to be less bothered by all of modern life’s distraction? I can’t speak from experience, having not driven the Revuelto yet, but standing next to the sharklike SV version, you can certainly begin to understand where Farmeschi and his colleagues are coming from. Be the car? Sure, I’ll be this car. And I’ll eat all others on the road for breakfast.

SV stands for Superveloce or “superfast,” which dates back to the iconic 1971 Miura SV. Lamborghini has also used the designation on higher-performance versions of the Diablo, Murciélago, and Aventador — and now the Revuelto, it’s flagship V12 supercar.

Previous Next







1 / 5

It’s a high-performance evolution of an already very fast, very high performing vehicle, which begs the question: How much is too much? The Revuelto SV’s hybrid-electric powertrain still features a 6.5-liter naturally aspirated V12 and three electric motors, which can put out 1,065cv (around 1,050 hp), or around a 50 hp boost over the standard Revuelto. The additional capability is supported by a revised battery package that retains the same basic shape and geometry but increases energy capacity by 7.3kWh and provides higher power output.

The battery improvements are intended not simply to produce a higher peak figure but to make the car’s performance more consistent during hard driving. Lamborghini wanted the SV to deliver a flatter and more consistent level of performance throughout a lap rather than experiencing larger variations in output, Farmeschi explained.

The transmission shifting time has also been reduced by 30 percent for a more responsive and effective acceleration. Carbon fiber is used extensively throughout the vehicle to shave crucial kilograms. The front bumper is completely new, while the rear wing, door panels, and new racing seats also use carbon fiber as part of the effort to slim down and improve performance. The result? The Revuelto SV posts a power-to-weight ratio of 1.66 kg/CV, as compared to 1.75kg/CV for the standard Revuelto. Every milligram matters.

Downforce has been increased by 80 percent, thanks to the new front bumper and rear wing, which Farmeschi explained incorporates two wing designs into one. The front-end changes alone provide a 100 percent increase in front downforce compared with the standard Revuelto, which gives the car greater stability as it enters corners and begins turning, effectively helping to “glue” the front of the car to the track. This enables a 0–62mph acceleration in just 2.4 seconds — on par with the limited-edition Fenomeno, which Lamborghini previously described as its “fastest” in production. (I guess the Fenomeno will have to share that distinction now.)

Previous Next







1 / 5

But for Farmeschi, it’s not just about track performance metrics — it’s also about emotion. “Because emotion is driving the car, it’s being so fast… enjoying the car, going beyond even your limits because the car also helps you to manage the performance,” he said.

Of course, enhanced acceleration and performance also demands enhanced braking. The Revuelto SV features a new CCM-R Plus braking system, as compared to the carbon-ceramic brakes used on the standard Revuelto. The discs are thicker and larger in diameter, with radial holes extending along the radius to improve cooling. The result is a braking system capable of handling greater levels of stress while allowing the driver to brake harder and later.

Speaking of driving dynamics, Lamborghini is introducing a new Pilota mode, derived from its GT racing program. The driver can activate Pilota mode using the helmet icon on the steering wheel and then choose one of five levels using the rotary controls. These settings alter how sensitive the car is to its stability systems. The vehicle incorporates ABS and stability-control systems as well as a six-dimensional sensor located in the center tunnel, which measures vertical, lateral, and longitudinal acceleration as well as roll, pitch, and other vehicle movements. Pilota mode uses this information to change the car’s behavior according to the driver’s selected level.

“The customer can select this, like in the race, where you want maybe the car a bit more, let’s say, loose, because you want to, let’s say, manage the car differently, maybe using better the track, the cornering, rather than being more precise,” Farmeschi said, “so it depends on the driving style.”

After scraping its plans to make a purely electric sports car, Lamborghini doubled down on its hybrid strategy. The electric motors in the Revuelto SV allow for better torque vectoring and driving dynamics, Farmeschi said, arguing that those reasons help justify the added weight from the 7.3kWh battery.

The hybrid system also has a practical social benefit, he said with a sly grin. Your neighbors may appreciate the courtesy of rolling out of your driveway silently under electric power, for example. (The idea of anyone living close enough to a Lamborghini Revuelto owner to hear any engine sounds seems slightly ludicrous, but I digress.) The electric-only range is approximately 15 kilometers, or about 10 miles — not enough for a commute, but it can be useful for driving through areas with restrictions on combustion-engine vehicles.

Lamborghini isn’t announcing pricing yet, but come on — we’re already talking a minimum of $612,000 for the non-SV trim. You can expect the new version to set you back at least $750,000 before any options are added in. I can already hear the crypto bros frantically checking their account balances.

There may not be an all-electric Lamborghini coming any time soon, and the public’s reception to the Ferrari Luce underscores the minefield these specialized automakers will need to navigate in the future. But for now, Lamborghini is making the most of its hybrid super cars — emphasis on “the most.”

Photography by Andrew J. Hawkins / The Verge

Tech.title: The X-Files creator Chris Carter wanted to make a more horrific movie
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

The version of The X-Files: I Want to Believe that premiered in 2008 was not exactly the movie co-writer / director Chris Carter intended to make. Carter wanted to bring agents Mulder and Scully back to the big screen with a grisly story about faith and the supernatural. But executives at 20th Century Fox felt that Carter’s ideas were too dark, and he was pushed to turn the project into a PG-13 feature. Now, almost two decades after I Want to Believe’s theatrical debut, Carter is back with a new director’s cut of the film for Hulu that’s much closer to his original vision.

“We got to tell a good X-Files story,” Carter said of the original cut during a recent conversation we had about the new release. ”We just didn’t get to tell it in the way that we had intended.”

The X-Files: I Want to Believe – Vrach Frankenshteyn’s Russian subtitle is meant to clue you into how heavily the movie leans into the series’ monster of the week-style storytelling. Mulder (David Duchovny) and Scully (Gillian Anderson) find themselves unwittingly investigating a string of gruesome kidnappings with the help of a predatory priest (Sir William Connolly) who claims to have psychic visions. Neither of the agents know what to make of the man’s supposed abilities, but they can’t ignore the way he consistently leads the FBI to dismembered body parts hidden in the frozen, West Virginian wilderness.

The new cut of I Want to Believe puts an emphasis on its Frankenstein elements that almost makes it feel like 20th Century Studios wanted to tap into Hollywood’s recent fascination with reimagining Mary Shelley’s seminal sci-fi novel. But Carter told me that he thinks his version is actually exploring some of the real world horrors that are woven into people’s desperate searches for youth and immortality.

“There’s this tech bro idea that if you do the right things and eat the right things, you might be able to live forever and ever,” Carter explained. “But if you’re able to transplant your head successfully onto younger and younger bodies, who’s to say that’s not everlasting life?”

While writing I Want to Believe back in the early aughts, Carter was inspired by the work of Robert J. White — a neurosurgeon and bioethicist who successfully managed to transplant the head of one living monkey onto another’s body in the 1970s. Before White’s death in 2010, Carter met with him in Ohio to speak about his work, and their conversation informed some of I Want to Believe’s beats. With Vrach Frankenshteyn, Carter wanted to highlight the visceral sense of fear that might be felt by someone undergoing experiments similar to White’s. The new cut spends less time focusing on Mulder and Scully’s personal relationship, and puts more of its energy into making you feel the terror of its victim characters.

“You have these women who have been stalked, violently taken from their cars, and then trapped in boxes, where they witness these terrible medical procedures they’re going to be subjected to,” Carter said. “If the audience now comes into this movie thinking about head transplants and this title, plot details like finding an arm in the ice and snow brings them into this story in a different way.”

David Duchovny, Gillian Anderson, and Chris Carter on the set of The X-Files: I Want to Believe. Image: Hulu / 20th Century Studios

Though I Want to Believe was met with mixed reviews when it first hit theaters, the series continued with two revival seasons on Fox that ran from 2016 to 2018. Those seasons and the rise of digital streaming brought a new generation of viewers into the X-Files fandom. Carter told me that he’s regularly surprised to meet young people who feel a deep connection to the world he created even though they weren’t alive when the show was originally airing. Carter appreciates that, for those fans, The X-Files is something they’re experiencing for the first time, and it’s markedly different from the new generation of streaming sci-fi series.

Carter — who’s currently working with his wife, Dori, on a movie about a woman forced to live her mother’s life in the 1950s titled Queens for a Day — knows the pleasure of watching truly original and distinct stories unfold. That’s why he has tried to keep himself in the dark about what Ryan Coogler is cooking up with his own upcoming spin on The X-Files. That said, while shooting Queens for a Day in Vancouver, Carter couldn’t stop some of the members from his production crew from visiting Coogler’s nearby set. And while Carter insisted about being kept in the dark about any “secret inside information,” he has faith that Coogler is going to “bring his stamp” to the franchise.

“Ryan is a filmmaker I completely respect,” Carter said. “I’ve made a point of not reading [his script] because I want to watch it like everyone else. But I’ve got an inkling about what he’s doing with his approach and this diverse cast, and it’s very exciting to me.”

The X-Files: I Want to Believe – Vrach Frankenshteyn is now streaming on Hulu.

Tech.title: Google’s best new camera feature is only for the Pixel 11 series
Tech.content:
Arguably the coolest new photo feature for the Pixel 11 lineup is Google’s new Camera Looks, which process image data differently at the sensor level to produce photos that don’t have that “smartphone” look. The result is new styles like “Digi,” which mimics the style of photos taken by older digital cameras. But to use Camera Looks, at least initially, you’ll need to have one of Google’s Pixel 11 phones.

Related Google is making the Pixel cameras better by making them worse

“Our latest camera updates are only available on our latest devices,” Google spokesperson Alex Moriconi tells The Verge. “We’re always looking to bring experiences to more users, but have nothing to share at this time.” That last sentence leaves some wiggle room for Camera Looks to come to older Pixel phones at some point in the future, though it’s unclear if or when that might actually happen.

If you want to learn more about how the Camera Looks feature works, check out David’s big article, which features an interview with Isaac Reynolds, the head of the Pixel camera team.

Tech.title: Mark Zuckerberg has an Instagzam
Tech.content:
Instagram’s wordmark is iconic. Well, was iconic. Apparently Instagram thought it looked old, so the company rolled out a new one this week. It doesn’t look like the old Instagram wordmark. Tech.title: You can now turn off Google Gemini’s visible watermarks
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google will now allow you to remove visible watermarks from the images, videos, and music made with AI tools. With the update, you can toggle off a new “Media watermark” setting in Gemini and Google’s AI video generator, Flow.

When toggled off, Google will remove the “sparkle” watermark that appears in the bottom-right corner of content generated with the company’s Nano Banana and Omni models. Though visible watermarks are now optional, AI-generated content will have invisible SynthID watermarks and C2PA metadata embedded in the background, according to Josh Woodward, the vice president of Google Labs, Gemini, and AI Studio. That means you can still verify if a piece of content has one of these markers by asking Gemini or Search if it’s AI-generated.

You can find the “Media watermark” option in Gemini’s settings menu. Screenshot: The Verge

While this change might make it more difficult to quickly discern if an image or video is AI-generated, many users have already been editing out visible watermarks. Other AI image generators, like OpenAI and Meta’s, also don’t apply visible watermarks. Instead, OpenAI relies on SynthID and C2PA to signal whether something is AI-generated, while Meta launched its own Content Seal standard. Anthropic also announced this week that it’s applying invisible watermarks to both AI-generated text and images.

Google plans on rolling out its new watermark setting to Search as well, but the toggle won’t launch in countries that require visible watermarks.
